Paul addresses Philemon, a Christian whose house was used for church meetings, and asks him to receive back his slave Onesimus as a beloved brother. Onesimus had become a Christian while with Paul. Its authenticity is almost universally accepted. The letter has been central to Christian discussions of slavery, reconciliation and fellowship.

The Book of Proverbs is a book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, and a classic example of biblical wisdom literature. Tradition ascribes it to King Solomon. Scholars instead see it as a "collection of collections" from different periods, with the final redaction often placed in the Persian or Hellenistic era. In short sayings and longer discourses it sets wise conduct against folly. It teaches that "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge" and personifies Wisdom as present at creation. Christian writers widely read Proverbs 8 in a Christological sense.

The Book of Psalms, or Psalter, is an anthology of Hebrew religious poetry in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It has 150 psalms in Jewish and Western usage, with a few more in Eastern churches, and is divided into five books. It includes hymns of praise, laments, royal psalms and thanksgivings. Many psalms are traditionally attributed to David, but scholars doubt this. They were composed over several centuries, before and after the Exile. The Psalms were central to Jewish and Christian worship, and early Christian writers commented on them extensively.

Revelation, also called the Apocalypse, is the last book of the New Testament and its only full apocalyptic work. Its author calls himself John and says he received his visions on the island of Patmos. Tradition identifies him with John the Apostle, but this has been disputed since antiquity. It is usually dated to about 95, under Domitian, though some scholars prefer an earlier date. It contains letters to seven churches in Asia and visions of judgement, the defeat of evil and the New Jerusalem. Its place in the canon was long contested, especially in the East.

The Epistle to the Romans is a letter of the apostle Paul to the Christian community at Rome and is part of the New Testament. Paul probably wrote it from Corinth around 55–58, before a planned visit to Rome and a journey on to Spain. It is the longest and most systematic of his letters. It sets out his teaching on sin, justification by faith, the place of Israel in God's plan, and Christian conduct. Romans has deeply shaped Christian theology, from Origen and Augustine to the Reformation. It was translated early into Syriac, Latin, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian and Georgian.

The Book of Ruth is a short anonymous Hebrew narrative in the Hebrew Bible. It is one of the Five Megillot in the Writings, while the Greek and Christian canons place it after Judges. The date is uncertain, but many scholars assign it to the Persian period. It tells how Ruth, a Moabite widow, stays loyal to her mother-in-law Naomi, goes with her to Bethlehem and marries their kinsman Boaz. Their son Obed became David's grandfather. Ruth appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, and the book is read in synagogues at Shavuot.

Sirach, also called Ecclesiasticus or the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, is a Jewish wisdom book. Jesus ben Sira, a scribe in Jerusalem, wrote it in Hebrew around 196–175 BC. His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt after 132 BC and added a prologue. The prologue is an early witness to the threefold division of the Hebrew scriptures. The book offers ethical teaching, praise of wisdom and a hymn to Israel's famous ancestors. Judaism excludes it from the Hebrew Bible, but it is in the Septuagint and was widely read in the early Church.

The Song of Songs, also called the Song of Solomon or Canticle of Canticles, is a book of Hebrew love poetry, one of the five megillot in the Ketuvim. Its superscription links it to Solomon, but its real author is unknown and its date is debated; many scholars place it in the Persian or Hellenistic period. In dialogues, dreams and rich imagery, a woman and her beloved express their desire. Jewish tradition reads it as an allegory of God and Israel. Christian commentators, from Origen onward, read it as an allegory of Christ and the Church or the soul.

The Epistle to Titus is a short New Testament letter written in Greek. It presents itself as Paul's letter to his co-worker Titus, whom he had left in Crete to organise the church there. Whether Paul wrote it is disputed: many scholars see it as a later pastoral letter, dated anywhere from the 60s to around 100. It sets out qualifications for elders and bishops, warns against false teachers, and urges sound doctrine and godly conduct. Together with 1 and 2 Timothy, it is one of the Pastoral Epistles.

Tobit is an anonymous Jewish narrative from the Second Temple period, usually dated to the 3rd or early 2nd century BC and probably first written in Aramaic or Hebrew. It tells of the pious, blinded exile Tobit in Nineveh and his son Tobias, who travels guided by the angel Raphael. On the way Tobias frees Sarah from the demon Asmodeus and marries her, and Tobit's sight is restored. The short recension, preserved in Codices Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, is one of several ancient forms of this deuterocanonical book.

The Book of Zechariah is the eleventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It is attributed to Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, a prophet active from about 520 BC under the Persian king Darius I. Chapters 1–8 contain eight night visions and oracles urging the returned exiles to repent and rebuild the Temple. Chapters 9–14, often assigned by scholars to later authors, hold oracles about a coming king and the future of Jerusalem. Christian writers frequently read these passages as messianic prophecy.

The Book of Zephaniah (Latin Sophonias) is the ninth of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew Bible, a short prophetic book of three chapters. It is attributed to Zephaniah, who prophesied in the reign of Josiah of Judah (640–609 BC). Many scholars date it to that period, though others think an original core was later expanded. It announces the coming "day of the Lord" as a day of judgement on Judah and the nations, and ends with promises that a humble remnant will be restored. Its imagery inspired the medieval hymn Dies irae.

The Apophthegmata Patrum, or Sayings of the Desert Fathers, are anonymous collections of short sayings and anecdotes linked to the monks and nuns of the Egyptian desert, especially Scetis, from the fourth and fifth centuries. The material began as oral tradition, partly in Coptic, and was written down and arranged mainly in Greek. Versions also circulated in Coptic, Latin, Syriac and other languages. Many sayings are named after figures such as Anthony, Arsenius, Poemen, Macarius and Moses, and they teach humility, watchfulness, fasting and staying in one's cell. These collections became foundational texts of Christian monastic spirituality.

Abraham Our Father is a Sahidic Coptic work by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery near Atripe in Upper Egypt. It belongs to his writings addressed to the monks and nuns of his monastic federation, probably from the late fourth or fifth century. The surviving text warns that impurity, sexual sin and hidden deceit within the community lead to punishment in hell. It also urges the monastics to support and serve one another, following the example of Christ, Paul, the apostles and the prophets.

The Letters of Besa are a collection of letters and sermons in Sahidic Coptic by Besa. He was the disciple and successor of Shenoute as head of the White Monastery federation near Atripe in Upper Egypt, and he wrote them in the second half of the fifth century. He addressed them mainly to the monks and nuns in his care. They urge repentance, obedience, humility and faithful keeping of the community's rules, and they draw heavily on the language of Scripture. Few Coptic writings of the period survive, so these texts are an important source for Egyptian monasticism after Shenoute.

The Dormition, or Repose, of John is an anonymous apocryphal account of the death of John the Apostle, preserved in Coptic. It comes from the closing section of the Greek Acts of John, known as the Metastasis. That section circulated on its own and was translated into many languages. Set in Ephesus, the account records John's last Sunday address to the brethren and his prayer. He then lies down in a grave dug for him and dies peacefully. The Coptic version's date is uncertain. The Greek tradition behind it probably goes back to the second or third century.

On Penitence and Abstinence is a homily on repentance and continence that survives in Coptic. Its heading attributes it to "Apa John, the Archbishop of Constantinople". This has been taken to mean John IV the Faster, patriarch from 582 to 595, but John Chrysostom could also be meant, so the true author and date remain uncertain. The sermon opens with the Apostle Paul, who disciplined his body for fear of being "a castaway". It argues that if even Paul feared, ordinary believers must take up fasting, self-control and penitence all the more seriously.

The Life of Aphou is an anonymous Coptic hagiography of Apa Aphou, an anchorite who became bishop of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt around the turn of the fifth century. It is commemorated on 21 Thout. The work describes his ascetic life in the desert among the antelopes and his secret attendance at the Easter sermon. Its best-known episode has Aphou travel to Alexandria to persuade Archbishop Theophilus that humans still bear the image of God. This makes the Life an important witness to the Origenist and anthropomorphite controversies. When it was written is uncertain.

The Life of Cyrus is an anonymous Coptic hagiography of Apa Cyrus (Kyros, Anba Karas), an anchorite venerated in the Coptic Church. It presents itself as the work of Apa Pambo, elder of the church of Scetis. After burying Hilaria, daughter of the Emperor Zeno, Pambo is sent by a vision to seek a hermit of exceptional holiness. The story places Cyrus in the late fifth century and records his death on 8 Epeiph. The date of composition is uncertain. The Life belongs to the Egyptian literature of desert monasticism.

This anonymous Coptic hagiography tells the legend of Saint Eustathius (Eustace), a Roman general, his wife Theopiste and their sons Agapius and Theopistus. Its date is uncertain, somewhere between the fourth and seventh centuries. The widely known legend tells of the general's conversion, the loss of his wealth, the family's separation and later reunion, and their martyrdom in Rome. The Coptic text places the martyrdom under Trajan on 20 Thoth, while other versions name Hadrian. This version shows how the legend, also known in Greek and Latin, spread into Egyptian Christianity.

This is an anonymous Coptic hagiography of John Calybites, "the Dweller in the Hovel", probably composed between the fifth and sixth centuries. It tells of the youngest son of Eutropius, a wealthy Roman official, and his wife Theodora. His parents gave him a gospel book bound in gold. He secretly left home to join the monastery of the "Sleepless" monks (Acoemetae). Later he came back and lived unrecognized in a hut at his parents' gate. He revealed himself only at his death, which the text places on 4 Mekhir. The legend circulated widely in both Eastern and Western traditions.

The Life of Longinus and Lucius is an anonymous hagiography written in Sahidic Coptic. Its subjects are two ascetics: Apa Longinus, superior of the Enaton monastic community outside Alexandria, who was active around 451–457, and his spiritual father Apa Lucius. The work tells of their ascetic lives and virtues, and their joint commemoration falls on 2 Emshir (Meshir). It opens with a rhetorical prologue in which the author calls their conduct angelic. The date of composition is uncertain. The text is a source for Egyptian monasticism in the period after the Council of Chalcedon.

The Life of Onnophrius is an anonymous Coptic hagiography, told in the first person by the monk Apa Paphnutius (Papnoute). Its date is uncertain, but it probably comes from late antiquity. Paphnutius tells how he travelled into the inner desert of Egypt to find hidden anchorites. He met several of them, above all Onnophrius, who had lived alone for decades, clothed only in his own hair. He then witnessed Onnophrius's death, dated to 16 Paone, and buried him. The account spread widely in other languages and became the basis for venerating Onuphrius across Eastern and Western Christianity.

The Life of Phib is a Coptic hagiography of Apa Phib, an anchorite from Sinemoun near Hermopolis in Middle Egypt. The text says it was written by Papohe, a disciple of Apa Apollo, usually identified with Apollo of Bawit, the monastic founder. It tells how Phib lived as a monk with Apollo, and how the two later practised asceticism together on the mountain of Titkooh. Much of the text also praises Apollo himself. It records Phib's death on 25 Paope. The date of composition is uncertain, probably between the fourth and sixth centuries.

This Coptic hagiographical encomium tells the life of Pisentius, bishop of Coptos (Qift) in Upper Egypt, who died in 632. According to its heading, John the Presbyter delivered it on the saint's commemoration, 13 Epep. It praises Pisentius as a monk and anchorite in the mountain of Tsenti in the Theban region and as a bishop. It records his asceticism, his miracles, his pastoral care and his gift of revealing hidden things. The work is a valuable witness to anti-Chalcedonian monastic and church life in Egypt in the late sixth and early seventh centuries.

The Mysteries of John is an anonymous Coptic apocryphal apocalypse that presents itself as the secrets revealed to John the apostle, called "the holy virgin", in heaven. After the Resurrection, Christ gathers the apostles on the Mount of Olives in a cloud. In answer to John's request, the heavens open, and a cherub guides him through the heavenly places, explaining cosmic and spiritual mysteries. Its date of composition is uncertain. It belongs to the later Egyptian Christian tradition of revelatory literature attributed to the apostles, and it is distinct from the Gnostic Apocryphon of John.

The Instructions of Pachomius are a Coptic catechesis, or spiritual exhortation, attributed to Pachomius (c. 287–348), the Egyptian founder of cenobitic monasticism, and probably composed during his leadership of the Tabennese communities. The best-known instruction is addressed to a monk who became angry with a man he had brought to Tabennese. It urges him toward obedience, humility, patience and ascetic discipline, citing Abraham, Jacob, Joseph and other biblical figures as models. It is among the few surviving works directly attributed to Pachomius, and it shows how spiritual teaching was given in early Pachomian monasticism.

These are sermons by Proclus of Constantinople (c. 390–446), bishop-designate of Cyzicus and later Archbishop of Constantinople from 434. He was famous as a preacher. He composed them in Greek, and they survive here in a Coptic translation. The opening homily is a Holy Week sermon on Christ's crucifixion and the reality of his incarnation. Its Coptic heading says it was preached in Constantinople with Nestorius present. Proclus's preaching played a central part in the Nestorian controversy and helped shape early devotion to Mary as Theotokos.

These are sermons preserved in Coptic that are attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria, who is called in them "Archbishop of Rakote", the Coptic name for Alexandria. Like much of the Pseudo-Athanasian literature, they were probably not written by Athanasius, and their authors and dates are uncertain. They may have been translated from Greek or composed in Egypt itself. One discourse explains Matthew's parable of the labourers in the vineyard, asking who the labourers, the vineyard and the master stand for. The sermons show how Athanasius's authority was used in Coptic preaching and how his name was attached to later homilies.

This is a collection of Coptic homilies and other writings that circulated under the name of Basil the Great, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (d. 379), but are not by him. They belong to the Egyptian tradition of attributing sermons to famous Church Fathers. Their authors are anonymous and their dates are uncertain. One homily treats the end of the world, the Temple of Solomon and the soul's departure from the body. It draws on Gospel prophecies of tribulation and judgement. These texts show how Basil's authority was received in Coptic Christianity.

This Coptic homily praises Saint Victor the General, a soldier-martyr venerated in Egypt. It presents itself as a sermon by Celestine, archbishop of Rome, given on Victor's feast, 27 Parmoute, at a martyr's shrine built for him in Rome while Emperor Valentinian looked on. The attribution to Pope Celestine I (422–432) is fictitious, and the real author and date are unknown. Along with praise of the martyr, the sermon urges repentance and describes the soul's fear at death and judgement. It belongs to the extensive Coptic literature about Victor.

This is a collection of Coptic sermons and discourses that are attributed to John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople (died 407), or that circulated with his name, but are not his work. They are generally dated to between the late fourth and the fifth century, though their dates and authors are uncertain. Some pieces carry other attributions, such as a discourse on the Canaanite woman assigned to a Bishop Eusebius of Caesarea in Cappadocia. The texts show how Chrysostom's reputation shaped Coptic preaching and homiletic literature.

This is a group of ascetic and homiletic writings that survive in Coptic and carry the name of Ephrem the Syrian, the fourth-century deacon and poet of Nisibis and Edessa. One of them is an "Asketikon of Apa Ephraim." It opens with the author's lament that instruction has fallen silent and sin has multiplied, and it urges monks to follow the teaching of the fathers. Ephrem's authorship is doubtful. Like much of the Greek "Ephrem" literature from which Coptic versions were probably made, these works are most likely pseudepigraphal, and their date is uncertain.

This Coptic hagiographical encomium praises Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria (Rakote) in the late second and early third centuries, and claims to have been delivered on his feast day. It is ascribed to a Flavianus, bishop of Ephesus, but the attribution is pseudepigraphic. Its date is uncertain, perhaps the fifth century or later. The sermon tells of miracles worked through Demetrius. It also turns to Peter, archbishop and martyr of Alexandria, and to an Antiochene woman martyred with her sons Philopator and Eutropius. Other sections discuss the impulse of the soul and a passage from Jeremiah.

The Discourse on Abbaton is a Coptic homily falsely attributed to Timothy, archbishop of Alexandria (Rakote). Its real author and date are unknown, though it is generally placed between the fifth and sixth centuries. The supposed archbishop says he found an apostolic book in Jerusalem, in which the Saviour tells the apostles how God made Abbaton, the terrifying Angel of Death. He was set over creation because of the sin of Adam and Eve, and his creation is commemorated on 13 Athor. The work is an important witness to Coptic angelology and apocryphal traditions about Adam.

A22 is a fragmentary Coptic text attributed to Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. It reads as a set of community regulations backed by curses. Anyone who hides a sin, or who offers sacrifice anywhere other than the community's gathering place, is to be cursed. The text marks the community's territory from a valley north of Atripe to the first desert dwelling of Apa Bishoy. It also requires nearby desert hermits to join the brothers' assemblies. It is valuable evidence for how Shenoute's monastic federation was governed.

Eagerness is a fragmentary Coptic work by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, composed between the late fourth and mid-fifth century. What survives is a moral exhortation that condemns traitors, thieves and apostates who commit abominations in holy places. Shenoute takes Judas's betrayal of Christ for thirty pieces of silver as his main example and attacks the love of money, wishing that gold did not exist. Like his other writings, it is an important witness to early Coptic literature and to Egyptian monastic preaching.

This polemical open letter by Shenoute of Atripe, abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, is often called "Not Because a Fox Barks" after its opening words. It was written in Sahidic Coptic in the fifth century. It answers a wealthy pagan of Panopolis, usually identified as Gessius, who had accused Shenoute of robbery after the abbot removed idols from his house. Shenoute casts himself as Christ's lion and his opponent as a fox. The letter is important evidence for monastic violence against pagan cults in late antique Egypt.

"Night" is a short Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Written in the first person, it describes a vision he had at dawn on the ninth of Tobe. Shenoute was praying over whether sinful members should stay in the monastic communities or be expelled when a figure with an air of authority confronted him, and he wrestled with it. The text shows his strict monastic discipline and his visionary sense of his role as leader.

This is a fragmentary Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Its beginning is lost. Shenoute writes as "father" to members of his monastic federation, including women, about how to care for a sick member sent among them. He also discusses whether wine may be drunk, insisting that kindness be offered willingly rather than under constraint, beyond what the Rule requires. He asks for a written report of their practice and tells them how to arrange their evening prayers. It shows how Shenoute governed his communities by letter.

"Those" is a fragmentary Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery near Panopolis (Akhmim) in Upper Egypt. As with many of his writings, its conventional title comes from its opening words, and the surviving portion begins mid-sentence. In a sharply polemical voice, it addresses opponents in Panopolis who reportedly twisted and misreported words about the monks, who had "made the desert into a city." Its exact date and where it belongs in his collected writings are uncertain.

"True" is a fragmentary Coptic text attributed to Shenoute of Atripe, abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, who died in 465. Like many of Shenoute's writings, it is known by a conventional title probably taken from its opening word, and its exact date is uncertain. The surviving portion deals with how monastic leaders should care for their communities. It covers who should teach the word of God, the Saturday gatherings for instruction, and yearly visits to villages. Citing Ephesians 4:11, it stresses that each person serves according to rank and calling.

The Apophthegmata Patrum, or Sayings of the Desert Fathers, are anonymous collections of short sayings and anecdotes linked to the monks and nuns of the Egyptian desert, especially Scetis, from the fourth and fifth centuries. The material began as oral tradition, partly in Coptic, and was written down and arranged mainly in Greek. Versions also circulated in Coptic, Latin, Syriac and other languages. Many sayings are named after figures such as Anthony, Arsenius, Poemen, Macarius and Moses, and they teach humility, watchfulness, fasting and staying in one's cell. These collections became foundational texts of Christian monastic spirituality.

Abraham Our Father is a Sahidic Coptic work by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery near Atripe in Upper Egypt. It belongs to his writings addressed to the monks and nuns of his monastic federation, probably from the late fourth or fifth century. The surviving text warns that impurity, sexual sin and hidden deceit within the community lead to punishment in hell. It also urges the monastics to support and serve one another, following the example of Christ, Paul, the apostles and the prophets.

The Gospel of Nicodemus, also called the Acts of Pilate, is an anonymous apocryphal gospel that claims to come from records kept by Nicodemus. It was probably written in Greek, and its sections date from different times; the work as it survives is usually placed in the fourth or fifth century. The first part tells of Jesus' trial before Pilate, his crucifixion and his resurrection. The second part describes Christ's descent into Hell. It was widely translated, including into Latin and Coptic, and shaped medieval accounts of the Harrowing of Hell.

The Letters of Besa are a collection of letters and sermons in Sahidic Coptic by Besa. He was the disciple and successor of Shenoute as head of the White Monastery federation near Atripe in Upper Egypt, and he wrote them in the second half of the fifth century. He addressed them mainly to the monks and nuns in his care. They urge repentance, obedience, humility and faithful keeping of the community's rules, and they draw heavily on the language of Scripture. Few Coptic writings of the period survive, so these texts are an important source for Egyptian monasticism after Shenoute.

The Dormition, or Repose, of John is an anonymous apocryphal account of the death of John the Apostle, preserved in Coptic. It comes from the closing section of the Greek Acts of John, known as the Metastasis. That section circulated on its own and was translated into many languages. Set in Ephesus, the account records John's last Sunday address to the brethren and his prayer. He then lies down in a grave dug for him and dies peacefully. The Coptic version's date is uncertain. The Greek tradition behind it probably goes back to the second or third century.

This Coptic hagiographical encomium is attributed to Stephen, bishop of Hnes (Heracleopolis Magna) in Middle Egypt. His dates are uncertain, but he is usually placed in the sixth or seventh century. The sermon was delivered at the shrine of the martyr Apa Elias (Helias) on his feast, 21 Phamenoth. It praises the saint through scriptural imagery and plays on his name, which it links to the Greek word for "sun." It also recounts his martyrdom. The work shows how martyr cults, shrines and festal preaching worked in late antique Egyptian Christianity.

The Canons of Apa Johannes are a Coptic monastic work attributed to a John, or Johannes, called the Archimandrite. Who he was is uncertain, and the text can only be dated loosely to between the fourth and sixth centuries. It is an exhortation in the tradition of Egyptian monastic rules. It warns against pride and disobedience, which it calls the sins that brought the devil down from heaven and send many to Amente, the underworld. It supports its teaching with Scripture, including Christ's saying "Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear."

On Penitence and Abstinence is a homily on repentance and continence that survives in Coptic. Its heading attributes it to "Apa John, the Archbishop of Constantinople". This has been taken to mean John IV the Faster, patriarch from 582 to 595, but John Chrysostom could also be meant, so the true author and date remain uncertain. The sermon opens with the Apostle Paul, who disciplined his body for fear of being "a castaway". It argues that if even Paul feared, ordinary believers must take up fasting, self-control and penitence all the more seriously.

The Lament of the Virgin Mary is an anonymous Christian apocryphal narrative in Coptic. It belongs to the cycle of Passion and Pilate texts that grew up around the canonical Gospels, and its date of composition is uncertain. The surviving portion tells events after the crucifixion. Pilate questions the soldiers who guarded Jesus' tomb, finds that their stories contradict one another, and goes to the tomb with the Jewish leaders, the centurion and the chief priests, where they find only the empty linen cloths. Texts of this kind show how Egyptian Christians developed the Passion story and devotion to Mary.

The Life of Aphou is an anonymous Coptic hagiography of Apa Aphou, an anchorite who became bishop of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt around the turn of the fifth century. It is commemorated on 21 Thout. The work describes his ascetic life in the desert among the antelopes and his secret attendance at the Easter sermon. Its best-known episode has Aphou travel to Alexandria to persuade Archbishop Theophilus that humans still bear the image of God. This makes the Life an important witness to the Origenist and anthropomorphite controversies. When it was written is uncertain.

The Life of Cyrus is an anonymous Coptic hagiography of Apa Cyrus (Kyros, Anba Karas), an anchorite venerated in the Coptic Church. It presents itself as the work of Apa Pambo, elder of the church of Scetis. After burying Hilaria, daughter of the Emperor Zeno, Pambo is sent by a vision to seek a hermit of exceptional holiness. The story places Cyrus in the late fifth century and records his death on 8 Epeiph. The date of composition is uncertain. The Life belongs to the Egyptian literature of desert monasticism.

This anonymous Coptic hagiography tells the legend of Saint Eustathius (Eustace), a Roman general, his wife Theopiste and their sons Agapius and Theopistus. Its date is uncertain, somewhere between the fourth and seventh centuries. The widely known legend tells of the general's conversion, the loss of his wealth, the family's separation and later reunion, and their martyrdom in Rome. The Coptic text places the martyrdom under Trajan on 20 Thoth, while other versions name Hadrian. This version shows how the legend, also known in Greek and Latin, spread into Egyptian Christianity.

This is an anonymous Coptic hagiography of John Calybites, "the Dweller in the Hovel", probably composed between the fifth and sixth centuries. It tells of the youngest son of Eutropius, a wealthy Roman official, and his wife Theodora. His parents gave him a gospel book bound in gold. He secretly left home to join the monastery of the "Sleepless" monks (Acoemetae). Later he came back and lived unrecognized in a hut at his parents' gate. He revealed himself only at his death, which the text places on 4 Mekhir. The legend circulated widely in both Eastern and Western traditions.

The Life of Longinus and Lucius is an anonymous hagiography written in Sahidic Coptic. Its subjects are two ascetics: Apa Longinus, superior of the Enaton monastic community outside Alexandria, who was active around 451–457, and his spiritual father Apa Lucius. The work tells of their ascetic lives and virtues, and their joint commemoration falls on 2 Emshir (Meshir). It opens with a rhetorical prologue in which the author calls their conduct angelic. The date of composition is uncertain. The text is a source for Egyptian monasticism in the period after the Council of Chalcedon.

The Life of Onnophrius is an anonymous Coptic hagiography, told in the first person by the monk Apa Paphnutius (Papnoute). Its date is uncertain, but it probably comes from late antiquity. Paphnutius tells how he travelled into the inner desert of Egypt to find hidden anchorites. He met several of them, above all Onnophrius, who had lived alone for decades, clothed only in his own hair. He then witnessed Onnophrius's death, dated to 16 Paone, and buried him. The account spread widely in other languages and became the basis for venerating Onuphrius across Eastern and Western Christianity.

The Life of Paul of Tamma is an anonymous Coptic hagiography of Apa Paul of Tamma, an Egyptian ascetic of the fourth and fifth centuries commemorated on 7 Paope. Its date is uncertain. The surviving text is fragmentary and is told in the first person by a disciple. Here the archangel Michael tells him that he will be the one to bury the holy man. The Life also tells of miracles, including Paul praying with his companions for bread from heaven. It is an important witness to the cult of a saint who is still venerated in the Coptic Church.

The Life of Phib is a Coptic hagiography of Apa Phib, an anchorite from Sinemoun near Hermopolis in Middle Egypt. The text says it was written by Papohe, a disciple of Apa Apollo, usually identified with Apollo of Bawit, the monastic founder. It tells how Phib lived as a monk with Apollo, and how the two later practised asceticism together on the mountain of Titkooh. Much of the text also praises Apollo himself. It records Phib's death on 25 Paope. The date of composition is uncertain, probably between the fourth and sixth centuries.

This Coptic hagiographical encomium tells the life of Pisentius, bishop of Coptos (Qift) in Upper Egypt, who died in 632. According to its heading, John the Presbyter delivered it on the saint's commemoration, 13 Epep. It praises Pisentius as a monk and anchorite in the mountain of Tsenti in the Theban region and as a bishop. It records his asceticism, his miracles, his pastoral care and his gift of revealing hidden things. The work is a valuable witness to anti-Chalcedonian monastic and church life in Egypt in the late sixth and early seventh centuries.

This anonymous Coptic hagiographical encomium on Saint Mercurius is presented as a eulogy that Acacius, bishop of Caesarea, delivered at the martyr's shrine on his feast, 20 Hathor. The attribution is almost certainly fictitious, and the date of composition is uncertain. The text praises Mercurius as a soldier who led the army of the emperor Decius against the barbarians. An angel gives him a heavenly sword, and the work goes on to tell of his conversion, his martyrdom and his miracles. It shows how the Coptic church venerated this popular military saint.

The Mysteries of John is an anonymous Coptic apocryphal apocalypse that presents itself as the secrets revealed to John the apostle, called "the holy virgin", in heaven. After the Resurrection, Christ gathers the apostles on the Mount of Olives in a cloud. In answer to John's request, the heavens open, and a cherub guides him through the heavenly places, explaining cosmic and spiritual mysteries. Its date of composition is uncertain. It belongs to the later Egyptian Christian tradition of revelatory literature attributed to the apostles, and it is distinct from the Gnostic Apocryphon of John.

The Instructions of Pachomius are a Coptic catechesis, or spiritual exhortation, attributed to Pachomius (c. 287–348), the Egyptian founder of cenobitic monasticism, and probably composed during his leadership of the Tabennese communities. The best-known instruction is addressed to a monk who became angry with a man he had brought to Tabennese. It urges him toward obedience, humility, patience and ascetic discipline, citing Abraham, Jacob, Joseph and other biblical figures as models. It is among the few surviving works directly attributed to Pachomius, and it shows how spiritual teaching was given in early Pachomian monasticism.

These are sermons by Proclus of Constantinople (c. 390–446), bishop-designate of Cyzicus and later Archbishop of Constantinople from 434. He was famous as a preacher. He composed them in Greek, and they survive here in a Coptic translation. The opening homily is a Holy Week sermon on Christ's crucifixion and the reality of his incarnation. Its Coptic heading says it was preached in Constantinople with Nestorius present. Proclus's preaching played a central part in the Nestorian controversy and helped shape early devotion to Mary as Theotokos.

These are sermons preserved in Coptic that are attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria, who is called in them "Archbishop of Rakote", the Coptic name for Alexandria. Like much of the Pseudo-Athanasian literature, they were probably not written by Athanasius, and their authors and dates are uncertain. They may have been translated from Greek or composed in Egypt itself. One discourse explains Matthew's parable of the labourers in the vineyard, asking who the labourers, the vineyard and the master stand for. The sermons show how Athanasius's authority was used in Coptic preaching and how his name was attached to later homilies.

This is a collection of Coptic homilies and other writings that circulated under the name of Basil the Great, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (d. 379), but are not by him. They belong to the Egyptian tradition of attributing sermons to famous Church Fathers. Their authors are anonymous and their dates are uncertain. One homily treats the end of the world, the Temple of Solomon and the soul's departure from the body. It draws on Gospel prophecies of tribulation and judgement. These texts show how Basil's authority was received in Coptic Christianity.

This Coptic homily praises Saint Victor the General, a soldier-martyr venerated in Egypt. It presents itself as a sermon by Celestine, archbishop of Rome, given on Victor's feast, 27 Parmoute, at a martyr's shrine built for him in Rome while Emperor Valentinian looked on. The attribution to Pope Celestine I (422–432) is fictitious, and the real author and date are unknown. Along with praise of the martyr, the sermon urges repentance and describes the soul's fear at death and judgement. It belongs to the extensive Coptic literature about Victor.

This is a collection of Coptic sermons and discourses that are attributed to John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople (died 407), or that circulated with his name, but are not his work. They are generally dated to between the late fourth and the fifth century, though their dates and authors are uncertain. Some pieces carry other attributions, such as a discourse on the Canaanite woman assigned to a Bishop Eusebius of Caesarea in Cappadocia. The texts show how Chrysostom's reputation shaped Coptic preaching and homiletic literature.

This is a group of ascetic and homiletic writings that survive in Coptic and carry the name of Ephrem the Syrian, the fourth-century deacon and poet of Nisibis and Edessa. One of them is an "Asketikon of Apa Ephraim." It opens with the author's lament that instruction has fallen silent and sin has multiplied, and it urges monks to follow the teaching of the fathers. Ephrem's authorship is doubtful. Like much of the Greek "Ephrem" literature from which Coptic versions were probably made, these works are most likely pseudepigraphal, and their date is uncertain.

This Coptic hagiographical encomium praises Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria (Rakote) in the late second and early third centuries, and claims to have been delivered on his feast day. It is ascribed to a Flavianus, bishop of Ephesus, but the attribution is pseudepigraphic. Its date is uncertain, perhaps the fifth century or later. The sermon tells of miracles worked through Demetrius. It also turns to Peter, archbishop and martyr of Alexandria, and to an Antiochene woman martyred with her sons Philopator and Eutropius. Other sections discuss the impulse of the soul and a passage from Jeremiah.

The Discourse on Abbaton is a Coptic homily falsely attributed to Timothy, archbishop of Alexandria (Rakote). Its real author and date are unknown, though it is generally placed between the fifth and sixth centuries. The supposed archbishop says he found an apostolic book in Jerusalem, in which the Saviour tells the apostles how God made Abbaton, the terrifying Angel of Death. He was set over creation because of the sin of Adam and Eve, and his creation is commemorated on 13 Athor. The work is an important witness to Coptic angelology and apocryphal traditions about Adam.

A22 is a fragmentary Coptic text attributed to Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. It reads as a set of community regulations backed by curses. Anyone who hides a sin, or who offers sacrifice anywhere other than the community's gathering place, is to be cursed. The text marks the community's territory from a valley north of Atripe to the first desert dwelling of Apa Bishoy. It also requires nearby desert hermits to join the brothers' assemblies. It is valuable evidence for how Shenoute's monastic federation was governed.

"Considering" is a short Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. It takes its name from its opening words. Speaking as the community's leader, Shenoute says he has long been considering how to prevent complaints and unfairness among the monks. He warns against lying, theft, grumbling and favouritism, and insists that true communal life means sharing equally. He then orders that particular foods, such as cheese and eggs, always be kept for the sick. The text is valuable evidence for the rules and daily life of Shenoute's monastic federation.

Crushed is a Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Like many of his writings, it is addressed to the "brothers and sisters" of his monastic community and refers to his other letters. Drawing on prophetic and apocalyptic imagery from Scripture, including the fallen angels bound in chains of darkness, the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the sword of judgment that will come upon Idumea, it warns of divine punishment and calls for repentance. It is a typical example of Shenoute's forceful Sahidic prose.

"Dirt" is a Coptic sermon or treatise by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. It is a moral exhortation that survives in fragments. Its surviving portion warns those who refuse to repent and urges them to turn to God. It contrasts obedient and disobedient children, using Jacob and Esau as examples: God, like a parent, blesses the child who submits to the church as mother and excludes the quarrelsome one from the inheritance. Its exact date and its place within Shenoute's writings are uncertain.

Eagerness is a fragmentary Coptic work by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, composed between the late fourth and mid-fifth century. What survives is a moral exhortation that condemns traitors, thieves and apostates who commit abominations in holy places. Shenoute takes Judas's betrayal of Christ for thirty pieces of silver as his main example and attacks the love of money, wishing that gold did not exist. Like his other writings, it is an important witness to early Coptic literature and to Egyptian monastic preaching.

This is a Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Its short title, "Errs", seems to come from its wording about everyone going astray. The surviving section reflects on wrongdoing throughout the whole earth and holds that God remains true even when every mouth speaks lies. It considers the image of a drawn sword, which human sin has called forth, and contrasts it with the avenging sword in the prophets. It shows Shenoute's typical style of heavily scriptural moral preaching.

This polemical open letter by Shenoute of Atripe, abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, is often called "Not Because a Fox Barks" after its opening words. It was written in Sahidic Coptic in the fifth century. It answers a wealthy pagan of Panopolis, usually identified as Gessius, who had accused Shenoute of robbery after the abbot removed idols from his house. Shenoute casts himself as Christ's lion and his opponent as a fox. The letter is important evidence for monastic violence against pagan cults in late antique Egypt.

A Coptic text known as "House", attributed to Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), the abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt and the most important author of early Coptic literature. It is a moral exhortation in Shenoute's typically forceful rhetorical style. It mourns the sins of the community, quoting Isaiah's words about the mother's certificate of divorce. It sets the praise that heaven, earth, sea and all creation give to God against human beings, who bless him with words alone while insulting him through ungodly and unnatural acts. Its exact date and place within Shenoute's writings are uncertain.

"Listen" is a Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, written for his monastic community. The opening survives only in fragments. In it Shenoute sharply rebukes members of the community who expect God to forgive defiling deeds committed after they have received instruction. He asks whether he can rightly gather or offer the offering with impure people who have not given up their wrongdoing. The work shows Shenoute's severe concern for purity and discipline within the monastery.

"Night" is a short Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Written in the first person, it describes a vision he had at dawn on the ninth of Tobe. Shenoute was praying over whether sinful members should stay in the monastic communities or be expelled when a figure with an air of authority confronted him, and he wrestled with it. The text shows his strict monastic discipline and his visionary sense of his role as leader.

This is a fragmentary Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Its beginning is lost. Shenoute writes as "father" to members of his monastic federation, including women, about how to care for a sick member sent among them. He also discusses whether wine may be drunk, insisting that kindness be offered willingly rather than under constraint, beyond what the Rule requires. He asks for a written report of their practice and tells them how to arrange their evening prayers. It shows how Shenoute governed his communities by letter.

A Coptic sermon or discourse attributed to Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt and one of the major writers of Coptic literature. The text speaks directly to the devil, the "instigator of evil" and "unclean spirit." It charges him with setting every vice against its matching virtue and attacking people through dreams and sinful passions. It also contrasts his weakness with the power of God in those who stay watchful and do good. Its exact date and original context are uncertain.

Seeks is a Coptic work by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, so it was written sometime in the late fourth or fifth century. It is preserved in fragments. The surviving opening is a moral exhortation built on Christ's saying that the people of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn this generation. Shenoute warns that the saints, martyrs and apostles, who will sit in judgment, will condemn people and angels who turned toward evil when they should have resisted Satan. The work's exact place among Shenoute's writings is uncertain.

"Those" is a fragmentary Coptic text by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery near Panopolis (Akhmim) in Upper Egypt. As with many of his writings, its conventional title comes from its opening words, and the surviving portion begins mid-sentence. In a sharply polemical voice, it addresses opponents in Panopolis who reportedly twisted and misreported words about the monks, who had "made the desert into a city." Its exact date and where it belongs in his collected writings are uncertain.

"Thundered" is a Coptic treatise by Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Like many of his writings, it is known by a short title taken from its opening words. Shenoute wrote it in Sahidic Coptic as a polemic against heretics and pagans. He sets the righteous, called friends of God like Abraham and the apostles, against heretics, whom he calls friends of Satan who fill books with abominable words. He condemns pagan sacrifice and ungodly kings, and warns that unbelievers will share the devil's punishment.

"True" is a fragmentary Coptic text attributed to Shenoute of Atripe, abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, who died in 465. Like many of Shenoute's writings, it is known by a conventional title probably taken from its opening word, and its exact date is uncertain. The surviving portion deals with how monastic leaders should care for their communities. It covers who should teach the word of God, the Saturday gatherings for instruction, and yearly visits to villages. Citing Ephesians 4:11, it stresses that each person serves according to rank and calling.

This is a fragmentary Coptic text attributed to Shenoute of Atripe (d. 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt. Its exact identity and its place among his writings are uncertain, and its date is unknown beyond his lifetime. The surviving portion is a prophetic warning about the last days. It lists the vices that the ungodly, men and women alike, will no longer count as sins, and condemns sexual immorality, idleness and luxury. It also warns that Satan will rise against those who fail to put these passions to death.

An untitled Coptic text attributed to Shenoute of Atripe, abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt, who died in 465. It has not been assigned to any of his known Canons or Discourses. Like much of Shenoute's writing, it survives only in fragments. The surviving opening strings together verses, mostly from the Psalms, about shame, reproach, mockery and persecution suffered by the righteous and by God's anointed. It then begins to discuss "the proof of their love". Its occasion and full argument are unknown.

Witness is a Coptic work by Shenoute of Atripe (died 465), abbot of the White Monastery in Upper Egypt and the most important writer of Sahidic Coptic literature. Its exact date is not known. In the surviving portion Shenoute sharply rebukes a group he accuses of secret wrongdoing "in these synagogues", in hidden corners and inside houses. He charges them with defiling the temple of God and grieving his Spirit, and warns them of judgment. He draws heavily on biblical language, which is typical of his forceful prophetic style of moral admonition.

This Coptic encomium is a festal sermon in praise of the archangel Michael. It is attributed to Theodosius I, the Miaphysite patriarch of Alexandria who died in 566, though the attribution is uncertain, as with many Coptic homilies circulating under famous names. The preacher recalls Michael's victory over the devil, who was bound and cast into the lake of fire. He then invites his hearers to a royal banquet given by Michael, where patriarchs, prophets, apostles and martyrs take their places first. The work is evidence for the strong devotion to Michael in Egyptian Christianity.

This is an anonymous Latin verse epitaph in elegiac couplets for Magnus Felix Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, a rhetorician and poet. It praises his noble family and his eloquence, and his part in ending the schism with the East and restoring "the faith of Peter" to the churches, which refers to his embassies to Constantinople during the Acacian schism. It also praises his generosity, his building of churches and his hymns. It closes by recording his burial on 17 July in the consulship of Valerius, that is, 521.

De Locis Sanctis ("On the Holy Places") is a Latin treatise in three books by Adomnán, abbot of Iona, written in the late seventh century. Adomnán based it largely on the account of Arculf, a Frankish bishop who had travelled to the Holy Land, Egypt and Constantinople and later visited Iona. It describes Jerusalem and its churches, Bethlehem, Hebron and other pilgrimage sites, and includes plans of several buildings. Bede made an abridgement of it, and it became an influential early medieval guide to the holy places.

The Apologia altera prophetae David (Second Apology for the Prophet David) is a Latin sermon handed down among the works of Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397), though scholars have long questioned whether he wrote it. It takes as its starting point the title of Psalm 50 (51), which tells of Nathan's visit after David's sin with Bathsheba, and the Gospel story of the woman taken in adultery. It defends David's public confession and Christ's pardon against readers who might take either as approval of sin. It treats repentance, humility and divine mercy.

The Apology of the Prophet David is a Latin exegetical treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, dedicated to the emperor Theodosius I. Its date is uncertain; some scholars link it to the emperor's penance after the massacre at Thessalonica in 390. It defends David's sins of adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah by reading the story in 2 Samuel and Psalm 50 (51). It presents David as a model of repentance, humility and penance for rulers who sin.

De benedictionibus patriarcharum (On the Blessings of the Patriarchs), also known as De patriarchis, is a short Latin exegetical treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, probably written late in his episcopate. Its exact date is uncertain. It opens by praising the honour children owe their parents. It then interprets Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh and his blessings of his twelve sons in Genesis 48–49. Ambrose reads these blessings typologically and morally, as prophecies of Christ, the Church and the calling of the Gentiles. The work is closely related to his treatise De Ioseph.

De Cain et Abel is a Latin exegetical treatise in two books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397). It was written as a sequel to his De paradiso, which treated the fall of Adam and Eve, and it comments on the story of Cain and Abel in Genesis 4. Ambrose reads the brothers allegorically as two opposed schools of thought. Cain stands for those who credit everything to their own minds, and Abel for those who refer everything to God. The work draws heavily on Philo of Alexandria and also discusses sacrifice and virtue.

De Helia et ieiunio (On Elijah and Fasting) is a Latin moral treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397. It was written from sermons preached in Lent, and its exact date is uncertain. Ambrose presents fasting as the Christian's battle before the Easter victory. He takes as models Christ's fast in the wilderness and the prophet Elijah, whose fasting gave him power over heaven. He sharply condemns gluttony, drunkenness and luxurious banquets. The work draws heavily on Basil of Caesarea's homilies on fasting and is an important witness to Lenten preaching in the Latin West.

De fuga saeculi (On Flight from the World) is a short Latin treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan. It was probably written late in his life, though its exact date is uncertain, and it may be based on sermons. It urges Christians to turn their hearts away from worldly desires and distractions, and it insists that this detachment is impossible without divine help. Ambrose draws on Scripture and on the allegorical exegesis of Philo of Alexandria, and he presents the cities of refuge, Jacob and Lot's wife as lessons in spiritual flight toward God.

De interpellatione Iob et David ("On the Complaint of Job and David") is a Latin moral-exegetical treatise in four books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan. It was probably first preached as sermons and later revised for reading. Scholars usually place it in the 380s, though the exact date is uncertain. Drawing on Job and on Psalms of David, starting with Psalm 41, Ambrose discusses human weakness, the suffering of the righteous and the apparent prosperity of the wicked. He argues that the hope of future glory outweighs the troubles of the present life.

De Iacob et vita beata ("On Jacob and the Happy Life") is a Latin moral treatise in two books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, probably written in the 380s and likely based on sermons. The first book argues that reason, aided by grace, can restrain the passions though not uproot them, and that the happy life lies in virtue. The second presents the patriarch Jacob, and then the Maccabean martyrs, as examples of the wise man. It drew on Philo and 4 Maccabees and is closely linked to Ambrose's De bono mortis.

De Joseph is a Latin treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, on the patriarch Joseph, son of Jacob. It was written probably in the late 380s and grew out of sermons preached to his congregation. It belongs to Ambrose's series of works on the patriarchs, alongside his writings on Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Ambrose presents Joseph as a "mirror of chastity" and a model of patience and forgiveness. He forgave the brothers who sold him long before the Gospel taught love of enemies. The work also reads episodes of Joseph's life as prefiguring Christ.

De Nabuthae (On Naboth) is a Latin moral treatise, probably first preached as sermons, by Ambrose, bishop of Milan. Its exact date is uncertain but is usually placed in the late 380s or 390s. Taking the story of King Ahab's seizure of Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21) as its starting point, it attacks the greed of the rich. Ambrose argues that the earth was made for all in common and that the poor are oppressed every day. It draws heavily on Basil of Caesarea's homilies on wealth and is a key text of early Christian social teaching.

De Noe (On Noah), sometimes called De Noe et arca, is an exegetical treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397). It comments on the Genesis account of Noah, the ark and the flood, and presents Noah, whose name it explains as "just" or "rest", as a model of righteousness for all to imitate. Its exact date is uncertain. Ambrose drew heavily on Philo of Alexandria's Questions on Genesis and read the narrative allegorically and morally. It belongs with his other treatises on Old Testament patriarchs, such as De Abraham and De Isaac.

De Paradiso (On Paradise) is a Latin exegetical treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan. It is among his earliest writings and is usually dated to the late 370s. It comments on the Genesis account of the garden of Eden, the fall of Adam and Eve and their expulsion. The treatise relies heavily on allegory and draws on Philo of Alexandria: paradise stands for the soul, Adam for the mind and Eve for the senses. Ambrose also answers objections to the Genesis story raised by the Marcionite thinker Apelles.

De Tobia (On Tobit) is a Latin moral treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397). It probably grew out of sermons, and its exact date is uncertain. It opens by praising the virtues of the biblical Tobit: his justice, mercy, hospitality, and his burial of the dead despite a royal ban. Most of the work then turns to a sharp attack on usury and the abuses of moneylenders, drawing on Scripture throughout. It is an important early Christian witness to Church teaching against lending at interest.

The Explanatio Psalmorum XII is a Latin commentary by Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397), on twelve psalms: Psalms 1, 35–40, 43, 45, 47, 48 and 61. Most of it seems to come from sermons preached in his last years and later revised. Ambrose's biographer Paulinus says he was still working on Psalm 43 when he died, and that commentary is unfinished. The opening exposition praises the psalms and introduces the theme of delight in God. Throughout, Ambrose reads the psalms morally and in relation to Christ, following the allegorical tradition of Origen and other Greek writers.

The Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam is a Latin commentary on the Gospel of Luke by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in ten books. It was compiled in the late 380s, largely from sermons he had preached, and it is his longest exegetical work. It opens by presenting Luke's Gospel as a historical narrative, then works through the text, reading it in literal, moral and allegorical senses, much influenced by Origen. It is one of the most important Latin Gospel commentaries of the fourth century.

The Expositio Psalmi CXVIII is a Latin commentary by Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397), on Psalm 118 (Psalm 119 in Hebrew numbering), the long alphabetic psalm in praise of God's law. It grew out of his preaching and is generally dated to the late 380s. After a prologue, it moves through the psalm's twenty-two eight-verse sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, in a matching series of sermons. Drawing partly on Origen, Ambrose reads the psalm as a guide to the moral and spiritual life. It is the longest of his exegetical works.

The Exameron (Hexameron) is an exegetical work by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, usually dated between 386 and 390. It is a commentary in six books on the six days of creation in Genesis, and it grew out of sermons preached over several days, probably during Holy Week. Ambrose begins by rejecting the philosophers' accounts of the eternity of matter and the world. He draws heavily on Basil of Caesarea's Greek homilies on the Hexaemeron, mixing natural history with moral and spiritual teaching. Through it, Greek creation exegesis reached the Latin West.

The Questions on the Old and New Testament is a Latin collection of short treatises in question-and-answer form. It was handed down among the works of Augustine, but it is now generally assigned to the anonymous Roman writer known as Ambrosiaster, who also wrote a commentary on Paul's epistles. It was composed in the later fourth century and survives in several recensions, including this one of 127 questions. It covers the nature of God, difficult biblical passages and doctrinal questions. It also argues against pagans, Jews and heretics, and it is valuable evidence for Roman Christianity of its time.

This Latin account of a pilgrimage to the holy places was written around 570 by an anonymous pilgrim from Piacenza. It was long wrongly attributed to "Antoninus of Piacenza" because its opening names the martyr Antoninus as the pilgrim's patron. The writer travels from Constantinople through Cyprus, the Syrian and Phoenician coast, Galilee, Jerusalem, Sinai and Egypt. He describes shrines, relics, monasteries, local customs and the damage left by earthquakes under Justinian. The text is an important witness to the Holy Land and to popular piety in the late sixth century.

This Latin account of a pilgrimage to the holy places was written around 570 by an anonymous pilgrim from Piacenza. It was long wrongly attributed to "Antoninus of Piacenza" because its opening names the martyr Antoninus as the pilgrim's patron. The writer travels from Constantinople through Cyprus, the Syrian and Phoenician coast, Galilee, Jerusalem, Sinai and Egypt. He describes shrines, relics, monasteries, local customs and the damage left by earthquakes under Justinian. The text is an important witness to the Holy Land and to popular piety in the late sixth century.

This Latin apologetic treatise in seven books was written by Arnobius, a rhetorician of Sicca Veneria in Roman North Africa, probably around 303, during the reign of Diocletian. Jerome calls it Adversus gentes, but the only surviving manuscript, from the ninth century, titles it Adversus nationes. Arnobius answers the pagan charge that Christianity had brought disaster on the world and driven away the gods. He then attacks pagan mythology, cult and sacrifice at length. The work is a valuable source for Roman religion and for an unusual early form of Christian thought.

The Confessions is an autobiographical work in thirteen books written in Latin by Augustine of Hippo between about 397 and 400. It is addressed to God as a long prayer. Books 1 to 9 tell the story of his restless youth, his attraction to Manichaeism and Neoplatonism, and his conversion to Christianity in 386. Book 10 examines memory, and the last three books are a commentary on the opening of Genesis. It is often called the first Western autobiography and has deeply shaped Christian spirituality and Western literature.

Adnotationes in Iob (Notes on Job) is a set of brief Latin comments on the Book of Job by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to around 399–400. It works through the biblical text phrase by phrase, offering short explanations that are often allegorical and moral. In his Retractationes, Augustine says the notes had been written in the margins of his copy of Job and were collected into a book by others. He doubted they should count as his work, since they were obscure and the copies were corrupt.

The City of God (De civitate Dei contra paganos) is a Latin apologetic and theological treatise in twenty-two books by Augustine of Hippo, written about 413–426. It was prompted by the Visigothic sack of Rome in 410 and dedicated to his friend Marcellinus. The first ten books answer pagan claims that Christianity caused Rome's misfortunes. The remaining twelve trace the origin, history and destiny of two cities: the earthly city, ruled by love of self, and the heavenly city, ruled by love of God. It deeply shaped Western theology and political thought.

De Fide et Symbolo (On Faith and the Creed) is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo. It began as an address he gave in 393, while still a presbyter, to the council of African bishops gathered at Hippo Regius. Augustine works through the baptismal creed article by article: God the Father, the Son's divinity and incarnation, the Holy Spirit, the Church, forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the body. Along the way he answers heretical misreadings, especially Manichaean and Arian ones. It is one of his earliest systematic accounts of Christian doctrine.

Augustine of Hippo wrote this long letter to Boniface, a Roman military officer in Africa who later became Count of Africa, around 417. It is often treated as a treatise on its own. Augustine explains how the Donatists differ from the Arians and defends the imperial laws that pressured Donatists to return to Catholic communion. He describes the violence of the Circumcellions and closes with a discussion of the sin against the Holy Spirit. The letter is a key source for Augustine's argument that the state may use coercion against schism and heresy.

The Letters of Augustine of Hippo are a Latin correspondence of more than two hundred letters, written from about 386, soon after his conversion, until his death in 430. The collection also includes letters written to him by others, among them Jerome and Paulinus of Nola. They cover philosophy, the interpretation of Scripture, pastoral care, church discipline and the Donatist and Pelagian controversies. The letters are an important source for Augustine's thought, for church life in Roman North Africa, and for the wider late Roman world.

The Breviculus Collationis cum Donatistis is a Latin summary by Augustine of Hippo of the Conference of Carthage, held in 411. By order of Emperor Honorius, Catholic and Donatist bishops met there to debate before the imperial tribune and notary Marcellinus, who acted as judge. Augustine wrote it soon after the conference. He condensed the long official record of its three sessions and keyed his summary to the record's numbered sections so readers could find each point. He presented the proceedings from the Catholic side, which won the judgment. The work is a key source for the Donatist controversy.

The Commonitorium on how to deal with Manichaeans who convert is a short Latin text of instructions for the Church. It is traditionally attributed to Augustine of Hippo, but its authorship is doubtful and it is often classed as pseudo-Augustinian. It tells how a bishop should receive former Manichaeans who submit a written confession: they are given a dated letter, placed under the watch of Catholic neighbours, and only cautiously admitted to baptism or reconciliation. It ends with a set form of anathemas against Manichaean teaching, such as the belief in two opposing principles of good and evil.

Contra Academicos (Against the Academics) is a philosophical dialogue in three books by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it in late 386 at Cassiciacum near Milan, after his conversion and before his baptism. It is dedicated to his patron Romanianus. The dialogue presents discussions with Augustine's pupils Licentius and Trygetius and his friend Alypius, and it argues against the scepticism of the New Academy, which held that certain knowledge is impossible. Augustine maintains that truth can be known and wisdom attained. It is among his earliest surviving works and shows Neoplatonic influence.

Contra Adimantum (Against Adimantus) is an anti-Manichaean treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written in the mid-390s while he was a presbyter at Hippo. Adimantus, a disciple of Mani, had written a work setting passages of the Old Testament against passages of the New to show that the two contradict each other. Augustine takes up these pairings in turn, beginning with the creation account in Genesis. He argues that the two Testaments agree, and he defends the unity of Scripture and of the God who inspired both.

Contra Cresconium (Against Cresconius) is an anti-Donatist treatise in four books by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to about 405–406. Cresconius, a Donatist layman and grammarian, had published a rebuttal of Augustine's earlier reply to Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Cirta. Augustine answers him point by point. He defends the validity of baptism given outside the Donatist communion and rejects the practice of rebaptism. He also turns the Donatists' own handling of the Maximianist schism against them. The work is a major source for Augustine's thinking on the Church and the sacraments.

This is a Latin pastoral letter by Augustine of Hippo to the Catholic faithful in his care, written during his controversy with the Donatists in Roman North Africa around the early 400s. He had already replied to a fragment of a letter by Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Constantine (Cirta). Once he obtained the complete letter, which was widely read, he answered it point by point, as if in a face-to-face debate. The work belongs to his writings against Petilian and defends Catholic unity against Donatist claims.

Against Two Letters of the Pelagians (Contra duas epistulas Pelagianorum) is a Latin treatise in four books by Augustine of Hippo, written about 420–421. It is addressed to Pope Boniface I, who had sent Augustine two Pelagian letters that slandered him. The first letter was attributed to Julian of Eclanum, and the second was issued by a group of Pelagian bishops. Augustine rejects their charge that he taught Manichaean doctrine. He also defends the Catholic teaching on original sin, grace, free will and the goodness of marriage. The work belongs to his later writings in the Pelagian controversy.

Contra epistulam fundamenti is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to about 396–397, early in his time as bishop. It refutes the "Fundamental Epistle", a foundational Manichaean letter attributed to Mani. Augustine quotes its opening passages and answers them one by one. Recalling his own years as a Manichaean hearer, he says he wants to heal his opponents, not crush them. The work contains his famous remark that he would not believe the Gospel unless moved by the authority of the Catholic Church. It also preserves fragments of the lost Manichaean text.

Against the Letter of Parmenian is an anti-Donatist treatise in three books by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to around 400. It answers a letter in which Parmenian, the Donatist bishop of Carthage who had died some years before, criticised the Donatist writer Tyconius. Tyconius had argued that no one's sin could cancel God's promise of a church spread throughout the world. Augustine defends this universal church and argues that it contains both good and bad members until the final judgment. He also argues that a sacrament does not depend on the holiness of the minister who performs it.

Reply to Faustus the Manichaean (Contra Faustum Manichaeum) is a polemical treatise in thirty-three books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 400. It answers a work by Faustus of Mileve, a Manichaean bishop whom Augustine had met in Carthage, as he recounts in the Confessions. Augustine quotes Faustus's arguments section by section and replies to each. He defends the Old Testament, the patriarchs and the unity of the two Testaments against Manichaean objections. The work also contains an influential early discussion of just war.

This Latin work is the stenographic record of a public debate held over two days in 392 at the Baths of Sossius in Hippo Regius. On one side was Augustine of Hippo, then a presbyter. On the other was Fortunatus, a Manichaean presbyter he had known before his conversion. Augustine argues that the Manichaean myth of a conflict between light and darkness makes God corruptible. The two men also debate the origin of evil, free will and the meaning of Scripture. After the debate Fortunatus reportedly left Hippo. It is an early witness to Augustine's anti-Manichaean polemic.

Contra Gaudentium Donatistarum Episcopum is a polemical treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 420. Gaudentius, Donatist bishop of Thamugadi, had threatened to burn himself and his followers inside his church rather than submit to the imperial laws enforcing Church unity. Those laws were being carried out by the tribune Dulcitius. Augustine quotes and refutes, point by point, the two letters Gaudentius sent to Dulcitius. The second book answers Gaudentius's reply to the first. The work is one of Augustine's last anti-Donatist writings and deals with martyrdom, suicide and the use of state coercion.

Answer to the Letters of Petilian (Contra litteras Petiliani) is a Latin polemical treatise in three books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 400–403 against Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Cirta (Constantina). Book I refutes the first part of a letter Petilian sent to his followers. Book II answers the whole letter point by point, and Book III replies to Petilian's response to Augustine. Augustine argues that the sacraments are valid whatever the holiness of the minister, and he defends the unity of the Catholic Church. The work is a major source for the Donatist controversy.

Against Lying (Contra Mendacium) is a treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 420 in reply to Consentius, a Catholic layman in Spain. Consentius had suggested that Catholics could expose hidden Priscillianists by pretending to share their beliefs. Augustine rejects this: no lie is permissible, even to unmask heretics. Lying about the faith is especially grave, and good ends never justify deceit. The work takes up the themes of his earlier On Lying (De mendacio) and became a classic statement of his strict view that lying is always wrong.

Contra partem Donati post gesta, also known as Ad Donatistas post collationem, is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 412. It followed the Conference of Carthage of 411, where Catholic and Donatist bishops debated before the imperial commissioner Marcellinus, who decided for the Catholics. Augustine addresses ordinary Donatists directly and urges them to stop following their bishops. He answers the claim that the judge had been bribed and uses the conference records to show that the Donatist case had been refuted.

Contra Secundinum Manichaeum is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated around 405–406. It answers a letter from Secundinus, a Manichaean auditor from Rome, who had written to Augustine with respect but criticised his departure from the sect and urged him to return. Augustine replies courteously but firmly, defending the Catholic faith and attacking Manichaean dualism and its teaching on the two natures and the origin of evil. In his Retractationes Augustine judged it the best of his writings against the Manichaeans.

Contra Felicem (Against Felix) is a Latin work in two books by Augustine of Hippo. It records a public debate held at Hippo Regius in December 404 between Augustine and Felix, a Manichaean teacher. The discussion starts from Mani's Letter of the Foundation and covers the authority of Mani's writings, the nature of God and the origin of evil. At the end Felix gives way and anathematizes Mani. The work is valuable both as anti-Manichaean polemic and as a near-verbatim record of an ancient debate.

De agone christiano (On the Christian Struggle) is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 396–397, early in his time as bishop. He wrote it in plain style for ordinary believers. It begins from Paul's image of the crown of victory. It explains that Christians fight against the devil, who rules through the love of passing things, and that Christ has already defeated him. It then sets out the rule of faith and briefly rejects the errors of heretical groups such as the Manichaeans, Arians and Donatists.

On the Soul and its Origin (De natura et origine animae) is a Latin treatise in four books by Augustine of Hippo, written about 419–420. It answers Vincentius Victor, a young man from Mauretania Caesariensis who had attacked Augustine's admitted uncertainty over whether individual souls are inherited from Adam or newly created for each person. One book is addressed to the monk Renatus, one to the presbyter Peter, and two to Victor himself. Augustine defends his hesitation on the question, insists that the soul is spirit rather than body, and refutes Victor's errors.

De Baptismo (On Baptism, Against the Donatists) is an anti-Donatist treatise in seven books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 400–401. Augustine argues that baptism given outside the Catholic communion by heretics or schismatics is valid and should not be repeated. However, it brings no spiritual benefit while the recipient stays separated from the Church. Much of the work answers the Donatist appeal to Cyprian of Carthage, and Augustine claims Cyprian's authority for his own position. The treatise shaped later Western teaching on the validity of sacraments.

De Beata Vita (On the Happy Life) is a short philosophical dialogue by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it in 386 at Cassiciacum near Milan, after his conversion and before his baptism. It is dedicated to Manlius Theodorus, and its prologue compares the approach to philosophy with a voyage to a harbour. The dialogue records conversations held over three days around Augustine's birthday with his mother Monica, his son Adeodatus and friends. It concludes that true happiness lies in possessing God, and it is one of his earliest surviving works.

De bono coniugali (On the Good of Marriage) is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 401 with its companion work On Holy Virginity. It responds to the controversy raised by Jovinian, who denied that virginity was superior to marriage. Augustine takes a middle course: marriage is a true good, grounded in human sociability and the creation of woman from man, while consecrated virginity remains the higher calling. His account of marriage's threefold good, offspring, fidelity and sacramental bond, became foundational for later Western theology and canon law on marriage.

On the Good of Widowhood (De bono viduitatis) is a letter-treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to about 414. Augustine wrote it to Juliana, a widow of the Roman noble family of the Anicii, after she had repeatedly asked him for it. It praises the vow of continent widowhood as a higher state than marriage, though below virginity, and holds that second marriages are not sinful. It also warns against attributing perseverance in virtue to human will alone instead of God's grace, which reflects Augustine's dispute with the Pelagians.
