The speech was given on Good Friday. Scholars disagree about its date and place, and they once doubted that Constantine wrote it, though many now accept it as his, probably translated from Latin. It attacks pagan polytheism and fatalism and defends divine providence and Christ's work. It is especially known for reading Virgil's Fourth Eclogue and an acrostic of the Erythraean Sibyl as prophecies of Christ.

This Greek panegyric by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, was delivered in Constantinople in 336 to mark the thirtieth anniversary of Constantine the Great's reign. Eusebius presents the emperor as the earthly image of the divine Logos and his monarchy as a reflection of God's heavenly rule. It also praises Constantine's suppression of polytheism and his support for the Church. Its later chapters are generally thought to come from a separate speech on Christ's sepulchre. The work is an important early statement of Christian imperial ideology, which later shaped Byzantine political thought.

The General Elementary Introduction is a Greek work in ten books by Eusebius of Caesarea. Its date is disputed: it may come from before the Great Persecution of 303 or from somewhat later. Only books six to nine survive, known as the Prophetic Extracts (Eclogae propheticae). They gather Old Testament prophecies about Christ, arranged by scriptural book and given brief commentary. They follow earlier books that argued for the faith without relying on Scripture. The work is an early source for Eusebius's exegesis and apologetic method.

The Ancoratus ("The Well-Anchored") is a Greek doctrinal treatise by Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia (Salamis) in Cyprus. He wrote it around 374 at the request of presbyters in Syedra in Pamphylia, whose letters stand at its beginning. It explains Christian teaching from Scripture and tradition: the consubstantiality of the Trinity, the full incarnation of Christ, and the resurrection and judgment. It argues against pagans, Jews and heretics, and lists the eighty heresies that Epiphanius later treated in the Panarion. It ends with two creeds, one of which closely resembles the creed associated with the Council of Constantinople of 381.

The Panarion ("medicine chest"), later known in Latin as Adversus haereses, is a Greek treatise against heresies by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis (Constantia) in Cyprus. He began it around 374–375 at the request of the Syrian archimandrites Acacius and Paul and finished it about three years later. It describes and refutes eighty sects and schools of thought, from the time of Adam to the late fourth century. The work preserves many otherwise lost documents and reports, including fragments of Jewish-Christian gospels such as the Gospel of the Ebionites.

The Anacephalaeosis ("Recapitulation") is a Greek epitome of the Panarion, the great catalogue of eighty heresies by Epiphanius of Salamis (d. 403). It is transmitted under his name, but its authorship is doubtful, and it is often treated as the work of a later hand. Tome by tome, it gives brief summaries of each heresy. It begins with the primal "mothers" of error, Barbarism, Scythism and Hellenism, which it traces through biblical history from Adam onward. It served as a convenient reference guide to Epiphanius's heresiology and circulated widely.

Christus patiens ("Christ Suffering") is a Greek religious drama of about 2,600 verses on the Passion, death and resurrection of Christ. Much of it is a cento, built from lines borrowed chiefly from Euripides. The Virgin Mary is the central speaker, and the cast also includes Christ, the Theologian, Joseph, Nicodemus, Mary Magdalene and Pilate. Manuscripts attribute it to Gregory of Nazianzus, but most scholars think it is a later Byzantine work, sometimes assigned to the twelfth century and possibly to Constantine Manasses. Its authorship and date are still disputed.

Oration 27 is the first of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople in 380, while he led the small Nicene community there. It serves as an introduction to the series and is aimed at the Eunomians, radical Arians known for their skill in dialectic. Gregory does not yet discuss the Trinity itself. Instead he asks who may speak about God, when, before whom and how far, arguing that theology requires purity of life, quiet and restraint rather than clever debate.

Oration 28 is the second of the five Theological Orations by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached them in Constantinople around 380, when he led the small Nicene community there against the Eunomians, who claimed that God's essence could be fully known. The first oration set out who may practise theology and under what conditions. This one argues that God's nature cannot be grasped by the human mind. Using the image of Moses on Sinai seeing only God's "back parts", Gregory shows that creation reveals that God exists, not what God is. The work is a classic statement of divine incomprehensibility.

The third of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arian groups. After setting out the monarchy of the Father, Gregory defends the full divinity of the Son. He argues that the Son is eternally begotten without time or passion, and answers his opponents' arguments from the terms "begotten" and "unbegotten." The oration closes with a set of antitheses contrasting Christ's human lowliness with his divine glory. Oration 30 continues the argument with a fuller treatment of the disputed passages of Scripture.

Oration 30 is the fourth of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus delivered in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arians. It is his second discourse on the Son. Gregory answers, one by one, the scriptural texts his opponents used to make the Son subordinate, such as "The Lord created me" (Proverbs 8:22) and "the Father is greater than I." He assigns the exalted expressions to Christ's divinity and the lowly ones to his assumed humanity. The oration ends with a discussion of the titles of the Son.

Oration 31 is the last of the five Theological Orations that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople, probably in 380, against the Eunomians and the Pneumatomachi, who denied that the Holy Spirit is fully divine. Gregory openly calls the Spirit God and consubstantial with the Father and the Son. He separates the Spirit's procession from the Son's generation and answers the objection that Scripture is silent on the matter with a theory of progressive revelation. The oration was an important statement of Cappadocian Trinitarian theology shortly before the Council of Constantinople of 381.

This short Greek poem by Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390) belongs to his moral poems (Carmina moralia). It is a series of one-line maxims in iambic trimeter, arranged as an alphabetic acrostic: each line begins with the next letter of the Greek alphabet. The maxims urge the reader to make God the beginning and end of all things, to control anger, speech and the flesh, to honour strangers, and to accept everything from God with thanksgiving. It shows how Gregory used classical gnomic verse for Christian moral teaching.

On the Incarnation of the Word is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius of Alexandria. It is the second part of a double work that opens with Against the Pagans, and both are addressed to a certain Macarius. Its date is disputed: some place it before the Arian controversy, around 318, while others place it in the 330s. It explains why the divine Word, through whom the world was made, took a human body to restore humanity from corruption and death. It also answers Jewish and pagan objections and remains a classic of Christian thought on the incarnation.

De Decretis is a Greek treatise in the form of a letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, usually dated to the 350s. It is written to an unnamed correspondent who had argued with supporters of Arius, including friends of Eusebius. Athanasius answers the Arian objection that the Council of Nicaea (325) used unscriptural terms, "of the essence" and "one in essence" (homoousios). He argues that these words express the meaning of Scripture about the Son's true divinity. The work is a major early defence of the Nicene formula. It also preserves documents connected with the council.

The Fourth Discourse Against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise that has come down with the three Orations Against the Arians of Athanasius of Alexandria (4th century). Most scholars doubt that Athanasius wrote it, and its true author and date are uncertain. It is a series of short arguments rather than a continuous discourse. Using Scripture, it argues that the Word is substantial and is the Father's own Son, and so preserves the single "Monarchy" of the Godhead. It attacks Arian teaching, and also views that separate the Word from the Son or merge Father and Son into one.

The First Discourse Against the Arians is the opening book of Athanasius of Alexandria's Greek polemical treatise against Arianism. Its date is disputed: scholars place it either around 339–346, during his exile in Rome, or in the later 350s. Athanasius argues that the Arians are sectaries named after their founder rather than Christians. He attacks the teaching of Arius's Thalia and defends the eternity of the Son and his unity of essence with the Father. He also begins interpreting disputed biblical texts such as Philippians 2:9–10 and Hebrews 1:4. It is a central text of Nicene theology.

The second of the Orations against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. Its date is debated, though it is often placed in the late 330s or 340s. It continues his defence of the Nicene faith by examining scriptural texts that his opponents used to argue that the Son of God is a creature. These include Hebrews 3:2, "faithful to him that made him", and Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me a beginning of his ways". Athanasius reads such passages as referring to the Son's incarnation rather than to his eternal being.

The third of the Greek Orations (Discourses) against the Arians by Athanasius of Alexandria, generally dated to around 340, though the exact date is debated. Its authenticity was questioned in modern scholarship but is widely accepted. Continuing the earlier discourses, it explains texts used by Arian opponents such as Asterius the Sophist, starting with John 14:10, "I in the Father and the Father in me." It argues for the mutual indwelling of Father and Son, who share one essence. It then attributes the Gospel accounts of Christ's ignorance, growth and suffering to the humanity the Word took on.

The Acts of Thomas is an anonymous apocryphal narrative, probably composed in Syriac in the early third century, likely at Edessa. It survives in Syriac and Greek versions, and scholars disagree about which is closer to the original. It tells how the apostle Judas Thomas was sold as a carpenter to the Indian king Gundaphoros, how he preached and worked miracles in India, and how he was martyred. It strongly favours sexual renunciation and includes liturgical prayers and celebrated poems, notably the Hymn of the Pearl. It is the chief source for the tradition of Thomas's mission to India.

The Fragmenta are the surviving remains of the writings of Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra (died c. 374), a supporter of the Council of Nicaea and opponent of Arianism. Most come from his treatise against Asterius the Sophist, written around the early 330s. They survive almost entirely as quotations in Eusebius of Caesarea's polemical works against him, with a few more in Epiphanius's Panarion 72. The fragments set out Marcellus's theology of the Word, which his critics condemned as Sabellian, and they are central to the history of the Arian controversy.

Against Celsus is an apologetic treatise in eight books by Origen of Alexandria, written around 248 at the request of his patron Ambrose. It refutes The True Word, an attack on Christianity by the second-century pagan philosopher Celsus. Origen answers him point by point, defending faith, the identity of Jesus, allegorical reading of Scripture and Christianity's relation to Greek religion. It survives complete in Greek and is among the most important works of early Christian apologetics. It also preserves most of what is known of Celsus's lost work.

This is a large Greek exegetical work by Origen of Alexandria, written for his patron Ambrose. He began it in Alexandria around the early 230s and continued it after moving to Caesarea. It originally ran to at least 32 books, but only a few survive, among them books 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 19, 20, 28 and 32. Origen reads the Fourth Gospel at both a literal and a spiritual level. He often argues against the Gnostic commentary of Heracleon, which makes this one of the earliest surviving Christian commentaries on John.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Gospel of John, preserved in the catenae: medieval chains of excerpts from earlier commentators arranged verse by verse. They are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253), whose large Commentary on John survives only in part. Catena attributions are often unreliable, so some passages may come from other writers or may have been reworded by later compilers. The fragments deal with themes such as the eternal Word, creation and the incarnation. They add to what is known of Origen's lost exegesis.

The Exhortation to Martyrdom is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, generally dated to about 235, during the persecution under the emperor Maximinus Thrax. It is addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Protoctetus, a presbyter of Caesarea, who were both facing arrest. Drawing heavily on Scripture, Origen urges them to stand firm, to reject idolatry and apostasy, and to see suffering for Christ as a contest that leads to glory. It is one of the most important early Christian writings on the meaning of martyrdom.

On Prayer (Peri euchēs) is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, usually dated around 233–234 and addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Tatiana. It is the earliest surviving systematic Christian study of prayer. Origen asks why prayer is worthwhile if God already knows all things, explains the kinds of prayer named in 1 Timothy 2:1, and argues that prayer in the strict sense should be offered to the Father through the Son. He gives a long commentary on the Lord's Prayer and ends with advice on posture, place and times for prayer.

Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) preached this series of sermons on the Book of Jeremiah at Caesarea in Palestine, probably in the 240s. Twenty homilies survive in Greek, which is unusual because most of Origen's preaching is known only through Latin translations. Jerome translated some of them into Latin. Working through the biblical text passage by passage, Origen reads the prophet's warnings as signs of God's patience and his call to repentance, and he moves from the literal history to spiritual and moral interpretation. The homilies are important evidence for early Christian preaching and for Origen's exegetical method.

This is a collection of short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Jeremiah, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts in the Byzantine catenae on the prophets, the chains of patristic comment arranged verse by verse. Some may come from Origen's lost homilies or notes on Jeremiah, though catena attributions are not always reliable. The fragments show his usual allegorical and moral reading, applying the prophet's images to sin, temptation and the soul's struggle, and they add to the Greek homilies on Jeremiah that survive in full.

These Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Lamentations are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive in the Byzantine catenae, or chains of commentary, on the prophets. They probably come from the commentary on Lamentations that Eusebius says Origen wrote at Alexandria and which is otherwise lost. The fragments discuss the alphabetic acrostic structure of Jeremiah's laments. They also read the Babylonian captivity allegorically, as the soul's captivity to hostile spiritual powers, from which Christ sets it free.

This short Greek exegetical fragment is attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). It comes from his lost commentary on Lamentations and survives only because it was quoted in a catena, or chain of patristic comments, on the Octateuch. The passage looks at the phrase "justly pursue what is just" and separates four cases by asking whether the act itself is right and whether the intention behind it is sound. Joseph, hypocritical almsgiving and Paul's zealous persecution of the church serve as examples. It is one witness to Origen's largely lost exegesis.

De Engastrimytho (On the Witch of Endor) is a homily by Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) on 1 Samuel 28, where the medium at Endor calls up Samuel for King Saul. It is one of the few homilies by Origen that survive in the original Greek. Four passages had been read, and the presiding bishop chose this one for the sermon. Origen reads the story literally and argues that Samuel really appeared and prophesied. He also holds that the souls of prophets, like Christ, went down to Hades. Eustathius of Antioch later wrote a treatise attacking this reading.

These are short Greek exegetical fragments on the First Book of Kingdoms (1 Samuel), attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) and preserved in a Byzantine catena on the books of Samuel and Kings. They comment on individual verses, among them the fate of Eli's sons, the capture of the ark and the fall of Dagon. One passage explains that the Bible's human language about God is figurative: God's "wrath" is discipline and his "repentance" is a change in his dispensation, not a passion. Attributions in catenae are often uncertain, so the authenticity of individual fragments may be questioned.

This short Greek exegetical fragment on the Song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2) is attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). It survives in a catena, or chain of excerpts, on the Song of Songs. Ascriptions in catenae are often unreliable, so the attribution is not certain. The fragment reads Hannah's song as teaching that whoever approaches God should place all hope in him alone and practise humility rather than boasting. God knows everything, judges each person by their conduct, and rules over life and death. People come to know him through good works.

The thirty-nine homilies on Luke's Gospel were preached by Origen of Alexandria, probably at Caesarea in the third century. They survive complete only in a Latin translation by Jerome, made around 390 at the request of Paula and Eustochium, while the Greek original is preserved only in fragments. Most of the homilies treat the first four chapters of Luke, especially the infancy narratives, and a few cover later passages. They are an important witness to Origen's preaching and exegesis and to Jerome's activity as a translator.

These are Greek exegetical fragments on the Gospel of Luke, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) and preserved in later catenae, the chains of excerpts from earlier commentators. They may come from his lost commentary on Luke or from his homilies on the Gospel. Not every catena attribution is certain. The comments follow the Gospel verse by verse. For example, on Christ rebuking the fever of Peter's mother-in-law, Origen asks whether harmful powers can afflict the body. The fragments keep some of Origen's Greek exegesis that would otherwise be lost.

The Philocalia is a Greek anthology of extracts from the writings of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The Greek text names Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen as its compilers, probably working in Pontus around 358–362. This attribution is widely accepted, though some scholars question it. It has twenty-seven chapters with titles added by the compilers, dealing with the inspiration and interpretation of Scripture, free will and providence. About a fifth comes from Contra Celsum. Because many of Origen's works are lost, the anthology also preserves Greek passages of On the First Principles.

Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) preached this series of sermons on the Book of Jeremiah at Caesarea in Palestine, probably in the 240s. Twenty homilies survive in Greek, which is unusual because most of Origen's preaching is known only through Latin translations. Jerome translated some of them into Latin. Working through the biblical text passage by passage, Origen reads the prophet's warnings as signs of God's patience and his call to repentance, and he moves from the literal history to spiritual and moral interpretation. The homilies are important evidence for early Christian preaching and for Origen's exegetical method.

This is Origen of Alexandria's verse-by-verse exegesis of the Gospel of Matthew, written in Greek at Caesarea late in his life, around 246–248. It originally ran to twenty-five books. Only books 10 to 17 survive in Greek, covering roughly Matthew 13:36 to 22:33. An anonymous early Latin translation preserves much of the rest, and a few fragments survive in other writers, including Origen's account of the order of the four Gospels. The commentary combines literal and allegorical interpretation and is a major witness to early Christian biblical scholarship.

This is Origen of Alexandria's verse-by-verse exegesis of the Gospel of Matthew, written in Greek at Caesarea late in his life, around 246–248. It originally ran to twenty-five books. Only books 10 to 17 survive in Greek, covering roughly Matthew 13:36 to 22:33. An anonymous early Latin translation preserves much of the rest, and a few fragments survive in other writers, including Origen's account of the order of the four Gospels. The commentary combines literal and allegorical interpretation and is a major witness to early Christian biblical scholarship.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the whole Psalter, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Most survive only as excerpts in later catenae, the Byzantine anthologies of biblical commentary. Origen wrote extensively on the Psalms, but compilers of catenae often confused or merged authors. Some material under his name is probably by others, such as Evagrius Ponticus, so the authenticity of individual fragments is doubtful. The comments read the Psalms morally and spiritually. Their opening reflection on Psalm 1 presents turning away from evil as the first step of the soul's progress toward God.

This Greek letter is Origen's reply to the Christian chronographer Julius Africanus, written from Nicomedia, probably around 240. Africanus had objected that the story of Susanna in the Book of Daniel was a late forgery. He pointed to Greek wordplays that could not have existed in a Hebrew original and to features he found implausible. Origen defends the story's place in the Church's Scriptures and discusses differences between the Hebrew and Greek texts of the Bible. The letter is one of Origen's few complete surviving letters and an important early witness to debates over the biblical canon and textual criticism.

Selecta in Genesim is a collection of Greek fragments of Origen of Alexandria's (c. 185–c. 253) exegetical writings on Genesis. Most survive in later catenae, the chains of excerpts that Byzantine compilers made from earlier commentators. Origen's own Commentary on Genesis, written in Alexandria, is largely lost. The collection opens with a passage from its third tome, preserved by Eusebius, on where the apostles went to preach. The other excerpts discuss particular verses: grammar, punctuation, the blessing to increase and multiply, and the creation of humanity in God's image. They are an important witness to Origen's lost interpretation of Genesis.

The Selecta in Exodum are Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Exodus attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive only in fragments, mostly preserved in later catenae (chains of excerpts from biblical commentators), and their exact relation to Origen's lost commentaries is uncertain. They comment on selected verses. A notable passage deals with the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, where Origen distinguishes between a heart described as "hardened", "strengthened" or "made heavy". This question of divine action and human free will recurs elsewhere in his writings.

Selecta in Leviticum ("Selections on Leviticus") is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Leviticus attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like other fragments of his biblical commentary, they survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, so how much of the wording is Origen's own is uncertain. The comments explain the book's title and defend its laws on priesthood and sacrifice against critics who thought them unworthy of the Creator. Drawing on Paul's statement that "the law is spiritual," they read the ritual prescriptions as hidden teaching worthy of God.

The Selecta in Numeros ("Selections on Numbers") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Numbers attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The notes survive as fragments, mainly through the catenae, the medieval chains of patristic commentary, and their authenticity is not always certain. They comment on individual verses, including the meaning of the word "manna", the prophesying of the seventy elders, Miriam's exclusion from the camp and the sending of the spies. They also read Joshua, son of Nun, as a type of Christ. The notes add to Origen's better-known Homilies on Numbers.

Selecta in Deuteronomium ("Selections on Deuteronomy") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Deuteronomy attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The notes survive as fragments rather than as a continuous commentary, mostly drawn from later catenae, and the authorship of some passages is uncertain. They comment briefly on individual verses. Topics include Moses as the prophetic voice of God, Joshua as his successor, the inheritance of Reuben and Gad, and how the divine "voice" at Sinai should be understood without suggesting that God has a bodily nature.

The Selecta in Jesum Nave are short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Joshua attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts, mainly through catenae, and so their exact wording and authenticity are not always certain. The notes comment on individual verses and mix literal remarks with allegorical readings. Rahab, for example, is presented as a figure of the Church gathered from the nations, and her lowering of the spies through the window is compared to Paul's escape from Damascus.

Selecta in Judices ("Selections on Judges") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Judges attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as fragments, mainly in exegetical catenae, so how much of the material is genuinely Origen's is uncertain. The notes take up individual verses. They discuss whether the Spirit was behind Jephthah's rash vow, the "shibboleth" password test, Samson's Nazirite hair, the ephod and teraphim, and the defeat of Benjamin. They also add to what survives of Origen's Homilies on Judges, which are preserved in Latin.

The Selecta in Job is a collection of short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Job attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like other Origenian "selecta", the comments survive as fragments rather than a continuous commentary. They are mostly preserved in later catenae, so some attributions are uncertain. The notes explain individual verses, often morally or allegorically. For example, they read Satan's attacks on Job's household as possible only through drunkenness, and they treat harsh words from Job's friends as a heavy burden on the soul.

The Selecta in Psalmos are a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Psalms attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, and their authenticity is doubtful in part because some passages may come from other writers, such as Evagrius Ponticus. The opening gathers philosophical definitions of "end" from Aristotle and Stoic sources to explain psalm titles. Even so, the fragments remain an important witness to Origen's lost commentaries and homilies on the Psalter.

The Fragmenta in Ezechielem are short Greek comments on passages of the Book of Ezekiel attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts in later manuscript collections rather than as a continuous work. Origen wrote a long commentary and homilies on Ezekiel, most of which are lost in Greek, so these pieces help preserve his exegesis of the book. They show his allegorical method, treating Pharaoh as a symbol of the devil and the closed eastern gate as God's mysteries. They also comment on the meaning of Hebrew words.

The Adnotationes in Genesim, headed in Greek "Eklogai eis tēn Genesin" (Selections on Genesis), are short exegetical notes on passages of Genesis attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like many such fragments, they come down mainly through later catenae, so it is uncertain whether particular notes are genuinely his. The surviving comments deal with episodes such as the Flood. They explain, for example, that God's "repentance" means a change in his plan of salvation, not a human emotion, because the divine nature is free from passions. They help preserve Origen's largely lost commentary work on Genesis.

Adnotationes in Exodum is a set of brief Greek exegetical notes on selected verses of Exodus, headed "Eklogai" ("selections") and attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like many of his lost commentaries, the material survives only in fragments, mostly from catenae, and the authenticity of individual pieces is uncertain. The notes explain why God tests his people, distinguish an "idol" from a "likeness" and worship from service, and comment on the high priest's vestments and the forty days of the giving of the Law.

This is a collection of short Greek exegetical notes on Leviticus attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts in later catenae, the anthologies of patristic comment arranged verse by verse. The comments cover passages on unintentional sin and sin offerings, which they connect to Christ offered for the sins of all. They also discuss childbirth, presenting the Virgin Mary as free from ritual impurity, and the laws about leprosy. Origen's surviving Greek commentary on Leviticus is very fragmentary. As with many catena excerpts, the attribution of individual fragments may be uncertain.

The Adnotationes in Numeros are a set of brief Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Numbers attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like many surviving fragments of his biblical scholarship, they come down as excerpts rather than a continuous commentary. They comment on selected verses from chapters 11 to 24. Topics include the manna, compared with the readings of Aquila and Symmachus; Miriam's leprosy as a warning to the people; and Balaam's oracles. They link Balaam's prophecy of the rising star to the Magi who came to Bethlehem.

The Adnotationes in Deuteronomium are short Greek exegetical notes on Deuteronomy attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive only as fragments in catenae, the Byzantine chains of excerpts from earlier commentators, so how much is authentically Origen's is uncertain. The notes compare readings such as Aquila's translation and give typological interpretations. Moses' exclusion from the promised land, for example, is read as a sign that the law cannot bring things to perfection. Joshua's succession to Moses is likened to Elisha receiving Elijah's spirit.

These are short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Joshua, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) and preserved as excerpts in later biblical catenae. They comment on individual verses. One question is why Jericho was placed under the ban: its spoils are explained as a firstfruits offering, and the city fell to trumpets without weapons as a sign of divine power. The notes also explain why plunder was allowed at Ai. Catena attributions are often uncertain. The fragments are separate from Origen's Homilies on Joshua, which survive mainly in Rufinus's Latin translation.

The Adnotationes in Judices, titled in Greek "Eklogai eis tous Kritas" (Selections on Judges), are short exegetical notes on the Book of Judges attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253). They survive as fragments, mostly from catenae, and comment on individual verses. Examples include the water that sprang from the jawbone in Samson's story and the war against the Benjaminites. The notes reflect on divine justice and read Jacob's blessing of Benjamin as a prophecy. Whether every fragment truly comes from Origen is uncertain.

These are exegetical fragments on the Book of Job attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They are traditionally linked to his lost homilies on Job, which Jerome lists as twenty-two in number. The fragments survive only as excerpts in Byzantine catenae, anthologies of patristic comment arranged verse by verse, so how far each one is authentic is uncertain. Short notes on individual verses dwell on the devil's assault on Job and the protection God gives the righteous. They help show how Job was read in early Greek Christian exegesis.

The Excerpta in Psalmos is a collection of short Greek exegetical notes on individual verses of the Psalms, handed down under the name of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253). Its authenticity is doubtful. Like much of Origen's lost Psalm commentary, the material survives as excerpts in later compilations, and parts may come from other authors. The notes read the text allegorically and morally: "the world" is the Church, Zion is the watchful soul, and God's judgment calls believers to avoid ungodly deeds and thoughts.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Proverbs, preserved in the catenae (chains of excerpts from biblical commentators) under the name of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Origen's full commentary on Proverbs is lost. The fragments explain the sayings of Solomon allegorically and morally, treating wisdom as spiritual knowledge and instruction as the governing of the passions. Their authenticity is uncertain, because modern scholars have shown that many scholia once ascribed to Origen belong to Evagrius Ponticus.

The Scholia on the Song of Songs are short Greek exegetical comments on the Song of Songs attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as fragments in a catena, the epitome of commentary that goes under the name of Procopius of Gaza, where they appear alongside excerpts from other Fathers. Origen reads the Song allegorically as the love between Christ the Bridegroom and the Church or soul as bride. These fragments supplement his Commentary and Homilies on the Song, which survive chiefly in Latin translation.

The Scholia in Matthaeum are a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Gospel of Matthew, handed down under the name of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like many fragments ascribed to Origen, they survive mainly through catenae, the medieval chains of commentary on Scripture. Their authenticity is uncertain, and some passages may belong to later writers. The notes go through Matthew verse by verse. They open with a theological distinction between Christ's "genesis" and "gennesis," comparing the incarnate Word to speech made visible in writing.

These Greek exegetical fragments on the Gospel of Luke are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253) and survive in catena manuscripts rather than as an independent work. They comment verse by verse on the Gospel. On Luke's prologue they contrast the four Gospels accepted by the Church with writings such as the Gospels according to the Egyptians, of the Twelve, of Thomas, of Basilides and of Matthias. They also reject docetic views of Christ's incarnation. Attributions within catenae are often uncertain, so the authenticity of individual fragments varies.

This is a large Greek exegetical work by Origen of Alexandria, written for his patron Ambrose. He began it in Alexandria around the early 230s and continued it after moving to Caesarea. It originally ran to at least 32 books, but only a few survive, among them books 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 19, 20, 28 and 32. Origen reads the Fourth Gospel at both a literal and a spiritual level. He often argues against the Gnostic commentary of Heracleon, which makes this one of the earliest surviving Christian commentaries on John.

These are Greek passages from Origen's homilies on Jeremiah that survive as excerpts in the Philocalia, the anthology of his writings traditionally said to have been compiled by Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen. Some overlap with homilies that survive elsewhere. Others, including material from the thirty-ninth homily, are known only through this anthology. The extracts deal with how Scripture should be read. They warn against rash speculation about God's hidden wisdom and insist that no stroke of the inspired text is empty, because every part comes from the divine fullness.

These are Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Job attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive in the catenae, the chains of patristic comment that Byzantine compilers arranged verse by verse. Origen is reported to have preached a series of homilies on Job, but the full series is lost, and the attribution of individual catena excerpts is often uncertain. The fragments comment on Job's righteousness, his losses, his wife's temptation and human life as a trial. They read the text morally and spiritually and stress endurance and the knowledge of God.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in nine books by Sozomen, a lawyer at Constantinople. He wrote it around the 440s and dedicated it to Emperor Theodosius II. It was meant to continue the work of Eusebius and covers events from the 320s to the 420s. The ninth book seems unfinished and stops short of the end date the author announced. Sozomen drew heavily on Socrates Scholasticus but added much material of his own, especially on monasticism, missions and the Church outside the empire. It is a key source for fourth- and early fifth-century Christianity.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in seven books by Socrates of Constantinople, also called Socrates Scholasticus. It was written in the 440s and continues Eusebius's history, covering events from 305 to 439: Constantine's conversion, the Arian controversy, the councils, and the affairs of the churches of the eastern empire. Socrates aimed for a plain style and drew on documents and on eyewitnesses. Sozomen used the work as a source. In the sixth century it was put into Latin as part of the Historia Tripartita, which carried it into the medieval West.

The Ecclesiastical History of Philostorgius (368–c. 439), a Cappadocian historian who followed the Anomoean teaching of Eunomius, was written in Greek in twelve books and appeared between about 425 and 433. It covered church history from the Arian controversy into the early fifth century from a non-Nicene point of view. The original is lost. It survives mainly through the epitome made by Photius of Constantinople in the ninth century. Photius summarised the work critically, but his epitome keeps a rare account of the period from the side of the losing party.

The Refutation of All Heresies, also called the Elenchus or Philosophumena, is a long Greek polemical treatise from the early third century. It is traditionally attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, but some scholars assign it to an unknown "Pseudo-Hippolytus", and it was once credited to Origen. The work argues that Christian heresies come from Greek philosophy, the mysteries and astrology. It surveys pagan thought and then describes some thirty-three Gnostic and other systems, which makes it a major source for early Christian heterodoxy. Books II and III are lost. Books IV–X were rediscovered at Mount Athos in 1842.

The Refutation of All Heresies, also called the Elenchus or Philosophumena, is a long Greek polemical treatise from the early third century. It is traditionally attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, but some scholars assign it to an unknown "Pseudo-Hippolytus", and it was once credited to Origen. The work argues that Christian heresies come from Greek philosophy, the mysteries and astrology. It surveys pagan thought and then describes some thirty-three Gnostic and other systems, which makes it a major source for early Christian heterodoxy. Books II and III are lost. Books IV–X were rediscovered at Mount Athos in 1842.

The Chronicon Paschale, or Paschal Chronicle, is an anonymous Greek world chronicle written in the seventh century, probably at Constantinople during the reign of Heraclius. Its author called it an epitome of the ages from Adam to the seventeenth year of Heraclius. Its name comes from its dating system, which follows the Christian Easter cycle. It opens with a discussion of the date of Easter that cites Philo and Peter of Alexandria. Although much of it draws on earlier works, it is an important independent source for events of the late sixth and early seventh centuries.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in six books by Evagrius Scholasticus, a lawyer at Antioch and aide to Patriarch Gregory of Antioch. He completed it around 593–594. It continues the histories of Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret, covering the period from the First Council of Ephesus in 431 to the reign of Emperor Maurice. Written from a Chalcedonian standpoint, it is a major source for the Christological controversies after Chalcedon, for imperial and Persian affairs, and for the plague of the 540s, which Evagrius survived.

This Greek church history in three books was written around 475 by an anonymous author, the son of a presbyter of Cyzicus, who worked in Bithynia. Following Photius, it was long misattributed to Gelasius of Cyzicus. Book I covers Constantine's reign up to 323, Book II the Council of Nicaea and Book III its aftermath. It draws on Eusebius, Rufinus and other historians, as well as on a parchment book that had belonged to Dalmatius of Cyzicus. The author aimed to show against the Eutychians that the Nicene Fathers did not teach Monophysite doctrine.

This Greek hagiography is attributed to Mark the Deacon, who presents himself as companion and deacon of Porphyry, bishop of Gaza from 395 to 420. It tells of Porphyry's ascetic life, his ordination, and his campaign to Christianize pagan Gaza. With imperial support, this ended in the destruction of the Marneion temple in 402. It is a vivid and detailed account of a city's Christianization, but its historical reliability is debated. Versions also survive in Latin and Georgian, and the Georgian may derive from a lost Syriac original.

The Acts of Philip is an anonymous Greek apocryphal work about the missionary journeys of the Apostle Philip. It was probably written in the mid-to-late fourth century. It was originally made up of fifteen separate episodes followed by a martyrdom account, and it mixes miracle stories with elements of heroic romance and ascetic teaching. In its best-known section, Philip preaches with Bartholomew and his sister Mariamne at Hierapolis (Ophioryma) in Asia. There he defeats a serpent cult and is martyred by crucifixion. The text matters as evidence for later apostolic legend and the ascetic piety of Asia Minor.

The Acts of Barnabas is an anonymous Greek apocryphal work, also called the Journeyings and Martyrdom of Barnabas. It claims to be written by John Mark, the companion of Paul and Barnabas. It tells of Mark's conversion and of Barnabas's split from Paul. It then follows Barnabas's mission through Cyprus, his martyrdom at Salamis and his burial by Mark. The work is usually dated to the fifth century. It is thought to reflect the Cypriot church's claim to apostolic foundation and independence from Antioch.

The Banquet of the Ten Virgins is a Greek dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. Its title and form deliberately echo Plato's Symposium. Gregorion tells Euboulios about a banquet held by Arete (Virtue) in a garden, where ten virgins give speeches in turn praising chastity and virginity. They draw heavily on allegorical readings of Scripture. Thekla gives the fullest speech, and the work ends with her hymn to Christ the Bridegroom. It is Methodius's only work to survive complete in Greek and an important early Christian treatise on virginity.

Concerning Free-Will (De libero arbitrio) is a Greek theological dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. In it, a speaker called Orthodoxus argues against a follower of Valentinian Gnosticism about where evil comes from. He rejects the idea that matter has always existed alongside God and is the source of evil. Instead, he argues that God created everything good and that evil comes from the misuse of free will by rational creatures. The work is an important early Christian treatment of human freedom and of why evil exists.

On Things Created (De creatis) is a Greek theological treatise by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. The full work is lost. It survives only in a summary of excerpts made by the ninth-century patriarch Photius in codex 235 of his Bibliotheca. The surviving passages argue against Origen and his followers. They criticize his allegorical reading of texts such as "cast not your pearls before swine" and dispute his view that the created world is coeternal with God. The work is an important witness to early opposition to Origen.

Against Porphyry was a Greek treatise by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. In it he answered the Neoplatonist philosopher Porphyry, whose attack on Christianity, Against the Christians, was widely read. Jerome mentions the work, but it is lost apart from a few short excerpts. These are moral and theological reflections: that true excellence is what God values, that repentance works best when it is immediate, and that human good lies in resembling God.

These are short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Job, preserved in the catenae (medieval chains of patristic commentary) under the name of Methodius, usually identified as Methodius of Olympus (died c. 311), bishop and martyr. Their authenticity cannot be fully confirmed, as is often the case with catena material. The fragments discuss Job's speeches to his friends. They argue that true wisdom, joined to piety, is beyond human discovery and comes only as God's gift through revelation. This is why Greek philosophers seeking God by their own strength failed.

This short Greek fragment comes from a lost discourse on martyrs attributed to Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and Church Father who died around 311. Only a brief passage survives, preserved as a quotation by later writers. It praises martyrdom as so admirable and desirable that Christ himself honoured it. Citing Philippians 2:6, it presents the Son's self-emptying descent to humanity as the source of this gift. The passage is a small witness to pre-Nicene reflection on martyrdom as an imitation of Christ, from the era of the last great persecutions.

This is a small collection of short Greek fragments of uncertain origin that later writers handed down under the name of Methodius of Olympus, the bishop and martyr who died around 311. They are not assigned to any known work, and their authenticity is doubtful. They include sayings on justice, described as the fulfilment of all the commandments and as "square", equal on every side. One passage, reporting Methodius's view, treats Adam, his begotten son and Eve, who "proceeded" from Adam, as types of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in five books by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was written around 449–450 and continues the history of Eusebius of Caesarea. It begins with the rise of Arianism under Constantine and ends in 429, with the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Theodoret writes from a firmly Nicene and Antiochene viewpoint and focuses on the struggle against Arianism. He quotes many letters, creeds and synodal documents in full. Along with the histories of Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen, it is one of the main sources for fourth-century church history.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in five books by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was written around 449–450 and continues the history of Eusebius of Caesarea. It begins with the rise of Arianism under Constantine and ends in 429, with the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Theodoret writes from a firmly Nicene and Antiochene viewpoint and focuses on the struggle against Arianism. He quotes many letters, creeds and synodal documents in full. Along with the histories of Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen, it is one of the main sources for fourth-century church history.

The Historia Religiosa, also called the Philotheos Historia ("History of the Lovers of God"), is a Greek hagiographical collection written by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, around 440. It gives thirty accounts of ascetics of Syria and Mesopotamia, beginning with Jacob of Nisibis. Among them is Symeon the Stylite, who was still living when Theodoret wrote. Theodoret knew many of these monks personally, and he tells of their hardships, miracles and teaching. A short treatise on divine love closes the work. It is a key source for early Syrian monasticism.

Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch from 412 to 444, wrote this Greek commentary on the twelve Minor Prophets, from Hosea to Malachi. It is usually dated to the earlier part of his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy. The preface admits that many have already explained the prophets but argues that further interpretation still helps readers. Cyril reads each prophet first in its historical setting and then spiritually, as pointing to Christ and the Church. It is the fullest surviving patristic commentary on these books.

The Catena on Matthew is an anonymous Greek commentary on the Gospel of Matthew. It belongs to the Byzantine genre of the catena, or "chain", in which excerpts from earlier Church Fathers are arranged verse by verse along the biblical text. The text is divided into numbered chapters (kephalaia) on episodes such as the Magi, the Beatitudes and the healing miracles. Among the Fathers it quotes, John Chrysostom's homilies on Matthew are especially prominent. Neither the compiler nor the date is known. Such catenae matter because they preserve fragments of patristic exegesis that are otherwise lost.

The Catena in Marcum is a Greek catena, or chain of excerpts from earlier Christian writers, that works through the Gospel of Mark passage by passage. It opens with a list of the traditional chapter headings (kephalaia) of Mark. It is traditionally attributed to Victor of Antioch, a presbyter of the fifth century, but who compiled it and when are uncertain. It draws heavily on earlier writers, especially John Chrysostom. It is often counted among the earliest surviving commentaries on Mark and is valued for comparing the Gospel accounts.

This is an anonymous Greek compilation that supplements John Chrysostom's homilies on the Gospel of Matthew and records variant readings of them. It survives in the tradition of the New Testament catenae, anthologies of patristic comment on Scripture. It opens with a list of exegetical questions arranged in the Gospel's order. They include why the Gospel is so called, the women in Christ's genealogy, the star of the Magi, the flight into Egypt and Christ's baptism. Its date and compiler are unknown.

The Catena on Luke is an anonymous Greek commentary on the Gospel of Luke. Like other catenae, it is a "chain" of excerpts from earlier Church Fathers, arranged passage by passage along the biblical text. It opens with the traditional list of the Gospel's chapter headings (kephalaia), covering episodes such as the census, the shepherds, Simeon and the Temptation. The compiler and the date of compilation are uncertain. Catenae of this kind matter because they preserve fragments of patristic exegesis, including passages from commentaries otherwise lost.

The Catena on John is an anonymous Greek catena, or "chain", of patristic commentary on the Gospel of John. It sets out the Gospel passage by passage and attaches excerpts from earlier Greek interpreters to each one. The commentary draws above all on John Chrysostom's homilies on John, and it opens with his account of the evangelist as an unlettered fisherman of Bethsaida. A list of chapter headings precedes the commentary. Neither the compiler nor the date of compilation is known. Like other catenae, it is valuable because it preserves fragments of early exegesis, some of which survive nowhere else.

This anonymous Greek collection supplies additional material and variant readings for a catena, or chain commentary, on the Gospel of Luke. Catenae are Byzantine compilations that set excerpts from earlier Church Fathers beside the biblical verses they explain. The collection is titled "Interpretation of various [Fathers] on the Gospel according to Luke". It opens with a list of numbered chapter headings covering episodes such as Luke's prologue, the Annunciation, Simeon and Anna, Christ's genealogy, and the parables. Its compiler and date are unknown. Texts like this matter because they keep fragments of patristic exegesis that are often lost elsewhere.

This is an anonymous Greek supplement to a catena on the Gospel of John, giving additional material and variant readings from a manuscript in the Bodleian Library, Oxford. A catena is a running commentary assembled from excerpts of earlier Church Fathers. This one opens with a list of chapter headings taken from John Chrysostom's homilies on John. The headings follow the Gospel's episodes, from the eternal generation of the Word through the Samaritan woman and the feeding of the five thousand to the man born blind. Its compiler and date are unknown.

The Catena on Acts is an anonymous Greek catena, or chain commentary, on the Acts of the Apostles. Its heading calls it an interpretation of Acts "by Chrysostom and various others". It follows the biblical text passage by passage and sets beside each one extracts from earlier interpreters, drawing above all on John Chrysostom's homilies on Acts. A prologue presents Luke as an Antiochene physician and disciple of Paul. The compiler and date are uncertain. The work matters because it preserves fragments of patristic exegesis, some of which survive nowhere else.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Epistle to the Romans belongs to the type named after its Vatican manuscripts. A catena is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier interpreters arranged verse by verse. Its compiler and date are unknown. It begins with a prologue that summarizes the letter. The prologue says Paul wrote it from Corinth and treats the calling of the Gentiles, the end of circumcision, and the undoing of Adam's transgression through Christ. Catenae of this kind matter because they preserve fragments of patristic exegesis that are otherwise lost.

This is an anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Epistle to the Romans. A catena is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier Church Fathers, each set against the verse it explains and labelled with its author's name. This form of the catena takes its name from a manuscript held in Munich. The surviving section begins at Romans 7:7 and opens with an excerpt from John Chrysostom on whether the Law is sin. Its compiler and date are unknown. Catenae of this kind matter because they preserve comments by Greek exegetes whose own works are partly or wholly lost.

The Catena on the First Epistle to the Corinthians is an anonymous Byzantine Greek commentary. Like other New Testament catenae, it strings together excerpts from earlier Greek interpreters, with John Chrysostom usually the main source, and arranges them verse by verse alongside Paul's letter. It opens with a summary of the letter's occasion: factions at Corinth, a case of incest, disputes over marriage and celibacy, food offered to idols, spiritual gifts and the resurrection. The compiler and date are uncertain.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier Church Fathers, arranged verse by verse. Its compiler and date are unknown. It opens with a summary of the letter's occasion. Paul writes from Macedonia after the Corinthians have disciplined the man who took his stepmother, and he urges them to receive him back now that he has repented. The summary also notes Paul's teaching on letter and spirit, the new creation in Christ, the collection for the saints, and his defence against false apostles.

The Catena on the Epistle to the Galatians is an anonymous Greek compilation of exegetical excerpts on Paul's letter to the Galatians. It belongs to the Byzantine catena tradition, in which compilers set extracts from earlier Church Fathers alongside the biblical text as a running commentary. Its date and compiler are unknown. The opening explains the occasion of the letter: Jewish-Christian teachers were pressing the Galatians to keep the Mosaic law and were questioning Paul's apostolic authority. Collections like this one are important because they preserve fragments of patristic commentaries that are otherwise lost.

The Catena on Ephesians is an anonymous Greek commentary on Paul's Letter to the Ephesians. Like other catenae ("chains"), it strings together excerpts from earlier Church Fathers, each marked with the name of its source. It opens with John Chrysostom's introduction to the letter, which describes Ephesus as the leading city of Asia, a centre of the cult of Artemis and of philosophy, and presents Paul writing as a prisoner in Rome. When and by whom the compilation was made is uncertain. It is valuable for preserving passages of patristic exegesis, including fragments of commentaries that are otherwise lost.

The Catena on the Epistle to the Philippians is an anonymous Greek exegetical anthology, a "catena" or chain of excerpts from earlier Church Fathers arranged to follow the text of Paul's letter verse by verse. Compilations of this kind were produced in the Byzantine period, but this one's compiler and exact date are unknown. It opens with an introduction to the church at Philippi and the circumstances of Paul's imprisonment, drawn from John Chrysostom's homilies. Catenae are valuable because they preserve patristic interpretation, sometimes including fragments of commentaries otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Epistle to the Colossians is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier patristic interpreters, arranged verse by verse. Its compiler and exact date are unknown, though such catenae belong to the Byzantine period. The opening passage draws on John Chrysostom's homilies on Colossians. It discusses the letter as one Paul wrote in captivity and places it in sequence with Romans, Philemon, Philippians and Timothy. Catenae like this one matter because they preserve fragments of patristic exegesis, some of which survive nowhere else.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's First Epistle to the Thessalonians is a chain of exegetical excerpts from earlier Church Fathers, arranged as a running commentary on the biblical text. Catenae of this kind were compiled in the Byzantine period, and the compiler and date of this one are unknown. It opens with an introduction to the letter: Paul writes from Athens and sends Timothy to strengthen the Thessalonians in affliction, console them about the dead, and teach about the resurrection and the uncertain day of Christ's coming. Catenae preserve patristic interpretations that are otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena is a chain of commentary on Paul's Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, presented as a volume of "exegetical selections". Like other New Testament catenae, it gathers excerpts from earlier Greek Church Fathers and arranges them verse by verse. Its opening draws heavily on John Chrysostom's homilies on the epistle. It explains that Paul wrote again because he could not visit, and to correct those who claimed that Christ's coming and the judgement were already at hand. The compiler and date are unknown.

The catena on the First Epistle to Timothy is an anonymous Greek commentary on Paul's letter. Like other catenae, or "chains", it is made of excerpts from earlier Church Fathers arranged in order along the biblical text. Its compiler and date are unknown. It opens with an introduction on Timothy as Paul's disciple, drawn from Acts. It explains why Paul wrote only to Timothy and Titus, then lists the chapter headings of the epistle, covering prayer, the qualities of bishops and the Incarnation. Catenae like this one preserve Greek exegesis, including passages from works that are otherwise lost.

This is an anonymous Greek catena, or "chain" commentary, on Paul's Second Epistle to Timothy. It is one of the Byzantine catenae on the New Testament. It presents exegetical extracts from earlier Greek writers verse by verse, with each excerpt attributed to its author, such as John Chrysostom and Theodore. Its opening asks why Paul wrote a second letter, explaining it as consolation for Timothy written near the apostle's death. Its compiler and date are uncertain. Catenae like this one preserve fragments of patristic commentaries that are otherwise lost.

The Catena on the Epistle to Titus is an anonymous Greek catena: a running commentary on Paul's letter to Titus built from excerpts of earlier patristic exegetes, arranged verse by verse. Its compiler and date are unknown, although Byzantine catenae of this kind were generally put together between about the sixth and tenth centuries. The opening comes from John Chrysostom's homilies on Titus. It discusses Titus's standing among Paul's companions, his charge over Crete, and why the letter is so short. Catenae like this one matter because they preserve fragments of commentaries that are otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena, or chain of commentary, on Paul's Epistle to Philemon gathers excerpts from earlier Church Fathers and arranges them verse by verse. It opens with a prologue that draws heavily on John Chrysostom's homilies on Philemon. The prologue tells how Onesimus, a runaway slave who had stolen from his master, was baptized by Paul in prison in Rome. It also defends the short letter's place in Scripture, arguing that it teaches care for slaves and for small matters. The compiler and the date of compilation are unknown.

This anonymous Greek catena on Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews is a chain of commentary in which brief excerpts from earlier Church Fathers are set beside the biblical text, passage by passage. Its prologue asks why Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, wrote to Jewish believers, probably in Jerusalem and Palestine, and how this fits his imprisonment in Rome. Such compilations were made in Byzantine times. Their compiler and date are uncertain. They matter because they keep fragments of patristic exegesis that would otherwise be lost.

This is an anonymous Greek catena, a chain of excerpts from earlier Church Fathers, on the Epistle of James. It belongs to a larger Byzantine commentary on the Catholic Epistles, and its date and compiler are uncertain. A prefatory summary sets out the epistle's themes: kinds of temptation, faith shown in works, the treatment of rich and poor, Job's patience, and anointing the sick. The comments cite Eusebius on doubts about the letter's authenticity and draw on Didymus the Blind and unnamed interpreters. Much patristic exegesis survives only through compilations like this one.

This anonymous Greek catena on the First Epistle of Peter is a running commentary built from excerpts of earlier Church Fathers, arranged verse by verse beside the biblical text. It opens with a summary of the letter's argument. The summary presents Peter writing to Jewish believers of the dispersion, and it touches on Christ's preaching in Hades and on readiness for judgement. The material is then grouped under chapter headings. Its compiler and date are unknown. Like other New Testament catenae, it matters chiefly for preserving fragments of patristic exegesis that are otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena is a Byzantine commentary on the Second Epistle of Peter. Its date and compiler are unknown. Like other catenae, it arranges the biblical text with excerpts from earlier Greek Church Fathers. It begins with a hypothesis, or prefatory summary, which presents the letter as Peter's reminder of earlier teaching before his approaching death. The summary notes the letter's warnings against false teachers and scoffers who deny the Lord's coming. It also notes the letter's teaching that a thousand years are as one day before God.

This anonymous Greek catena on the First Epistle of John strings together brief excerpts from earlier Greek Church Fathers, arranged verse by verse as a running commentary. It opens with a hypothesis, or summary, of the letter. The summary presents John as the author of both the Gospel and the epistle. It names the letter's main themes: the eternal Word, God as light, mutual love, the children of God and of the devil, the discernment of spirits, and sin that leads to death. Like other Byzantine catenae, it is anonymous and hard to date, and it preserves fragments of commentaries that are otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena, or "chain" commentary, covers the Second Epistle of John. It sets brief excerpts from earlier Greek interpreters alongside the biblical text. It opens with a summary of the letter's occasion. The Elder writes to the "elect lady" and her children, praises their faithful conduct and urges love. He warns against deceivers who deny that Christ came in the flesh and forbids receiving them. The comments ask whether the "lady" was a church or an actual woman. Such compilations preserve fragments of patristic exegesis that are otherwise lost.

This anonymous Greek catena on the Third Epistle of John is a chain of exegetical comments drawn from earlier Church Fathers and arranged alongside the biblical text. It is part of the Byzantine catena tradition on the Catholic Epistles, and its date and compiler are uncertain. It opens with a summary (hypothesis) presenting the letter as a teaching on hospitality. The comments praise Gaius for welcoming travelling brethren, condemn Diotrephes for hindering such charity, and commend Demetrius. The text is divided into chapters with headings and explains why the letter is so brief.

This is an anonymous Greek catena, or chain of commentary, on the Epistle of Jude. It follows the biblical text section by section and sets excerpts from earlier Greek patristic interpreters beside it. An introductory summary (hypothesis) says Jude wrote to believers to warn them against intruders who taught that sin was a matter of indifference and who denied the Lord. The comments that follow deal with Christology, the fallen angels and the judgement of the ungodly. The compiler and date are unknown. Byzantine catenae like this one preserve exegetical material that would otherwise be lost.

This is an anonymous Greek preface to a Byzantine compilation of explanations of the Book of Revelation, gathered from earlier Church writers. In the manuscript tradition it is ascribed to Oecumenius, bishop of Trikka in Thessaly, and to Arethas of Caesarea, but it is not by Oecumenius, so it is known as Pseudo-Oecumenian. The preface defends the Apocalypse as inspired and as the genuine work of John the Evangelist. It cites Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, Methodius of Olympus, Cyril of Alexandria and Hippolytus in support, and presents John as a prophet as well as an apostle. Its exact date is uncertain.

This is a Greek commentary on the Book of Revelation attributed to Arethas, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the early tenth century and a leading Byzantine scholar. It relies heavily on the earlier commentary of Andrew of Caesarea, which it abridges, supplements and sometimes corrects. It works through the Apocalypse in numbered sections, beginning with the prologue, the letters to the seven churches and the opening of the seals. Its interpretation is mainly spiritual and ecclesial. The work is a witness to how Revelation was received in the Byzantine Church.

This Greek commentary on the Book of Revelation is by Andrew, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and dates from the late sixth or early seventh century. It explains the Apocalypse verse by verse, mainly through spiritual and moral readings, and often draws on and corrects the earlier commentary of Oecumenius. Andrew divided it into twenty-four discourses and seventy-two chapters. It became the standard Greek interpretation of Revelation and helped the book gain acceptance in the Eastern Church. It also shaped how the Greek text of Revelation was handed down.

The History of the Franks is a Latin history in ten books, properly titled Decem Libri Historiarum. Gregory, bishop of Tours (c. 538–594), wrote it between about 573 and 594. It starts with the Creation and a short account of world and church history, then covers Gaul. Most of it describes the Merovingian kingdoms of the sixth century, many of whose events Gregory saw himself. It is often the only source for the period. Its lively and sometimes partisan stories have earned Gregory the title "father of French history."

The Etymologies (Etymologiae, or Origines) is a Latin encyclopedia compiled by Isidore, bishop of Seville, in Visigothic Spain during the early seventh century. It was still unfinished at his death in 636, and his friend Braulio of Zaragoza arranged it into twenty books. It covers the liberal arts, medicine, law, chronology, Scripture and the Church, languages and peoples, animals, geography, building, warfare and everyday objects. It explains things mainly through the supposed origins of their names. Drawing on many classical and Christian authors, it became one of the most widely copied reference works of the Middle Ages.

This Greek hagiography is attributed to Mark the Deacon, who presents himself as companion and deacon of Porphyry, bishop of Gaza from 395 to 420. It tells of Porphyry's ascetic life, his ordination, and his campaign to Christianize pagan Gaza. With imperial support, this ended in the destruction of the Marneion temple in 402. It is a vivid and detailed account of a city's Christianization, but its historical reliability is debated. Versions also survive in Latin and Georgian, and the Georgian may derive from a lost Syriac original.

The Missale Gallicanum Vetus is an anonymous Latin sacramentary from Merovingian Gaul, usually dated to the eighth century. It survives only in fragments. It holds prayers for parts of the church year, including Advent, Lent and the Easter Vigil, together with baptismal rites. It is one of the few surviving witnesses to the Gallican liturgy before Carolingian reforms replaced it with Roman usage. It is also one of the earliest sources for the Easter proclamation known as the Exsultet.

The Missale Gallicanum Vetus ("Old Gallican Missal") is an anonymous Latin liturgical book from eighth-century Francia. Despite its name, it is a sacramentary: it gives only the celebrant's prayers. It survives incompletely and gathers material from several sources. It opens with a Mass for Germanus of Auxerre, and its other formularies cover feasts and seasons of the church year. It is one of the few surviving witnesses to the Gallican rite used in Gaul before Carolingian reforms brought in Roman liturgical books, so it is important for studying early Western liturgy.

The Missale Gothicum is an anonymous Latin sacramentary of the Gallican Rite, compiled around the late seventh or early eighth century and usually linked with Burgundy, probably Autun. It was once called "Gothic" because scholars thought it came from Visigothic territory. The book is incomplete at its start. It gives the variable prayers of the Mass for the liturgical year, beginning with the Eve of the Nativity, and some of its collects are borrowed from Roman sources. It is one of the main surviving witnesses to the Gallican liturgy before Carolingian Romanization.

The Mone Masses are a group of anonymous Latin mass formularies of the Gallican rite. They survive in a palimpsest manuscript from the abbey of Reichenau, which is why they are also called the Missale Richenovense. They are named after Franz Joseph Mone, who discovered and published them in 1850. The manuscript is usually dated to the seventh century, but when the prayers themselves were written is uncertain. They include Sunday masses and a mass for Saint Germanus of Auxerre. They are among the earliest surviving witnesses to the liturgy of Merovingian Gaul.

The Bobbio Missal is an anonymous Latin liturgical book of the Gallican tradition, usually dated to the late seventh or early eighth century. Jean Mabillon found its only manuscript at the monastery of Bobbio in northern Italy. It combines elements of a sacramentary, a lectionary and a ritual, setting Gallican prayers beside a form of the Roman canon. It also mentions Sigismund of Burgundy, which led some nineteenth-century scholars to name it after Besançon. Its origin is still disputed. It is an important witness to early medieval liturgy before the Carolingian reforms.

The Anaphora of the Apostles is an anonymous Eucharistic prayer and the ordinary anaphora of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, preserved in Ge'ez. It is closely based on the Eucharistic prayer of the Apostolic Tradition, traditionally attributed to Hippolytus, which reached Ethiopia through the collection known as the Church Ordinances. Its date is uncertain. It includes an invocation of the Holy Spirit on the offering, and scholars compare it with other Ethiopic anaphoras, such as the Anaphora of Our Lord, to trace how early liturgical prayer developed.

The Anaphora of Saint Athanasius is a eucharistic prayer in Ge'ez, one of the anaphoras used in the liturgy of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. It is attributed to Athanasius, the fourth-century patriarch of Alexandria, but the attribution is traditional, and its real author and date are unknown. It is appointed for the Christian Sabbath. The text opens with exhortations from the deacon and priest that call the clergy and people to reconciliation and to exclude grave sinners. It also shows the Ethiopian Church's special regard for the Sabbath.

The Anaphora of Saint John Chrysostom is a eucharistic prayer of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, preserved in Ge'ez and counted among the anaphoras of the Ethiopic liturgy. It bears the name of John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople (d. 407), but it is a different text from the Byzantine anaphora that carries his name, and the attribution is traditional. When and by whom it was written is unknown. It opens with a long hymn on God's eternal essence, with the refrain "was He in His essence" repeated before each act of creation.

The Anaphora of Saint Cyril is a eucharistic prayer, or "Thanksgiving", from the Ethiopian liturgical tradition. It survives in Ge'ez and is attributed to Cyril of Alexandria, but its real author is unknown and its date is uncertain. It should not be confused with the Coptic Anaphora of Saint Cyril, which is related to the Liturgy of Saint Mark. The prayer opens with praise of God's hidden, incomprehensible essence. It then describes the seraphim, cherubim and ranks of "watchers" singing the Sanctus, using imagery with roots in Isaiah and Enochic tradition.

The Anaphora of Saint Dioscorus is a eucharistic prayer of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. It is one of the anaphoras of the Ge'ez liturgy and was composed in Ge'ez. Tradition attributes it to Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria (444–451), who is honoured by the non-Chalcedonian churches. The real author is unknown and the date of composition is uncertain; it is probably much later than Dioscorus. It opens with a hymnic litany that praises God reigning in his kingdom before creation. Prayers on the Trinity and the Incarnation follow, set out as alternating parts for priest and deacon.

The Anaphora of Saint Epiphanius is a eucharistic prayer in Ge'ez. It is one of the fourteen anaphoras of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo liturgy. Tradition credits it to Epiphanius, the fourth-century bishop of Salamis, but the author is unknown. It was most likely composed later within the Ethiopian tradition, and its date is uncertain. The prayer opens with a long list of praises of God's greatness and incomprehensibility. It then moves to the sending of the Son as Saviour, with the deacon's responses set between the priest's prayers. It shows the rhetorical style typical of Ethiopian anaphoras.

The Anaphora of St. Gregory of Alexandria is an anonymous eucharistic prayer, or anaphora, used in the Ethiopian liturgical tradition, where it belongs to the Church's large collection of alternative anaphoras. Its attribution to a "Gregory of Alexandria" is traditional and does not match any securely identified author, and when it was written is uncertain. The text sets the deacon's calls against the priest's prayers of thanksgiving. It praises God's mercy and creation, then the incarnation of Christ, who came down without setting aside the glory of his Godhead and gave life through his death.

The Anaphora of Saint Gregory of Armenia is a eucharistic prayer from the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, preserved in Ge'ez and one of the anaphoras of the Ethiopian liturgy. Tradition attributes it to Gregory the Illuminator, the fourth-century apostle of Armenia, but this attribution is not considered historical. The actual date and place of composition are uncertain. The prayer begins with a long hymn of praise to God, who is exalted above angels, watchers and seraphim, and leads into the Sanctus. The text includes directions for the priest and the deacon.

The Anaphora of James (Jacob) of Serugh is a eucharistic prayer used in the Ge'ez liturgy of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. It is one of the church's many anaphoras and bears the name of Jacob of Serugh, the Syriac poet and bishop who died in 521. The attribution is traditional, and the prayer's actual date and origin are uncertain. Its exchanges between deacon and priest begin with intercessions for the departed and for the presiding patriarch and bishop. They then praise the authority and majesty of the Son, whom the angels worship.

The Anaphora of Saint John the Evangelist, also titled the Eucharistic Thanksgiving of Saint John the Son of Thunder, is one of the anaphoras, or eucharistic prayers, of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. It is preserved in Ge'ez and attributed to the apostle John, but its real author is unknown. When it was composed is also uncertain, and scholars disagree about how old the Ethiopian anaphoras are.
