The Chronicle of Zuqnin is an anonymous Syriac world chronicle finished around 775 by a monk of the Zuqnin monastery near Amida, on the upper Tigris. It was once wrongly attributed to Dionysius of Tel Mahre, and its author is sometimes identified as Joshua the Stylite. In four parts, it runs from the creation to the year 1087 of the Seleucid era (775/76). It draws on the Bible, John of Ephesus and other sources, and it preserves otherwise lost texts such as the Revelation of the Magi. Its eyewitness account of life under early Abbasid rule is especially valuable.

This anonymous apocryphal narrative tells of the death, or "departure", of the apostle John at Ephesus. It is a Syriac version of the account known in Greek as the Metastasis, which closes the apocryphal Acts of John. On a Sunday, John urges the assembled brethren to stay faithful and celebrates the Eucharist. He then has a grave dug, prays, and lies down in it to die in peace. Its date of composition is uncertain, perhaps the fourth or fifth century. It shaped later traditions about John's end.

The Disputation between the Apostle Peter and Nero is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal text. Its date is uncertain, but it was probably composed between the fifth and seventh centuries. It opens with an allegorical prologue: the world is a stormy sea, the twelve apostles are ships carrying great wealth, the devil is the king of the sea who stirs up the waves, and the kingdom is the harbour where they find rest. It then presents the Emperor Nero as the devil's willing servant in opposing Peter's preaching.

The Prose Refutations are a group of polemical discourses in Syriac by Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), the deacon and theologian of Nisibis and Edessa. They are aimed at the three main rival teachings of his region: Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan. The first discourse is a letter to a certain Hypatius. In it Ephrem argues against dualist ideas about light and darkness, matter and the body, and defends free will and the goodness of creation. The work is a rare example of Ephrem's prose. It is also an important witness to early Manichaean, Marcionite and Bardaisanite thought.

The Exhortation of the Apostle Peter is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal discourse on admonition, attributed to the apostle Peter. Its date is uncertain; it is generally placed between the fourth and sixth centuries. Speaking to a crowd that has gathered for instruction, Peter warns his hearers not to become attached to worldly things but to be ready for death. He illustrates the point with a parable about two servants banished by their master: one puts down roots in exile, while the other turns his earnings into a gold crown engraved with images of his master and his master's son.

The History of John, the Son of Zebedee is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal narrative about the apostle John, probably composed in the fifth century. It tells how, after Pentecost, the apostles dispersed to preach and John went to Ephesus, where he preached, worked wonders, baptised and turned the city from pagan worship to Christianity. Its heading claims Eusebius of Caesarea as author and says it was translated from a Greek book, but this attribution is not credited. The work is a witness to Syriac traditions about John and his Ephesian ministry.

The History of Karka d-Beth Slokh is an anonymous Syriac local history and martyr narrative from the Church of the East, probably written in the late sixth or early seventh century. It covers Karka d-Beth Slokh, usually identified with modern Kirkuk. The story begins with a legendary founding by an Assyrian king named Sardana, linked to Jonah's preaching at Nineveh, and follows the city's later rulers. It then tells of the city's Christian martyrs under Sasanian Persian rule. The work matters as a source for northern Mesopotamian Christianity and for how a Christian community remembered its local past.

The History of Philip, the Apostle and Evangelist is an anonymous Syriac apocryphal narrative, probably composed between the fifth and seventh centuries; its exact date is uncertain. It tells how Christ appears to Philip in a night vision at Jerusalem and sends him to preach in "Carthage, which is in Azotus." There he drives out Satan's power and converts the city through wonders and preaching. The work blends Philip the Apostle with Philip the Evangelist of Acts, and it reflects the Syriac tradition of legendary apostolic acts.

The History of Mar Qardagh is an anonymous Syriac martyr legend of the Church of the East, probably composed in the early seventh century in northern Mesopotamia, near Arbela. Set in the reign of the Sasanian king Shapur II, it tells of Qardagh, a Persian noble and governor descended from Nimrod. The hermit ʿAbdishoʿ converts him to Christianity, and he is then martyred by stoning. Drawing on Persian epic ideals of the warrior and hunter, it is an important source for Christian identity and culture in the late Sasanian Empire.

The Hymn of the Soul, also called the Hymn of the Pearl or Hymn of the Robe of Glory, is an anonymous Syriac poem preserved within the apocryphal Acts of Thomas. In the Acts, the apostle Judas Thomas sings it while imprisoned in India. A royal prince is sent from the East to Egypt to bring back a pearl guarded by a serpent. He forgets his mission, is woken by a letter from his parents, and returns to receive his glittering robe. The poem is widely read as an allegory of the soul's descent and redemption. It may be older than the Acts, and its date and authorship are disputed. Some scholars have linked it to Bardaisan of Edessa.

On the End Times is a Syriac metrical homily (memra) attributed to Isaac of Antioch, a fifth-century Syriac poet whose death the Chronicle of Edessa places around 451–452. Writing is ascribed to several authors named Isaac, so which one wrote it is uncertain. In the poem, a personified Truth wakes the speaker and orders him to announce that the last times have come. It points to Scripture, the prophets, the apostles and the decay of nature as signs of the end. It urges readers to repent and seek refuge in God against Satan and an evil earthly ruler.

The First Part of Isaac of Nineveh's writings is a collection of Syriac discourses on monastic life, asceticism and prayer. It was composed in the late seventh century by the Church of the East bishop also known as Isaac the Syrian or Isaac of Qatar. It opens by calling the fear of God the beginning of virtue, and it teaches withdrawal from worldly affairs, meditation on Scripture, patient endurance, humility and stillness. It was translated into Greek early on and later into many other languages, and it became one of the most widely read ascetic works in Eastern Christianity.

The Letters are a collection of more than one hundred Syriac letters by Ishoʿyahb III of Adiabene, Patriarch of the Church of the East from 649 to 659. They are traditionally arranged by the stages of his career: as bishop of Nineveh, as metropolitan of Adiabene, and as catholicos. Written to clergy, monks and laypeople, they deal with church discipline, doctrinal disputes and pastoral affairs. They include letters to the Christians of Beth Qatraye. The collection is an important witness to Christian life in the earliest decades of Islamic rule.

The Memre are the verse homilies of Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the Syriac poet-theologian who became bishop of Batnan in 519. Most are written in the twelve-syllable metre associated with him. They cover biblical narratives, feasts, saints and moral exhortation, as in the opening homily on admonition, which presents praise of God as humanity's duty to its Creator. Jacob is said to have composed 763 works. Around 400 survive, and they were copied widely across the Syriac churches.

This saint's life of Peter the Iberian (c. 417–491) was written by his disciple John Rufus, an anti-Chalcedonian priest who may have become bishop of Maiuma. It was composed in Greek around the end of the fifth century and survives only in a Syriac translation. It follows Peter's life as a Georgian royal prince, a hostage at the court in Constantinople, a monk and monastery founder in Palestine, and bishop of Maiuma near Gaza. It is an important source for Palestinian monasticism and for early opposition to the Council of Chalcedon.

The Plerophoriae ("Assurances") is an anti-Chalcedonian collection of anecdotes by John Rufus, a priest of Antioch, disciple of Peter the Iberian and bishop of Maiuma near Gaza. It was written in the early sixth century, probably in Greek, and survives in a Syriac version. It gathers visions, revelations and miraculous testimonies, many of them told by Peter the Iberian, that present the Council of Chalcedon (451) and the doctrine of two natures in Christ as condemned by God. It is a key witness to early miaphysite piety and to Palestinian monastic opposition to Chalcedon.

The Dialogue on the Soul is a Syriac treatise attributed to John the Solitary, often identified with John of Apamea, a fifth-century ascetic writer. It is framed as a conversation in which two disciples, Eutropius and Eusebius, visit John in his cell and question him. Among the topics are why the soul was placed in the human body, and how the passions of body, soul and spirit differ. The work sets out John's threefold scheme of the spiritual life and shows the influence of Evagrius Ponticus. It is an important early witness to Syriac ascetic and mystical thought.

On Prayer is a short Syriac treatise on spiritual contemplation (theoria) in prayer, associated with Joseph Hazzaya, an 8th-century monk and mystic of the Church of the East. The manuscript heading attributes it to "Mar Abdisho". Several of Joseph's writings circulated under the name Abdisho, which was also the name of his brother, so the authorship is uncertain. The work describes how monks who have purified their hearts of the passions are drawn in prayer beyond the senses. It speaks of a "fiery movement" of the indwelling Holy Spirit, received at baptism, which transforms the soul into its own likeness.

The Julian Romance is an anonymous Syriac prose narrative giving a fictionalized, Christian account of the reign of the emperor Julian the Apostate. It was written sometime between Julian's death in 363 and the sixth century, probably at Edessa. It has three parts: Julian's accession and persecution of Christians, his conflict with Eusebius of Rome, and, in the form of a letter, his Persian campaign, death and the accession of the Christian Jovian. It is one of the major narrative works of Syriac literature, and an Arabic adaptation existed by the tenth century.

The Book of Steps (Syriac Ktaba d-Masqata, Latin Liber Graduum) is an anonymous Syriac treatise of thirty discourses (memre). It was probably written in the late fourth or early fifth century by an author living in the Sasanian Empire, who addressed it to his own Christian community. It separates the "upright", who keep the lesser commandments, from the "perfect", who follow the greater commandments of renunciation and celibacy. It also describes the visible church as working alongside a heavenly church. It is an important witness to early Syriac asceticism and spirituality.

The Life of Jacob of Serugh is an anonymous Syriac hagiography of Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the Miaphysite poet, homilist and late in life bishop of Batnan. Its date is uncertain but is usually placed between the mid-sixth and seventh centuries. It opens by calling itself "another account" of the saint. It tells of his birth to a barren mother after prayer at a shrine, and of a childhood miracle in which he received divine inspiration at the Eucharist. It then follows his upbringing in Hawra, his hymn-writing as a visiting priest and his time as bishop.

The Life of Rabbula is an anonymous Syriac hagiography of Rabbula, bishop of Edessa from about 411 to 435/6. It was written by an unnamed member of the Edessene church, probably within a few decades of his death. It praises him as an ascetic champion of the faith. The work follows his conversion and ascetic life, then his time as bishop: his care for the poor, his strict discipline of clergy and monks, and his struggles against heretics and civil rulers. It is an important witness to Christianity in Edessa in the early fifth century.

This is a short anonymous Syriac martyr act, one of the Acts of the Persian Martyrs, which record Christians who died in the persecution under the Sasanian king Shapur II. It tells how Jacob, priest of the village of Tel Shlila, and his sister Mary, a "daughter of the covenant" (a consecrated woman), were arrested in the seventh year of the persecution. On the orders of Narses Tamshapur they were flogged for refusing to eat blood. A Christian layman named Mahdad then beheaded them at Tel Dara on the Great Zab, on 17 Adar.

An anonymous Syriac hagiography, one of the Persian martyr acts, about Miles, bishop of Susa, and his companions Aborsam the priest and Sinai the deacon. They were executed by the Sasanian authorities in 340 or 341, at the start of the persecution under Shapur II. The account opens with a rhetorical prologue in praise of the martyrs. Its date is uncertain. Sozomen summarized a Syriac account of Miles in the fifth century, but the fuller surviving Acts have been dated as late as the end of the sixth century.

The Memre on Joseph are a cycle of verse homilies (mēmrē) in Syriac by Jacob of Serugh (c. 451–521), the poet-theologian and late bishop of Batnan. They are written in the twelve-syllable metre linked with Jacob, and they retell the story of the patriarch Joseph from Genesis in a series of discourses. The first opens with a prayer to Christ as the source of all beauty. Jacob presents Joseph's beauty and virtue as a reflection of Christ, which fits the Syriac tradition of reading Old Testament figures as types of Christ.

On the Soul is a Syriac theological treatise by Moses bar Kepha (died 903), a Syriac Orthodox bishop and one of the most celebrated writers of his church in the ninth century. It begins by setting out the many senses of the word "soul" in Scripture and in ordinary usage. It can mean the divine nature, the whole human person, the body, the blood, or the life-giving power in plants. It then discusses the nature of the human soul. The work draws on earlier Greek patristic and philosophical thought, and it is a valuable witness to Syriac Christian anthropology.

The Memre are the verse homilies of Narsai (c. 399 – c. 502), a leading poet-theologian of the Church of the East who taught at the School of Edessa and later headed the School of Nisibis. About eighty-one survive. They are metrical sermons on biblical themes, feasts and doctrine. Many were linked to the liturgical year, for example a discourse on the revelations to Abraham for the first Sunday of the Annunciation. They reflect the exegetical tradition of Theodore of Mopsuestia and rank among the major works of classical Syriac preaching, alongside those of Jacob of Serugh.

The Bazaar (or Book) of Heracleides is a theological and autobiographical apology attributed to Nestorius, the archbishop of Constantinople deposed at the Council of Ephesus in 431. He wrote it in exile late in his life, around 451–452. The Greek original is lost, and the work survives only in a Syriac translation preserved by the Church of the East and rediscovered in the nineteenth century. In it Nestorius defends his Christology against Cyril of Alexandria and recounts the events of his condemnation. The work has prompted scholars to reassess his actual teaching.

The Odes of Solomon are a collection of 42 early Christian hymns. Their author is unknown, and the attribution to King Solomon is traditional, not historical. Most scholars date them to the late first or early second century, though some place them later. Whether they were first written in Greek or Syriac is also debated. The poems are lyrical and mystical. They celebrate union with the Lord through love, the gift of the Spirit, salvation and immortality, and each ends with "Hallelujah." They are among the oldest surviving Christian hymnbooks, and they share notable affinities with the Gospel of John.

This anonymous Syriac collection of letters is attributed to correspondence with Papa bar Aggai, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in the early fourth century, who is traditionally regarded as the first catholicos of the Church of the East. Writers such as Eusebius, called "patriarch of the Romans", and Judas Cyriacus of Jerusalem praise Papa and send gifts from Constantine and his mother. The letters are spurious and were probably composed between the sixth and eighth centuries. They likely served to support the dignity and apostolic standing of the see of Seleucia-Ctesiphon.

The Ascetic Discourses are a collection of thirteen Syriac discourses on the Christian and monastic life by Philoxenus of Mabbug (died 523), the Miaphysite bishop of Hierapolis. They were written in the late fifth or early sixth century, though the exact date is uncertain. The work sets out a gradual path of discipleship that starts from faith and simplicity and moves through the fear of God and renunciation of the world. It then turns to the struggle against gluttony and fornication, with spiritual love and perfection as the goal. It is among the most important works of early Syriac spirituality.

The Admonitions to Monks is a short set of disciplinary rules in Syriac attributed to Rabbula, bishop of Edessa (Urhay) from about 411 to 435/6. It governs life in the monasteries of his diocese. Its numbered precepts ban women from entering monasteries and limit monks' contact with villages and lay households to an appointed "Visitor". They also forbid drinking wine and restrict ascetic practices such as wearing long hair, iron chains or hair garments outside the monastery. The text is important evidence for early Syrian monasticism and for Rabbula's efforts to bring it under church discipline.

This polemical Syriac letter by Simeon of Beth Arsham, the early sixth-century Miaphysite bishop known as the "Persian Debater", sets out a hostile history of the Nestorian heresy and how it reached Persia. Simeon traces the belief that Christ was a mere man to Annas, Caiaphas and the Jews who rejected him, and then to Simon Magus. The chain continues through later teachers to Barsauma of Nisibis, the late fifth-century bishop who promoted Dyophysite doctrine in the Church of the East. The letter is an important witness to the Miaphysite–Nestorian conflict in the Persian Empire.

This is a Syriac prefatory letter by Simeon, abbot of the monastery of Mary, Mother of God, in Beth Liqnis. It is addressed to the priest Barlaha (Barlahe), a recluse living in the enclosure of Mar Elisha of Markabta. Simeon replies to Barlaha's repeated requests, carried by the deacon Damian, that he translate a book from Greek into Syriac. He professes himself unfit for the task but credits Barlaha's prayers with giving him the strength to attempt it. The letter's exact date and the identity of the translated work are uncertain.

The Testament of Adam is an anonymous Christian pseudepigraphon, preserved mainly in Syriac, in which Adam speaks to his son Seth. Its date is uncertain, but it is usually placed between the third and fifth centuries. It has three parts. The first is a horarium listing the worship offered by each creature at each hour of the night and day. The second is a prophecy of the Flood and of Christ's incarnation. The third describes the hierarchy of the angels. Versions also exist in Arabic, Ethiopic, Armenian and Georgian.

This Syriac treatise explains the feast of Christ's birth in the flesh. It was written by Thomas of Edessa (died c. 540), a theologian of the Church of the East, at the request of Mar Moses. Its chapters ask why the feast is celebrated and what benefits came through Christ. They also explain why God was revealed through a human being born of a virgin, and why the conception took place in Nisan. Reflecting the theology of Theodore of Mopsuestia, it is among the oldest surviving examples of the ʿelltā, or "cause", genre of feast explanations.

Against the Manichaeans is a polemical treatise in four books by Titus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia (died c. 378), written in Greek probably in the 360s or 370s. The Greek original survives only in part. The complete work is preserved in an early Syriac translation, attested in a manuscript of 411. Titus rejects Mani's doctrine of an eternal evil principle opposed to God. He defends divine providence and human free will as the source of sin, arguing first from reason and then from Scripture. It is a major early Christian source on Manichaean teaching.

The Travels of Peter is an anonymous Christian apocryphal narrative that survives in Syriac. Its date is uncertain, though it is generally placed somewhere between the fifth and eighth centuries. It tells of the apostle Simon Peter preaching baptism and the true faith from city to city. In its opening episode Peter meets a demon waiting to kill a newborn child, raises the dead infant to life and questions the demon about its attacks on children. That episode connects the text with traditions of protecting mothers and infants from demons. It is distinct from the Greek Pseudo-Clementine "Circuits of Peter."

The General Elementary Introduction is a Greek work in ten books by Eusebius of Caesarea. Its date is disputed: it may come from before the Great Persecution of 303 or from somewhat later. Only books six to nine survive, known as the Prophetic Extracts (Eclogae propheticae). They gather Old Testament prophecies about Christ, arranged by scriptural book and given brief commentary. They follow earlier books that argued for the faith without relying on Scripture. The work is an early source for Eusebius's exegesis and apologetic method.

The Ancoratus ("The Well-Anchored") is a Greek doctrinal treatise by Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia (Salamis) in Cyprus. He wrote it around 374 at the request of presbyters in Syedra in Pamphylia, whose letters stand at its beginning. It explains Christian teaching from Scripture and tradition: the consubstantiality of the Trinity, the full incarnation of Christ, and the resurrection and judgment. It argues against pagans, Jews and heretics, and lists the eighty heresies that Epiphanius later treated in the Panarion. It ends with two creeds, one of which closely resembles the creed associated with the Council of Constantinople of 381.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Gospel of John, preserved in the catenae: medieval chains of excerpts from earlier commentators arranged verse by verse. They are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253), whose large Commentary on John survives only in part. Catena attributions are often unreliable, so some passages may come from other writers or may have been reworded by later compilers. The fragments deal with themes such as the eternal Word, creation and the incarnation. They add to what is known of Origen's lost exegesis.

This is a collection of short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Jeremiah, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts in the Byzantine catenae on the prophets, the chains of patristic comment arranged verse by verse. Some may come from Origen's lost homilies or notes on Jeremiah, though catena attributions are not always reliable. The fragments show his usual allegorical and moral reading, applying the prophet's images to sin, temptation and the soul's struggle, and they add to the Greek homilies on Jeremiah that survive in full.

These Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Lamentations are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive in the Byzantine catenae, or chains of commentary, on the prophets. They probably come from the commentary on Lamentations that Eusebius says Origen wrote at Alexandria and which is otherwise lost. The fragments discuss the alphabetic acrostic structure of Jeremiah's laments. They also read the Babylonian captivity allegorically, as the soul's captivity to hostile spiritual powers, from which Christ sets it free.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the whole Psalter, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Most survive only as excerpts in later catenae, the Byzantine anthologies of biblical commentary. Origen wrote extensively on the Psalms, but compilers of catenae often confused or merged authors. Some material under his name is probably by others, such as Evagrius Ponticus, so the authenticity of individual fragments is doubtful. The comments read the Psalms morally and spiritually. Their opening reflection on Psalm 1 presents turning away from evil as the first step of the soul's progress toward God.

The Selecta in Psalmos are a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Psalms attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, and their authenticity is doubtful in part because some passages may come from other writers, such as Evagrius Ponticus. The opening gathers philosophical definitions of "end" from Aristotle and Stoic sources to explain psalm titles. Even so, the fragments remain an important witness to Origen's lost commentaries and homilies on the Psalter.

These are exegetical fragments on the Book of Job attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They are traditionally linked to his lost homilies on Job, which Jerome lists as twenty-two in number. The fragments survive only as excerpts in Byzantine catenae, anthologies of patristic comment arranged verse by verse, so how far each one is authentic is uncertain. Short notes on individual verses dwell on the devil's assault on Job and the protection God gives the righteous. They help show how Job was read in early Greek Christian exegesis.

The Excerpta in Psalmos is a collection of short Greek exegetical notes on individual verses of the Psalms, handed down under the name of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253). Its authenticity is doubtful. Like much of Origen's lost Psalm commentary, the material survives as excerpts in later compilations, and parts may come from other authors. The notes read the text allegorically and morally: "the world" is the Church, Zion is the watchful soul, and God's judgment calls believers to avoid ungodly deeds and thoughts.

This is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Proverbs, preserved in the catenae (chains of excerpts from biblical commentators) under the name of Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Origen's full commentary on Proverbs is lost. The fragments explain the sayings of Solomon allegorically and morally, treating wisdom as spiritual knowledge and instruction as the governing of the passions. Their authenticity is uncertain, because modern scholars have shown that many scholia once ascribed to Origen belong to Evagrius Ponticus.

The Historia Religiosa, also called the Philotheos Historia ("History of the Lovers of God"), is a Greek hagiographical collection written by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, around 440. It gives thirty accounts of ascetics of Syria and Mesopotamia, beginning with Jacob of Nisibis. Among them is Symeon the Stylite, who was still living when Theodoret wrote. Theodoret knew many of these monks personally, and he tells of their hardships, miracles and teaching. A short treatise on divine love closes the work. It is a key source for early Syrian monasticism.

This is a Greek commentary on the Book of Revelation attributed to Arethas, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the early tenth century and a leading Byzantine scholar. It relies heavily on the earlier commentary of Andrew of Caesarea, which it abridges, supplements and sometimes corrects. It works through the Apocalypse in numbered sections, beginning with the prologue, the letters to the seven churches and the opening of the seals. Its interpretation is mainly spiritual and ecclesial. The work is a witness to how Revelation was received in the Byzantine Church.

The Lefafa Sedq ("Bandlet of Righteousness") is an anonymous Ethiopian funerary text in Ge'ez. It is a sequence of prayers that contain secret names of God and of Christ. According to tradition, Christ revealed it to the Virgin Mary to secure the salvation of believers. The text was copied onto a strip of parchment, often about the height of the dead person, and buried with the body. It was meant to protect the soul on its passage after death and gain it entry into heaven. Its date and origin are uncertain, and some scholars suggest Egyptian or Coptic influence.

Mysteries of Heaven and Earth is an anonymous apocryphal work that survives in Ge'ez, the classical language of Ethiopia. Its date and origin are uncertain. It is presented as mysteries that the apostle Peter revealed to his disciple Clement, which places it among the writings that circulated under Clement's name. The text gives an account of creation and a summary of biblical history down to the reign of King Jehoram. It also includes discourses on God's mercy toward humankind and on the role of Christ as Saviour.

The Sinodos is an anonymous Ethiopian collection of church order and canon law, counted among the books of the broader Ethiopian Orthodox biblical canon. It brings together earlier Christian material dating roughly from the third to the seventh centuries, including the Apostolic Tradition, the Apostolic Canons, and canons of councils such as Nicaea, Ancyra, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea and Chalcedon. It also includes letters of Constantine, Athanasius and Cyril of Alexandria, along with liturgical and baptismal texts. The Ge'ez text was translated from Arabic, and it remains an important source for church discipline and early liturgy.

The Ethiopian Synaxarion (Senkessar) is a liturgical collection of short commemorative notices of saints, martyrs, angels, prophets and church events. The notices are arranged day by day through the Ethiopian year, beginning with the month of Maskaram. It derives from the Arabic Synaxarion of the Coptic Church. Its preface attributes that work to Michael, bishop of Athribis and Malig, John, bishop of Burullus, and others, and dates it to the year 963 of the Martyrs (1246–47). It was probably translated into Ge'ez around 1400, later expanded with Ethiopian saints, and survives in more than one recension.

The Hudra ("Cycle") is the main choir book of the East Syriac liturgical tradition used by the Church of the East. It contains the proper hymns, anthems and prayers of the Divine Office for the Sundays, feasts and fasts of the liturgical year. Its core is traditionally linked to the reform of the Patriarch Ishoyahb III in the seventh century, following the use of the Upper Monastery at Mosul. Later poets added material to it over many centuries. This first volume opens with the ordinary weekday office, the Book of Before and After, and its rules for the alternating choirs.

Contra Marcellum (Against Marcellus) is a polemical treatise in two books by Eusebius of Caesarea. It was written around 336–337, after Marcellus of Ancyra was deposed by a synod at Constantinople. Eusebius accuses Marcellus of attacking respected churchmen out of envy, among them Asterius the Sophist and Eusebius of Nicomedia. He charges him with Sabellianism for denying that the Son exists as a distinct person. Eusebius continued the argument in his Ecclesiastical Theology. Both works are important because they preserve many fragments of Marcellus's otherwise lost writings.

De ecclesiastica theologia ("On Ecclesiastical Theology") is a Greek theological treatise in three books written by Eusebius of Caesarea late in his life, probably around 337–338. It is dedicated to Flacillus, bishop of Antioch. It follows Eusebius's earlier two books Against Marcellus, which mostly quoted Marcellus of Ancyra's own words. Here Eusebius refutes Marcellus's teaching directly. Eusebius saw that teaching as Sabellian. Against it, he argues that the Son exists as a distinct being alongside the Father. The work is an important witness to the theological debates that followed the Council of Nicaea.

The Exhortation to Martyrdom is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, generally dated to about 235, during the persecution under the emperor Maximinus Thrax. It is addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Protoctetus, a presbyter of Caesarea, who were both facing arrest. Drawing heavily on Scripture, Origen urges them to stand firm, to reject idolatry and apostasy, and to see suffering for Christ as a contest that leads to glory. It is one of the most important early Christian writings on the meaning of martyrdom.

The Fragmenta are the surviving remains of the writings of Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra (died c. 374), a supporter of the Council of Nicaea and opponent of Arianism. Most come from his treatise against Asterius the Sophist, written around the early 330s. They survive almost entirely as quotations in Eusebius of Caesarea's polemical works against him, with a few more in Epiphanius's Panarion 72. The fragments set out Marcellus's theology of the Word, which his critics condemned as Sabellian, and they are central to the history of the Arian controversy.

This Greek church history in three books was written around 475 by an anonymous author, the son of a presbyter of Cyzicus, who worked in Bithynia. Following Photius, it was long misattributed to Gelasius of Cyzicus. Book I covers Constantine's reign up to 323, Book II the Council of Nicaea and Book III its aftermath. It draws on Eusebius, Rufinus and other historians, as well as on a parchment book that had belonged to Dalmatius of Cyzicus. The author aimed to show against the Eutychians that the Nicene Fathers did not teach Monophysite doctrine.

On the Letters is a short Old Church Slavonic treatise attributed to Chernorizets Hrabar ("Hrabar the Monk"), a writer linked to the Preslav Literary School in the First Bulgarian Empire. It is usually dated to the late ninth or early tenth century. The work defends the Slavic alphabet created by Constantine-Cyril the Philosopher and argues that it is equal in dignity to the Hebrew, Greek and Latin scripts. It also describes how the letters were made in imitation of Greek. It is a key early witness to Slavic literacy and to the Cyrillo-Methodian mission.

The Euchologium Sinaiticum is an anonymous Old Church Slavonic prayer book (euchologion), mostly translated from Greek liturgical sources. It is preserved in a Glagolitic manuscript kept at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai, usually dated to the eleventh century, though the translations may be older. Besides sacramental and penitential material, it contains many occasional blessings for daily life. Examples include prayers for planting a vineyard, blessing grapes and restoring wine that has turned sour. It is one of the most important witnesses to early Slavonic liturgical language and practice.

The Kiev Missal, also called the Kiev Folios, is an anonymous Old Church Slavonic manuscript written in Glagolitic script. It is usually held to be the oldest and most archaic Old Church Slavonic manuscript and is dated no later than the second half of the tenth century. Its seven small parchment folios contain Mass prayers of the Roman rite translated from a Latin sacramentary, among them propers for Saint Clement and Saint Felicity. It is important evidence for early Slavonic use of the Western liturgy.

De paenitentia (Concerning Repentance) is a Latin treatise in two books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, written during his episcopate (374–397). It is aimed against the Novatians, who denied that the Church could forgive grave sins committed after baptism. Ambrose praises gentleness as a virtue that church leaders need, following the example of Christ the Good Shepherd. He argues from Scripture that the Church has received the power to bind and loose, and he urges sinners to do sincere penance. It is an important witness to early Western teaching and practice of penance.

De virginibus is a Latin treatise in three books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, addressed to his sister Marcellina, a consecrated virgin. Usually dated to about 377, early in his episcopate, it seems to have grown out of his sermons. It praises consecrated virginity as a heavenly way of life. It holds up models such as the martyr Agnes, the Virgin Mary and Thecla, and it recalls the address Pope Liberius gave at Marcellina's veiling in Rome. It is among the earliest major Latin works on virginity and shaped later Western ascetic teaching.

De Viduis (Concerning Widows) is a Latin treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, usually dated to about 377. Ambrose wrote it soon after his three books On Virgins, which it follows directly. It praises widowhood as a state of chastity devoted to God, close in honour to virginity. Its models include the widow of Zarephath who received Elijah, Anna, Naomi, Judith and Deborah, and it stresses hospitality, prayer and self-restraint. It discourages widows from remarrying without condemning second marriage. It belongs to Ambrose's influential ascetical writings on Christian women.

De Fide ad Gratianum is a dogmatic treatise in five books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, written at the request of the Western emperor Gratian. Books one and two are usually dated to about 378, and books three to five to about 380. Ambrose relies mainly on the authority of Scripture and the Council of Nicaea to defend the full divinity of the Son and his equality with the Father against Arian teaching. It is one of the main Latin anti-Arian works of the fourth century, and Ambrose followed it with his treatise On the Holy Spirit.

This is a pair of funeral orations by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, for his brother Satyrus, who gave up a public career to manage the church's secular affairs. Satyrus died unexpectedly at Milan, probably in 378, at a time of fear over barbarian invasions. Ambrose delivered the first book at the funeral. It praises his brother's virtues and expresses personal grief. The second, delivered a week later at the tomb, is a treatise on the resurrection. The work draws on classical consolation literature and is an important early Christian example of the genre.

De officiis ministrorum is a Latin ethical treatise in three books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, addressed to his clergy. Its date is debated, but it is usually placed in the late 380s or early 390s. Modelled closely on Cicero's De officiis, it reworks classical Stoic ethics in Christian terms, using biblical examples to discuss duty, the cardinal virtues, and the relation between the honourable and the useful. It is often regarded as the first systematic treatise on Christian ethics.

De Spiritu Sancto is a Latin theological treatise in three books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan. He addressed it to the emperor Gratian and completed it around 381. It defends the full divinity of the Holy Spirit and the Spirit's equality with the Father and the Son, against Arian and Pneumatomachian views. Ambrose built his argument from scriptural exegesis and typology, such as Gideon's fleece, and drew heavily on Greek writers, especially Basil of Caesarea and Didymus the Blind. This transmitted Eastern pneumatology to the Latin West, although Jerome criticised the work for its borrowings.

On the Mysteries (De Mysteriis) is a short Latin mystagogical treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397. Its exact date is uncertain. It is addressed to the newly baptized, and explains the rites of Christian initiation only after they have received them. It covers the opening of the ears, the baptismal font, the anointing and spiritual seal, and the Eucharist, which it reads through Old Testament types. It closely parallels De Sacramentis, and it is an important witness to fourth-century Western liturgy and sacramental theology.

The first class of the letters of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in the traditional Benedictine arrangement: sixty-three letters written between about 374 and 397. They include his correspondence with the emperors Gratian, Valentinian II and Theodosius I. Among them are his letters opposing the restoration of the Altar of Victory in the Roman Senate, with the pagan prefect Symmachus's petition (Relatio III) preserved alongside. The collection also contains his sermon against Auxentius on surrendering the basilicas. It is a key source for relations between church and state in the late fourth century.

The Iambics to Seleucus is a didactic Greek poem in iambic verse, now generally attributed to Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, and written in the later fourth century. It was once transmitted among the poems of Gregory of Nazianzus. Addressed to a young man named Seleucus, it urges him toward virtue and sound learning. Its closing section lists the inspired books of Scripture. It notes that some add Esther and that many reject Revelation. This list was later ratified by the Council in Trullo, which makes it an important witness to the history of the biblical canon.

Pope Anastasius I wrote this Latin letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem, around 400–401. It belongs to the controversy over Origen. After Theophilus of Alexandria urged him to act, Anastasius had condemned Origenism. Rufinus of Aquileia, who was ordained in Jerusalem, had translated Origen's On First Principles into Latin, and Rome took this as a defence of Origen's views. The letter replies to John's inquiry about Rufinus. It opens with warm praise of John and then distances Rome from Rufinus and condemns Origen's writings. Jerome cites the letter. Rufinus doubted it was genuine, but it is generally accepted as authentic.

The Demonstrations (Taḥwyātā) are twenty-three Syriac prose treatises by Aphrahat, the "Persian Sage," written in the Sasanian Empire between 337 and 345. Prefaced by a letter from an inquirer asking about the faith, the first twenty-two are arranged as an alphabetical acrostic. They address faith, love, fasting, prayer, humility, the "sons of the covenant," Passover, circumcision and the sabbath, often in debate with Jewish practice, and the persecution under Shapur II. They are the earliest major surviving works of Syriac Christianity, largely untouched by Greek theological influence.

The thirty-ninth Festal Letter is an Easter letter that Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, sent to the churches of Egypt in 367. To counter heretics' use of apocryphal writings, it lists the books "received through tradition" as canonical. These are twenty-two Old Testament books, including Baruch but not Esther, and the twenty-seven books of the New Testament. Other works, such as Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit, the Didache and the Shepherd of Hermas, may be read for instruction. It is the earliest known list that matches today's New Testament canon exactly.

De Decretis is a Greek treatise in the form of a letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, usually dated to the 350s. It is written to an unnamed correspondent who had argued with supporters of Arius, including friends of Eusebius. Athanasius answers the Arian objection that the Council of Nicaea (325) used unscriptural terms, "of the essence" and "one in essence" (homoousios). He argues that these words express the meaning of Scripture about the Son's true divinity. The work is a major early defence of the Nicene formula. It also preserves documents connected with the council.

The First Discourse Against the Arians is the opening book of Athanasius of Alexandria's Greek polemical treatise against Arianism. Its date is disputed: scholars place it either around 339–346, during his exile in Rome, or in the later 350s. Athanasius argues that the Arians are sectaries named after their founder rather than Christians. He attacks the teaching of Arius's Thalia and defends the eternity of the Son and his unity of essence with the Father. He also begins interpreting disputed biblical texts such as Philippians 2:9–10 and Hebrews 1:4. It is a central text of Nicene theology.

The Festal Letters are the annual pastoral letters that Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, sent between 329 and 373 to announce the date of Easter and the start of the Lenten fast. Each letter pairs that announcement with teaching on fasting, the feast, virtue and the defence of Nicene faith. Athanasius wrote them in Greek, but they survive mainly in a Syriac translation rediscovered in 1842, along with Coptic and Greek fragments. The Thirty-Ninth Letter (367) is especially important because it lists the twenty-seven books of the New Testament as canonical.

The Fourth Discourse Against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise that has come down with the three Orations Against the Arians of Athanasius of Alexandria (4th century). Most scholars doubt that Athanasius wrote it, and its true author and date are uncertain. It is a series of short arguments rather than a continuous discourse. Using Scripture, it argues that the Word is substantial and is the Father's own Son, and so preserves the single "Monarchy" of the Godhead. It attacks Arian teaching, and also views that separate the Word from the Son or merge Father and Son into one.

On the Incarnation of the Word is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius of Alexandria. It is the second part of a double work that opens with Against the Pagans, and both are addressed to a certain Macarius. Its date is disputed: some place it before the Arian controversy, around 318, while others place it in the 330s. It explains why the divine Word, through whom the world was made, took a human body to restore humanity from corruption and death. It also answers Jewish and pagan objections and remains a classic of Christian thought on the incarnation.

This is a small group of personal letters by Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), bishop of Alexandria and leading opponent of Arianism, written over the course of his long and repeatedly interrupted episcopate. The first, sent from the Council of Serdica in 343–344 to the clergy and people of the Mareotis, praises their steadfastness under persecution and reports that the council deposed his opponents Theodore, Valens and Ursacius. The other letters, to individual correspondents, give a glimpse of Athanasius's pastoral concerns and the church politics of the Arian controversy.

The second of the Orations against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. Its date is debated, though it is often placed in the late 330s or 340s. It continues his defence of the Nicene faith by examining scriptural texts that his opponents used to argue that the Son of God is a creature. These include Hebrews 3:2, "faithful to him that made him", and Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me a beginning of his ways". Athanasius reads such passages as referring to the Son's incarnation rather than to his eternal being.

The third of the Greek Orations (Discourses) against the Arians by Athanasius of Alexandria, generally dated to around 340, though the exact date is debated. Its authenticity was questioned in modern scholarship but is widely accepted. Continuing the earlier discourses, it explains texts used by Arian opponents such as Asterius the Sophist, starting with John 14:10, "I in the Father and the Father in me." It argues for the mutual indwelling of Father and Son, who share one essence. It then attributes the Gospel accounts of Christ's ignorance, growth and suffering to the humanity the Word took on.

Against Lying (Contra Mendacium) is a treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 420 in reply to Consentius, a Catholic layman in Spain. Consentius had suggested that Catholics could expose hidden Priscillianists by pretending to share their beliefs. Augustine rejects this: no lie is permissible, even to unmask heretics. Lying about the faith is especially grave, and good ends never justify deceit. The work takes up the themes of his earlier On Lying (De mendacio) and became a classic statement of his strict view that lying is always wrong.

Contra epistulam fundamenti is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to about 396–397, early in his time as bishop. It refutes the "Fundamental Epistle", a foundational Manichaean letter attributed to Mani. Augustine quotes its opening passages and answers them one by one. Recalling his own years as a Manichaean hearer, he says he wants to heal his opponents, not crush them. The work contains his famous remark that he would not believe the Gospel unless moved by the authority of the Catholic Church. It also preserves fragments of the lost Manichaean text.

Against Two Letters of the Pelagians (Contra duas epistulas Pelagianorum) is a Latin treatise in four books by Augustine of Hippo, written about 420–421. It is addressed to Pope Boniface I, who had sent Augustine two Pelagian letters that slandered him. The first letter was attributed to Julian of Eclanum, and the second was issued by a group of Pelagian bishops. Augustine rejects their charge that he taught Manichaean doctrine. He also defends the Catholic teaching on original sin, grace, free will and the goodness of marriage. The work belongs to his later writings in the Pelagian controversy.

Answer to the Letters of Petilian (Contra litteras Petiliani) is a Latin polemical treatise in three books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 400–403 against Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Cirta (Constantina). Book I refutes the first part of a letter Petilian sent to his followers. Book II answers the whole letter point by point, and Book III replies to Petilian's response to Augustine. Augustine argues that the sacraments are valid whatever the holiness of the minister, and he defends the unity of the Catholic Church. The work is a major source for the Donatist controversy.

This is a short treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 421–422 in reply to Paulinus, bishop of Nola. Paulinus had asked whether it helps the dead to be buried near a saint's shrine. The question arose after the widow Flora had her son Cynegius buried in the basilica of Saint Felix. Augustine argues that the place of burial does the soul no good in itself. Funeral rites mainly comfort the living, while prayers, the Eucharist and almsgiving offered for the faithful departed truly help them. He also discusses dreams and apparitions of the dead.

De catechizandis rudibus is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated around 400. He wrote it for Deogratias, a deacon of Carthage who had asked how to teach the Christian faith to beginners seeking admission to the Church. Augustine advises catechists to tell the story of salvation from creation to the present age, to adapt their teaching to each listener and to teach with cheerfulness. He ends with a long and a short model address. The work is an important early handbook of Christian religious instruction.

The City of God (De civitate Dei contra paganos) is a Latin apologetic and theological treatise in twenty-two books by Augustine of Hippo, written about 413–426. It was prompted by the Visigothic sack of Rome in 410 and dedicated to his friend Marcellinus. The first ten books answer pagan claims that Christianity caused Rome's misfortunes. The remaining twelve trace the origin, history and destiny of two cities: the earthly city, ruled by love of self, and the heavenly city, ruled by love of God. It deeply shaped Western theology and political thought.

The Confessions is an autobiographical work in thirteen books written in Latin by Augustine of Hippo between about 397 and 400. It is addressed to God as a long prayer. Books 1 to 9 tell the story of his restless youth, his attraction to Manichaeism and Neoplatonism, and his conversion to Christianity in 386. Book 10 examines memory, and the last three books are a commentary on the opening of Genesis. It is often called the first Western autobiography and has deeply shaped Christian spirituality and Western literature.

Augustine of Hippo wrote this long letter to Boniface, a Roman military officer in Africa who later became Count of Africa, around 417. It is often treated as a treatise on its own. Augustine explains how the Donatists differ from the Arians and defends the imperial laws that pressured Donatists to return to Catholic communion. He describes the violence of the Circumcellions and closes with a discussion of the sin against the Holy Spirit. The letter is a key source for Augustine's argument that the state may use coercion against schism and heresy.

This Latin work is the stenographic record of a public debate held over two days in 392 at the Baths of Sossius in Hippo Regius. On one side was Augustine of Hippo, then a presbyter. On the other was Fortunatus, a Manichaean presbyter he had known before his conversion. Augustine argues that the Manichaean myth of a conflict between light and darkness makes God corruptible. The two men also debate the origin of evil, free will and the meaning of Scripture. After the debate Fortunatus reportedly left Hippo. It is an early witness to Augustine's anti-Manichaean polemic.

The Enchiridion, or handbook on faith, hope and love, is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it around 421, soon after Jerome's death, for a layman named Laurentius who had asked for a brief guide to Christian doctrine. Under faith, Augustine expounds the Apostles' Creed and refutes heresies. Under hope, he briefly explains the Lord's Prayer. He ends with a discussion of love as the goal of the law. The work offers a compact summary of Augustine's mature theology, especially on sin, grace and redemption.

The Enarrationes in Psalmos are Augustine of Hippo's commentary on all 150 psalms, written over about three decades, from roughly 392 to 422. Some are sermons preached to congregations in North Africa and taken down by stenographers. Others are expositions he dictated. Together they form the longest of his works. Augustine reads the psalms mainly as being about Christ, often hearing in them the voice of the "whole Christ", head and body, meaning Christ and the Church. The collection became one of the most influential Psalm commentaries of the Latin Middle Ages.

De Fide et Symbolo (On Faith and the Creed) is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo. It began as an address he gave in 393, while still a presbyter, to the council of African bishops gathered at Hippo Regius. Augustine works through the baptismal creed article by article: God the Father, the Son's divinity and incarnation, the Holy Spirit, the Church, forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the body. Along the way he answers heretical misreadings, especially Manichaean and Arian ones. It is one of his earliest systematic accounts of Christian doctrine.

De fide rerum quae non videntur (On Faith in Things Not Seen) is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo. Some once doubted that he wrote it, but he names it in his letter to Count Darius (Letter 231). A reference to laws against idols suggests it was written after 399. It answers critics who mock Christianity for asking belief in what cannot be seen. Augustine points out that people already trust unseen things, such as a friend's goodwill. He then presents fulfilled prophecy and the spread of the Church among the nations as visible grounds for faith.

On the Gift of Perseverance (De dono perseverantiae) is a late theological treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 428–429. It is the second book of a pair with On the Predestination of the Saints, and both were addressed to Prosper of Aquitaine and Hilary. Augustine answers objections raised by monks in southern Gaul. He argues that perseverance in faith until the end of life is an unmerited gift of God, and that no one can be certain of having received it while still alive. The work is a key statement of his mature teaching on grace and predestination.

De bono coniugali (On the Good of Marriage) is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 401 with its companion work On Holy Virginity. It responds to the controversy raised by Jovinian, who denied that virginity was superior to marriage. Augustine takes a middle course: marriage is a true good, grounded in human sociability and the creation of woman from man, while consecrated virginity remains the higher calling. His account of marriage's threefold good, offspring, fidelity and sacramental bond, became foundational for later Western theology and canon law on marriage.

On the Good of Widowhood (De bono viduitatis) is a letter-treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to about 414. Augustine wrote it to Juliana, a widow of the Roman noble family of the Anicii, after she had repeatedly asked him for it. It praises the vow of continent widowhood as a higher state than marriage, though below virginity, and holds that second marriages are not sinful. It also warns against attributing perseverance in virtue to human will alone instead of God's grace, which reflects Augustine's dispute with the Pelagians. It belongs with his other treatises on marriage and virginity.

On Grace and Free Will (De gratia et libero arbitrio) is a late anti-Pelagian treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 426–427. He addressed it to Valentinus, abbot of the monastery at Hadrumetum in North Africa, where monks had disputed whether preaching grace meant denying free will. Augustine argues from Scripture that both are real: human beings have free will, but grace is not given according to merit, and even good works and faith are God's gifts. With its companion treatise On Rebuke and Grace, it shaped later debates over predestination.

On the Grace of Christ, and on Original Sin is an anti-Pelagian treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it in 418, after Popes Innocent I and Zosimus condemned Pelagianism, and addressed it to Albina, Pinianus and Melania the Younger. The first book argues that Pelagius, despite claiming to honour grace, reduced it to nature, free will, law or teaching. It also attacks his view that grace is given according to merit. The second book defends original sin against Pelagius and Caelestius. Together the books are a key statement of Augustine's teaching on grace.

De consensu evangelistarum (On the Agreement of the Evangelists) is a Latin treatise in four books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 400 while he was also working on On the Trinity. It sets out to show that the four canonical Gospels do not contradict one another. The first book answers pagan critics who said Christ's disciples had exaggerated his divinity, and it defends the worship of the God of Israel alone. The later books work through the Gospel narratives and reconcile passages that seem to conflict. The work shaped Western thinking about how the Gospels relate to each other.

De sancta virginitate (Of Holy Virginity) is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 401 as a companion to his On the Good of Marriage. Both works answer the controversy raised by Jovinian, who denied that consecrated virginity was more meritorious than marriage. Augustine holds that virginity dedicated to God is the higher gift, yet marriage remains good, and the married patriarchs of Israel are not to be despised. Much of the treatise warns consecrated virgins against pride and urges humility, with Mary held up as their model.

Ten sermons by Augustine of Hippo on the First Epistle of John, preached at Hippo during Easter week. He paused his series of tractates on John's Gospel to give them. They are often dated to around 407, but the date is disputed. The Latin title reflects an old tradition that the letter was addressed to the Parthians. Augustine calls charity the epistle's central theme and develops it against the Donatist schism, linking love of God to love of neighbour and the unity of the Church. The seventh homily contains his famous maxim "Love, and do what you will."

The Letters of Augustine of Hippo are a Latin correspondence of more than two hundred letters, written from about 386, soon after his conversion, until his death in 430. The collection also includes letters written to him by others, among them Jerome and Paulinus of Nola. They cover philosophy, the interpretation of Scripture, pastoral care, church discipline and the Donatist and Pelagian controversies. The letters are an important source for Augustine's thought, for church life in Roman North Africa, and for the wider late Roman world.

On Marriage and Concupiscence (De nuptiis et concupiscentia) is a Latin anti-Pelagian treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 419–421 and addressed to Count Valerius. The Pelagians claimed that Augustine's doctrine of original sin condemned marriage. In reply, he argues that marriage is good and that the concupiscence of the flesh is not its fault, since conjugal chastity makes good use of that evil in begetting children. Julian of Eclanum attacked the first book, and Augustine wrote the second to answer extracts from Julian's work. The treatise began their long controversy.

This Latin treatise in three books by Augustine of Hippo was written around 411–412, in reply to questions sent from Carthage by the imperial official Marcellinus. It was Augustine's first written work against Pelagianism. He defends the baptism of infants as necessary because of original sin, inherited from Adam. He also argues that justification comes by God's grace and that no one in this life is entirely without sin. The third book is really a letter, and it mentions Pelagius respectfully by name. The work shaped later Western teaching on original sin and grace.

De moribus ecclesiae catholicae et de moribus Manichaeorum is a Latin treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo. He began it in Rome around 387–388, soon after his baptism, and finished it after returning to Africa. The first book sets out Catholic ethics, with God as the highest good of human beings. It presents the four cardinal virtues as forms of love for God and points to Christian ascetics as examples of holy living. The second book attacks Manichaean moral teaching and practice. Augustine had himself been a Manichaean, and the work is one of his earliest anti-Manichaean writings.

De moribus ecclesiae catholicae et de moribus Manichaeorum is a Latin treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo. He began it in Rome around 387–388, soon after his baptism, and finished it after returning to Africa. The first book sets out Catholic ethics, with God as the highest good of human beings. It presents the four cardinal virtues as forms of love for God and points to Christian ascetics as examples of holy living. The second book attacks Manichaean moral teaching and practice. Augustine had himself been a Manichaean, and the work is one of his earliest anti-Manichaean writings.

On Nature and Grace (De natura et gratia) is a Latin treatise in one book that Augustine of Hippo wrote in 415. He addressed it to Timasius and Jacobus. It answers a book by Pelagius, "On Nature", which defended the natural ability of human beings to live without sin. Augustine argues that human nature, damaged by Adam's sin, needs God's grace to be healed and set free. In the Retractations he notes that sayings he had attributed to Bishop Xystus were really by the pagan philosopher Sextus. It is an important early work of the Pelagian controversy.

De Natura Boni (On the Nature of the Good) is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around the turn of the fifth century against the Manichaeans, whose sect he had once belonged to. It argues that God alone is the highest, unchangeable good and that everything He created from nothing is good, though changeable. Evil is not a nature or substance but a corruption of a nature's measure, form and order. It is one of the clearest statements of Augustine's view of evil as a privation of good.

De Baptismo (On Baptism, Against the Donatists) is an anti-Donatist treatise in seven books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 400–401. Augustine argues that baptism given outside the Catholic communion by heretics or schismatics is valid and should not be repeated. However, it brings no spiritual benefit while the recipient stays separated from the Church. Much of the work answers the Donatist appeal to Cyprian of Carthage, and Augustine claims Cyprian's authority for his own position. The treatise shaped later Western teaching on the validity of sacraments.

De doctrina Christiana (On Christian Doctrine, or On Christian Teaching) is a Latin treatise in four books by Augustine of Hippo on how to interpret and teach Scripture. He began it around 397 and finished it around 426, adding the fourth book then. Book 1 sets out the things to be enjoyed or used, centring on the love of God and of neighbour. Books 2 and 3 deal with signs and with interpreting obscure or ambiguous passages. Book 4 adapts classical rhetoric to Christian preaching. The work shaped medieval biblical interpretation and education.

De Continentia (On Continence) is a Latin treatise in the form of a sermon by Augustine of Hippo. Its date is uncertain. It does not appear in his Retractationes, but Augustine mentions it in a letter to Count Darius, and Possidius lists it among his works. Erasmus doubted that Augustine wrote it, but the attribution is generally accepted. The work argues that continence is a gift of God rather than a human achievement. It treats self-restraint as the discipline of the whole person against sinful desire and attacks the Manichaean view that the body is evil.

De Mendacio (On Lying) is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 395, shortly before he became bishop. It asks what counts as a lie and whether lying is ever allowed, even with good or charitable intent. Augustine defines a lie, sorts lies into eight kinds by how serious they are, and argues that every lie is sinful. In his Retractations he admits the work was obscure. He returned to the subject around 420 in Against Lying. Both treatises shaped the strict Western Christian tradition on truthfulness.

De Patientia (On Patience) is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo. Its exact date is uncertain, but it is usually placed late in his career. It begins by explaining how God, who cannot suffer, can still be called patient. It then turns to human patience, separating true Christian endurance from the endurance of wicked people who suffer hardship for bad ends. Augustine uses examples such as Job and the martyrs and argues that genuine patience is a gift of God's grace, not an achievement of the human will alone.

On the Creed: A Sermon to the Catechumens is a Latin sermon attributed to Augustine of Hippo, bishop of Hippo Regius in North Africa. Its exact date is uncertain. It was preached to candidates preparing for baptism when the creed was formally handed over to them. Augustine tells them to learn the creed by heart rather than write it down, then explains it clause by clause: God the almighty Father, Christ's birth, passion and resurrection, the Holy Spirit, the Church, forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the body. It shows how creeds were taught in the early Church.

De Trinitate is a theological treatise in fifteen books by Augustine of Hippo, written in Latin over about two decades, roughly between 400 and 420. The early books use Scripture and the Church's teaching to show that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one and equal, and they answer texts cited against the Son's equality. The later books look for analogies of the Trinity in the human mind, notably memory, understanding and will. Some scholars see it as Augustine's masterpiece, and it deeply shaped Western Trinitarian theology.

De perfectione iustitiae hominis is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo against the Pelagians, usually dated to about 415. He addressed it to the bishops Eutropius and Paulus. It answers a paper of "Definitions" said to be by Caelestius, a disciple of Pelagius, which claimed that people are able to live without sin. Augustine first answers each proposition briefly and then examines the Bible passages cited in the paper. He argues that perfect, sinless righteousness cannot be reached without grace and is never fully attained in this life.

On the Predestination of the Saints (De praedestinatione sanctorum) is a late Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written about 428–429. It is addressed to Prosper of Aquitaine and Hilary, who had reported objections to his teaching on grace among monks in southern Gaul, later called semi-Pelagians. Augustine argues that the very beginning of faith, and not only its growth, is God's gift. Citing 1 Corinthians 4:7, he admits that he had held a different view in his early exposition of Romans. Its companion is On the Gift of Perseverance, and both shaped later debates on grace and predestination.

De Gestis Pelagii (On the Proceedings of Pelagius) is a Latin treatise in one book by Augustine of Hippo, addressed to Bishop Aurelius of Carthage and written around the beginning of 417. It examines the acts of the Synod of Diospolis in Palestine (December 415), where fourteen bishops acquitted Pelagius. Augustine goes through each charge and Pelagius's reply. He argues that Pelagius was cleared only because he condemned the propositions read against him, so the synod did not approve his teaching. The treatise is a major source for what happened at the synod.

De Utilitate Credendi (On the Profit of Believing) is a short treatise by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it around 391–392, soon after his ordination as a priest at Hippo. It is addressed to his friend Honoratus, whom Augustine had earlier drawn into Manichaeism. Augustine defends the Old Testament against Manichaean attacks and sets out ways of interpreting Scripture. He argues that believing on the authority of the Catholic Church is a reasonable first step toward understanding truth, not a betrayal of reason. The work is an early statement of his view of how faith and reason relate.

On Rebuke and Grace (De correptione et gratia) is a treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written about 426–427 and addressed to Valentinus, abbot of Hadrumetum, and his monks. It answers an objection raised among them: if good conduct depends wholly on God's grace, then no one should be rebuked for failing to keep the commandments, only prayed for. Augustine defends the usefulness of correction while maintaining that grace alone frees the will for good. He also discusses perseverance and predestination. It belongs to his late anti-Pelagian writings.

Reply to Faustus the Manichaean (Contra Faustum Manichaeum) is a polemical treatise in thirty-three books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 400. It answers a work by Faustus of Mileve, a Manichaean bishop whom Augustine had met in Carthage, as he recounts in the Confessions. Augustine quotes Faustus's arguments section by section and replies to each. He defends the Old Testament, the patriarchs and the unity of the two Testaments against Manichaean objections. The work also contains an influential early discussion of just war.

De sermone Domini in monte is a Latin commentary by Augustine of Hippo on the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 5–7. He wrote it around 393, while he was still a priest at Hippo. Augustine calls the sermon "a perfect standard of the Christian life." The work has two books. The first covers Matthew 5, including the Beatitudes, which Augustine links to the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit. The second covers chapters 6 and 7 and includes a short theology of prayer based on the Lord's Prayer. It is one of his earliest works of biblical exegesis.

This is a collection of Latin sermons that Augustine of Hippo preached to his congregations, mostly at Hippo Regius in North Africa, during his years as priest and bishop (c. 391–430). In the Benedictine edition they belong to the sermons "on the Scriptures" and comment on New Testament readings heard in the liturgy. The English collection of this title covers sermons 51 to 147. They expound passages from the Gospels and the apostolic writings. The first deals with how Matthew's and Luke's genealogies of Christ can be reconciled. Together they show Augustine as a pastoral preacher and biblical interpreter.

The Soliloquies are a philosophical dialogue in two books by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote them in 386–387 during his retreat at Cassiciacum, after his conversion and before his baptism. Augustine converses with a personified Reason, an inner voice, and states his aim as knowing God and the soul. The first book looks at how God can be known and at the moral purification needed to know him. The second argues for the soul's immortality from the permanence of truth. Augustine coined the word "soliloquia" for the work. An Old English adaptation is attributed to Alfred the Great.

On the Soul and its Origin (De natura et origine animae) is a Latin treatise in four books by Augustine of Hippo, written about 419–420. It answers Vincentius Victor, a young man from Mauretania Caesariensis who had attacked Augustine's admitted uncertainty over whether individual souls are inherited from Adam or newly created for each person. One book is addressed to the monk Renatus, one to the presbyter Peter, and two to Victor himself. Augustine defends his hesitation on the question, insists that the soul is spirit rather than body, and refutes Victor's errors.

De Spiritu et Littera is a Latin theological treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 412 for the imperial official Marcellinus. Marcellinus had been puzzled by Augustine's claim that a person could, with God's help, live without sin, even though no one ever had. In reply, Augustine expounds Paul's saying, "The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life." He argues that the law alone cannot make anyone righteous and that justification comes from grace poured into the heart by the Holy Spirit. It is one of his first anti-Pelagian works and later shaped Reformation debates.

The Tractates on the Gospel of John are a series of 124 Latin homilies by Augustine of Hippo. Together they form a continuous commentary on the whole of the Fourth Gospel. Most were preached to his congregation at Hippo, and some were later dictated. Their dating is debated, but they are generally placed between about 406 and the early 420s. They take up Christ as the eternal Word, grace, the sacraments, charity and the unity of the Church, often against the Donatists and Arians. They are among Augustine's most important exegetical works.

De duabus animabus (On Two Souls) is a short anti-Manichaean treatise in one book by Augustine of Hippo, written around 391–392, soon after he was ordained a priest at Hippo. Augustine had once been a Manichaean hearer. Here he rejects their teaching that each person has two souls, a good one from God's substance and an evil one not created by God. He argues that every soul, because it is a form of life, comes from God, and that sin comes from the will, not from an evil nature. He later reviewed the work in his Retractationes.

De Opere Monachorum (Of the Work of Monks) is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 400 at the request of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. It deals with monks in Carthage who refused manual labour and claimed to live only by prayer and the gifts of the faithful. Some also wore their hair long. Augustine draws on Paul's words, "If any will not work, neither let him eat," and on the apostle's own example. He argues that monks should support themselves by working with their hands. The treatise is an important early Western text on monastic life.

The Conferences (Collationes Patrum) is a Latin work by the monk John Cassian, written in southern Gaul in the 420s. It follows his Institutes and consists of twenty-four dialogues, issued in three parts. In them, Egyptian desert fathers, especially the anchorites of Scetis, teach Cassian and his companion Germanus about prayer, discretion, purity of heart and the monastic goal. The Thirteenth Conference's teaching on grace and free will drew criticism from Prosper of Aquitaine. The Rule of Benedict recommends the work, and it became a key channel of Eastern monastic spirituality to the Latin West.

The Institutes (De institutis coenobiorum) is a Latin treatise in twelve books on monastic life by John Cassian. He wrote it in the 420s in southern Gaul at the request of Bishop Castor of Apt, who was founding a monastery. The first four books describe the dress, prayer, psalmody and rules of the monasteries of Egypt and Palestine. The remaining eight books deal with the eight principal vices and their remedies, a scheme that draws on Evagrius Ponticus. Together with Cassian's Conferences, the work helped bring Eastern monastic practice to the Latin West and influenced the Rule of Saint Benedict.

De Incarnatione Domini contra Nestorium is a Latin theological treatise in seven books by the monk John Cassian. He wrote it at Marseille around 429–430, after his Conferences, at the request of the Roman deacon Leo, later Pope Leo I. It was one of the first Western replies to Nestorius of Constantinople. Cassian defends the unity of Christ's person and the title Theotokos, "God-bearer", for Mary, and connects Nestorius's teaching with Pelagianism. He supports his case with Scripture, the creed and earlier Fathers. The work came out shortly before the Council of Ephesus in 431.

The Commentary on Galatians is a Greek exposition of Paul's Epistle to the Galatians by John Chrysostom. It is usually dated to his years as a priest at Antioch (386–398). Unlike most of his work on Paul, it is a continuous commentary rather than a series of homilies. It follows the epistle verse by verse, explaining Paul's sharp tone, his defence of his apostleship and his teaching on faith, the Mosaic Law and Christian freedom. It is an important witness to Antiochene literal exegesis.

The Oration to the Assembly of the Saints is a Greek speech attributed to the emperor Constantine the Great. Eusebius of Caesarea preserved it as an appendix to his Life of Constantine. The speech was given on Good Friday. Scholars disagree about its date and place, and they once doubted that Constantine wrote it, though many now accept it as his, probably translated from Latin. It attacks pagan polytheism and fatalism and defends divine providence and Christ's work. It is especially known for reading Virgil's Fourth Eclogue and an acrostic of the Erythraean Sibyl as prophecies of Christ.
