This is a cycle of Syriac teaching hymns (madrāšê) for the feast of the Epiphany, traditionally attributed to Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), deacon of Nisibis and Edessa. Scholars have questioned whether all of them are his. Each hymn has a refrain. They celebrate Christ's baptism in the Jordan and the baptism of believers, and read Old Testament episodes as types of the sacrament: Elisha's washings, the sweetening of the waters at Marah, the guiding cloud and the crossing of the sea. They are an important witness to early Syriac baptismal theology and liturgical poetry.

The Hymns on the Nativity are a cycle of Syriac madrāšê, or teaching hymns, by Ephrem the Syrian. He was a deacon and poet who worked at Nisibis and later at Edessa, and he composed these hymns in the mid-fourth century. They celebrate the birth of Christ as the fulfilment of the prophets, kings and types of the Old Testament. They dwell on paradoxes such as the Creator becoming an infant and on the Virgin Mary's role. They are among the best-known works of early Syriac poetry and incarnational theology.

The Carmina Nisibena ("Nisibene Hymns") are a collection of Syriac madrāšê, or teaching hymns, by Ephrem the Syrian, written between about 350 and 373. About 77 of them survive. The early hymns deal with Nisibis, Ephrem's home city, and its sieges by the Persian king Shapur II. They pray for deliverance from the floodwaters turned against the city walls and praise its bishops. Other hymns concern Edessa and Harran. The later hymns dramatise Christ's descent into Sheol and his contest with Death and Satan. The collection is valuable both as poetry and as a historical source.

The Pearl is a set of seven Syriac teaching hymns (madrāšê) by Ephrem the Syrian, the fourth-century deacon and poet of Nisibis and Edessa. They belong to his larger cycle of Hymns on Faith. Ephrem turns a single pearl over in his hand and finds in it images of Christ, the Virgin, the Church, baptism and the Kingdom. He uses the pearl to argue that the Son cannot be fully understood and to warn against prying debate about the divine nature. The hymns are among the best-known examples of his symbolic theology.

A group of three sermons in Syriac attributed to Ephrem the Syrian, the fourth-century deacon and poet of Nisibis and Edessa. They were composed before his death in 373. The first, the Homily on Our Lord, is a long meditation in elevated prose on the Incarnation and the saving work of Christ. It describes his passage from the Godhead to the Virgin's womb, and from Sheol to the Kingdom, to bring humanity to life. The second homily deals with admonition and repentance. The third deals with the sign God gave to Hezekiah.

This letter was sent by the Christian communities of Vienne and Lyon (Lugdunum) in Gaul to the churches of Asia and Phrygia. It gives an eyewitness account of the persecution of about 177, under Marcus Aurelius. It describes mob violence, trials and the deaths of martyrs such as the aged bishop Pothinus and the slave woman Blandina. Its author is unknown, though some have suggested Irenaeus. The letter survives only in the excerpts Eusebius of Caesarea quoted in Book 5 of his Ecclesiastical History. It is one of the most important early Christian martyr accounts.

Eusebius of Caesarea wrote this Greek letter to his church at Caesarea in 325, soon after the Council of Nicaea. In it he explains why he signed the council's creed. He quotes the baptismal creed of his own church, which he says he read before Emperor Constantine and which was approved. He then sets out the Nicene formula with its additions and explains how he understood terms such as "of the substance" and "consubstantial" (homoousios). Athanasius, Socrates and Theodoret preserved the letter, and it is a key eyewitness source for the council's debates.

The Life of Constantine is a Greek work in four books by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, written in honour of the emperor Constantine the Great. Eusebius composed it after Constantine's death in 337 and left it unfinished when he died in 339. It mixes panegyric and biography. It presents Constantine as a model Christian ruler and recounts his conversion, including the vision of the cross, his wars, his church building and his religious policy. It is one of the fullest sources for the religious history of his reign, and it quotes several imperial letters and documents.

The Martyrs of Palestine is a Greek account by Eusebius of Caesarea of the Christians who died in Palestine during the Great Persecution. It begins with Diocletian's edicts of 303 and continues to the persecution's end about 311. Eusebius lived in Caesarea at the time and witnessed many of the events, including the sufferings of his teacher Pamphilus. The work survives in two forms. This shorter recension is attached to Book VIII of some manuscripts of his Ecclesiastical History. A longer version survives mainly in Syriac. The work is an important eyewitness source for the last Roman persecution.

This Greek panegyric by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, was delivered in Constantinople in 336 to mark the thirtieth anniversary of Constantine the Great's reign. Eusebius presents the emperor as the earthly image of the divine Logos and his monarchy as a reflection of God's heavenly rule. It also praises Constantine's suppression of polytheism and his support for the Church. Its later chapters are generally thought to come from a separate speech on Christ's sepulchre. The work is an important early statement of Christian imperial ideology, which later shaped Byzantine political thought.

The Festal Index, or Chronicon Athanasianum, is an anonymous annotated list of the festal letters that Athanasius of Alexandria sent each year to the churches of Egypt and Libya to announce the date of Easter. It was compiled after his death in 373 and survives in Syriac. For each year from 328 onward, it records the Easter date, consuls, indiction, prefect of Egypt, and events such as Athanasius' exiles and returns. Scholars value it for the chronology of his career and for Roman Egypt's administration. The traditional numbering of the letters comes from it.

This Greek encyclical letter was issued by Gennadius I, patriarch of Constantinople from 458 to 471, together with a synod meeting in the capital. It is usually dated to about 459. Addressed to the metropolitans and to the pope of Rome, it condemns simony, the buying or selling of ordination. It argues that clergy must be ordained freely, as Christ ordained the apostles without payment, and it appeals to the Gospel and to the Council of Chalcedon's canon against simoniacal ordinations. The letter was later preserved among collections of Eastern canon law.

This Latin catalogue of Christian writers, usually called De viris illustribus, was written by Gennadius, a priest of Marseilles, in the later fifth century. Its exact date is uncertain. It continues Jerome's work of the same name, which ended in 392–393. In about ninety short notices it covers Greek, Latin and Syriac authors from the late fourth century to Gennadius's own time, describing their lives and listing their writings. Some notices were probably added by later hands. Many of the writers it records are otherwise poorly documented, so it is an important source for the literary history of the period.

Oration 27 is the first of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople in 380, while he led the small Nicene community there. It serves as an introduction to the series and is aimed at the Eunomians, radical Arians known for their skill in dialectic. Gregory does not yet discuss the Trinity itself. Instead he asks who may speak about God, when, before whom and how far, arguing that theology requires purity of life, quiet and restraint rather than clever debate.

Oration 28 is the second of the five Theological Orations by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached them in Constantinople around 380, when he led the small Nicene community there against the Eunomians, who claimed that God's essence could be fully known. The first oration set out who may practise theology and under what conditions. This one argues that God's nature cannot be grasped by the human mind. Using the image of Moses on Sinai seeing only God's "back parts", Gregory shows that creation reveals that God exists, not what God is. The work is a classic statement of divine incomprehensibility.

The third of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arian groups. After setting out the monarchy of the Father, Gregory defends the full divinity of the Son. He argues that the Son is eternally begotten without time or passion, and answers his opponents' arguments from the terms "begotten" and "unbegotten." The oration closes with a set of antitheses contrasting Christ's human lowliness with his divine glory. Oration 30 continues the argument with a fuller treatment of the disputed passages of Scripture.

Oration 30 is the fourth of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus delivered in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arians. It is his second discourse on the Son. Gregory answers, one by one, the scriptural texts his opponents used to make the Son subordinate, such as "The Lord created me" (Proverbs 8:22) and "the Father is greater than I." He assigns the exalted expressions to Christ's divinity and the lowly ones to his assumed humanity. The oration ends with a discussion of the titles of the Son.

Oration 31 is the last of the five Theological Orations that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople, probably in 380, against the Eunomians and the Pneumatomachi, who denied that the Holy Spirit is fully divine. Gregory openly calls the Spirit God and consubstantial with the Father and the Son. He separates the Spirit's procession from the Son's generation and answers the objection that Scripture is silent on the matter with a theory of progressive revelation. The oration was an important statement of Cappadocian Trinitarian theology shortly before the Council of Constantinople of 381.

This short Greek theological treatise in letter form is addressed to Eustathius, a physician whom the author praises for healing minds as well as bodies. It is usually attributed to Gregory of Nyssa, but it was also handed down among the letters of his brother Basil of Caesarea. It was probably written in the late 370s or early 380s. It defends the full divinity of the Holy Spirit against those who denied it. Its main argument is that Father, Son and Spirit share one operation, and therefore one nature. It is an important witness to Cappadocian Trinitarian theology.

The Book of Pastoral Rule (Regula Pastoralis) is a Latin treatise on the duties of bishops and clergy, written by Pope Gregory I around 590, soon after his election. It is addressed to John, bishop of Ravenna, who had criticised Gregory for trying to avoid the papacy. Its four parts deal with who should take up spiritual rule, how the pastor should live, how he should teach people of differing character, and how he should stay humble. It became one of the most influential medieval guides to ministry, and King Alfred had it translated into Old English.

The Register of the Epistles is the collected official correspondence of Pope Gregory I (the Great), written during his pontificate from 590 to 604. It survives in fourteen books arranged by indiction year and contains around 850 letters in Latin. They deal with the management of the papal estates, church discipline, and relations with bishops, emperors, Frankish and Lombard rulers. They also cover the mission to the English and the dispute over the title "ecumenical patriarch." The collection is a major source for the history of the late sixth-century Church and of Italy.

It survives in fourteen books arranged by indiction year and contains around 850 letters in Latin. They deal with the management of the papal estates, church discipline, and relations with bishops, emperors, Frankish and Lombard rulers. They also cover the mission to the English and the dispute over the title "ecumenical patriarch." The collection is a major source for the history of the late sixth-century Church and of Italy.

De Synodis ("On the Councils", also called "The Faith of the Easterns") is a Latin treatise by Hilary of Poitiers. He wrote it around 358–359, while exiled in Asia Minor during the Arian controversy. Hilary addressed it to the bishops of Gaul and Britain. In it he sets out and comments on the creeds of several Eastern councils, including those of Antioch, Sirmium and Ancyra. He argues that the term homoiousios ("of like substance") can be understood in an orthodox sense. The work sought to bring together Western Nicene bishops and the moderate Eastern Homoiousians against the more radical Arians.

The Tractatus super Psalmos is a Latin series of homilies on the Psalms by Hilary of Poitiers. It is generally dated to his last years, after he returned from exile in the East around 360. Only part survives, covering selected psalms, including Psalms 1, 53 and 130. Hilary drew heavily on Origen's exegesis. He reads the Psalms mainly as speaking of Christ, and he holds that interpretation begins by asking in whose person the psalmist speaks and whom he addresses. The work is among the earliest substantial Latin commentaries on the Psalter.

De Trinitate is a Latin theological treatise in twelve books by Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. He wrote most of it during his exile in Phrygia in the later 350s, and it was completed by about 360. Its first book opens with an autobiographical account of Hilary's search for truth, which led him to faith. The treatise argues against Arianism, defending the full divinity of the Son and his unity of nature with the Father from Scripture. It is the first major Latin work on the Trinity, and it brought Eastern theological debates to Western readers.

The Historia Acephala, or "headless history" because its opening is lost, is an anonymous Alexandrian chronicle of the career of Athanasius of Alexandria. It was composed in Greek, probably soon after his death in 373, but survives only in a Latin translation. It runs from his return to Alexandria in 346 through his later exiles and restorations to his death and succession. Events are dated precisely by Egyptian months and consular years. Together with the Festal Index, it is a key source for the chronology of Athanasius and the Arian controversy.

Jerome wrote this Latin polemical treatise in Rome around 383, while Damasus was bishop there. It answers Helvidius, a layman who claimed that the Gospels' references to the "brothers" and "sisters" of the Lord show that Mary had other children with Joseph, and who ranked marriage as equal to virginity. Jerome argues that Mary remained a virgin, that these "brothers" were the Lord's cousins, and that virginity is superior to marriage. Helvidius's own work is lost and is known only through this reply.

To Pammachius Against John of Jerusalem is a Latin polemical treatise by Jerome, written in the late 390s during the Origenist controversy. It is addressed to his Roman friend Pammachius. Jerome attacks John II, bishop of Jerusalem, for allegedly sheltering Origenist errors on the resurrection of the body, the soul and related doctrines. He also defends himself and Epiphanius of Salamis in the quarrel over Epiphanius' ordination of Jerome's brother Paulinian. The work is an important source for the controversy in Palestine and for church politics there at the time.

Against Jovinianus is a Latin polemical treatise in two books by Jerome, written in 393. It answers Jovinian, a Roman monk condemned at synods in Rome and Milan. Jovinian had taught that virgins are no better than wives, that abstinence is no better than eating with thanksgiving, that the baptized cannot sin, and that all sins and rewards are equal. Book I praises virginity over marriage, and Book II rejects the other claims. Many readers found its attack on marriage excessive, and Jerome defended it in letters to Pammachius. The treatise was later widely quoted in medieval writing against marriage.

The Dialogue Against the Pelagians is a Latin polemical work in three books by Jerome. He wrote it in Bethlehem late in life, around 415 to 417, and it was his last major controversial writing. It takes the form of a debate between Atticus, a Catholic, and Critobulus, who speaks for Pelagius. The work attacks the claim that a person can live without sin by free will alone and defends the necessity of divine grace, drawing heavily on Scripture. It was written while Pelagius was in Palestine, and it set Jerome beside Augustine in the Pelagian controversy.

Against Vigilantius (Contra Vigilantium) is a short polemical treatise by Jerome, written at Bethlehem in 406. Jerome says he dictated it in a single night. It answers a lost work by Vigilantius, a presbyter from Aquitaine who had once been Jerome's guest. Vigilantius had attacked the veneration of martyrs' relics, vigils at their tombs, clerical celibacy, monasticism and the sending of alms to Jerusalem. Jerome defends these practices in fierce, sarcastic terms, mocking his opponent as "Dormitantius" ("the sleepy one"). The treatise is an important witness to the cult of the saints in the early fifth century.

Jerome wrote this polemical Latin treatise at Bethlehem in about 401–402, during the Origenist controversy. Its first two books are addressed to Pammachius and Marcella. They answer Rufinus of Aquileia's Apology, which Jerome knew only from summaries sent to him and from passages his brother Paulinianus had memorized. A third book followed after Rufinus sent a letter in reply. Jerome defends his own orthodoxy and his translations, attacks Rufinus's Latin version of Origen's On First Principles and its preface, and denies any sympathy for Origen's errors. The work marks the bitter end of a long friendship.

The Dialogue Against the Luciferians is a Latin polemical dialogue by Jerome. It is one of his early works, usually dated around 379, though some scholars place it a few years later. In it, a follower of Lucifer of Cagliari debates an orthodox Christian. The Luciferians refused communion with bishops who had compromised with Arianism. Against them, Jerome argues that such bishops, especially those who signed the formula of Ariminum in 359, should be received back, and that baptism given by heretics is valid. The work includes his famous remark that the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.

This is the collected correspondence of Jerome of Stridon. It spans roughly fifty years, from his earliest surviving letter to Innocent (c. 370) until shortly before his death at Bethlehem in 420. The collection also includes letters written to Jerome by correspondents such as Pope Damasus and Augustine of Hippo. The letters deal with ascetic and virginal life, biblical interpretation and the principles of translation, as well as the Origenist controversy and personal disputes. They are polished examples of Latin prose and an important source for the church and society of the late fourth century.

The Life of Saint Hilarion is a Latin hagiography written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 390. It tells the story of Hilarion, a fourth-century hermit from near Gaza who was a disciple of Antony of Egypt and is regarded as the founder of monastic life in Palestine. It follows his ascetic struggles, miracles and later wanderings, which took him to Egypt, Sicily, Dalmatia and finally Cyprus, where he died. Jerome wrote it to promote the ascetic ideal. Alongside his Lives of Paul and Malchus, it shaped Latin monastic hagiography.

The Life of Malchus, the Captive Monk is a short Latin hagiography written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 391. Jerome says he heard the story from Malchus himself, an aged monk living at Maronia in Syria. Malchus had left his monastery and was captured by Bedouin raiders. He was enslaved and forced to marry a fellow captive, but the two lived together chastely and finally escaped. The work celebrates chastity and monastic obedience, and it is the only record of Malchus.

The Life of Paul the First Hermit (Vita Sancti Pauli Eremitae) is a short Latin saint's life by Jerome. He wrote it around 375–376, probably while living as a hermit in the Syrian desert. Jerome argues that Paul of Thebes, not Antony, was the first Christian hermit. In his story, Paul flees the Decian persecution and lives for decades in an Egyptian desert cave, fed by a raven. Antony visits him and later buries him, and lions dig the grave. Jerome's first saint's life, it strongly shaped medieval monastic devotion, though scholars have questioned whether Paul really existed.

De viris illustribus (On Illustrious Men) is a Latin collection of short biographies and bibliographies of Christian writers. Jerome compiled it at Bethlehem in 392–393 and dedicated it to Nummius Aemilianus Dexter. It has a preface and 135 chapters, running from the apostles to Jerome himself. He modelled it on Suetonius's lives of pagan men of letters, presented it as a defence of Christian learning and took much of the early material from Eusebius. It was continued by Gennadius of Massilia and later by Isidore of Seville, and it is a key source for early Christian literary history.

Jerome wrote this preface to his Latin translation of the Book of Daniel from the Hebrew and Aramaic around 392 and addressed it to Paula and Eustochium. He explains that the churches read Theodotion's Greek version rather than the Septuagint, which he judged far from the original. He notes that parts of Daniel are written in Aramaic ("Chaldee") and recalls how hard he worked to learn that language. He also observes that the Jews counted Daniel among the Hagiographa rather than the Prophets, and that the Greek additions, such as Susanna, are absent from the Hebrew.

Jerome wrote this preface to his Latin translation of the Book of Job, made directly from the Hebrew around 392–393, while he was living in Bethlehem. He defends his work against critics who saw it as an attack on the Septuagint. He points out that Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion had already produced other Greek versions, and that Origen had marked the Old Testament with obeli and asterisks to show where the older Greek was defective. Jerome stresses that this was especially true of Job, where the Septuagint lacked many passages. The preface shows how he justified translating from the Hebrew.

The Prologus galeatus, or "Helmeted Preface," is Jerome's Latin preface to his translation from Hebrew of the books of Samuel and Kings, written about 391–392 and addressed to Paula and Eustochium. It was the first of his prefaces to his Hebrew-based translations. In it he sets out his method and lists the books of the Hebrew canon, which he counts as twenty-two to match the Hebrew alphabet. He classes Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit and the Shepherd of Hermas as outside the canon. This made it a key text in later debates over the Old Testament canon.

This short Latin preface was written by Jerome for his translation of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs from the Hebrew. It is addressed to the bishops Chromatius of Aquileia and Heliodorus of Altinum and is usually dated to the 390s. Jerome thanks them for paying for his secretaries and copyists, and says that, though weakened by illness, he finished the work in three days. The preface is best known for its view of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus: the Church may read them to build up the people, but not to establish doctrine.

This Latin dedicatory letter, known from its opening words as Novum opus, is the preface Jerome addressed to Pope Damasus I with his revised Latin text of the four Gospels. It is usually dated to about 383. Jerome explains that, at the pope's request, he corrected the widely differing Old Latin copies against Greek manuscripts. He expects to be attacked as a forger and defends the work. He also explains how to use the Eusebian Canons. The letter introduced the Vulgate Gospels and was copied at the start of many medieval Gospel books.

This is a collection of the Latin prefaces that Jerome (c. 347–420) wrote between about 380 and 415. They introduce his early translations, such as Eusebius's Chronicle, which he translated at Constantinople in 381–82. Others open his Old Testament versions, later part of the Vulgate, and his biblical commentaries. Addressed to friends and patrons, they explain how he went about translating, defend his return to the Hebrew text over the Septuagint and answer his critics. They are key evidence for his views on scholarship, the biblical canon and translation.

The Letters are the surviving correspondence of Leo the Great, bishop of Rome from 440 to 461. The collection includes some letters sent to Leo as well as his own. Writing to bishops, emperors, empresses and councils, Leo dealt with church discipline, Pelagian, Manichaean and Priscillianist errors, and the Eutychian controversy. The best known is Letter 28, the Tome to Flavian of Constantinople, which set out the two natures of Christ in one person and shaped the Council of Chalcedon. The letters are a major source for the growth of papal authority.

This is a collection of Latin sermons, also known as Tractatus, preached in Rome by Pope Leo I (Leo the Great) during his pontificate from 440 to 461. Most follow the liturgical year, with sermons for Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, the Passion, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost and the seasonal fasts. Others mark the anniversaries of his ordination, the feast of Peter and Paul, and collections for the poor. Written in polished, rhythmic prose, they set out Leo's teaching on the two natures of Christ and on the authority of Peter's see, and they shaped later Latin preaching and liturgy.

The Epistolae Septem, or Doubtful Letters, are seven Latin letters handed down under the name of Sulpicius Severus, the late fourth- and early fifth-century Aquitanian writer and biographer of Martin of Tours. His authorship is doubted or rejected, and the real writer or writers and the date are uncertain. The letters are personal and spiritual. Some are addressed to a woman the writer calls his sister, encouraging ascetic Christian living, renunciation of the world and perseverance in the Lord's precepts. They show the devotional and ascetic correspondence circulating in the Latin West in late antiquity.

Rufinus of Aquileia wrote this short Latin treatise, usually called De adulteratione librorum Origenis, around 397. He addressed it to Macarius and attached it to his Latin translation of Pamphilus the Martyr's Apology for Origen. Rufinus argues that heretics had tampered with Origen's writings, and he cites cases where the works of other respected Church writers were also corrupted. The treatise was his reason for removing apparently unorthodox passages when he translated Origen's On First Principles. It became part of the bitter Origenist controversy between Rufinus and Jerome.

This is a collection of the prefaces and closing remarks that Rufinus of Aquileia attached to his Latin works and translations from Greek, written between his return to Italy in 397 and about 410. They introduce his commentary on Jacob's blessings of the twelve patriarchs, written at Paulinus of Nola's request, and his versions of Pamphilus's Apology for Origen, Origen's Peri Archon and other works, the pseudo-Clementine Recognitions, the Sentences of Sextus and Eusebius's Church History. The prefaces explain how Rufinus translated and defend his handling of Origen, a matter at the centre of his quarrel with Jerome.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in seven books by Socrates of Constantinople, also called Socrates Scholasticus. It was written in the 440s and continues Eusebius's history, covering events from 305 to 439: Constantine's conversion, the Arian controversy, the councils, and the affairs of the churches of the eastern empire. Socrates aimed for a plain style and drew on documents and on eyewitnesses. Sozomen used the work as a source. In the sixth century it was put into Latin as part of the Historia Tripartita, which carried it into the medieval West.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in nine books by Sozomen, a lawyer at Constantinople. He wrote it around the 440s and dedicated it to Emperor Theodosius II. It was meant to continue the work of Eusebius and covers events from the 320s to the 420s. The ninth book seems unfinished and stops short of the end date the author announced. Sozomen drew heavily on Socrates Scholasticus but added much material of his own, especially on monasticism, missions and the Church outside the empire. It is a key source for fourth- and early fifth-century Christianity.

The Dialogues are a Latin hagiographical work by Sulpicius Severus, the Aquitanian writer and biographer of Martin of Tours, composed in the early fifth century. Written as conversations between the author, his friend Postumianus, just back from the East, and Gallus, a Gaulish disciple of Martin, they first tell of the monks and hermits of Egypt and the East. They then turn to further miracles and deeds of Martin, presenting him as the equal of the famous Eastern ascetics. The work adds to Sulpicius's earlier Life of Martin and is an important source for early Western monasticism.

The three Latin letters of Sulpicius Severus (c. 363 – c. 425), a Christian writer from Aquitaine, add to his Life of Saint Martin of Tours. The first, to the priest Eusebius, answers a critic who asked why Martin, said to have worked miracles, had himself been put in danger by a fire. The second, to the deacon Aurelius, tells of a vision of Martin and mourns his death in 397. The third, to Bassula, the author's mother-in-law, describes Martin's last days and funeral. Together they form an important part of the early cult of Martin.

The Vita Sancti Martini is a Latin biography of Martin, bishop of Tours, written by the Aquitanian writer Sulpicius Severus, who knew him personally. It was completed around 396–397, apparently while Martin was still alive, and is introduced by a dedicatory letter to Desiderius. It covers Martin's military service, including the famous sharing of his cloak with a beggar, his monastic life, his work as bishop and his many miracles. It became one of the most influential models for later Western hagiography.

The Chronica, also called the Sacred History, is a Latin universal chronicle in two books by Sulpicius Severus, the Aquitanian writer best known for his Life of Saint Martin of Tours. Written in the early fifth century, it covers events from the creation of the world to the author's own time. It summarises the Old Testament and the life of Christ, then the persecutions, the Arian controversy and the Priscillianist affair, using secular historians to fix dates. Its brief, classical style earned Sulpicius the name "the Christian Sallust." Its accounts of fourth-century church conflicts are a valuable historical source.

The first class of the letters of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in the traditional Benedictine arrangement: sixty-three letters written between about 374 and 397. They include his correspondence with the emperors Gratian, Valentinian II and Theodosius I. Among them are his letters opposing the restoration of the Altar of Victory in the Roman Senate, with the pagan prefect Symmachus's petition (Relatio III) preserved alongside. The collection also contains his sermon against Auxentius on surrendering the basilicas. It is a key source for relations between church and state in the late fourth century.

This is a polemical Christological treatise by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, written around 430–431. It answers in turn each of the Twelve Anathemas that Cyril of Alexandria attached to his letter to Nestorius. Speaking from the Antiochene tradition, Theodoret argues that God the Word is immutable and was not changed into flesh but took flesh. He also insists that Christ's divine and human natures remain distinct. The work survives mainly through the quotations in Cyril's reply. Because it opposed Cyril, it was condemned posthumously as one of the Three Chapters at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in five books by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was written around 449–450 and continues the history of Eusebius of Caesarea. It begins with the rise of Arianism under Constantine and ends in 429, with the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Theodoret writes from a firmly Nicene and Antiochene viewpoint and focuses on the struggle against Arianism. He quotes many letters, creeds and synodal documents in full. Along with the histories of Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen, it is one of the main sources for fourth-century church history.

The Apocalypse of Moses is the Greek version of the Life of Adam and Eve. It is an anonymous apocryphal narrative presented as a revelation given to Moses through the archangel Michael. It tells of Adam and Eve after their expulsion from paradise, including Abel's murder, Adam's final illness, Eve's own account of the Fall, Adam's death and burial, and the promise of resurrection. Its date and origin are disputed. Some scholars see a Jewish work of the first century, while others regard it as a Christian Greek composition from as late as the fifth century.

This short Latin letter is attributed to Pope Deusdedit (Adeodatus I, 615–618) and addressed to a Bishop Gordianus, styled bishop of Seville. During the crowded Easter Vigil baptisms, some parents had unknowingly received their own children from the font as sponsors. The bishop asked whether these couples could resume married life. Citing precedents attributed to Popes Julius, Innocent and Celestine, the letter orders such couples to separate. It also forbids a man to marry his co-godmother (commater). Its authenticity is doubted, partly because Isidore, not Gordianus, held the see of Seville at that time.

This short Latin decree on the election of the Roman pontiff is issued in the name of Pope Deusdedit (Adeodatus I, 615–618). It survives in the collection of Udalric of Bamberg, and its authenticity is doubtful. The same text is also attributed to Stephen IV, to Stephen VI, or to a forger. It orders that a new pope be chosen by the bishops and clergy, at the request of the senate and people. He is then to be consecrated in public, with imperial legates present, so that disorder is prevented and the emperor's honour is preserved.

De Antichristo, also known as De ortu et tempore Antichristi, is a Latin treatise in letter form. Adso, a monk and later abbot of Montier-en-Der, wrote it around 949–954 for Queen Gerberga, wife of Louis IV of West Francia. Drawing on biblical exegesis, the Church Fathers and Sibylline lore, it tells the Antichrist's life like a saint's life in reverse: his birth from the tribe of Dan, his deceptions, persecution and destruction. It also predicts that a last Frankish king will reign before him. It became the most widely copied medieval account of the Antichrist.

This short Latin doctrinal letter, the "Letter to Armenius on the Rule of Faith", is attributed to Agnellus, bishop of Ravenna from 557 to 570. It was written at the request of a certain brother Martinus to support Armenius, whose faith someone had unsettled with conflicting arguments. Citing Scripture, the letter defends Catholic teaching on God and the Trinity. It argues that God was always Father and the Son eternally begotten, a position directed against Arian views. It reflects Agnellus's work to establish Catholic orthodoxy in Ravenna after the end of Arian Gothic rule.

The Interpretatio mystica progenitorum Christi is a short Latin exegetical treatise attributed to Ailerán the Wise, an Irish scholar associated with Clonard who died in 664 or 665. It takes the names in the genealogy of Christ and interprets them allegorically and morally, drawing on earlier authorities for the meanings of Hebrew names. It is an important witness to biblical learning in seventh-century Ireland. Early modern editors printed it with the sermons attributed to Columbanus because it was too short to publish alone.

This Latin exegetical treatise is attributed to Ailerán the Wise, an Irish scholar associated with Clonard who died in 664 or 665. It forms the moral part of his interpretation of the names in Christ's genealogy. It follows a mystical reading of the same names and reinterprets each ancestor, from Abraham, Isaac and Jacob onward, as an image of the virtues a Christian should gain and the vices to be uprooted. It draws on Cassian and on the established meanings of Hebrew names. It is an early example of Hiberno-Latin biblical scholarship.

This is a set of excerpts from the theological question-and-answer writings of Alcuin of York (c. 735–804), the Anglo-Saxon scholar at Charlemagne's court and later abbot of Tours. It draws on his questions on the Trinity, addressed to his pupil Fredegisus, and on his questions on Genesis. In short questions and answers, it explains the unity of substance and trinity of persons in God, the properties of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and matters of Christ's incarnation and divinity. The format is typical of Carolingian teaching.

This short Latin charter is attributed to Alphanus, bishop of Benevento. It is dated to the twenty-fourth year of Arichis, duke of the Lombards, in the fourth indiction, which probably places it in the early seventh century. In it the bishop frees the church of Saint Martin from episcopal claims. The church was built and consecrated on the estate of Trasemund, a Lombard schultheis. The charter gives Trasemund and his heirs the right to choose its priest, who was still to be ordained by the bishop. It is a rare witness to private church foundations in Lombard southern Italy.

The Questions on the Old and New Testament is a Latin collection of short treatises in question-and-answer form. It was handed down among the works of Augustine, but it is now generally assigned to the anonymous Roman writer known as Ambrosiaster, who also wrote a commentary on Paul's epistles. It was composed in the later fourth century and survives in several recensions, including this one of 127 questions. It covers the nature of God, difficult biblical passages and doctrinal questions. It also argues against pagans, Jews and heretics, and it is valuable evidence for Roman Christianity of its time.

The Conflict of Vices and Virtues is a Latin moral treatise by Ambrose Autpert, the Frankish Benedictine abbot of San Vincenzo al Volturno, written between about 760 and his death in 784. In the Middle Ages it circulated under the names of Augustine and Isidore of Seville. Taking up Paul's saying that all who live godly lives will suffer persecution, it argues that in peaceful times Christians are persecuted from within by the vices. It then pairs each vice with the virtue that opposes it. The treatise was widely copied and read as a guide to the spiritual life.

The Conflict of Vices and Virtues is a Latin moral treatise by Ambrose Autpert, the Frankish Benedictine abbot of San Vincenzo al Volturno, written between about 760 and his death in 784. In the Middle Ages it circulated under the names of Augustine and Isidore of Seville. Taking up Paul's saying that all who live godly lives will suffer persecution, it argues that in peaceful times Christians are persecuted from within by the vices. It then pairs each vice with the virtue that opposes it. The treatise was widely copied and read as a guide to the spiritual life.

This Latin synodal letter was sent by Ambrose of Milan and his fellow bishops to Pope Siricius, probably around 393. It answers Siricius's report that a Roman synod had condemned the monk Jovinian and his followers. The bishops summarise and refute Jovinian's teachings: that marriage equals virginity in merit, that Mary did not remain a virgin in giving birth, and that fasting has no value. They argue that his views on Christ's birth support the Manichaeans, and they endorse the condemnation. The letter is an important early witness to the doctrine of Mary's perpetual virginity.

De interpellatione Iob et David ("On the Complaint of Job and David") is a Latin moral-exegetical treatise in four books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan. It was probably first preached as sermons and later revised for reading. Scholars usually place it in the 380s, though the exact date is uncertain. Drawing on Job and on Psalms of David, starting with Psalm 41, Ambrose discusses human weakness, the suffering of the righteous and the apparent prosperity of the wicked. He argues that the hope of future glory outweighs the troubles of the present life.

The Apology of the Prophet David is a Latin exegetical treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, dedicated to the emperor Theodosius I. Its date is uncertain; some scholars link it to the emperor's penance after the massacre at Thessalonica in 390. It defends David's sins of adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah by reading the story in 2 Samuel and Psalm 50 (51). It presents David as a model of repentance, humility and penance for rulers who sin.

The Apologia altera prophetae David (Second Apology for the Prophet David) is a Latin sermon handed down among the works of Ambrose, bishop of Milan (c. 339–397), though scholars have long questioned whether he wrote it. It takes as its starting point the title of Psalm 50 (51), which tells of Nathan's visit after David's sin with Bathsheba, and the Gospel story of the woman taken in adultery. It defends David's public confession and Christ's pardon against readers who might take either as approval of sin. It treats repentance, humility and divine mercy.

De officiis ministrorum is a Latin ethical treatise in three books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, addressed to his clergy. Its date is debated, but it is usually placed in the late 380s or early 390s. Modelled closely on Cicero's De officiis, it reworks classical Stoic ethics in Christian terms, using biblical examples to discuss duty, the cardinal virtues, and the relation between the honourable and the useful. It is often regarded as the first systematic treatise on Christian ethics.

De Fide ad Gratianum is a dogmatic treatise in five books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, written at the request of the Western emperor Gratian. Books one and two are usually dated to about 378, and books three to five to about 380. Ambrose relies mainly on the authority of Scripture and the Council of Nicaea to defend the full divinity of the Son and his equality with the Father against Arian teaching. It is one of the main Latin anti-Arian works of the fourth century, and Ambrose followed it with his treatise On the Holy Spirit.

De Spiritu Sancto is a Latin theological treatise in three books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan. He addressed it to the emperor Gratian and completed it around 381. It defends the full divinity of the Holy Spirit and the Spirit's equality with the Father and the Son, against Arian and Pneumatomachian views. Ambrose built his argument from scriptural exegesis and typology, such as Gideon's fleece, and drew heavily on Greek writers, especially Basil of Caesarea and Didymus the Blind. This transmitted Eastern pneumatology to the Latin West, although Jerome criticised the work for its borrowings.

De incarnationis dominicae sacramento ("On the Mystery of the Lord's Incarnation") is a Latin treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, usually dated to about 381–382. It began as preaching delivered after Arian opponents had challenged him. It opens with the offerings of Cain and Abel, then turns to Christology. Ambrose defends both the full divinity of the Son against Arian teaching and the completeness of Christ's human nature, including a human soul, against Apollinarian views. The work is an important witness to Western teaching on the incarnation in the decades after the Council of Nicaea.

This short Latin confession of faith on the person of Christ is attributed to Ambrose of Milan, bishop from 374 to 397. It survives as a fragment quoted by Theodoret of Cyrrhus in his patristic florilegia. It confesses one Christ, the only-begotten Son, who is eternally begotten of the Father and became incarnate of the Virgin Mary. He is consubstantial with the Father in his divinity and with us in his humanity, and his two perfect natures are united without mixture or change. Its authenticity is doubted, because its terminology closely resembles the Christological formulas of the fifth century.

The first class of the letters of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in the traditional Benedictine arrangement: sixty-three letters written between about 374 and 397. They include his correspondence with the emperors Gratian, Valentinian II and Theodosius I. Among them are his letters opposing the restoration of the Altar of Victory in the Roman Senate, with the pagan prefect Symmachus's petition (Relatio III) preserved alongside. The collection also contains his sermon against Auxentius on surrendering the basilicas. It is a key source for relations between church and state in the late fourth century.

De virginibus is a Latin treatise in three books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, addressed to his sister Marcellina, a consecrated virgin. Usually dated to about 377, early in his episcopate, it seems to have grown out of his sermons. It praises consecrated virginity as a heavenly way of life. It holds up models such as the martyr Agnes, the Virgin Mary and Thecla, and it recalls the address Pope Liberius gave at Marcellina's veiling in Rome. It is among the earliest major Latin works on virginity and shaped later Western ascetic teaching.

This group of Latin letters by Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397, makes up what the Benedictine editors called the "second class" of his correspondence. It gathers letters with no clear internal evidence of date and arranges them by subject instead of chronologically. The first are expositions of passages of Scripture, such as the opening letter to Irenaeus presenting Christ's Body as the true manna. Next come discussions of mainly doctrinal questions, and the group ends with brief letters of friendship. Together they show Ambrose's allegorical exegesis and his pastoral guidance.

This is a pair of funeral orations by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, for his brother Satyrus, who gave up a public career to manage the church's secular affairs. Satyrus died unexpectedly at Milan, probably in 378, at a time of fear over barbarian invasions. Ambrose delivered the first book at the funeral. It praises his brother's virtues and expresses personal grief. The second, delivered a week later at the tomb, is a treatise on the resurrection. The work draws on classical consolation literature and is an important early Christian example of the genre.

De Obitu Valentiniani Consolatio is a Latin funeral oration by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, for the young Western emperor Valentinian II. Valentinian was found dead in Gaul in May 392, and the speech was delivered at Milan later that year. Ambrose mourns the emperor and praises his piety and his willingness to come to Italy's defence. He also consoles Valentinian's sisters. Because Valentinian died while still preparing for baptism, Ambrose argues that his desire for it was enough to save him. The work is therefore an important early witness to the idea of "baptism of desire."

De Obitu Theodosii is the Latin funeral oration Ambrose, bishop of Milan, gave for the emperor Theodosius I, who died in January 395. Ambrose delivered it in Milan on the fortieth day after the emperor's death, with the young emperor Honorius present. He praises Theodosius for his piety, his mercy and his public penance. He also urges the army to stay loyal to the emperor's sons. The speech is known for its account of the empress Helena finding the True Cross. It is an important example of the Christian imperial funeral speech.

This is a collection of Latin liturgical hymns attributed to Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397. They are written in iambic dimeter and grouped in four-line stanzas. They include "Aeterne rerum conditor", a hymn for cockcrow, "Deus creator omnium", for evening, and "Iam surgit hora tertia", for the third hour. Augustine confirms that these three, with "Veni redemptor gentium", are by Ambrose. Many other hymns traditionally ascribed to him are of doubtful authorship. Ambrose introduced congregational hymn-singing at Milan, and his hymns became the model for Latin hymnody in the West.

De Viduis (Concerning Widows) is a Latin treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, usually dated to about 377. Ambrose wrote it soon after his three books On Virgins, which it follows directly. It praises widowhood as a state of chastity devoted to God, close in honour to virginity. Its models include the widow of Zarephath who received Elijah, Anna, Naomi, Judith and Deborah, and it stresses hospitality, prayer and self-restraint. It discourages widows from remarrying without condemning second marriage. It belongs to Ambrose's influential ascetical writings on Christian women.

De virginitate is a Latin treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397. It is usually dated to around 377–378, shortly after his three books De virginibus, and is distinct from that earlier work. It opens with an allegorical reading of Solomon's judgement between the two women and goes on to the story of Jephthah's daughter. Ambrose praises consecrated virginity and answers critics of his teaching on the subject. With his other ascetic writings, it shaped Latin thought on the religious life of women.

De institutione virginis is a Latin treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, usually dated to about 391–392. It is addressed to a father named Eusebius, generally identified as a man from Bologna, on the consecration of his daughter Ambrosia as a virgin. Ambrose praises virginity and modesty, holding up Mary as the model for consecrated women. He also defends her perpetual virginity against contemporary deniers, notably Bonosus. It is one of his several writings on virginity and an important early witness to Marian doctrine in the Latin West.

The Exhortatio virginitatis (Exhortation to Virginity) is a Latin treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, usually dated to about 393–394. It was delivered as a sermon at Florence for the dedication of a basilica founded by a widow named Juliana, where Ambrose placed relics of the martyrs Vitalis and Agricola, recently found at Bologna. The work opens with the story of these martyrs, a slave and his master. Through Juliana's words to her children, it then praises consecrated virginity and widowhood. It is one of Ambrose's several writings on the ascetic life.

De lapsu virginis consecratae (On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin) is a short Latin treatise of the late fourth century. It has come down among the works of Ambrose of Milan, but his authorship is doubted, and many scholars assign it to Nicetas of Remesiana. The author mourns publicly over a noble, educated virgin dedicated to Christ who has fallen into sexual sin and borne a child. He rebukes her and her seducer and urges her to do lifelong penance. It is an important witness to early Christian ideals of consecrated virginity and to the practice of ecclesiastical penance.

On the Mysteries (De Mysteriis) is a short Latin mystagogical treatise by Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397. Its exact date is uncertain. It is addressed to the newly baptized, and explains the rites of Christian initiation only after they have received them. It covers the opening of the ears, the baptismal font, the anointing and spiritual seal, and the Eucharist, which it reads through Old Testament types. It closely parallels De Sacramentis, and it is an important witness to fourth-century Western liturgy and sacramental theology.

De Sacramentis is a Latin work in six books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397. It consists of mystagogical sermons given during Easter week to the newly baptized, apparently taken down as they were preached. They explain the rites of initiation: the opening of the ears ("Ephphatha"), baptism, anointing, the Eucharist and the Lord's Prayer. Its authorship was long disputed, but most scholars now accept it as Ambrose's. It closely parallels his De mysteriis and contains the earliest surviving witness to the Roman Canon of the Mass.

De paenitentia (Concerning Repentance) is a Latin treatise in two books by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, written during his episcopate (374–397). It is aimed against the Novatians, who denied that the Church could forgive grave sins committed after baptism. Ambrose praises gentleness as a virtue that church leaders need, following the example of Christ the Good Shepherd. He argues from Scripture that the Church has received the power to bind and loose, and he urges sinners to do sincere penance. It is an important witness to early Western teaching and practice of penance.

This is a Latin commentary on Paul's Second Letter to the Thessalonians. It belongs to a series of commentaries on the Pauline epistles that was long transmitted under the name of Ambrose of Milan. Modern scholarship generally credits the series to the anonymous writer known as Ambrosiaster, who worked in Rome in the later fourth century. The commentary goes through the letter verse by verse. Its prologue says Paul writes, though obscurely, about the end of the Roman kingdom, the appearance and condemnation of Antichrist, and the restlessness of some members of the community.

This Latin commentary on Paul's First Epistle to Timothy has long been transmitted among the works of Ambrose of Milan. Scholars now attribute it to the anonymous writer known as Ambrosiaster, who wrote at Rome in the later fourth century, probably during the pontificate of Damasus (366–384). It is one part of his commentary on the thirteen Pauline epistles. A prologue describes Timothy's background and his circumcision, and calls the letter Paul's instruction to a newly appointed bishop on how to order the Church. The commentary then explains the epistle verse by verse, with attention to its plain sense.

This is a Latin commentary on Paul's Second Epistle to Timothy. It forms part of a series of commentaries on the Pauline letters that was long transmitted under the name of Ambrose of Milan. Since Erasmus, scholars have attributed it to the anonymous author now called Ambrosiaster, who probably wrote in Rome in the later fourth century. The commentary follows the letter verse by verse. It stresses Paul's encouragement of Timothy towards steadfastness and martyrdom, the faithful handing on of sound teaching, and warnings against false doctrines.

This is a Latin commentary on Paul's Epistle to Titus, part of a verse-by-verse commentary on the thirteen Pauline letters. It was long transmitted among the works of Ambrose of Milan, but scholars now attribute it to the anonymous author known as "Ambrosiaster," who wrote in Rome in the later fourth century, probably during the pontificate of Damasus (366–384). The commentary treats Titus as a bishop Paul appointed in Crete. It deals with the qualifications for clergy, church order and the correction of Judaizing opponents.

This is a short Latin commentary on Paul's Letter to Philemon that works through the epistle verse by verse. It was long transmitted and printed among the works of Ambrose of Milan. Most scholars now assign it to the anonymous author known as Ambrosiaster, who wrote commentaries on the Pauline epistles in Rome in the later fourth century, probably during the pontificate of Damasus (366–384). The prologue presents Philemon as a respected layman rather than a cleric. It explains that Paul writes on behalf of Philemon's slave Onesimus, asking that Philemon forgive him and receive him as a beloved brother.

This Latin commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Romans was long transmitted among the works of Ambrose of Milan. Since Erasmus, scholars have attributed it to an unknown author known as Ambrosiaster, who probably wrote in Rome under Pope Damasus (366–384). Its prologue explains the origins of the Roman church among Jewish believers who kept the Law. The commentary goes on to explain the epistle verse by verse. It is an important early witness to the Old Latin text of Paul and to Latin teaching on grace, sin and justification before Augustine.

The Explanatio symboli ad initiandos is a short Latin catechetical sermon attributed to Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397. It was preached to candidates for baptism at the ceremony of the "handing over of the Creed" and seems to have been taken down by a listener. Ambrose explains the word symbolum, says the Creed was composed jointly by the apostles, and stresses the equal divinity of the Trinity. The sermon is an important witness to the baptismal creed used at Milan and to fourth-century catechesis.

This is a Latin commentary on Paul's First Epistle to the Corinthians. It has long been transmitted among the works of Ambrose of Milan, but it is now generally assigned to the anonymous author known as Ambrosiaster. He wrote commentaries on the Pauline letters, probably in Rome around 366–384. A prologue lists the reasons Paul wrote to Corinth, including factions, worldly philosophy, the incestuous man, lawsuits, marriage and virginity. The commentary then explains the letter verse by verse. It is an important early witness to Latin biblical interpretation and to the Old Latin text of Paul.

This is a Latin commentary on Paul's Second Epistle to the Corinthians. It was long transmitted among the works of Ambrose of Milan, but since Erasmus scholars have attributed it to the anonymous writer known as Ambrosiaster. That writer was active in Rome in the later fourth century, probably under Pope Damasus. Its prologue says Paul wrote the letter to comfort the Corinthians after the sharp rebukes of the first epistle. It then explains the text verse by verse, keeping to the literal and historical sense, and is an important witness to the Old Latin text of Paul.

A Latin commentary on Paul's Letter to the Galatians, long transmitted among the works of Ambrose of Milan but now generally assigned to the anonymous author known as Ambrosiaster. It belongs to his series of commentaries on the thirteen Pauline epistles, probably written in Rome during the pontificate of Damasus (366–384). The prologue opposes Christians who keep the Mosaic Law, such as the Symmachians, whose view of Christ it likens to Photinus'. It argues that faith alone is enough for salvation and that circumcision, sabbaths and food laws have ceased.

This Latin commentary on Paul's Letter to the Ephesians was long transmitted under the name of Ambrose of Milan. Scholars now generally attribute it to the anonymous author called "Ambrosiaster," who wrote commentaries on the thirteen Pauline epistles at Rome, probably during the pontificate of Damasus (366–384). After a short prologue noting that Paul strengthened rather than founded the Ephesian church and wrote while in custody at Rome, it explains the letter verse by verse. It is an important witness to early Latin exegesis and the Old Latin biblical text.

This is a Latin commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Philippians. It belongs to a commentary series on the thirteen Pauline letters that was long transmitted under the name of Ambrose of Milan. Scholars now generally credit the series to the anonymous writer called Ambrosiaster, who probably worked in Rome in the later fourth century. A prologue explains the letter's background and praises the Philippians' steadfast faith. The commentary then explains the text verse by verse, emphasising its literal and historical sense and attacking heresies such as those of Photinus and the Manichaeans.

This is a Latin commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Colossians, part of a commentary on the thirteen Pauline letters that was long transmitted under the name of Ambrose of Milan. Modern scholars attribute it to an anonymous writer known as "Ambrosiaster", who probably worked in Rome in the later fourth century, under Pope Damasus. A short prologue explains that false apostles were trying to lead the Colossians astray with philosophy. The commentary then works through the text verse by verse, giving a mainly literal and historical reading of it.

This is a Latin commentary on Paul's First Epistle to the Thessalonians. It has long been transmitted among the works of Ambrose of Milan, but it belongs to the Pauline commentaries now generally credited to the anonymous author known as Ambrosiaster, who wrote in Rome in the later fourth century. A short prologue explains that Paul praises the Thessalonians for persevering under persecution so that their example will encourage others. The commentary then goes through the letter verse by verse, giving a concise, mainly literal explanation of its moral and doctrinal teaching.

The Sermones tres are three short Latin sermons attributed to Ambrose, bishop of Milan from 374 to 397. They survive in a manuscript once held in the Sessorian library at Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Rome, which gives the collection its name. The first, "De perfecto", treats Christ's command in Luke 12:33 to sell all one's possessions and give alms, and reads it as a call to Christian perfection. Their attribution to Ambrose is uncertain, and scholars have generally treated them as doubtful or spurious.

A short Latin poem in hexameters arranged as a series of quatrains. Each quatrain has a heading and describes a scene from the Old or New Testament, starting with Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel and Noah's ark. Under the name Amoenus, an otherwise unknown figure, the poem has been transmitted and printed as an "Enchiridion of the Old and New Testament". It is generally identified with the Dittochaeon (Tituli historiarum) of Prudentius, from around 400. The verses read like captions for a sequence of biblical pictures, perhaps church murals, and they show early Christian typological reading of Scripture.

This short Latin hexameter poem is attributed to Amoenus, an obscure Christian poet. It tells of a miracle connected with Saint Martin of Tours. A ship sailing across the Tyrrhenian Sea towards Rome is caught in a violent storm, and the crew is helpless. An Egyptian on board, not yet a Christian, cries out "God of Martin, save us!", and the sea at once grows calm. The story matches a miracle told in Sulpicius Severus's writings on Martin. The poem's date is uncertain. It is probably from the late fourth or fifth century.

This Latin abecedarian hymn is attributed in some collections to an obscure poet named Amoenus. It is more commonly printed among the poems of Venantius Fortunatus. It celebrates Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, coming back to his church. A false report of his death had led a rival to plot for his see, and the poem condemns that ambition. It holds up Hilary, Martin and Gregory as clergy who did not seek office. It also describes the city's joy when Leontius returned. Because of these disputes, the authorship and date remain uncertain.

This short Latin dedicatory letter is by Anastasius Bibliothecarius, librarian of the Roman see, and dates from the mid-ninth century. He addressed it to Landuleus, bishop of Capua, whose church held relics of the protomartyr Stephen. With it he sent his Latin translation of a Greek account of the translation of Stephen's body, which he had made while staying in Mantua on a papal legation to the emperors. He also enclosed his translation of a sermon by Amphilochius of Iconium on Anna, Simeon and virginity. The letter shows how Anastasius brought Greek hagiography and homilies into Latin.

This is a collection of Latin letters and decrees by Anastasius I, bishop of Rome from 399 to 401. Most belong to the Origenist controversy. The best known is his letter to Bishop John of Jerusalem, which Jerome copied into the second book of his Apology against Rufinus. In it Anastasius condemns Origen's writings, which had recently been translated into Latin, and criticises Rufinus as their translator. Other pieces deal with church affairs in the West, including encouragement to the African Church in its struggle against Donatism.

Pope Anastasius I wrote this Latin letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem, around 400–401. It belongs to the controversy over Origen. After Theophilus of Alexandria urged him to act, Anastasius had condemned Origenism. Rufinus of Aquileia, who was ordained in Jerusalem, had translated Origen's On First Principles into Latin, and Rome took this as a defence of Origen's views. The letter replies to John's inquiry about Rufinus. It opens with warm praise of John and then distances Rome from Rufinus and condemns Origen's writings. Jerome cites the letter. Rufinus doubted it was genuine, but it is generally accepted as authentic.

This Latin letter was written around 400–401 by Pope Anastasius I to John, bishop of Jerusalem, about Rufinus of Aquileia. It was prompted by the controversy over Rufinus's Latin translation of Origen's On First Principles. Anastasius thanks John for his praise, condemns Origen's writings and distances himself from Rufinus and his translation. Jerome cites the letter in his Apology against Rufinus, while Rufinus questioned whether it was genuine. The letter survives among manuscripts of Marius Mercator's writings and is an important document of the Origenist controversy.

These anonymous Latin fragments of Arian (Homoian) theological writing survive only in palimpsest leaves now in Milan and the Vatican. They were first published by Angelo Mai, who added his own refutations. They probably date from the late fourth or early fifth century, but who wrote them and where is unknown. The surviving portions instruct a "dearest brother" in the faith and answer opponents who charged that calling Christ God's Son implied many gods. They are rare direct evidence of Latin Arian thought, which mostly survives only through its critics.

This is a collection of fragmentary Latin sermons preserved in a palimpsest manuscript of the Ambrosian Library in Milan, where the older writing survives beneath a later text. They are anonymous and are attributed to an Arian or Homoian preacher of the late fourth or early fifth century. The surviving pieces are numbered sermons or excerpts from them. They speak of Christ as the foundation and cornerstone of the Church, of the union of heaven and earth in the incarnation, and of believers being transformed "from glory to glory." They are rare evidence for Latin Arian preaching.

The Sermo Arianorum is an anonymous Latin statement of Arian (Homoian) doctrine from the early fifth century. A copy was sent to Augustine of Hippo around 418–419, and he answered it point by point in his Contra sermonem Arianorum, with matching numbers marking each passage. The text presents the Son as the only-begotten God, established by the Father's will before all ages, who created all things at the Father's command and is subordinate to him. It places the Holy Spirit below the Son. It is a rare surviving witness to Latin Arian teaching in North Africa.

The Liberian Catalogue is an anonymous Latin list of the bishops of Rome. It forms part of the Chronography of 354, a collection compiled in Rome in that year. Beginning with Peter and ending with Liberius (bishop 352–366), after whom it is named, it gives the length of each episcopate in years, months and days, with the consuls and emperors of the time. Its early sections are thought to draw on older lists, possibly including one by Hippolytus. It is the earliest surviving papal list of this kind, and the later Liber Pontificalis drew on it.

This is a set of Latin excerpts recording the deaths of martyrs and other events, drawn from two anonymous lists of Roman consuls found in a manuscript once owned by the humanist Johannes Cuspinianus. Both lists begin with Julius Caesar. The older one ends in the late fifth century and the other in 536. An early modern editor copied the notes on saints and events, often with Roman calendar dates, together with the consuls of each year so they could be dated. Their tie to the Chronography of 354 is uncertain.

This is the short biographical entry on Pope Stephen I (bishop of Rome c. 254–257) in the Liber Pontificalis, the anonymous Latin collection of papal lives. Its earliest form was compiled in Rome around the 530s. In the collection's usual format, the entry names Stephen as a Roman by birth and son of Julius, gives the length of his pontificate, and records his disciplinary measures and ordinations. It is late and often unreliable as history. Its value lies in showing how sixth-century Rome remembered a third-century pope, best known for his dispute with Cyprian of Carthage over rebaptism.

This is the short biography of Pope Simplicius (bishop of Rome 468–483) from the Liber Pontificalis, the anonymous collection of papal lives whose first edition was compiled in Rome around the 530s. It records that Simplicius was a native of Tibur, the son of Castinus, and gives the length of his pontificate. It also notes his dedication of Roman churches, including Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill and a basilica of Saint Andrew, and his condemnation of an Eutychian bishop of Alexandria named Peter after a report from Acacius of Constantinople.

This is the short biography of Pope Mark, bishop of Rome for most of 336 under Constantine, as given in the Liber Pontificalis. That anonymous collection of papal lives was first compiled in Rome around the 530s. The notice states that Mark was Roman by birth and the son of Priscus, and gives the length of his pontificate. It also credits him with decreeing that the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates the bishop of Rome, should wear the pallium. Like other early entries in the collection, it mixes historical record with later tradition.

These are anonymous fragments of a Greek onomasticon, a glossary that explains the meanings of Hebrew names found in Scripture. It belongs to the tradition of the "Onomastica sacra". Short entries give symbolic or etymological meanings for patriarchs, places, prophets and angels, and for terms such as Amen, Alleluia, Seraphim and Cherubim. For example, Bethlehem is "house of bread" and Abraham is "father of mercies". Its date and author are unknown. Glossaries like this one were used in allegorical exegesis. This one is usually read alongside Jerome's Latin book of Hebrew names, which drew on similar Greek material.

The Lexicon Origenianum nominum Hebraicorum is an anonymous Latin glossary of biblical proper names. It is arranged alphabetically and gives one or more Latin meanings for each Hebrew, Aramaic or Greek name, such as Adam, "earthly man" or "red earth". It belongs to the tradition of sacred onomastica, which was associated with Origen and is best known in the West through Jerome's book of Hebrew names. Such lists served allegorical exegesis, where the meaning of a name could carry spiritual sense. Its date and compiler are unknown.

This anonymous Latin glossary explains the meanings of biblical proper names. It is one version of the so-called "Origenian lexicon", a tradition of name lists that ancient writers linked to Origen, whose work Jerome reworked in his own book on Hebrew names. The entries are arranged alphabetically under Old Testament headings and give short etymologies, such as "Adam, earthly, or red earth" and "Abraham, father of nations". Neither its compiler nor its date is known. Lists like this one gave early Christian interpreters a tool for allegorical and spiritual readings of Scripture.

De decem Dei nominibus is a short anonymous chapter on the ten Hebrew names of God, transmitted among the Onomastica sacra, the early Christian glossaries that explain biblical names. Its author and date are unknown. It closely parallels Jerome's letter to Marcella on the same ten names. It survives in a badly corrupted Greek manuscript and is valued for showing that Greek commentators wrote the Tetragrammaton in Hebrew letters. Some readers mistook those letters for the Greek ΠΙΠΙ and read the name as "Pipi."

This is a short anonymous Greek chapter on the ten Hebrew names of God, including the Tetragrammaton, transmitted with the Onomastica sacra, the early Christian lists explaining biblical names. This is a second copy of the chapter, which also circulated as a fragment ascribed to Evagrius Ponticus. The accompanying editorial preface compares a single faulty Colbertine manuscript with royal manuscripts of the Evagrian fragment. It uses them to restore corrupted forms of the divine names, including the reading Iao. Its date and authorship remain uncertain.

The Liber nominum Hebraicorum ex operibus Philonis collectus is an anonymous Latin glossary of biblical proper names. It is arranged alphabetically, and each Hebrew name of a person or place is followed by a short Latin interpretation, for example "Adam, terra" and "Israel, Deum videns." As its title says, the etymologies were gathered from the works of Philo of Alexandria, whose allegorical exegesis relied heavily on such name meanings. Its date and compiler are unknown. It belongs to the tradition of early Christian onomastica, or lists of sacred names, used as aids to reading Scripture.

The Liber nominum Hebraicorum ex operibus Josephi collectus is an anonymous glossary of Hebrew names, made up of entries taken from the writings of the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus. It belongs to the tradition of onomastica sacra, the lists of biblical names and their meanings that were used in early Christian interpretation of the Bible. The entries are in alphabetical order and give short etymologies, such as Adam as "red," Babel as "confusion" and Bethel as "house of God." It comes with a parallel Greek list. Its author and date are unknown.

This anonymous collection of Latin Mass formularies honours Saint Zeno, the fourth-century bishop of Verona, and was drawn from old sacramentaries. Each Mass gives the proper prayers for his feast: collects, a secret (prayer over the offerings), a preface and related orations. The texts call Zeno "priest and confessor" and praise his steady faith, his chastity, his miracles and his daily preaching to his people. Their date and place of composition are not known. They show how Zeno was venerated in the liturgy, especially at Verona.

Three anonymous Latin collects for the liturgical commemorations of Zeno, fourth-century bishop of Verona. They come from the records of a monastery of St Zeno in the diocese of Salzburg, and their date is unknown. The prayers belong to three feasts: his main feast on 12 April, the translation of his relics on 21 May, and his episcopal ordination on 9 December. They praise Zeno as a teacher and preacher of the Catholic faith and ask for his intercession to obtain forgiveness of sins. They show how his cult spread beyond Verona.

This is an anonymous collection of Latin liturgical texts for the cult of Saint Zeno, the fourth-century bishop of Verona. The selections include antiphons and responsories for the Office of his feast, Mass prayers and the Gospel reading for his commemoration, among them material from the Ambrosian (Milanese) rite. The texts date from different periods, and none can be assigned to a known author. They show how Zeno was venerated in Verona and elsewhere, including the later custom of honouring him as a martyr as well as a confessor bishop.

Contra Arianos Fragmentum is a short, anonymous Latin piece of anti-Arian polemic, tentatively dated between about 360 and 450. It defends Nicene teaching on the Son. It takes up the Arian argument from the terms "begotten" and "unbegotten," which Basil of Caesarea, Ambrose and Augustine also answered. The piece is incomplete and survives as part of a larger lost work. Its first editor cautiously suggested that it might come from Augustine's lost treatises against the Arians, but he admitted that it could belong to another Father. Its authorship remains unknown.

Sermones Dominicales is an anonymous Latin collection of sermons for Sundays. Its date and authorship are uncertain, and it has been tentatively placed between the late fourth and mid-fifth centuries. The sermons address "dearly beloved brethren" and explain the day's scriptural reading. The opening sermon takes up Paul's image of the race in the stadium. It describes the ancient athletic contest, its crown and the runners' abstinence, and then reads these allegorically as the Christian's course through this present life toward salvation. The collection is a witness to early Latin preaching on the liturgical year.

The Expositio Fidei is an anonymous Latin statement of faith, probably composed between the later fourth and mid-fifth centuries. Its author and place of origin are unknown. It professes one God in an undivided Trinity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who share one essence and substance in three persons, and it explicitly rejects Arius' teaching of three unequal natures. It argues that the Father has always been Father, so the Son is eternal too. It is a witness to anti-Arian Trinitarian confession in the Latin West.

The Breviarium fidei adversus Arianos haereticos is an anonymous Latin treatise against Arianism, usually placed between the later fourth and mid-fifth centuries. Its heading calls the author uncertain but very ancient. It sets out to prove the equality of the three divine persons from many passages of Scripture. It begins by arguing that heretics go wrong because they do not see that Christ is one person in two substances. Sayings such as "the Father is greater than I," along with Christ's hunger, weariness and weeping, belong to his humanity, while his miracles show his divinity.

The Calendar of Carthage is an anonymous Latin liturgical calendar of the Church of Carthage, usually dated to the early sixth century, when North Africa was under Vandal rule. It lists the feasts the Carthaginian church kept each year, both the anniversaries (natalitia) of martyrs and the burial days (depositiones) of its bishops. The list begins in April with the African martyr Mappalicus, whom Cyprian praised. It also names Roman and other saints. The calendar is an important witness to the cult of saints and to the liturgy of the late antique African church.

The Acta (or Passio) of Saint Sebastian is an anonymous Latin martyr narrative, usually dated to the fifth century and sometimes attributed to Arnobius the Younger. It presents Sebastian, a native of Milan and citizen of Narbonne, as a commander in the imperial guard under Diocletian and Maximian. He secretly strengthens imprisoned Christians, including the twin brothers Marcellianus and Marcus, and is then shot with arrows, survives, and is finally clubbed to death. This text is the main source for the later cult and iconography of Sebastian.

This anonymous Latin topographical register of the city of Rome belongs to the fourth-century "Regionary Catalogues," surviving in two related versions known as the Curiosum and the Notitia. It is usually dated to the reign of Constantine or his sons, roughly 334–357. It goes through the fourteen Augustan regions in turn, listing temples, baths, arches, warehouses and other landmarks, with counts of streets, shrines, apartment blocks and bakeries.
