An expanded version, later issued under the name of Publius Victor, is not authentic. The catalogues are a key source for the topography of late antique Rome.

The Exhortatio ad monachos is a short Latin ascetic exhortation addressed to monks and transmitted under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria, though he did not write it. Its polished Latin style shows it to be the work of an unknown Latin author. It survives in the collection of monastic rules compiled by Benedict of Aniane in the late eighth or early ninth century, together with a companion exhortation to virgins, the sponsae Christi. It urges abstinence, fasting, patience, constant prayer, and reading or listening to Scripture as the basis of monastic life. Its date is uncertain.

The Exhortation to a Bride of Christ is an anonymous Latin treatise on consecrated virginity. It was handed down under the name of Athanasius of Alexandria, but the attribution is spurious. Its author and date are uncertain, though it is generally placed in the late antique West. The work praises virginity as a life above ordinary human nature. It presents veiled virgins as brides joined to Christ in a spiritual marriage and as a living sacrifice offered to God, citing Paul's letters. It then urges the virgin to keep her vocation through strict discipline and inner virtue.

De laudibus Domini is an anonymous Latin poem in hexameters, once attributed to Juvencus. It was probably written in Gaul, apparently near Autun in the territory of the Aedui, during the reign of Constantine, around 317–324. The poem begins with a local miracle near the river Arar (Saône) and moves on to praise God as creator and Christ as the divine Word. It closes with a tribute to Constantine and his sons. It is valued as one of the earliest surviving Christian Latin poems, and its learned classical style has been widely admired.

The Consultationes Zacchaei Christiani et Apollonii philosophi is an anonymous Latin apologetic dialogue, usually dated to the early fifth century (about 408–410). Apollonius, a pagan philosopher, questions the Christian Zacchaeus about the faith. Zacchaeus answers step by step, setting out the main points of Christian belief and rejecting fate and astrology, until Apollonius accepts the faith. The work goes on to defend Trinitarian doctrine against heresies and to discuss Christian and ascetic life. Its authorship is unknown, and older proposals naming a particular writer remain speculative.

This anonymous Latin legend of Eugenia, virgin and martyr, was probably written in the late fifth or sixth century. It tells how Eugenia, daughter of Philip, prefect of Egypt under Commodus, came to the Christian faith by reading Paul's letters. Dressed as a man, she joined a monastery near Alexandria under Bishop Helenus and later became its abbot. Falsely accused by a woman named Melanthia, she revealed her sex, and her family converted. She was later martyred at Rome. The text is a well-known example of the legend of a woman disguised as a monk.

The Abbreviatio chronicae is a short anonymous Latin chronicle, printed as an appendix to the "Divina bibliotheca", the edition of the Latin Bible associated with Jerome. It is a summary of world history divided into ages. It follows the biblical generations from Adam to Noah and the Flood, then from Shem to Abraham, and onward to the Exodus, adding up the years for each age. Its author, date and place of origin are unknown.

The Martyrologium Hieronymianum is an anonymous Latin martyrology, a calendar listing the commemorations of martyrs and saints. Spurious prefatory letters falsely attribute it to Jerome. It was probably compiled in Italy in the mid-fifth century, and the form that survives reflects a later revision made in Gaul around 600. It draws on Roman, African and Eastern calendars, giving for each day little more than places and names. It is the oldest surviving general martyrology of the Latin West and a basic source for later martyrologies and for the early cult of the saints.

This is an anonymous Latin preface to a set of questions on the Gospels; its author and date are unknown. It praises the Gospel above the rest of Scripture as the fulfilment of the Law and the Prophets, and gives special honour to John the Evangelist. Drawing on traditional patristic material, it says John wrote after returning from exile under Domitian, to oppose heretics who denied Christ's divinity. It explains his eagle symbol and says he filled gaps left by the other three Gospels.

This anonymous Latin martyr account describes the deaths of Vibia Perpetua, a young noblewoman, the slave Felicitas and their companions, who were executed in the arena at Carthage in 203. At its core is Perpetua's own prison diary, written in the first person and recording her visions, together with a vision narrated by her fellow martyr Saturus. An editor framed these with a preface and an account of the martyrdom. Some have identified the editor as Tertullian, but this is disputed. The work is among the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman. A Greek version also exists.

The Muratorian Canon, or Muratorian Fragment, is an anonymous Latin list of New Testament books that may be the oldest of its kind. Ludovico Antonio Muratori published it from an eighth-century codex that came from Bobbio Abbey. It is usually dated about 170–200 and thought to translate a Greek original, but some scholars place it in the fourth century. Its opening and ending are lost. The surviving 85 lines comment on the Gospels, Acts and the epistles, and name the books accepted, disputed or rejected by the churches the compiler knew.

The Liber generationis is an anonymous Latin chronicle reckoning world history from Adam to the time of the emperor Severus Alexander, ending around 235. It is generally regarded as a Latin rendering of the Greek Chronicle attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, though the attribution has been questioned. Its preface lists genealogies of the patriarchs, the division of the earth among Noah's three sons and the nations that came from them, and lists of judges, kings, prophets, priests, Persian, Macedonian and Roman rulers, and bishops of Rome. It is an important early example of Christian chronography.

This is a short Latin editorial notice on the authorship of the anonymous treatise Ad Novatianum, a mid-third-century work against the rigorist schismatic Novatian, who refused to readmit Christians who had lapsed in persecution. The notice argues that the author was a contemporary of Cyprian. It holds that he wrote early in Valerian's reign, after the Decian persecution, and was probably an African bishop. It points to his pun on Felicissimus and his rejection of heretical baptism. It also cites Tillemont, who was reluctant to assign the treatise to Cyprian because of its different style.

The Acta Proconsularia is a short Latin martyr account recording the trials and execution of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. It gives his examination by the proconsul Paternus on 30 August 257, which ended in his exile to Curubis. It then covers his second hearing before Galerius Maximus and his beheading on 14 September 258, during the persecution under Valerian and Gallienus. Its author is anonymous, though it is often transmitted alongside the Life of Cyprian by his deacon Pontius. It is among the most important early Latin acts of the martyrs.

This anonymous Latin account, usually called the Acta Proconsularia, records the trial and martyrdom of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. It was probably composed soon after his death in 258, during the persecution under Valerian. The narrative describes his recall from exile at Curubis and his arrest on 13 September. It then gives his examination before the proconsul Galerius Maximus and his beheading on 14 September. Its brevity and closeness to official court records make it one of the most valuable early Christian martyr acts. It complements the more rhetorical Life of Cyprian by his deacon Pontius.

This anonymous hagiographical legend tells how the relics of Stephen the Protomartyr were moved from Jerusalem to Byzantium (Constantinople). The senator Alexander builds an oratory for Stephen in Jerusalem and is buried beside the martyr. Years later his widow Juliana sets out to take her husband's body to Byzantium, and the story turns on the arrival there of Stephen's remains. The legend comes from a Greek original of uncertain date and author. This Latin version is credited to Anastasius the Librarian, the ninth-century Roman translator of Greek texts, and it helped spread the legend in the West.

This anonymous Latin hagiographical work in two books records miracles attributed to relics of Stephen the Protomartyr at Uzalis in North Africa. It was written around 420–425 at the request of Evodius, bishop of Uzalis and a friend of Augustine of Hippo. Stephen's relics reached Africa after they were discovered in Palestine in 415. The work describes healings and other wonders, sometimes quoting witnesses directly. It is valuable evidence for the early cult of relics and for Christian life in Roman Africa.

A short Latin anti-Donatist treatise, also called Contra Fulgentium Donatistam, handed down among the works of Augustine of Hippo. Its authenticity is widely doubted, and it is usually treated as the work of an anonymous Catholic writer of roughly the same period. The text answers a booklet by a Donatist named Fulgentius. It quotes his arguments point by point and replies to each from Scripture. The main issues are the single baptism, the Church as an "enclosed garden" with a "sealed fountain", the holy chrism, and the Donatist practice of rebaptizing Catholics.

The Gallic Chronicle of 452 is an anonymous Latin chronicle, written in southern Gaul and once wrongly attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine. It continues Jerome's Chronicle from the death of the emperor Valens in 378 to the early 450s. It arranges brief notices by regnal year. They cover emperors, usurpers such as Magnus Maximus, barbarian invasions, church figures like Martin of Tours, Ambrose and Augustine, and heresies. It is a valuable independent source for fifth-century Gaul and is especially noted for its entries on Britain falling under Saxon control.

The Praedestinatus is an anonymous Latin treatise in three books, usually dated to about 432–440 and probably written in Rome. Its author is unknown, though some scholars have proposed Arnobius the Younger. The first book catalogues ninety heresies, drawing largely on Augustine's De haeresibus, and ends with the "predestinarians". The second presents a treatise said to be by a predestinarian and falsely passed off as Augustine's. The third refutes it. The work is an important witness to the hostility to Augustine's teaching on predestination in the decades after his death.

The Sacramentarium Veronense, also called the Leonine Sacramentary, is the oldest surviving collection of Roman Mass prayers. It is anonymous and was probably compiled in the sixth century. The old attribution to Pope Leo the Great is no longer accepted, though some prayers may go back to him and to Popes Gelasius and Vigilius. It is not a true sacramentary but a private gathering of Mass booklets (libelli missarum) arranged by the months of the year. The opening months are lost, so the text begins in April. It remains an important witness to early Roman liturgy and its prayer style.

This anonymous Latin liturgical address, known from its opening words "Adest, o venerabilis pontifex", was spoken by the archdeacon to the bishop during the public reconciliation of penitents. In the Roman tradition this rite took place on Maundy Thursday. The archdeacon declares that the time of forgiveness has come and draws on psalms and the Beatitudes to describe the penitent's tears, fasting and confession. He then asks the bishop to restore the sinner to the Church. The text belongs to early Western penitential liturgy, and its exact date and origin are uncertain.

This is an anonymous Latin epitaph in elegiac couplets for Perpetuus, bishop of Tours in the later fifth century. It praises him for building the lofty basilica over the tomb of Saint Martin, where he was himself buried near Martin's feet. The poem recalls his distinguished senatorial ancestry and says he made Christ his heir, gave golden vessels for the Eucharist and distributed his wealth to the poor. It closes by asking him to watch over his flock. The poem is evidence for the cult of Martin and the episcopate of Gaul in late antiquity.

This anonymous Latin verse epitaph was written for Sidonius Apollinaris, the Gallo-Roman aristocrat, poet and bishop of Clermont. It is composed in hendecasyllables and praises his noble rank and his secular offices as administrator and judge. It also credits him with restraining "barbarian fury" by law and bringing peace between warring kingdoms. It recalls his lasting writings and his later episcopate, and asks visitors to pray at his tomb. The closing dating formula places his burial on 21 August in the reign of the emperor Zeno, so the poem dates to the late fifth century.

The Libellus de genealogiis patriarcharum is a short anonymous Latin treatise on the genealogies of the biblical patriarchs. Its author and date are unknown. It opens with the creation of Adam and Eve and the entry of death through the devil's envy, and sets Eve against the Virgin Mary: as death came through a woman, so did the resurrection. It then retells Genesis, starting with Cain and Abel, and reads Abel as the first martyr and Cain as the first murderer. In this it follows the early Christian practice of reading biblical genealogy typologically.

The Libellus de computo paschali is an anonymous Latin treatise on computus, the calculation of the date of Easter. It was written in Vandal North Africa and dates itself by the reign of King Geiseric, giving the present year as his sixteenth, about 455. The author explains lunar cycles and embolismic years, building the nineteen-year cycle from ogdoads and hendecads (periods of eight and eleven years). He dates the Passion to 25 March and the Resurrection to 27 March. The treatise is evidence for Easter reckoning in fifth-century Africa.

This is an anonymous Latin account of the monastic way of life said to have been followed at Culross (Kil-ros) in Scotland. It credits the monastery's foundation, around 448, to Servanus (Saint Serf), described as a disciple of Palladius. It calls the monks Culdees, or Kiledei, and presents them as followers of Egyptian monasticism. The account describes their single daily meal of bread and vegetables, abstinence from meat, silence at table, communal sleeping and night prayer. Its date and origin are uncertain, and it is not regarded as a reliable early witness.

The Carmen de laudibus Domini (Praises of the Lord) is an anonymous Latin poem in hexameters, usually dated to the reign of Constantine, around 317–324. It is among the earliest surviving Christian Latin poems. It opens with a miracle from the territory of the Aedui, near Autun in Gaul: a dead wife stretches out her hand in the tomb to welcome her husband's body. The poet treats this as a sign of the resurrection and goes on to praise Christ as the eternal Son and Creator. The poem ends by praising Constantine.

The Regula monasterii Tarnatensis is an anonymous Latin monastic rule written in sixth-century Gaul for a community at Tarnate, probably in the Rhône valley, though its exact location is uncertain. It sets out how postulants are to be received and tested, and requires them to give up all private property. It also teaches that servants who enter with their masters become their equal brothers. The rest covers obedience, prayer, work and discipline. The rule draws heavily on Augustinian and Lérinian monastic traditions.

The Regula cujusdam patris ad monachos ("Rule of a certain father for monks") is an anonymous Latin monastic rule, probably from the seventh century. Its author and place of origin are unknown. It warns readers to read Scripture humbly rather than by their own judgement. It then sets out the love of God and neighbour, obedience to the abbot and elders "even unto death", and mutual service among the brethren. It also lays down penalties for disobedience, including confinement and finally expulsion from the community. Its strict penitential discipline is typical of early medieval Western monasticism.

The Regula consensoria monachorum is a short anonymous Latin monastic rule that has come down among the spurious works attributed to Augustine of Hippo. Its date and origin are disputed. It is usually placed in seventh-century Spain, although some scholars have argued for an earlier origin. The rule takes the form of a common agreement among the monks. Citing the Acts of the Apostles, it requires them to be of one mind and to hold all property in common. It also tests newcomers carefully before admitting them and sets out how the community should live and be disciplined.

The Ordo monasterii, also called the Regula secunda, is a short Latin monastic rule handed down in the corpus of rules linked to Augustine of Hippo. Its authorship and date are disputed: some scholars place it in Augustine's circle around 400, and others treat it as an anonymous later composition. It sets out a daily schedule of psalms, antiphons and readings, with manual work in the mornings, reading in the afternoons, common ownership modelled on the apostolic community of Acts, obedience, silence at meals and moderate use of wine.

This anonymous Latin liturgical directive dates probably from the eighth century. It opens as a "Breviarium ecclesiastici ordinis" and describes how monks should celebrate Mass, the feasts of the saints and the divine office through the liturgical year. It claims to follow both the authority of the Roman Church and the Rule of Saint Benedict. It covers Advent readings from Isaiah, the station days and fasts, and the four seasons for ordaining clergy. It is an important witness to how Roman liturgical practice was adapted in Frankish monasteries.

The Carmen de laudibus Domini (Praises of the Lord) is an anonymous Latin poem in hexameters, usually dated to the reign of Constantine, around 317–324. It is among the earliest surviving Christian Latin poems. It opens with a miracle from the territory of the Aedui, near Autun in Gaul: a dead wife stretches out her hand in the tomb to welcome her husband's body. The poet treats this as a sign of the resurrection and goes on to praise Christ as the eternal Son and Creator. The poem ends by praising Constantine.

This Latin critical appendix lists the main variant readings of Scripture found in an ancient Gallican lectionary. It was printed as the second appendix to Jean Mabillon's seventeenth-century work on the Gallican liturgy. The lectionary itself dates from roughly the seventh or eighth century. The appendix notes that its biblical text mostly follows the Vulgate, and that where it differs, it often agrees with the Greek. It then goes through the variant readings book by book. This makes it evidence for the Latin Bible used in the early Church of Gaul.

The Sacramentarium Gallicanum, better known as the Bobbio Missal, is an anonymous Latin liturgical book from about the late seventh or early eighth century. It survives from the monastery of Bobbio, and Jean Mabillon first published it in 1687. Whether it was made in southeastern Gaul or northern Italy is debated. It places Scripture readings alongside the prayers of the Mass, making it an early example of a complete missal. Its mix of Gallican material with Roman elements, including the Roman canon, makes it an important witness to pre-Carolingian worship in the West.

The Antiphonary of Bangor is an anonymous Latin liturgical collection thought to have been compiled at the monastery of Bangor, in present-day Northern Ireland, in the late seventh century. A dating to about 680–691 is usually based on a hymn listing Bangor's abbots, which ends with Crónán. The collection contains canticles, hymns, collects and antiphons for the monastic office. Among them are the hymn "Hymnum dicat turba fidelium", attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, and the communion hymn "Sancti venite". It is one of the most important witnesses to early Irish liturgy and monastic devotion.

This is an anonymous early medieval Latin treatise on where the Church's chant and liturgical offices (the "cursus") came from. Its date and place of origin are uncertain, though it is generally thought to come from an Insular or Irish-influenced milieu. It traces the Gallican office back through Irenaeus and Polycarp to John the Evangelist, and other forms of the office to Mark, Peter and other apostolic founders. It also discusses the "cursus Scottorum", the Irish office. Its lineages are legendary, but the text is valuable evidence for how early medieval writers understood the history of the liturgy.

The Antiquum martyrologium Gallicanum ("Ancient Gallican Martyrology") is an anonymous Latin calendar of saints from Gaul. Its date and place of origin are uncertain. Working through the year from January, it lists each day's commemorations with brief notes of place: martyrs of the East, Africa and Rome alongside Gallic bishops and saints such as Genovefa of Paris, Melanius of Rennes, Hilary of Poitiers and Remigius of Reims. Like other early Western martyrologies, it appears to draw on the Hieronymian tradition. It is evidence for the cult of saints and for local liturgical commemoration in Gaul.

The Calendarium Anglicanum is an anonymous Latin liturgical calendar from early medieval England. Its author and exact date are unknown. It goes through the year month by month. For each month it gives the Hebrew, Egyptian, Greek, Latin and Old English names, such as Giul for January and Solmonath for February, along with notes on the moon and the zodiac. It then lists feasts of Christ and saints' days by Roman dating. Besides universal saints, it includes English and Frankish figures such as Cuthman, Eormenhild, Radegund and Brigid. This makes it evidence for the cult of saints in Anglo-Saxon England.

The Veteres litaniae Anglicanae ("Old English Litanies") are an anonymous Latin litany of the saints, associated with early medieval England and printed by Jean Mabillon in his Vetera analecta. They begin with the Kyrie and invocations of Christ, then call on the Virgin Mary, the archangels and the nine angelic choirs, the apostles and a long list of martyrs, each followed by the response "ora pro nobis". Their exact date and origin are uncertain. They are evidence of how saints were venerated in the early medieval West.

An anonymous Latin verse epitaph for the tomb of three siblings honoured as saints in Visigothic Spain: Leander and Isidore, both bishops of Seville, and their sister Florentina, a consecrated virgin. It must date from after Isidore's death in 636. The poem describes the shared grave, with Isidore lying between his brother and sister. It invites the reader to judge the brothers by their books and to look up at their painted images. A prose note follows, recording the date of Leander's death according to the Spanish era.

This is an anonymous preface to the Greek translation of the Dialogues of Pope Gregory the Great, a four-book collection of miracles and lives of Italian saints. It praises those who leave edifying writings for later generations and places Gregory's lives of Italian holy men beside the earlier accounts of Eastern and Egyptian monks. It says that 165 years after the Dialogues were written, nobody had yet put them into Greek, until Pope Zacharias (741–752) undertook the task. The preface is an important witness to how the work reached the Greek-speaking world.

The Gregorian Sacramentary is a Latin liturgical book of the Roman Church. It contains the prayers a bishop or priest said at Mass through the liturgical year, along with the Roman Canon and texts for ordinations and other rites. Tradition credits it to Pope Gregory the Great (590–604), but its core more likely reflects papal liturgy of the seventh century. Pope Hadrian I sent a copy, known as the Hadrianum, to Charlemagne around 790. With later Frankish supplements, this text became the main basis of the medieval Roman Missal.

This is an anonymous collection of Latin liturgical texts attached to the Liber sacramentorum, the Mass book traditionally linked with Pope Gregory the Great. It gathers supplementary material from early medieval Western liturgy. It opens with an "old Mass" for Easter Sunday taken from the codex of Ratoldus, abbot of Corbie. Its rubrics and prayers guide a bishop through private preparation and the vesting, with a blessing for each garment. The pieces come from different periods, so their dates are uncertain. Together they show how the Roman sacramentary tradition grew and was adapted in the Frankish lands.

The Liber antiphonarius is an anonymous Latin chant book of the Roman Mass, traditionally associated with Pope Gregory the Great but in fact compiled in the Frankish era, probably between the eighth and ninth centuries. It is arranged by the liturgical year, beginning with the first Sunday of Advent. For each feast it gives the texts of the proper chants: introit antiphon with psalm verse, gradual responsory, alleluia, offertory with verses, and communion. As an early witness to the Mass repertory later called Gregorian chant, it is important for the history of Western liturgy and music.

This anonymous Latin liturgical supplement is appended to the early medieval Roman chant book known as the Liber antiphonarius, traditionally linked with Gregory the Great. It is drawn from a Compiègne manuscript and probably dates from the Carolingian period. It lists the chant texts for a weekly cycle of votive Masses: for sins, the angels, wisdom, charity, the Holy Cross and virgins. For each it gives the incipits of the antiphon, psalm, respond, verse, alleluia, offertory and communion. Marian pieces and sequences follow, showing how the Frankish lands added to and adapted the Roman repertory.

The Liber responsalis sive antiphonarius is an anonymous Latin liturgical book of the Carolingian period. It collects the antiphons and responsories sung at the Divine Office throughout the church year, beginning with the vigil of the First Sunday of Advent and following the cycle of feasts and seasons. Tradition placed it under the name of Pope Gregory the Great, but the attribution is legendary. It is known from a late ninth-century codex from Compiègne. It is an important early witness to the Office chant of the Frankish church, which drew on Roman practice.

This anonymous Latin saint's life tells of Sulpicius, called Pius ("the Pious"), bishop of Bourges in the early seventh century. It should not be confused with his predecessor Sulpicius Severus of Bourges. The author was a monk of the monastery Sulpicius founded, who calls him his patron and writes as a near-contemporary, probably in the later seventh century. The Life praises the bishop's asceticism, charity and pastoral care. A shorter abridged version also survives, along with an appended book of miracles that may be by a different author. It is a useful witness to Merovingian Gaul.

This is a short anonymous Latin list of the early bishops of Toledo, printed as an editorial appendix. It is drawn from Juan de Grial's edition and the collection of the Toledan Fathers. It numbers the succession from a legendary Saint Eugenius, said to have been sent by Dionysius of Paris, through figures such as Melantius, Audentius, Montanus, Helladius and Eugenius II and III, down to Ildefonsus (657). Brief notes give approximate dates, council signatures and cross-references to Ildefonsus's De viris illustribus. These make it a guide to the Visigothic-era see.

The Chronica regum Visigothorum is a short anonymous Latin list of the kings of the Visigoths. Its author and date of composition are unknown. It starts with Athanaric and follows the succession through Alaric, Athaulf and the later rulers in Gaul and Hispania. For each king it gives the year of accession, counted by the Spanish era, and the length of the reign, often noting other figures found in other copies. It was copied alongside the Visigothic law code and continued at various points, and it is a useful reference for the chronology of the Visigothic kingdom.

This is an anonymous Latin list of the Gothic kings, giving each ruler's length of reign with brief notes on his deeds and death, and dating events by the reigning Roman emperors. It starts with Athanaric, who is said to have brought the Goths into Arianism under Valens, and then follows Alaric, Ataulf, Sigeric, Wallia, Theodoric I, Thorismund and their successors. Its date and author are unknown. It belongs to the early medieval tradition of Visigothic regnal lists, which is closely tied to Isidore of Seville's History of the Goths.

Liber glossarum is an anonymous Latin glossary, usually dated to the second half of the eighth century. It is an alphabetical list of rare, obscure or late Latin words, each followed by a brief explanation or synonym, such as "Abaia, infima domus." It was compiled from earlier glossaries and passed down under the name of Isidore of Seville, though he did not write it. Glossaries of this kind matter as evidence for early medieval Latin vocabulary, learning and teaching, and for the early development of the Romance languages.

This anonymous Latin panegyric was delivered at Trier in 313, probably before Constantine left to campaign on the German frontier. It belongs to the collection known as the Panegyrici Latini. The orator praises Constantine's victory over Maxentius in 312. He describes how the emperor crossed the Alps with a small part of his army, against the advice of his friends and unfavourable omens, then tells of the campaign in northern Italy and the battle at the Milvian Bridge. Some early scholars attributed it to Nazarius, but the author is unknown. It is an important near-contemporary witness to Constantine's rise.

The Gesta Liberii is an anonymous Latin apocryphal narrative about Pope Liberius (352–366). It is usually counted among the so-called Symmachian forgeries, written in Rome in the early sixth century, around the Laurentian schism. The text tells of Liberius's conflict with the emperor Constantius, his exile to a cemetery near Rome, and his baptizing activity there, and it names Damasus as his vicar. The story is historically unreliable: it confuses the Constantinian emperors and misplaces the exile, which actually took place at Beroea. It draws on the legendary Acts of Silvester.

This Latin panegyric by an unknown orator was delivered in 307, probably at Trier, to celebrate the marriage of Constantine to Fausta, daughter of the former emperor Maximian. Maximian had come out of retirement and returned to power, and at this time he recognised Constantine as Augustus. The speech praises Constantine by comparing him with his father Constantius, then praises Maximian's campaigns in Gaul, across the Rhine and in Mauretania. It belongs to the collection known as the Panegyrici Latini and is an important source for the politics of the Tetrarchy.

The Epistola ad Florianum is a short dedicatory verse letter in elegiac couplets by Arator, a sixth-century Christian poet from Liguria who served as a subdeacon of the Roman church. He addressed it to Florianus, an abbot, and sent it with a copy of his hexameter poem De Actibus Apostolorum, a verse history of the Apostles presented in Rome in 544. The letter offers the work for the abbot's judgement and is one of several dedicatory epistles that accompany the poem.

The Epistola ad Vigilium is a short dedicatory letter in Latin elegiac verse. Arator, a Ligurian poet and subdeacon of the Roman Church, addressed it to Pope Vigilius. It accompanied his epic De Actibus Apostolorum, a verse retelling of the Acts of the Apostles, when he presented the poem to the pope in 544. In it Arator offers the work to Vigilius with deference, honouring him as first among bishops. The letter shows how the poem was received in mid-sixth-century Rome, and it is regularly transmitted together with the epic.

De Actibus Apostolorum is a Latin biblical epic in two books of hexameters by Arator, a subdeacon of the Roman church. It retells the Acts of the Apostles, with the first book centred on Peter and the second on Paul. The poem does not simply paraphrase the narrative. It explains the episodes through allegorical and typological interpretation. Arator presented the work to Pope Vigilius in 544, and it was then read publicly in Rome to great acclaim. It became a widely studied school text throughout the Middle Ages.

The Epistola ad Parthenium is a Latin verse letter in elegiac couplets by Arator, a subdeacon of the Roman church and poet from Liguria. It was written in the 540s, probably soon after 544, to Parthenius, an aristocrat holding the titles of magister officiorum and patricius. Arator praises his friend's noble ancestry and virtues and recalls their earlier ties. The letter seems to have accompanied a copy of his verse epic De Actibus Apostolorum. It is a minor but revealing witness to literary friendship and patronage in sixth-century Italy and Gaul.

The Conflictus de Deo trino et uno is a Latin theological dialogue in two books, written in the mid-fifth century, probably in Rome. It presents a formal debate before judges between Arnobius, a Catholic, and Serapion, an Egyptian. The debate deals with the Trinity against the Sabellians and Arians, with the Incarnation against the Nestorians and Eutychians, and with grace and free will. It is often ascribed to Arnobius the Younger, but this is disputed, and some scholars think it is the work of a follower of Augustine.

The Commentarii in Psalmos is a Latin commentary on the Psalter by Arnobius the Younger, a cleric probably of African origin who wrote in Rome around the mid-fifth century. It is dedicated to two bishops, Leontius and Rusticus, and goes through the Psalms one by one with brief allegorical and mystical readings, many of them pointing to Christ and the Church. It shows the influence of Tyconius. Its opposition to Augustine's teaching on predestination has led scholars to call it semi-Pelagian. Erasmus first printed it in 1522 and wrongly attributed it to the elder Arnobius.

The Annotationes ad quaedam Evangeliorum loca are a short Latin collection of explanatory notes on selected Gospel passages. They are attributed to Arnobius the Younger, a fifth-century cleric active in Rome around 460 and the author of an allegorical commentary on the Psalms. The notes were once wrongly ascribed to the earlier African apologist Arnobius of Sicca. They begin with the prologue of John and the wedding at Cana. The exegesis is mainly spiritual and allegorical: the Cana wedding, for example, is read as the union of Christ and the Church.

This is the very small surviving correspondence of Augustine of Canterbury, the Roman monk whom Pope Gregory I sent to convert the Anglo-Saxons of Kent and who became the first Archbishop of Canterbury (597 to c. 604). He must have written many letters, but almost all are lost. What remains comes mainly from the questions he sent to Gregory about church order, marriage, liturgy and relations with other bishops. These survive only within Gregory's reply, known as the Libellus responsionum, and they are an important witness to the early English mission.

The Fundatio abbatiae S. Augustini Cantuariensis is a Latin narrative of the founding of the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul, later St Augustine's Abbey, at Canterbury. It is sometimes attributed to Augustine of Canterbury, but its retrospective style, its Anno Domini dating and its reference to an existing Life of Augustine point to a later medieval author whose date is uncertain. It recalls Pope Gregory I's mission of 597, King Æthelberht's baptism, Augustine's consecration at Arles and the endowment of the abbey. It belongs to the house traditions the abbey kept about its own origins.

This Latin charter of privilege is attributed to Augustine of Canterbury, the first Archbishop of Canterbury (d. c. 604). It confirms that King Æthelberht of Kent founded and endowed the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul outside Canterbury, later St Augustine's Abbey. In Augustine's name it forbids his successors and all secular or church authorities to claim power over the house, its lands or its churches, and it protects the monks' free election of their abbot. Scholars generally regard it as spurious, probably written later at the abbey to support its claim to be exempt from the archbishops' control.

De mirabilibus sacrae Scripturae is a Latin treatise in three books, written in Ireland around 655 by an anonymous author now called Augustine the Irishman. It was long transmitted among the works of Augustine of Hippo. The work covers the miracles of the Pentateuch, the Prophets and the New Testament. It explains them as far as possible through natural causes, holding that God's creation was complete after six days and that miracles draw on properties already present in nature. It is an important witness to early Irish learning and natural science.

The Soliloquies are a philosophical dialogue in two books by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote them in 386–387 during his retreat at Cassiciacum, after his conversion and before his baptism. Augustine converses with a personified Reason, an inner voice, and states his aim as knowing God and the soul. The first book looks at how God can be known and at the moral purification needed to know him. The second argues for the soul's immortality from the permanence of truth. Augustine coined the word "soliloquia" for the work. An Old English adaptation is attributed to Alfred the Great.

Principia Dialecticae, also known as De dialectica, is a short, unfinished Latin treatise on logic and language attributed to Augustine of Hippo. Its authenticity has long been disputed, though many scholars now accept it as genuine. If so, it probably belongs to his planned handbooks on the liberal arts, begun around 387. It defines dialectic as "the science of arguing well" and goes on to discuss simple and combined words, statements, the signification of words, their origins and the causes of ambiguity and obscurity. It is valued as an early statement of Augustine's theory of signs.

The Categoriae decem is an anonymous Latin paraphrase of Aristotle's Categories, written in the later fourth century and addressed to the author's son. It explains the parts of speech and the ten categories, beginning with substance (ousia). Medieval copyists attributed it to Augustine of Hippo, perhaps because he recalls reading the Categories in his Confessions, but scholars regard the attribution as spurious. It was a key logic textbook in Carolingian schools, where Alcuin promoted it, and it stayed influential until Boethius's translation replaced it.

Principia Rhetorices, also called De rhetorica, is a short Latin handbook of rhetoric handed down under the name of Augustine of Hippo. It is often linked with the series of works on the liberal arts that Augustine says he began in Milan around 386–387. Its authenticity is disputed, however, and many scholars doubt that he wrote it. Following Cicero and Greek theory, it defines the orator's duties as invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. It then discusses the orator's goal and how to classify political questions. It is a witness to the school rhetoric of late antiquity.

The Regula consensoria monachorum is a short anonymous Latin monastic rule that has come down among the spurious works attributed to Augustine of Hippo. Its date and origin are disputed. It is usually placed in seventh-century Spain, although some scholars have argued for an earlier origin. The rule takes the form of a common agreement among the monks. Citing the Acts of the Apostles, it requires them to be of one mind and to hold all property in common. It also tests newcomers carefully before admitting them and sets out how the community should live and be disciplined.

The Ordo monasterii, also called the Regula secunda, is a short Latin monastic rule handed down in the corpus of rules linked to Augustine of Hippo. Its authorship and date are disputed: some scholars place it in Augustine's circle around 400, and others treat it as an anonymous later composition. It sets out a daily schedule of psalms, antiphons and readings, with manual work in the mornings, reading in the afternoons, common ownership modelled on the apostolic community of Acts, obedience, silence at meals and moderate use of wine.

De Immortalitate Animae (On the Immortality of the Soul) is a short philosophical treatise by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it in Milan in 387, after the Soliloquies and before his baptism, as notes toward completing that work. It sets out a series of arguments in a Platonic style. For example, it argues that the soul is the subject of unchanging knowledge (disciplina) and of truth, so it cannot cease to live. In the Retractationes, Augustine called it obscure and said it had circulated without his consent.

De Quantitate Animae (On the Greatness of the Soul) is a Latin philosophical dialogue by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it at Rome around 387–388, soon after his baptism. In it Augustine answers questions about the soul put to him by his friend Evodius. The dialogue centres on the question of how "great" the soul is. Augustine argues that the soul is incorporeal and has no size or place in space, though it has great power. He then describes seven ascending levels of the soul's activity, rising from giving life to the body up to the contemplation of God.

De Musica (On Music) is a Latin treatise in six books by Augustine of Hippo, written as a dialogue between a master and a disciple. Augustine began it in Milan around 387, soon after his baptism, as part of a planned series on the liberal arts, and finished it in Africa a few years later. The first five books cover rhythm, metre and verse in technical detail. The sixth moves from sounding numbers to the numerical harmony of the soul and its ascent to God. It is an important source for early medieval ideas about music and number.

De Magistro (On the Teacher) is a philosophical dialogue in Latin by Augustine of Hippo, written about 389 after his return to Africa. It records a conversation between Augustine and his son Adeodatus on how language works and how teaching happens. They examine words as signs and how signs relate to things. The dialogue concludes that words only prompt learning, and that real knowledge comes from the inner Teacher, Christ, the eternal truth within the mind. It is a key early text in the philosophy of language and the theory of signs.

De libero arbitrio (On Free Choice of the Will) is a philosophical dialogue in three books by Augustine of Hippo, conducted with his friend Evodius, later a bishop. Book One was begun in Rome around 388; Books Two and Three were completed in Africa between about 391 and 395. Asking where evil comes from, Augustine argues that sin arises from the free will of creatures, not from God. The work also offers a proof of God's existence. Written against Manichaeism, it was later cited by Pelagians, and Augustine defended it in his Retractationes.

De moribus ecclesiae catholicae et de moribus Manichaeorum is a Latin treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo. He began it in Rome around 387–388, soon after his baptism, and finished it after returning to Africa. The first book sets out Catholic ethics, with God as the highest good of human beings. It presents the four cardinal virtues as forms of love for God and points to Christian ascetics as examples of holy living. The second book attacks Manichaean moral teaching and practice. Augustine had himself been a Manichaean, and the work is one of his earliest anti-Manichaean writings.

The Regula ad servos Dei, known as the Rule of Saint Augustine, is a short Latin monastic rule attributed to Augustine of Hippo. It is usually dated to around 397–400. Taking the Jerusalem community of Acts 4 as its model, it asks monks to share one mind and heart in God, to hold all property in common, and to practise prayer, moderation, chastity, mutual correction and obedience. A version addressed to women survives in Augustine's Letter 211. In the Middle Ages the Rule became the basis for the Augustinian canons and friars, the Dominicans and other orders.

De Grammatica is a short Latin grammatical handbook handed down under the name of Augustine of Hippo. It sets out the endings of Latin nouns and their genders, with examples drawn from proper names, Greek loanwords and classical authors such as Sallust. In his Retractations Augustine says he wrote a book on grammar around 387, as part of a planned series on the liberal arts, but that it was later lost. Whether the surviving treatise is that work, a reworking of it, or a later school text is disputed. Many scholars doubt that it is authentic.

De doctrina Christiana (On Christian Doctrine, or On Christian Teaching) is a Latin treatise in four books by Augustine of Hippo on how to interpret and teach Scripture. He began it around 397 and finished it around 426, adding the fourth book then. Book 1 sets out the things to be enjoyed or used, centring on the love of God and of neighbour. Books 2 and 3 deal with signs and with interpreting obscure or ambiguous passages. Book 4 adapts classical rhetoric to Christian preaching. The work shaped medieval biblical interpretation and education.

De vera religione (On True Religion) is a single-book treatise by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it around 390, as a layman in North Africa, shortly before he became a priest, and dedicated it to his patron Romanianus. It argues that true religion, the worship of one God, is found not among pagan philosophers or sects but only in the Catholic Church. It refutes Manichaean teaching about two natures and the origin of evil. It also sets out how God leads people by authority and by reason, and it shows Augustine's early Neoplatonic thought.

On Genesis against the Manichaeans is a Latin treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo. He is generally thought to have written it around 388–389, soon after his return to Africa following his baptism. It defends the opening chapters of Genesis against Manichaean ridicule of the Old Testament. Book one covers the creation account up to God's rest on the seventh day, and book two treats paradise and the fall, often reading them figuratively. Augustine deliberately wrote in a plain style so that unlearned readers could follow. It is the first of his several commentaries on Genesis.

De sermone Domini in monte is a Latin commentary by Augustine of Hippo on the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 5–7. He wrote it around 393, while he was still a priest at Hippo. Augustine calls the sermon "a perfect standard of the Christian life." The work has two books. The first covers Matthew 5, including the Beatitudes, which Augustine links to the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit. The second covers chapters 6 and 7 and includes a short theology of prayer based on the Lord's Prayer. It is one of his earliest works of biblical exegesis.

Quaestiones Evangeliorum ("Questions on the Gospels") is a Latin exegetical work in two books by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to around 400. Its prologue says it was not a continuous commentary. Instead it records answers Augustine dictated, as time allowed, to questions about obscure passages raised by a companion while they read the Gospels together. These answers were later collected and given numbered headings. The first book deals with passages from Matthew and the second with Luke. Augustine reviews the work in his Retractationes.

The Seventeen Questions on the Gospel according to Matthew is a short Latin collection of exegetical notes, transmitted under the name of Augustine of Hippo. It is usually printed as an appendix to his Quaestiones evangeliorum, and its date is uncertain. Each question takes a passage of Matthew, such as the slaughter of the Innocents, the sword that divides households or the healing of the leper, and gives it a brief allegorical reading. The Church set against the Synagogue and the earthly city is a recurring theme.

The Tractates on the Gospel of John are a series of 124 Latin homilies by Augustine of Hippo. Together they form a continuous commentary on the whole of the Fourth Gospel. Most were preached to his congregation at Hippo, and some were later dictated. Their dating is debated, but they are generally placed between about 406 and the early 420s. They take up Christ as the eternal Word, grace, the sacraments, charity and the unity of the Church, often against the Donatists and Arians. They are among Augustine's most important exegetical works.

Ten sermons by Augustine of Hippo on the First Epistle of John, preached at Hippo during Easter week. He paused his series of tractates on John's Gospel to give them. They are often dated to around 407, but the date is disputed. The Latin title reflects an old tradition that the letter was addressed to the Parthians. Augustine calls charity the epistle's central theme and develops it against the Donatist schism, linking love of God to love of neighbour and the unity of the Church. The seventh homily contains his famous maxim "Love, and do what you will."

Augustine of Hippo wrote this short Latin commentary around 394–395 at Carthage, while he was still a presbyter. It grew out of questions that fellow Christians asked while the Epistle to the Romans was being read together. The work is a series of brief notes on chosen verses. Augustine states at the outset that the letter's central issue is works of the Law and grace. He sets out four stages of human life: before the Law, under the Law, under grace and in peace. Later, in the Retractations, he revised his early views on Romans 7, election and foreseen faith.

The Epistolae ad Romanos inchoata expositio (Unfinished Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans) is a Latin exegetical work by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it around 394–395, while still a presbyter at Hippo. It deals only with the letter's opening greeting (Romans 1:1–7). Augustine presents Romans as concerned with whether the gospel of grace comes to all nations, Jews and Gentiles, without prior merit from works of the Law. Much of the work is a long digression on the sin against the Holy Spirit. In his Retractations, Augustine says he abandoned the commentary because the task was too large.

This Latin commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, the Expositio Epistolae ad Galatas, was written by Augustine of Hippo around 394–395, while he was still a presbyter at Hippo. It is his only complete running commentary on a Pauline letter. It explains the text in order, presenting the epistle as Paul's teaching that believers under grace are no longer under the burdens of the Law. Augustine discusses at length Paul's rebuke of Peter at Antioch, which he took to be a genuine correction. This reading was also central to his correspondence with Jerome.

The Enarrationes in Psalmos are Augustine of Hippo's commentary on all 150 psalms, written over about three decades, from roughly 392 to 422. Some are sermons preached to congregations in North Africa and taken down by stenographers. Others are expositions he dictated. Together they form the longest of his works. Augustine reads the psalms mainly as being about Christ, often hearing in them the voice of the "whole Christ", head and body, meaning Christ and the Church. The collection became one of the most influential Psalm commentaries of the Latin Middle Ages.

This is a collection of Latin sermons that Augustine of Hippo preached to his congregations, mostly at Hippo Regius in North Africa, during his years as priest and bishop (c. 391–430). In the Benedictine edition they belong to the sermons "on the Scriptures" and comment on New Testament readings heard in the liturgy. The English collection of this title covers sermons 51 to 147. They expound passages from the Gospels and the apostolic writings. The first deals with how Matthew's and Luke's genealogies of Christ can be reconciled. Together they show Augustine as a pastoral preacher and biblical interpreter.

The Sermones de tempore are the second class of Augustine of Hippo's sermons to the people, as arranged by the Maurist editors. They are Latin homilies preached at Hippo and elsewhere in North Africa, probably between about 391 and 430, and follow the liturgical year: Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, Holy Week, Easter, the Ascension and Pentecost. In them Augustine explains the Incarnation, the Passion and the Resurrection to ordinary congregations. They give important evidence for the preaching, liturgy and pastoral teaching of the late antique Western Church.

This is the third class of Augustine of Hippo's sermons to the people in the Maurist arrangement, the sermons "on the saints" (Sermons 273–340). He preached them as bishop of Hippo, mostly on the feast days of martyrs and saints, including Stephen, Peter and Paul, John the Baptist, Cyprian, and the Spanish martyrs Fructuosus, Augurius and Eulogius. In them he praises the martyrs' courage, explains the meaning of martyrdom and the veneration of martyrs, and teaches about grace, death and resurrection. Together they are an important witness to the cult of the saints in late Roman North Africa.

The Sermones de diversis are the fourth class of Augustine of Hippo's sermons to the people in the Maurist arrangement, beginning with Sermon 341. Augustine preached them as bishop of Hippo between his ordination and his death in 430. They cover a range of occasional and doctrinal subjects that do not fit the classes on Scripture, the liturgical seasons or the saints. The opening sermon, preached against the Arians, sets out three ways Scripture speaks of Christ. These are as God equal to the Father, as the incarnate mediator, and as the "whole Christ" of head and body, the Church.

This is a group of Latin sermons transmitted under the name of Augustine of Hippo (354–430). They make up the fifth and final class of his Sermones ad populum in the arrangement made by the Benedictine Maurist editors, who placed here the sermons whose authenticity they considered doubtful. The series opens with Sermon 364, on Samson. It argues that Samson's strength came from the Spirit of God and from grace, not from nature, and reads his deeds as prophetic figures. Scholars still disagree about who wrote individual pieces in the group.

This is a collection of fragments from sermons by Augustine of Hippo (354–430) whose full texts are lost. The fragments survive as quotations in later writers and compilers, among them Eugippius. The first comes from a sermon against the Pelagians. In it Augustine reports what his fellow bishop Urbanus of Sicca heard in Rome: a Pelagian claimed that the Lord's Prayer asks God only for protection from outward harm, because people can overcome temptation to sin by their own will. Augustine refutes this and defends the necessity of grace. The individual pieces cannot be dated precisely.

De diversis quaestionibus LXXXIII (Eighty-Three Different Questions) is a Latin collection by Augustine of Hippo. It gathers short answers he gave to questions put to him by his companions between his return to Africa in 388 and the start of his episcopate around 396. Augustine later had them collected into a single book and discussed it in his Retractations. The questions range over philosophy, theology and biblical interpretation, including the soul, free will, the origin of evil, the Trinity and difficult passages of Scripture. Question 46, on the divine ideas, is a key witness to his Christian adaptation of Platonism.

De disciplina Christiana (On Christian Discipline) is a Latin sermon by Augustine of Hippo, preached during his years as bishop. Its exact date is uncertain. It takes as its starting point Sirach's words "Receive discipline in the house of discipline" and describes the Church as a school in which Christ is the only true teacher. Augustine explains what it means to live well, what reward a good life brings, and who true Christians are. He centres his teaching on the twofold commandment to love God and neighbour.

Sermo de cantico novo ("Sermon on the New Song") is a Latin catechetical sermon passed down among the works of Augustine of Hippo. It is addressed to candidates preparing for baptism and urges them to pass from the "old" to the "new": the old covenant, old song and old man give way to the new covenant, new song and new man. It draws on Jeremiah, the Psalms and Paul. It travels in manuscripts with the sermons on the Creed to catechumens. Augustine's authorship is disputed, and many scholars assign the group to Quodvultdeus of Carthage in the fifth century.

This Latin sermon, also called De quarta feria, has come down among the works of Augustine of Hippo, but its authenticity is doubted. The Maurist editors grouped it with the sermons De cataclysmo and De tempore barbarico as probably spurious. Modern scholars often attribute this group to Quodvultdeus of Carthage. The preacher treats the Church as the Lord's field, which must be ploughed and prepared for the rain of grace. He draws on Paul's words about planting and watering, and turns the five yoke of oxen in the Gospel parable of the great supper (Luke 14) into an allegory.

The Sermo de utilitate jejunii ("Sermon on the Usefulness of Fasting") is a Latin sermon by Augustine of Hippo, preached at an uncertain date during his ministry in North Africa. It argues that fasting is an offering only humans can make to God, because angels already enjoy the full and unfailing food of God himself. Using the beatitude on hungering and thirsting for righteousness and the example of the Apostle Paul, Augustine presents fasting as self-denial of the body that gains the mind, preparing the soul to be filled in the life to come.

Sermo de urbis excidio ("Sermon on the Destruction of the City") is a Latin sermon by Augustine of Hippo, preached in North Africa soon after Alaric's Goths sacked Rome in 410. It answers Christians who complained against God over the disaster. Augustine cites Daniel confessing his own sins and the righteous Noah, Daniel and Job of Ezekiel 14. He argues that the city was chastised rather than destroyed and that suffering tests and corrects believers. It is an early statement of themes he later developed in The City of God.

Augustine of Hippo wrote this Latin treatise in two books around 396–397, soon after he became bishop. It answers questions sent by Simplician, a priest of Milan who later succeeded Ambrose as bishop. The first book explains Romans 7 on the law and sin, and Romans 9 on the election of Jacob over Esau. The second book takes up difficult passages from the Books of Kings. Augustine's reading of Romans 9 stressed that grace comes before any human merit. He later saw this as a turning point in his teaching on grace.

De octo Dulcitii quaestionibus (On Eight Questions of Dulcitius) is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written late in his life, probably in the 420s. It answers questions sent from Carthage by Dulcitius, an imperial official in Africa. Where he had already dealt with a question, Augustine mostly answers by quoting his earlier writings. The topics include the fate of baptized sinners, prayer for the dead, the appearance of Samuel to Saul through the medium at Endor, and why God called David a man after his own heart.

De fide rerum quae non videntur (On Faith in Things Not Seen) is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo. Some once doubted that he wrote it, but he names it in his letter to Count Darius (Letter 231). A reference to laws against idols suggests it was written after 399. It answers critics who mock Christianity for asking belief in what cannot be seen. Augustine points out that people already trust unseen things, such as a friend's goodwill. He then presents fulfilled prophecy and the spread of the Church among the nations as visible grounds for faith.

The Enchiridion, or handbook on faith, hope and love, is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it around 421, soon after Jerome's death, for a layman named Laurentius who had asked for a brief guide to Christian doctrine. Under faith, Augustine expounds the Apostles' Creed and refutes heresies. Under hope, he briefly explains the Lord's Prayer. He ends with a discussion of love as the goal of the law. The work offers a compact summary of Augustine's mature theology, especially on sin, grace and redemption.

De agone christiano (On the Christian Struggle) is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 396–397, early in his time as bishop. He wrote it in plain style for ordinary believers. It begins from Paul's image of the crown of victory. It explains that Christians fight against the devil, who rules through the love of passing things, and that Christ has already defeated him. It then sets out the rule of faith and briefly rejects the errors of heretical groups such as the Manichaeans, Arians and Donatists.

De catechizandis rudibus is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated around 400. He wrote it for Deogratias, a deacon of Carthage who had asked how to teach the Christian faith to beginners seeking admission to the Church. Augustine advises catechists to tell the story of salvation from creation to the present age, to adapt their teaching to each listener and to teach with cheerfulness. He ends with a long and a short model address. The work is an important early handbook of Christian religious instruction.

On the Creed: A Sermon to the Catechumens is a Latin sermon attributed to Augustine of Hippo, bishop of Hippo Regius in North Africa. Its exact date is uncertain. It was preached to candidates preparing for baptism when the creed was formally handed over to them. Augustine tells them to learn the creed by heart rather than write it down, then explains it clause by clause: God the almighty Father, Christ's birth, passion and resurrection, the Holy Spirit, the Church, forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the body. It shows how creeds were taught in the early Church.

Contra sermonem Arianorum (Against an Arian Sermon) is a Latin polemical treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to about 418–419. It answers, point by point, an anonymous Homoian Arian sermon that had been sent to him. The Arians called Christ God but denied that he was true God, one God with the Father. Against this, Augustine argues from Scripture for the Son's full divinity, his coeternity with the Father and the unity of the Trinity. The work is an important witness to Latin Arianism in Augustine's last years.

The Collatio cum Maximino Arianorum episcopo is the Latin record of a public debate held at Hippo Regius, usually dated to about 427–428. In it Augustine of Hippo faced Maximinus, a Homoian ("Arian") bishop who had come to Africa with the Gothic count Sigisvult. Clergy and laity were present. Maximinus based his faith on the creed of the Council of Ariminum (359) and would accept only arguments drawn from Scripture. The two men disputed the relation of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Maximinus spoke at such length that Augustine afterwards wrote a fuller reply, Contra Maximinum.

Contra Maximinum Haereticum Arianorum Episcopum (Against Maximinus, the Arian Bishop) is a Latin treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 427–428. It follows a public debate at Hippo with Maximinus, a Homoian (Arian) bishop who came to Africa with Gothic troops. Maximinus spoke at such length that the debate ran out of time, and he afterwards claimed victory. In the first book Augustine shows that Maximinus never refuted his arguments. In the second he answers Maximinus's own claims, defending the equality and unity of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It is among Augustine's last anti-Arian writings.

De Trinitate is a theological treatise in fifteen books by Augustine of Hippo, written in Latin over about two decades, roughly between 400 and 420. The early books use Scripture and the Church's teaching to show that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are one and equal, and they answer texts cited against the Son's equality. The later books look for analogies of the Trinity in the human mind, notably memory, understanding and will. Some scholars see it as Augustine's masterpiece, and it deeply shaped Western Trinitarian theology.

De Haeresibus (On Heresies) is a Latin catalogue of heresies written by Augustine of Hippo around 428–429, near the end of his life. He wrote it at the repeated request of Quodvultdeus, a deacon of Carthage. The first part briefly describes eighty-eight heretical groups, from the Simonians to the Pelagians. For the earlier groups it draws on Epiphanius and Filastrius of Brescia. A second part was planned to explain what makes someone a heretic, but Augustine never wrote it. The work became a standard reference for later Latin heresiology.

The Tractatus adversus Judaeos is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, usually placed among the works of his final years. It is written in the style of a sermon and starts from Paul's image of the olive tree in Romans 11. Augustine argues that the Jews were broken off for unbelief and the Gentiles grafted in through faith. He then sets out to show the Jews' blindness from the Old Testament, which they themselves accept, citing passages from the Psalms and the Prophets. It is one of the main sources for Augustine's view of Judaism.

Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets is a Latin treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo, usually dated to around 420. Some brethren had sent him an anonymous heretical book that was being sold and eagerly read in a street by the sea. Its author rejected the Old Testament and condemned the God who made the world. Augustine could not tell which sect the writer belonged to, though he noted that such views resembled Marcionite ideas. He answers the book's objections passage by passage, starting with Genesis, and defends the unity of the two Testaments.

Contra Priscillianistas et Origenistas is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written about 415. It replies to the Commonitorium of the Spanish priest Orosius, who had asked Augustine about errors spreading in his homeland. Augustine refutes the Priscillianist claim that the soul is a part of God's substance, pointing to his earlier arguments against the Manichaeans. He then turns to opinions attributed to Origen, rejecting the idea that the punishments of hell will end and that all rational creatures will be restored. The work documents Western reactions to Origenism and Priscillianism in the early fifth century.

Contra partem Donati post gesta, also known as Ad Donatistas post collationem, is a Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 412. It followed the Conference of Carthage of 411, where Catholic and Donatist bishops debated before the imperial commissioner Marcellinus, who decided for the Catholics. Augustine addresses ordinary Donatists directly and urges them to stop following their bishops. He answers the claim that the judge had been bribed and uses the conference records to show that the Donatist case had been refuted.

De perfectione iustitiae hominis is a short Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo against the Pelagians, usually dated to about 415. He addressed it to the bishops Eutropius and Paulus. It answers a paper of "Definitions" said to be by Caelestius, a disciple of Pelagius, which claimed that people are able to live without sin. Augustine first answers each proposition briefly and then examines the Bible passages cited in the paper. He argues that perfect, sinless righteousness cannot be reached without grace and is never fully attained in this life.

On Rebuke and Grace (De correptione et gratia) is a treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written about 426–427 and addressed to Valentinus, abbot of Hadrumetum, and his monks. It answers an objection raised among them: if good conduct depends wholly on God's grace, then no one should be rebuked for failing to keep the commandments, only prayed for. Augustine defends the usefulness of correction while maintaining that grace alone frees the will for good. He also discusses perseverance and predestination. It belongs to his late anti-Pelagian writings.

On the Predestination of the Saints (De praedestinatione sanctorum) is a late Latin treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written about 428–429. It is addressed to Prosper of Aquitaine and Hilary, who had reported objections to his teaching on grace among monks in southern Gaul, later called semi-Pelagians. Augustine argues that the very beginning of faith, and not only its growth, is God's gift. Citing 1 Corinthians 4:7, he admits that he had held a different view in his early exposition of Romans. Its companion is On the Gift of Perseverance, and both shaped later debates on grace and predestination.

De Gestis Pelagii (On the Proceedings of Pelagius) is a Latin treatise in one book by Augustine of Hippo, addressed to Bishop Aurelius of Carthage and written around the beginning of 417. It examines the acts of the Synod of Diospolis in Palestine (December 415), where fourteen bishops acquitted Pelagius. Augustine goes through each charge and Pelagius's reply. He argues that Pelagius was cleared only because he condemned the propositions read against him, so the synod did not approve his teaching. The treatise is a major source for what happened at the synod.

On the Grace of Christ, and on Original Sin is an anti-Pelagian treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo. He wrote it in 418, after Popes Innocent I and Zosimus condemned Pelagianism, and addressed it to Albina, Pinianus and Melania the Younger. The first book argues that Pelagius, despite claiming to honour grace, reduced it to nature, free will, law or teaching. It also attacks his view that grace is given according to merit. The second book defends original sin against Pelagius and Caelestius. Together the books are a key statement of Augustine's teaching on grace.

This is a Latin letter from Augustine of Hippo to Valerius, a Christian count of high rank at the imperial court. It is usually identified as Letter 200 in his correspondence and dated around 418–419. Augustine says he has received three letters from Valerius after a long silence, some brought by Bishop Vindemialis and the presbyter Firmus. He praises the count's Catholic faith, his humility in high office and his good works. The letter went with the first book of On Marriage and Concupiscence, which Augustine dedicated to Valerius during the Pelagian controversy.

On Marriage and Concupiscence (De nuptiis et concupiscentia) is a Latin anti-Pelagian treatise in two books by Augustine of Hippo, written around 419–421 and addressed to Count Valerius. The Pelagians claimed that Augustine's doctrine of original sin condemned marriage. In reply, he argues that marriage is good and that the concupiscence of the flesh is not its fault, since conjugal chastity makes good use of that evil in begetting children. Julian of Eclanum attacked the first book, and Augustine wrote the second to answer extracts from Julian's work. The treatise began their long controversy.

Contra Julianum is a Latin polemical treatise in six books by Augustine of Hippo, generally dated around 421–422. It answers the four books in which the Pelagian bishop Julian of Eclanum attacked the first book of Augustine's De nuptiis et concupiscentia and accused him of Manichaeism. The first two books gather testimonies from earlier Greek and Latin Fathers, including Basil and John Chrysostom, to show that the Church had always taught original sin. The remaining books refute Julian's arguments on concupiscence, marriage and grace. Augustine later began a second reply, the unfinished Opus imperfectum contra Julianum.

Augustine of Hippo wrote these two Latin letters, numbered 214 and 215 among his correspondence, around 426–427 to Valentinus, abbot of a monastery at Hadrumetum in North Africa. Two monks, Cresconius and Felix, had reported that the community was divided. Some brothers were stressing grace so strongly that they denied free will and judgment according to works. Augustine argues that God's grace and human free will must both be affirmed. The letters accompany his treatise On Grace and Free Will and are early documents of the controversy later called Semi-Pelagian.

On Grace and Free Will (De gratia et libero arbitrio) is a late anti-Pelagian treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 426–427. He addressed it to Valentinus, abbot of the monastery at Hadrumetum in North Africa, where monks had disputed whether preaching grace meant denying free will. Augustine argues from Scripture that both are real: human beings have free will, but grace is not given according to merit, and even good works and faith are God's gifts. With its companion treatise On Rebuke and Grace, it shaped later debates over predestination.

On the Gift of Perseverance (De dono perseverantiae) is a late theological treatise by Augustine of Hippo, written around 428–429. It is the second book of a pair with On the Predestination of the Saints, and both were addressed to Prosper of Aquitaine and Hilary. Augustine answers objections raised by monks in southern Gaul. He argues that perseverance in faith until the end of life is an unmerited gift of God, and that no one can be certain of having received it while still alive. The work is a key statement of his mature teaching on grace and predestination.

Augustine of Hippo's last major polemical work, usually called the Opus imperfectum ("Unfinished Work"), is a reply to Julian of Eclanum, the leading Pelagian theologian. Julian had written eight books attacking the second book of Augustine's On Marriage and Concupiscence. Augustine quotes Julian's text passage by passage and answers each in turn. He began the work around 428–429 and had finished six books when he died in 430. In it he defends his teaching on original sin, concupiscence, grace and the transmission of Adam's fault, and it preserves much of Julian's otherwise lost writing.

This is a Latin collection of sermons attributed to Augustine of Hippo, bishop of Hippo Regius in North Africa (354–430). The pieces were published from manuscripts after the standard editions of his works had appeared, which is why they are called "unpublished". As the title says, the genuine sermons are mixed with others whose authenticity is doubtful. The first piece is a Holy Saturday sermon on the paschal candle. It treats the candle and the bee as figures of Christ and the just, and Samson killing the lion as a type of Christ. Its attribution to Augustine is itself questioned.

This is a collection of ten Latin sermons attributed to Augustine of Hippo (354–430). They were found in manuscripts at the Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino and first published by Ottavio Fraja Frangipane, a monk of that house. He dedicated the edition to a pope who had once been a Benedictine monk. Like other modern finds of sermons credited to Augustine, the group's authenticity needs to be judged piece by piece. Scholars accept some sermons in such collections as genuine and doubt others. The collection added to the known body of Augustine's preaching.

This Latin homily for the Second Sunday of Advent has come down under the name of Augustine of Hippo. Its authenticity is doubtful, since the liturgical framing suggests a later origin, and its date and real author are uncertain. Starting from the Gospel reading on the tribe from which Christ would be born, the preacher cites Psalm texts and Nathan's oracle to David in Chronicles. He argues that the promise of an everlasting throne for David's offspring cannot refer to Solomon, who began to reign while David was still alive, and must be fulfilled in Christ.

This is a Latin sermon for the feast of the Lord's Circumcision, handed down under the name of Augustine of Hippo (354–430). Its authenticity is doubtful, and its date and origin are uncertain. The preacher marks the yearly feast by reflecting on the mystery of the Incarnation. He stresses that the Son of God freely took on true flesh and true death out of mercy, not because of any human merit. He urges his hearers to give humble thanks for this unearned grace and to believe without hesitation in Christ's real humanity.

This is a small group of four Latin sermons attributed to Augustine of Hippo (354–430). They belong to the larger body of sermons that Cardinal Angelo Mai found in manuscripts and published in the nineteenth century. The first sermon explains Matthew 14:22 and following, where the disciples face a storm at sea and Christ comes to them. It compares Christ to a swallow teaching its young to fly, staying close so they do not fall. As with many sermons in Mai's collection, whether Augustine really wrote these is uncertain.

The Council of Auxerre was a diocesan synod held by Bishop Aunarius (Aunacharius) of Auxerre with the abbots and priests of his diocese in the late sixth century. Older editions date it to about 578, but its exact date is uncertain. Its Latin canons ban pagan New Year customs on the Kalends of January, auguries and divination. They also regulate vigils, baptism, burial, Sunday observance, clerical continence, monastic discipline and forbidden marriages. The canons are valuable evidence for pastoral practice and popular religion in Merovingian Gaul.

Aunarius, bishop of Auxerre (c. 540–c. 603), wrote this short Latin letter in the late sixth century to Stephen, a priest. Aunarius praises Stephen's learning and notes that readers differ in taste: some prefer prose, others verse. He therefore asks Stephen to put the life of Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, into verse and to write the life of Amator, Germanus's predecessor, in prose. The letter documents the bishop's support for writing about the saints of Auxerre and explains how the hagiography of the see's founding bishops came to be written.

The Regula ad monachos is a Latin monastic rule written by Aurelian, bishop of Arles from 546 to 551. He wrote it for a community of monks he founded at Arles with the support of the Frankish king Childebert I, probably around 548. The prologue urges the monks to give up worldly pleasures for chastity and the love of God. The rule then sets out their discipline and common life. It draws heavily on the rules of Caesarius of Arles. Aurelian also wrote a companion rule for nuns. Both are important witnesses to monasticism in sixth-century Gaul.

The Regula ad virgines (Rule for Virgins) is a Latin monastic rule written by Aurelian, bishop of Arles from 546 to 551, for the nuns of the monastery of Saint Mary that he founded within the walls of Arles. A prologue addressed to the sisters is followed by a list of short precepts. These require lifelong enclosure, the giving up of personal property, and obedience to the abbess, and they regulate correspondence, speech and community life. The rule draws heavily on the earlier rule for nuns by Caesarius of Arles. Aurelian also wrote a companion rule for monks.

This is a Latin letter, surviving only in excerpts, from Aurelian, bishop of Arles (546–551), to King Theodebert.
