The king is generally taken to be Theodebert I, Frankish king of Austrasia, who died in 548. That would place the letter between 546 and 548. In ornate, highly rhetorical prose, Aurelian apologises for writing late and modestly plays down his own eloquence. He then praises the king's piety, clemency and glory. The letter is a short example of how bishops in sixth-century Gaul addressed Merovingian rulers.

This circular letter in Latin, addressed to all bishops, was written by Aurelius, bishop of Carthage (c. 391–c. 430) and primate of the African Church. It concerns the condemnation of the heretics Pelagius and Caelestius. Its salutation names Donatianus, primate of Byzacena, and other bishops. Aurelius sent the letter together with an imperial constitution of Emperor Honorius against the Pelagians, and he required the bishops to subscribe to their condemnation. It is usually dated to about 419. It shows how the African episcopate and the imperial authorities worked together to enforce the anti-Pelagian decisions.

This brief synodal notice concerns Aurelius, bishop of Carthage from about 391 to about 430. It is preserved in Greek with a Latin translation and was drawn from the medieval Greek compilation known as the Libellus Synodicus. It records that after the deaths of the emperor Theodosius I and Nectarius of Constantinople, a provincial synod of 127 fathers met at Carthage under Aurelius. The synod acted against the Donatists, other heresies and local abuses, and issued canons that stayed in force until the reign of Theodosius II. The notice is a late summary, not a work written by Aurelius himself.

This brief Latin letter is addressed to Pope Damasus I in the name of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. It asks the pope to send copies of the decrees issued by the apostolic see from the death of Saint Peter to the start of Damasus's pontificate, so that violations of the apostolic canons can be identified. The attribution is chronologically impossible. Damasus died in 384, and Aurelius became bishop only around 391. The letter and the reply credited to Damasus are therefore regarded as spurious. They are generally linked to later forged collections of papal decretals.

This is the collected surviving writings of Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. 310 – c. 395), a Latin poet and teacher of rhetoric from Burdigala (Bordeaux) who tutored the future emperor Gratian and became consul in 379. It opens with a letter attributed to Emperor Theodosius asking for his writings, followed by the poet's verse reply. The corpus includes the Mosella, the Ephemeris with its Christian prayer, the Parentalia, the Commemoratio professorum Burdigalensium, epigrams, a speech thanking Gratian, and letters, including his exchange with his former pupil Paulinus of Nola.

This Latin verse letter was written around 470–475 by Auspicius, bishop of Toul, to Arbogast, the Roman count governing Trier. Auspicius recalls meeting Arbogast at Toul and praises his noble birth, his father Arigius, his mother and his upright character. He contrasts Arbogast's Christian faith with his famous pagan namesake and ancestor, the general Arbogast. The poem is written in accentual iambic stanzas, an early example of Latin verse based on stress rather than syllable length. It is also a rare witness to Roman life in Gaul as imperial rule collapsed.

This short Latin charter is attributed to Autbert (Aubert), bishop of Cambrai in the mid-seventh century. In it the bishop takes under his protection the estate of Wallare. King Dagobert is said to have given the estate to Landelin so that he could build a monastery there. The charter also grants Landelin and his successors the tithes of the property. It is generally considered spurious, a later forgery made to support a royal diploma of doubtful authenticity. Its stated dates contradict one another and do not match the monastery's actual foundation.

This is a Latin covering letter written around 415–416 by Avitus, a priest of Braga living in the Holy Land. He addressed it to Bishop Palchonius and to the clergy and people of Braga. Avitus regrets that the barbarian invasions of Hispania stopped him from returning home. He sends relics of the protomartyr Stephen, whose tomb had recently been found near Jerusalem, along with his Latin translation of the Greek account of the discovery by the priest Lucian. Gennadius mentions the letter, which is important evidence for the early spread of Stephen's cult in the West.

This is a short Latin collection of excerpts from the writings of Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul (died c. 518), arranged under verses of Paul's First Epistle to the Corinthians. Each lemma, such as "God chose the base and despised things of the world", is followed by a passage from Avitus, drawn for example from a sermon at a bishop's ordination and his books Contra Phantasma. The work preserves fragments of otherwise lost writings and shows how Avitus's theology was later read as Pauline commentary.

This is a short Latin collection of excerpts from the sermons of Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul (d. c. 518), arranged under passages of Paul's Second Epistle to the Corinthians. The passages include the veiled glory of Moses' face, being "away from the Lord" while in the body, God reconciling the world in Christ, and the "unspeakable words" Paul heard. Each excerpt names the sermon it comes from, such as homilies on the Creed and for Eastertide. Many of these homilies are otherwise lost, so the fragments help preserve Avitus's preaching.

This short Latin collection gathers passages from the writings of Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul (died c. 518), and arranges them under verses of Paul's Epistle to the Galatians. The verses include the one mediator, God sending his Son "made of a woman", and glorying only in the cross. The excerpts come from his anti-heretical books Contra Phantasma, a text on Christ's nativity, his letters and a Rogation sermon. Together they show how Avitus used Galatians in his Christological teaching. It is unclear who compiled the collection or when.

This is a short Latin collection of theological excerpts by Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul (died c. 518). The excerpts are grouped under verses of the Epistle to the Ephesians, such as "one Lord, one faith, one baptism". Most come from his lost books against the Arians. They argue for the unity and equality of the Trinity, citing Scripture such as Abraham's welcome of the three visitors at Mamre. The work survives only through a later compilation, and these fragments preserve parts of Avitus's polemic against the Arianism of the Burgundian court.

This short Latin collection of excerpts is attributed to Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul (died c. 518). It gathers his comments on Paul's hymn to Christ in Philippians 2:6–11. The passages are drawn mainly from a work cited as "Contra Phantasma," which is otherwise lost. They argue that Christ, while truly God, took the form of a servant and truly died as a man. They also explain his exaltation and the name above every name. The fragments preserve part of Avitus's lost anti-heretical writing on Christology.

This Latin collection of short excerpts is drawn from the writings of Avitus of Vienne, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul (died c. 518), and arranged under verses of Paul's Epistle to the Colossians. The opening passage comes from a sermon for the first day of Easter. It comments on Colossians 1:18, where Christ is called "firstborn from the dead". Avitus explains that others raised from death, such as Lazarus, died again. Christ alone rose never to die, and he is the first of the resurrection promised to the faithful.

This is a short Latin collection of passages from the sermons of Avitus, bishop of Vienne (died c. 518), that comment on verses of Paul's First Letter to the Thessalonians. They centre on 1 Thessalonians 4, where Paul describes the Lord coming at the voice of the archangel and the faithful caught up in the clouds to meet Christ. The excerpts come from Avitus's sermons on the Ascension and the Rogations, and they survive mainly as fragments of his otherwise largely lost preaching.

The Sententiae ex epistola I ad Timotheum is a short collection of excerpts from the writings of Avitus, bishop of Vienne (died c. 518). The passages are arranged as comments on verses of Paul's First Epistle to Timothy. They are drawn from several of his works, including his books against the Arians and a sermon on the ordination of a bishop. Topics include Christ as the one mediator, both God and man in one person, the qualities required of a bishop, young widows, and contentment with worldly goods. The collection shows how Avitus's theology was later sorted by biblical verse.

A short collection of Latin extracts from the writings of Avitus, bishop of Vienne (c. 450–517/518), arranged under verses of Paul's Second Epistle to Timothy. The opening passage comes from a sermon for the third day of Rogations. It takes the image in 2 Timothy 2:20 of gold, silver, wooden and earthen vessels in a great house and reads them as martyrs, virgins, married people and penitents, each able to offer a pure gift to God. These fragments preserve parts of Avitus's preaching that are otherwise largely lost.

This is a short Latin collection of excerpts from Avitus, bishop of Vienne (died c. 518), arranged under five verses of the Epistle to the Hebrews. The passages come from his otherwise largely lost writings, including a work on the divinity of Christ and books against the Arians. They interpret such texts as "Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee" and "Thou madest him a little lower than the angels". Together they preserve parts of Avitus's anti-Arian defence of Christ's full divinity, written in Burgundian Gaul.

Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul, wrote this Latin epic in hexameters on biblical history around the turn of the sixth century. Its five books cover the creation of the world, original sin, God's judgement and the expulsion from Paradise, the Flood, and the crossing of the Red Sea. A prose prologue dedicates it to his brother Apollinaris, bishop of Valence, and argues that Christian poetry must keep to the truth rather than poetic invention. It is a major work of late Latin biblical epic, and its account of the Fall has often been compared with Milton's Paradise Lost.

This is a small group of four Latin letters by Avitus, bishop of Vienne (died c. 518). They were brought together as a supplement to Jacques Sirmond's earlier collection of his correspondence. The first is addressed to Gundobad, king of the Burgundians. It answers the king's question about Christ's promise of a hundredfold reward (Matthew 19:29), reading it spiritually: God weighs the giver's intention, not the size of the gift. The letters show Avitus as theological adviser to the Burgundian court in the years around 500.

De Divinitate Spiritus Sancti is a Latin theological treatise by Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul (died c. 518). He wrote it against the Arian Burgundian king Gundobad. The work is lost and survives only in fragments quoted by later writers concerned with the procession of the Holy Spirit. Drawing on the Pauline letters, Acts and John, the fragments defend the full divinity of the Spirit. They also affirm that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, which makes them an early Gallic witness to the Filioque doctrine.

This Latin sermon by Avitus, bishop of Vienne (c. 490–518), was preached on the Tuesday of the Rogations. These three days of penitential processions and prayer before Ascension had been introduced in Vienne by his predecessor Mamertus. Avitus compares the Rogations to the heavenly food that sustained Elijah on his long journey. He defends the observance against people who scorned it as a recent novelty, and he calls everyone to penance. He then expounds the prophecy of Amos read at the service ("You only have I known of all the families of the earth").

The Epistolae are the collected Latin letters of Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus, bishop of Vienne (died c. 518), written between about 490 and 518. Some are the bishop's own correspondence with Burgundian kings, popes, bishops and lay aristocrats, and some he drafted for the Burgundian court. The collection opens with answers to theological questions from King Gundobad and includes arguments against Arianism and a famous letter congratulating Clovis on his baptism. The letters are an important source for church life, doctrinal controversy and politics in Gaul after Roman rule ended.

The Homily on the Rogations is a Latin sermon by Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul from about 490 until his death around 518. It explains where the Rogations came from: the penitential litanies and processions held before Ascension Day. Avitus claims the custom for the church of Vienne, where Bishop Mamertus introduced it in the later fifth century after a series of terrors: frequent fires, earthquakes, strange noises at night and wild animals appearing in the town. The homily is an early witness to the origin of a liturgical observance that spread across the Latin West.

Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul (died c. 518), preached the homilies that survive here only as fragments, along with the titles and opening words of eight of them. Many were given at church dedications and restorations, including a basilica at Geneva, the baptistery at Vienne, and a church of Saint Peter built by a bishop of Tarentaise. One was preached when the monastery of the Agaunum martyrs was renewed. Another marks a royal conversion from Arianism. Though incomplete, they show Avitus as a preacher and reflect the religious life of the Burgundian kingdom.

This Latin collection gathers passages on verses of Paul's Epistle to the Romans from the writings of Avitus, bishop of Vienne in Burgundian Gaul (died c. 518). It is not a continuous commentary. Excerpts from his works, including his treatise against the Eutychians (Contra phantasma), are arranged in eleven sections following the order of the epistle. They cover Christ's descent from David according to the flesh, the two natures of Christ, Adam and justification, grace, and the depth of God's wisdom. The compiler and date of compilation are uncertain.

The Professio Fidei (also called Libellus de fide) is a short Latin statement of faith by Bachiarius, a monk probably from Galicia or elsewhere in Hispania, written in the late fourth or early fifth century. It is addressed to a bishop, probably the bishop of Rome, as Gennadius reports. Bachiarius complains that he is suspected because of his home province rather than his words, a likely reference to Priscillianism, and he sets out orthodox teaching to clear himself. It is a valuable witness to the Priscillianist controversy.

The Liber de reparatione lapsi, also known as De recipiendis lapsis, is a Latin letter by Bachiarius, an early fifth-century writer who was probably a Galician monk. He addresses a fellow Christian, Januarius, about a man who had fallen into grave sin, generally understood as a monk who had seduced a consecrated virgin. Drawing heavily on Scripture, Bachiarius pleads for mercy and argues that a sinner who does penance should be restored to communion. It is one of only two works securely attributed to him.

This short Latin letter fragment is addressed to the patriarch of Grado and attributed to Pope Benedict I, bishop of Rome from 575 to 579. Its authenticity is doubtful. It survives as a palea, a later addition to Gratian's Decretum. The letter answers a question from a man named John: could his surviving daughter marry the young man who had been betrothed to her dead sister? Arguing from Genesis that only physical union makes two "one flesh", it rules that a betrothal by words alone creates no impediment, so the marriage may go ahead.

The Epistola ad David episcopum is a short Latin letter attributed to Pope Benedict I (575–579), addressed to a Bishop David. It answers his report that some people in the province of Baetica, in southern Spain, denied that the Trinity could be shown to be a unity. The letter gathers scriptural proofs of the Trinity in unity, such as the threefold "Holy" of Isaiah 6 and Genesis, and much of it is drawn from the anti-Arian treatise Contra Varimadum. Its authenticity is doubtful.

The Rule of Saint Benedict is a Latin monastic rule written by Benedict of Nursia, probably for his community at Monte Cassino, sometime between about 529 and his death around 547. It opens with the words "Listen, my son" (Ausculta, o fili). A prologue and seventy-three chapters set out how a monastery should be governed: the abbot's authority, obedience, humility, the daily Divine Office, manual work, reading, and common life. It draws on John Cassian and the earlier Rule of the Master and is known for its moderation. It became the most influential monastic rule in the Western Church.

The Expositio super septem visiones libri Apocalypsis is a Latin commentary on the Book of Revelation, attributed to Berengaudus. He is traditionally identified as a ninth-century Benedictine monk of Ferrières, but both the attribution and the date have been questioned. The work divides Revelation into seven visions and interprets them allegorically, verse by verse. It opens by defending the apostle and evangelist John as the book's author. It was once printed among the works of Ambrose. By the twelfth century it was widely copied, and it later accompanied many illuminated English Gothic Apocalypse manuscripts in Old French translation.

This is the will of Bertram (Bertechramnus), bishop of Le Mans from about 587 to 623, dated 27 March in the thirty-second year of King Chlothar II, usually reckoned as 616. Dictated to his notary Ebbo, it names the church of Le Mans and the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul, which Bertram built, as his heirs. It lists extensive estates, bequests and freed slaves. It survives because it was copied into the Le Mans episcopal deeds, and it is an important source for Merovingian landholding, law and church wealth.

De institutione arithmetica, in two books, is a Latin treatise on number theory by the Roman statesman and philosopher Boethius. It was probably written early in his career, in the first years of the sixth century. It freely adapts the Introduction to Arithmetic of the Greek Neopythagorean Nicomachus of Gerasa, and its preface dedicates the work to Boethius's father-in-law Symmachus. The treatise covers the classification of numbers, ratios and proportions, and introduces the term quadrivium. It became the standard arithmetic textbook of medieval Western schools.

De institutione musica, often called De musica, is a Latin treatise on music theory by the Roman philosopher and statesman Boethius, written in the early sixth century. It survives in five books, the last incomplete. It draws chiefly on Greek sources, especially Nicomachus and Ptolemy, and treats music as a mathematical discipline concerned with ratios, consonances and scales. It distinguishes cosmic, human and instrumental music. As part of the quadrivium, it became the standard authority on music theory in medieval schools and universities.

Boethius (c. 480–524) wrote two Latin commentaries on Porphyry's Isagoge, the Neoplatonist introduction to Aristotle's Categories. The first, in two books, is a dialogue between Boethius and his friend Fabius, set on a winter night in the mountains. It explains the Latin translation by Marius Victorinus and opens with the six standard preliminary questions of late-antique commentary. The second, in five books, is based on Boethius's own translation. Both belong to his early logical works, and they shaped medieval discussion of genera, species and the problem of universals.

De divisione is a short Latin treatise on logical division by Boethius, the Roman senator and philosopher (c. 480–524). Its exact date is uncertain. It was written as an introduction for Latin readers and draws on the Peripatetic tradition, citing Andronicus, Plotinus and Porphyry. It sets out the kinds of division: genus into species, a whole into its parts, and a word with several meanings into those meanings. It also covers three kinds of division by accident. With his other logical writings, it became a standard source for medieval teaching in logic.

The Liber de diffinitione (On Definition) is a short Latin treatise on the logical and rhetorical theory of definition. It was long transmitted among the works of Boethius, but modern scholarship generally attributes it to the fourth-century rhetorician Marius Victorinus. The author starts from Cicero's Topics and argues that any dispute needs an agreed definition of its subject, because words are ambiguous or obscure. He then defines definition itself and classifies its various kinds. The treatise is an important witness to the teaching of dialectic and rhetoric in late antiquity, and it was read widely in the Middle Ages.

This is the Latin translation of Aristotle's Topics, in eight books, made by the Roman philosopher and statesman Boethius in the early sixth century. It was part of his plan to make Aristotle's logical works available in Latin. The Topics sets out a method of dialectical reasoning from generally accepted premises. The opening defines the syllogism and separates demonstrative, dialectical and contentious reasoning. Boethius's version was little used at first. It became widely known in the twelfth century as part of the "new logic" of the medieval schools.

This is the Latin translation, in two books, of Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations (De sophisticis elenchis), made by Boethius in the early sixth century. It belonged to his plan to make Aristotle's logical works, the Organon, available in Latin. Aristotle's treatise examines fallacious arguments: reasonings that only seem to be valid syllogisms or refutations. It sorts them into fallacies that depend on language, such as ambiguity, and those that do not. The version came back into use in the twelfth century as part of the "new logic" and shaped medieval teaching on fallacies.

This Latin commentary by the Roman philosopher and statesman Boethius (c. 480–524) explains Cicero's Topica, a treatise on finding arguments from "topics" or commonplaces. Boethius dedicated it to Patricius, a skilled rhetorician who had asked for it. He presents his work as adding to the earlier four-book commentary by Marius Victorinus. It discusses invention and judgement in dialectic and how to define place and argument, and it survives incomplete in six books. Its exact date is uncertain. Together with Boethius's De topicis differentiis, it passed the ancient theory of topics on to medieval logic and rhetoric.

De differentiis topicis ("On Topical Differences") is a Latin treatise in four books by the Roman philosopher Boethius, written in the early sixth century. It deals with the logic of discovering arguments: the topics, or "places" (loci), from which arguments are drawn. Boethius sets out two classifications of the topics, one drawn from Greek sources and one from Cicero's Topica, shows how each can be fitted within the other, and explains how dialectical topics differ from rhetorical ones. It became a standard textbook of medieval logic and rhetoric.

The Speculatio de rhetoricae cognatione ("On the Kinship of Rhetoric") is a short Latin treatise attributed to Boethius, the Roman statesman and philosopher (c. 480–524). Earlier teachers had treated each rule of rhetoric separately. This treatise instead sets out what the whole art has in common: its genus, a faculty; its three species, judicial, demonstrative and deliberative; its subject matter, mostly civil questions; and its parts, instrument, work, the speaker's duty and its end. It draws on Ciceronian rhetoric and shows how late antique teaching on rhetoric was passed on to the Middle Ages.

The Locorum rhetoricorum distinctio is a short Latin treatise on rhetorical topics, attributed to Boethius (c. 480–524), although its authenticity is uncertain. Drawing on Cicero's De inventione, it explains how arguments in a legal case come from the attributes of the person and of the act. It lists the circumstances that make up the substance of a question: who, what, why, where, when, how and by what means. It then divides these, following Cicero, into eleven attributes of the person and several attributes of the act. It belongs with Boethius's work on rhetoric and the theory of topics.

Boethius (c. 480–524) wrote two Latin commentaries on Porphyry's Isagoge, the Neoplatonist introduction to Aristotle's Categories. The first, in two books, is a dialogue between Boethius and his friend Fabius, set on a winter night in the mountains. It explains the Latin translation by Marius Victorinus and opens with the six standard preliminary questions of late-antique commentary. The second, in five books, is based on Boethius's own translation. Both belong to his early logical works, and they shaped medieval discussion of genera, species and the problem of universals.

Quomodo Trinitas unus Deus ac non tres dii, usually called De Trinitate, is a short Latin theological treatise by the Roman statesman and philosopher Boethius. It was written in the early sixth century, before his execution in 524, and is dedicated to his father-in-law Symmachus. It is one of his Opuscula sacra. Using Aristotelian categories, it argues that God's unity rests on a single substance, while the distinction of Persons arises only from relation. Gilbert of Poitiers, Thierry of Chartres and Thomas Aquinas wrote commentaries on it, and it strongly influenced medieval Scholastic theology.

This brief Latin treatise by the Roman statesman and philosopher Boethius (c. 480–524) is addressed to John the Deacon. It is the second of his five theological tractates, the Opuscula sacra, and was written in the early sixth century. Using Aristotelian logic, Boethius asks which terms apply to God's substance. He concludes that names such as God, truth and goodness apply to the single divine substance and to each Person. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, however, name relations rather than substance. The tractate influenced medieval scholastic thinking about the Trinity.

This short Latin treatise by Boethius (c. 480–524) is commonly known as De hebdomadibus and is one of his theological tractates, the Opuscula sacra. It is addressed to the deacon John, probably the later Pope John I. Boethius sets out axioms in the manner of a mathematical proof. He then asks how created things can be good simply because they exist when they are not goodness itself. His answer is that their being comes from God, the first Good. The treatise strongly influenced medieval discussions of being and goodness.

This Latin theological treatise by the Roman philosopher and statesman Boethius is one of his short theological tractates, the Opuscula sacra. It is addressed to John the Deacon and was prompted by a debate in a Roman assembly over a bishop's letter about whether Christ is "from" two natures or "in" two natures. It is usually dated to around 512. Boethius uses Aristotelian logic to reject both Nestorius and Eutyches and to defend the Chalcedonian faith. In the treatise he defines a person as "an individual substance of a rational nature", a definition that became central to medieval theology.

This is a Latin commentary in four books on Aristotle's Categories by Boethius, the Roman senator and philosopher (c. 480–524). It is usually dated to around 510. It was written after his commentaries on Porphyry's Isagoge and is deliberately kept at an elementary level, setting aside deeper questions. Boethius explains Aristotle's ten categories as a theory of words that signify things. The commentary was part of his plan to make Aristotle's logic available in Latin, and it shaped how the Categories were read in the early medieval West.

This is the first and shorter of the two Latin commentaries that Boethius wrote on Aristotle's De interpretatione (Peri hermeneias), composed in the early sixth century. In the preface Boethius says that this edition offers a brief, step-by-step explanation of the text for beginners, and that harder questions are left to the longer second commentary. Following Aristotle's order, it explains interpretation as meaningful speech and then covers nouns, verbs and declarative sentences that can be true or false. It became an important channel through which Aristotelian logic reached the Latin Middle Ages.

This is the second and longer of Boethius's two Latin commentaries on Aristotle's De interpretatione, in six books, and is often called the "major commentaries." He wrote it in the early sixth century in Ostrogothic Italy. It goes through Aristotle's treatise step by step, beginning with a definition of the spoken sound (vox) and moving on to the noun, the verb, the proposition, opposition and modality. Boethius draws on earlier Greek commentators, especially Porphyry. His discussion of future contingents strongly influenced how medieval Latin thinkers understood logic, language and freedom.

This is the Latin translation of Aristotle's Prior Analytics, in two books, made by the Roman philosopher and statesman Boethius (c. 480–524) in the early sixth century. It was part of his plan to put Aristotle's logical works into Latin. The treatise defines the proposition, the term and the syllogism, then sets out the figures and moods of syllogistic reasoning and separates demonstrative from dialectical argument. Boethius's version was little used at first. It gained wide circulation in the twelfth century and became a basic text of medieval Latin logic.

This is a Latin translation of Aristotle's Posterior Analytics, the treatise of the Organon on demonstration, scientific knowledge and how first principles are known. It opens with the claim that all teaching and learning come from prior knowledge. It is traditionally printed among the works of Boethius (c. 480–524), who planned to translate all of Aristotle into Latin. Its authenticity is doubtful, however: no translation of this work by Boethius is known to survive. The earliest securely attested medieval Latin version is that of James of Venice in the twelfth century.

The Introductio ad syllogismos categoricos is a short Latin logical treatise by the Roman philosopher and statesman Boethius (c. 480–524). It was probably written in the early sixth century, though its exact date is uncertain. It is an elementary introduction to Aristotelian categorical logic. After a prologue on teaching beginners, it covers the groundwork needed for syllogisms: terms, nouns and verbs, and the kinds of categorical propositions and how they relate to one another. It is closely related to Boethius's De syllogismo categorico, and is often thought to be a revised and unfinished treatment of the same material.

De syllogismo categorico is a Latin treatise on logic in two books by the Roman philosopher and statesman Boethius (c. 480–524). It is generally dated to the earlier part of his scholarly career, though the exact date is uncertain. It is an introduction to the theory of the categorical syllogism set out in Aristotle's Prior Analytics, also drawing on later Greek Peripatetic writers. The work covers the kinds of propositions, their opposition and conversion, and the figures and moods of the syllogism. It was one of the main channels through which Aristotelian syllogistic reached the early medieval Latin West.

De Syllogismo Hypothetico (On the Hypothetical Syllogism) is a Latin treatise on logic by the Roman philosopher and statesman Boethius (c. 480–524), written in the early sixth century. Boethius dedicates it to an unnamed friend who already knew categorical syllogisms. It explains conditional and disjunctive arguments, a subject Aristotle never treated and on which Theophrastus and Eudemus, by Boethius's account, wrote only briefly. Boethius says he found no Latin treatment of the topic. The work was the main channel through which the ancient theory of hypothetical reasoning reached medieval Western logic.

This is the collected Latin correspondence and decrees of Boniface I, bishop of Rome from 418 to 422. The collection opens with documents on his contested election and the schism with the rival claimant Eulalius. These include reports by Symmachus, prefect of Rome, rescripts of Emperor Honorius, and a petition from the Roman presbyters defending Boniface's ordination. Other letters deal with church discipline and with the rights of the Gallic sees of Narbonne and Vienne against Arles. Some also assert Roman jurisdiction over Illyricum. Together they are an important source for papal authority in the early fifth century.

The Decreta ex epistolis excerpta is a short Latin collection of canonical decrees attributed to Pope Boniface I, bishop of Rome from 418 to 422. The excerpts were gathered from Gratian's Decretum and older manuscripts. They cover church discipline: thirty as the minimum age for ordaining a priest, appeals from metropolitans to primates, the inviolability of property consecrated to God, and the exemption of bishops from secular courts. Several items come from much later sources, including Justinian's Novels and Carolingian capitularies. That shows the attribution to Boniface is largely spurious.

This is a small collection of Latin letters and decrees issued by Pope Boniface II during his brief pontificate (530–532). The best known is his letter to Caesarius of Arles. Writing at Caesarius's request, Boniface confirms with the authority of the apostolic see the teaching of the Council of Orange (529). Against certain Gallic bishops, it holds that even the beginning of faith comes from God's prevenient grace and not from human nature or free will. The letter was decisive in ending the Semi-Pelagian controversy in the West.

The Roman Council of 610 was a synod of Italian bishops held at Rome under Pope Boniface IV, dated to 27 February in the eighth year of the emperor Phocas. Bede reports that it dealt with the life and discipline of monks. Mellitus, the first bishop of London, attended and consulted the pope on the needs of the young English Church. Bede says its canons were lost, but a synodal decree defending the right of monks to exercise priestly ministry has come down under its name. Whether that decree is authentic is disputed.

This short Latin decree is attributed to Pope Boniface IV and dated to a Roman synod held in 610, a council that Bishop Mellitus of London is known to have attended. It answers critics who said monks were "dead to the world" and therefore unfit to hold priestly office. Against them it argues that ordained monks may lawfully exercise the power to bind and loose, absolve penitents and administer the sacraments. Its examples include Gregory the Great, Augustine of Canterbury, Martin of Tours and the Rule of Benedict. Scholars have questioned whether the text is authentic.

This is a short Latin letter attributed to Pope Boniface IV (608–615), sent after a Roman synod to Æthelberht, king of Kent. Bede records that Mellitus, bishop of London, attended this synod around 610. The letter praises the king's faith. It grants his request, made through Mellitus, that monks living under a rule should staff the monastery of the Holy Saviour at Canterbury, which Augustine consecrated and Laurence then led. It threatens with anathema anyone who undoes the grant. Its authenticity has been questioned, and it may be a later Canterbury forgery.

This is a small group of three Latin letters by Pope Boniface V, who was bishop of Rome from 619 to 625. The first is addressed to Justus, formerly bishop of Rochester and now Mellitus's successor as archbishop of Canterbury. It praises him for bringing King Eadbald of Kent (Adaluald) to the faith, sends him the pallium and gives him the right to ordain bishops. Bede preserves other letters by Boniface to King Edwin of Northumbria and his queen Æthelburh. These letters are important evidence for papal involvement in the conversion of Anglo-Saxon England.

This Latin letter is addressed in the name of Pope Boniface V (619–625) to Justus, archbishop of Canterbury. It welcomes news that many pagans in Kent had been converted and that King Eadbald had turned to the true faith. It then confirms Pope Gregory the Great's arrangement making Canterbury (Dorobernia) the metropolitan and primatial see of the English, with authority over the whole island. It is not the authentic letter of Boniface to Justus that Bede preserves. Its genuineness is doubted, and it is generally associated with the later Canterbury claims to primacy over York.

This Latin commentary is by Bovo, abbot of Corvey in Saxony (900–916). It explains a single poem, the hymn "O qui perpetua mundum ratione gubernas" from Book III, metre 9 of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy. Bovo wrote it for a kinsman, the bishop Bovo, after first explaining the passage to him in person. He finished it amid civil wars and pagan raids. He identifies the poem's Platonic teachings on the world-soul and the soul's origin and judges them against Christian doctrine, warning readers about where they go wrong.

The Epistolae are the collected Latin letters of Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza (c. 585–651), a leading churchman of Visigothic Hispania. Written roughly between 631 and 651, the collection includes letters Braulio received as well as those he sent. Among them is his correspondence with Isidore of Seville, which shows Braulio urging his friend to finish the Etymologies. Other letters went to Visigothic kings, a pope and fellow clerics. The collection is an important source for the Church, learning and politics of seventh-century Spain.

This Latin hagiography by Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, tells the life of Aemilianus (San Millán), a sixth-century hermit and priest in northern Hispania. Braulio wrote it after 631 and dedicated it to his brother, the priest Fronimian. He says he first took up the task when their elder brother John, his predecessor as bishop, asked him to. He drew on a memorandum of testimony from the abbot Citonatus, the priests Sophronius and Gerontius, and the religious woman Potamia. The work describes the saint's miracles and ascetic life. It is the chief early source for his cult in Visigothic Spain.

The Acta de martyribus Caesaraugustanis is a Latin hagiographical account of the Christians of Caesaraugusta (Zaragoza) who were put to death in the persecution under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, traditionally dated to 303. It is attributed to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza (c. 585–651), though the attribution is uncertain. A rhetorical prologue contrasts the pagan custom of honouring heroes in histories, poems and inscriptions with the Christian duty to celebrate Christ's soldiers. It then tells of the imperial edicts against Christians and the martyrs' sufferings. It is evidence for the cult of Zaragoza's martyrs in Visigothic Spain.

These are three Latin letters by Bulgaranus (Bulgar), a Visigothic count writing about 610–612, during the reign of King Gundemar. They are addressed to bishops in Francia. The letters deal with the conflict among the Merovingian rulers. Bulgaranus reports rumours that Brunhild and King Theuderic II were stirring up war against King Theudebert II. He proposes public litanies and prayers for the Catholic cause and asks for news of envoys and diplomatic negotiations. The letters are a rare source for relations between the Visigothic kingdom and the Franks in the early seventh century.

The Expositio in Apocalypsim is a Latin commentary on the Book of Revelation, written as a series of homilies addressed to "dearest brethren". It was long transmitted among the works of Augustine, but is now generally attributed to Caesarius, bishop of Arles (d. 542), and dates from the early sixth century. It reads the Apocalypse spiritually ("secundum anagogen"), chiefly as a figure of the Church and of Christ, its head. It draws heavily on the lost commentary of the Donatist Tyconius, so it is an important witness to his interpretation.

These are Latin sermons of Caesarius, bishop of Arles (died 542), the leading churchman of early sixth-century Gaul and a famously active popular preacher. Written to be clear and easy to repeat, they mostly teach morals: charity, penance, getting ready for judgement and giving up pagan customs. Caesarius encouraged other clergy to reuse them, so many circulated under Augustine's name, and older printed collections combine genuine pieces with doubtful ones, such as homilies on Easter and Christ's descent into hell. The sermons are an important witness to Christian life in late antique Gaul.

De canonibus observandis is a short Latin text preserving the decisions of a synod of bishops held at Arles, usually dated to 524. The bishops met to dedicate the basilica of Saint Mary, and Caesarius of Arles presided. Its four canons set rules for ordaining clergy. A deacon must be at least twenty-five years old, and a layman may not become bishop or priest before turning thirty. Candidates must first spend a year in religious conversion. Penitents and men who had remarried could not be ordained, and a bishop who received another church's cleric was to be excommunicated.

De viduitate servanda ("On Keeping Widowhood") is a short Latin exhortation to a widow, traditionally attributed to Caesarius, bishop of Arles in southern Gaul (died 542). It addresses the reader as a "forsaken daughter" and urges her not to remarry. Drawing heavily on Paul's instructions about widows in 1 Timothy 5, it calls her to trust in God rather than worldly support, and to live in prayer, humility, sobriety and good management of her household. Its authorship is not fully certain.

The Regula ad monachos (Rule for Monks) is a short Latin monastic rule written by Caesarius, bishop of Arles from 502 to 542, for communities of men. A preface says it was passed on by the priest Tetradius, Caesarius's nephew, and that the bishop had sent it to various monasteries. In brief chapters it requires lifelong stability, the giving up of all private property, a shared dormitory, and rules against swearing and lying. It draws on Augustine and the tradition of Lérins, and is a companion to his longer Rule for Virgins.

The Regula ad virgines (Rule for Virgins) is a Latin monastic rule by Caesarius, bishop of Arles (d. 542). He wrote it for the convent of St John, which he founded at Arles around 512 and which his sister Caesaria led as first abbess. Caesarius revised it over many years. Drawing on Augustine and John Cassian, it requires lifelong enclosure, shared property, obedience, set psalmody and manual work such as copying books. It is generally regarded as the first Western rule written specifically for women, and later communities adopted it, notably Radegund's Holy Cross at Poitiers.

The Epistolae are the surviving Latin letters of Caesarius of Arles (c. 470–542), bishop of Arles and the leading churchman of early sixth-century Gaul. They date from his episcopate (502–542). Several are exhortations on the monastic life. The first is addressed to the abbess Caesaria and her community at the women's monastery Caesarius founded in Arles. Written at her repeated request, it urges her toward virginity, humility and obedience to God's will. Together with his Rule for nuns and his sermons, the letters show his pastoral and ascetic teaching.

The Testamentum is the Latin will of Caesarius of Arles (d. 542), bishop of Arles in southern Gaul, probably written late in his life. It is addressed to the clergy, to the abbess Caesaria and to the community of nuns. Caesarius makes the monastery of St John at Arles, which he had founded, his heir, with the bishop of Arles as co-heir, and places it under episcopal authority. He also frees slaves and makes bequests. It is an important source for the history of late Roman testamentary law, church property and women's monasticism in Gaul.

This short Latin homily on the parable of the ten virgins (Matthew 25:1–13) is attributed to Caesarius, bishop of Arles from 502 to 542. Although it is titled a letter, it is addressed to "dearly beloved brothers" and reads as a sermon. It explains the parable allegorically: the sleep of the virgins stands for death, midnight for the unknown hour of the Day of Judgement, and the oil for mercy and charity. Listeners are urged to store up enough of these good works in their souls to last for eternity. This moral emphasis is typical of Caesarius's popular preaching.

This short Latin homily on the monastic life is transmitted among the works of Caesarius of Arles (d. 542), the bishop and preacher of Merovingian Gaul. Its heading, however, presents it as the teaching of Abbot Macarius for those living in monasteries, so the attribution to Caesarius is doubtful. It describes the monk's spiritual progress: knowing oneself and seeking God, repenting past negligence, and practising fasting, vigils, prayer, humility and contempt of the world. It also warns of the devil's temptations to give up the effort.

This is a short critical notice in Latin about the one decree credited to Pope Caius, bishop of Rome from 283 to 296. It is a later scholarly discussion, not a work by Caius. It notes that no genuine letter of his survives or is even mentioned. The Liber Pontificalis says he ordered that a future bishop must first pass through every grade of ministry, from doorkeeper to presbyter. Drawing on Cyprian, Cornelius and the Council of Serdica (c. 343), the notice argues that the custom was older than Caius but that the strict law came later than his time.

A short Latin theological treatise addressed to the rhetorician Marius Victorinus by Candidus, an Arian otherwise known only from this correspondence. It was probably written in the late 350s. Candidus argues that all generation is a kind of change and God is immutable, so God is unbegotten and cannot beget. From this he concludes that the Son is not generated from the Father's substance but is the Father's first work. Victorinus replied with his treatise Ad Candidum. Some scholars have suggested that Candidus was a literary fiction created by Victorinus himself.

This short Latin letter is addressed to the Roman rhetor and Christian Neoplatonist Marius Victorinus and attributed to Candidus, an Arian. It dates from around 355–360 and belongs to their exchange on the generation of the Son. Candidus argues that Christ was made, not begotten. As support, he gives Latin versions of Arius's letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia and of Eusebius's letter to Paulinus of Tyre. These are early witnesses to Arian documents in Latin. Scholars disagree about whether Candidus was a real person or a figure invented by Victorinus.

The surviving Latin letters of Capreolus, bishop of Carthage in the early 430s. The best known is addressed to the Council of Ephesus (431). In it Capreolus explains why no African delegation could attend: Theodosius II's summons had been meant for Augustine, who had already died, and the Vandal invasion had cut off travel across Africa. The letter defends the single person of Christ, God and man, against Nestorius. It was read in the council's proceedings, and Ferrandus later quoted it. A second letter, sent to correspondents in Spain, also deals with the unity of Christ's person.

The Chronica, or Chronicle, is a short Latin world chronicle by the Roman statesman Cassiodorus. He compiled it in 519 at the request of Eutharic, son-in-law of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric the Great, to mark Eutharic's consulship that year. Its preface says it was meant to correct the consular lists. It begins with Adam and the Flood, runs through the Assyrian kings and other ancient rulers, and then lists the Roman consuls down to 519. It draws on Eusebius and Jerome, Livy and Prosper of Aquitaine, and it presents Gothic rule in a favourable light.

The Computus Paschalis is a short Latin manual of calendar reckoning, traditionally attributed to Cassiodorus, though the attribution is not certain. Its worked examples use the twenty-first year after the consulship of Basilius the Younger, which points to composition around 562. It gives arithmetical rules for finding the year since the Incarnation, the indiction, the epacts (lunar additions) and the concurrents (solar weekday numbers), all of which are needed to fix the date of Easter. It is an early witness to the spread of the Dionysian Anno Domini era in sixth-century Italy.

The Variae, in twelve books, is a collection of official letters and documents written in Latin by Cassiodorus while he held high office under the Ostrogothic rulers of Italy, from Theodoric the Great to Witigis. It was published around 537–538. The preface says friends urged him to gather his writings so that later readers would know of his labours and his honest conduct in office. The letters, written in an elaborate rhetorical style, include model formulae for appointing officials. The collection is a major source for the government, society and culture of Ostrogothic Italy.

The Historia ecclesiastica tripartita, or Tripartite History, is a Latin church history in twelve books. It was compiled under the direction of Cassiodorus, and Epiphanius Scholasticus translated it from the Greek. It brings together excerpts from the church histories of Socrates Scholasticus, Sozomen and Theodoret, covering the period from Constantine to Theodosius II, roughly 324 to 439. It is usually dated to around 550, although some scholars have argued for an earlier date. Together with Rufinus's Latin version of Eusebius, it became the standard manual of church history in the medieval West.

The Expositio Psalmorum is a Latin commentary on all 150 psalms by Cassiodorus. He wrote it in the mid-sixth century, after leaving public office under the Ostrogoths, and finished it in connection with his monastery at Vivarium. It draws heavily on Augustine's Enarrationes in Psalmos. Each psalm receives a Christological and moral reading. The commentary also explains the psalm titles and points out rhetorical figures and material from the liberal arts. It was widely copied and abridged, and it became one of the standard psalm commentaries of the medieval West.

De Institutione Divinarum Litterarum is the first book of the Institutiones, written by Cassiodorus around the mid-sixth century for the monks of his Vivarium monastery in southern Italy. He explains that he and Pope Agapetus had planned a Christian school in Rome, modelled on Alexandria and Nisibis, but war prevented it. The book became a guide instead. It surveys the books of Scripture and their best commentators, and it gives advice on copying and correcting texts. It strongly shaped monastic learning and libraries in the medieval West.

This Latin treatise on the seven liberal arts is the second book of the Institutiones by Cassiodorus (c. 485 – c. 585). He wrote it in the later part of his life, after leaving Ostrogothic government service and founding the monastery of Vivarium in southern Italy. The first book guides the reader through sacred literature. This one surveys secular learning in seven sections: grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic, music, geometry and astronomy. Cassiodorus justifies the number seven from Scripture. The book passed classical learning on to the monks and became a basic textbook in medieval education.

De Orthographia is a Latin treatise on correct spelling, compiled by Cassiodorus near the end of his long life, probably around 580, for the monks of his foundation at Vivarium in southern Italy. In the preface he says the monks asked how to write correctly the texts they studied and copied. In response he gathered excerpts from twelve earlier grammarians, among them Donatus and Priscian. The preface also looks back over his earlier works, including the Psalm commentary and the Institutiones. The treatise shows the practical care for accurate copying behind monastic scholarship.

De anima ("On the Soul") is a short Latin treatise by Cassiodorus, the Roman statesman and scholar who served the Ostrogothic court and later founded the Vivarium monastery. He wrote it around 540, just after finishing the twelve books of his official letters, the Variae, and it was often transmitted as their thirteenth book. Friends had asked him for an account of the soul. The treatise covers the soul's substance, origin, form, moral virtues and fate after death, drawing especially on Augustine and Claudianus Mamertus. It is often seen as marking Cassiodorus's turn from public life to Christian learning.

The Complexiones in Epistolis Apostolorum are short Latin commentaries by Cassiodorus, the Roman statesman who in later life founded the Vivarium monastery in southern Italy. They were written late in his life, when he was devoted to Christian learning. Each one briefly summarises a passage from the apostolic letters, the Acts of the Apostles or the Apocalypse. The commentary on Romans begins by stressing Paul's apostolic calling and the Trinity. The work reflects Cassiodorus's aim of giving monks simple guides for reading Scripture.

This short Latin letter is attributed to Castor, bishop of Apt in southern Gaul, and addressed to John Cassian. It probably dates from about 419–426. Castor calls himself a novice in the monastic life. Because Cassian knew the monasteries of Egypt, the Thebaid and Palestine, including Bethlehem, Castor asks him to write down their rules in simple language for a newly founded monastery in Provence. Cassian answered with his Institutes, whose preface is addressed to Castor. The letter therefore shows how Eastern monastic practice was carried into Gaul.

The Contra Maximinum Arianum is a short Latin anti-Arian treatise by Cerealis, Catholic bishop of Castellum in Roman North Africa, written around 484 during the Vandal persecution. According to its introduction, Cerealis came to Carthage and was challenged by Maximinus, an Arian bishop, to support each of a series of propositions with two or three scriptural testimonies. Cerealis answered with many more. Under headings on the Son's equality with the Father, the divinity and creative power of the Holy Spirit, and the unity of the Trinity, he sets out collections of biblical proof-texts. Gennadius of Marseille also records the work.

This is a short Latin letter sent to Pope Leo the Great around 450–451 by three bishops of southern Gaul: Ceretius of Grenoble, Salonius of Geneva and Veranus of Vence. Salonius and Veranus were sons of Eucherius of Lyon. The bishops thank Leo for his Tome to Flavian, his statement of Christological doctrine against Eutyches. They say they have had a copy made and ask him to look it over and correct any errors. The letter survives among Leo's correspondence and shows how widely the Tome was received in the West before the Council of Chalcedon.

This Latin royal decree was issued by Childebert I, Merovingian king of Paris from 511 to 558. It was sent to bishops and to all the people. It orders landowners to destroy idols and shrines dedicated to demons on their estates, and not to hinder priests who remove them. It also bans drunken night vigils, coarse songs and dancing on Easter, Christmas, other feasts and Sundays. Slaves who break it are to be flogged, and free persons punished more severely. The decree shows Frankish kings using royal power to enforce church discipline and Christianize rural Gaul.

This short Latin letter, issued by the Frankish king Clovis I to the bishops of his realm, dates from soon after his campaign against the Visigoths of 507. Clovis says that before entering Gothic territory he ordered his army not to harm churches, nuns, widows, clerics, their children, or church slaves. Any such persons taken captive were to be returned without delay. For lay captives, the bishops could intercede, sending sealed letters confirmed by oath to prevent false claims. It is an early witness to relations between the Merovingian king and the Gallic episcopate.

The Constitutio Generalis, also known as the Praeceptio Chlotharii, is a short Latin royal decree issued by a Merovingian king named Chlothar to all his officials. It is traditionally ascribed to Chlothar I (reigned 511–561), though some scholars assign it to Chlothar II. The decree orders judges to follow established law and forbids condemning anyone unheard. It lets Romans settle disputes under Roman law and gives bishops a role in correcting unjust judges. It also bans forced marriages of widows, girls and nuns, and protects bequests to churches.

This is a short Merovingian legal decree in Latin, printed among the Frankish capitularies under the name of King Chlothar II (reigned 584–629). Its provisions closely match the peace-keeping decree often ascribed to Childebert I and Chlothar I, so the attribution is uncertain. It makes local units called centenae responsible for catching thieves and repaying stolen goods. It also sets out procedures for proof by lot, for accused slaves of the Church, the fisc or private owners, and for the duties of masters.

The Edict of Paris is a Latin royal decree issued by the Merovingian king Chlothar II in 614, after a council of bishops met at Paris. It confirms the authority of church canons and rules on the Church's relations with the crown. A bishop is to be elected by clergy and people and consecrated by his metropolitan with royal approval. No bishop may name his own successor, and clerics may not go over their bishop's head to the king. The edict also deals with secular administration, and historians disagree on how far it limited royal power.

The Praeceptum pro monasterio Sancti Dionysii is a Latin royal charter issued by the Merovingian king Chlothar II (reigned 584–629). Its exact date is unknown. At the request of Dodo, abbot of the basilica of Saint Denis, the king confirms the will of John, a former merchant. John left property, including lands, houses and slaves, to Saint-Denis, to other holy places in Paris and to his relatives. The text survives only in fragments. It is early evidence for the endowment of Saint-Denis and for Merovingian chancery Latin.

This is a short Latin letter attributed to the Frankish king Chlothar II (584–629), written to Arnulf, bishop of Metz. Arnulf had repeatedly asked the king to choose a successor so that he could give up his see. In reply, Chlothar refuses to appoint anyone in his place and urges him not to leave the court or withdraw his fellowship. The date is uncertain. Earlier editors proposed several years, and Bouquet placed it around 625. The letter shows how much Merovingian kings relied on bishops as counsellors.

This is a Latin sermon on the eight Beatitudes of Matthew 5, attributed to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia from about 388 to his death around 407. The preacher opens by taking the crowd gathered for a market as his occasion. He offers the Beatitudes to his hearers as precious pearls to be "bought" and describes them as steps laid down by Christ, leading the faithful upward to the kingdom of heaven. It has often been grouped with Chromatius's tractates on Matthew's Gospel, sometimes as the first of them.

This is the prologue to the Latin tractates, or sermons, on the Gospel of Matthew by Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia from about 388 until his death around 407. It introduces the commentary by setting out the gospel as the special vessel of the mystery of salvation. It then names the four evangelists and the order in which they wrote. According to the prologue, Matthew wrote first and John last, after his exile on Patmos, to answer rising heresies. It also stresses that Matthew and John were apostolic eyewitnesses. The collection of tractates survives only in part.

The Dicta are short sayings of Chromatius, later bishop of Aquileia (died c. 406/407). They survive in the acts of the Council of Aquileia of 381, which met under Bishop Valerian and was led by Ambrose of Milan. Chromatius, then a presbyter of the Aquileian church, spoke at the council against the Arian bishops Palladius and Secundianus. His brief remarks charge Palladius with denying the true power and divinity of the Son and press for his condemnation. They are among the earliest records of Chromatius's role in defending Nicene orthodoxy in northern Italy.

This Latin hymn on Christ's Passion opens "Pange lingua gloriosi proelium certaminis." It is generally credited to Venantius Fortunatus, writing in the late sixth century, although some older editions assign it to the fifth-century Gallo-Roman theologian Claudianus Mamertus. In trochaic verse, it traces salvation from Adam's fall through the tree to the Incarnation and Crucifixion. It then addresses the Cross as the one noble tree. Its stanzas, including "Crux fidelis," became part of the Western liturgy of Holy Week and Good Friday.

The Gratiarum Actio is a Latin speech of thanks (panegyric) by Claudius Mamertinus to the emperor Julian. Mamertinus gave it in Constantinople on 1 January 362, when he took up the consulship that Julian had granted him. Julian had already given him the treasury and the praetorian prefecture of Illyricum. The speech praises Julian's virtues, his campaigns in Gaul and his reforms of the corrupt administration of his predecessor Constantius II. It survives in the Panegyrici Latini and is an important contemporary witness to Julian's brief reign.

The Vita S. Brigidae is a Latin Life of Brigid of Kildare, written by the Irish monk Cogitosus, probably around 650–680. It is usually counted among the earliest surviving Irish hagiographies. Cogitosus says he wrote it at the request of his brethren. He presents Brigid mainly through her miracles and describes how she founded the monastery at Kildare, calling the anchorite Conláed from the wilderness to serve as its bishop. The work strongly promotes Kildare's claim to pre-eminence among Irish churches. Its account of the church at Kildare is a rare early description of an Irish church building.

This is the prefatory material and table of chapters of the Collectio Hispana, the great canon-law collection of the Visigothic Spanish Church. It was compiled anonymously in the seventh century, probably around the Fourth Council of Toledo (633), and later revised. It was long attributed to Isidore of Seville, but that attribution is uncertain. The collection gathers canons of Greek, African, Gallic and Spanish councils together with papal decretals. The preface opens with a verse dialogue in which the personified Codex describes its authority over the faith, worship and discipline of the Church.

The Graecorum concilia is the section of the Collectio Hispana that gives Latin versions of the canons of the Eastern councils. The Hispana is an anonymous canonical collection compiled in Visigothic Spain, probably around or after the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633, and was traditionally but doubtfully linked to Isidore of Seville. The section opens with a preface on the four principal ecumenical councils. It names Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon and the heresies each condemned. It then gives the conciliar canons. It was an important channel through which Greek church legislation reached the Latin West.

The Africae concilia is the section of the Collectio Hispana that holds the canons of church councils held in Roman North Africa. The Hispana is an anonymous Latin collection of canon law compiled in Visigothic Spain in the seventh century. The section opens with the Council of Carthage held under Bishop Gratus around 345–348, after the emperor Constans sent Paul and Macarius to end the Donatist schism. Its canons begin by forbidding the repetition of baptism given in the name of the Trinity. The section helped pass African conciliar legislation into later Western canon law.

This Latin collection of canons from church councils held in Gaul forms the Gallic section of the Collectio Hispana. The Hispana was a canon-law compilation made in Visigothic Spain, probably around the Fourth Council of Toledo (633), and traditionally linked with Isidore of Seville. The series begins with the Council of Arles of 314, held under Bishop Marinus and addressed to Pope Silvester, which ruled on the date of Easter, clerical stability and the excommunication of charioteers and actors. Later Gallic synods, such as Agde (506), follow. The collection preserved these disciplinary decrees for the Western Church.

This is the collection of canons from councils held in Spain, preserved in the Collectio Hispana, the canon-law compilation of Visigothic Spain. The Hispana was assembled anonymously, probably around the Fourth Council of Toledo (633), and was expanded in later recensions. Its attribution to Isidore of Seville is traditional but disputed. The Spanish section opens with the Council of Elvira, held in the early fourth century, and continues with the councils of Toledo and other synods. It is a key source for Iberian church discipline and later shaped the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals.

The Epistolae decretales are the second part of the Collectio Hispana, the canon-law collection compiled in Visigothic Spain from about 633 and revised later in the seventh century. Its compiler is unknown; the traditional attribution to Isidore of Seville is uncertain. This section gathers letters on doctrine and church discipline from twenty bishops, mostly popes from Damasus to Gregory the Great. It opens with Damasus's letter to Paulinus of Antioch on the full humanity of Christ. The collection was a major channel for passing papal decretals into early medieval canon law.

The Regula Coenobialis ("Communal Rule") is a Latin monastic rule attributed to the Irish missionary Columbanus (d. 615). It was probably composed between about 590 and 615 for the monasteries he founded in Gaul and northern Italy, such as Luxeuil and Bobbio. It is a companion to his Regula Monachorum and sets fixed penalties for faults in community life, often fasting, silence or strokes of the lash. Its strict discipline shaped Irish-influenced monasticism on the Continent until the Benedictine Rule gradually replaced it.

This Latin penitential is attributed to Columbanus, the Irish monk who founded Luxeuil and Bobbio, and was probably written during his work on the Continent around 590–615. It begins by defining true penance as weeping for sins committed and not committing them again. It then sets out a scale of penances, often fasting on bread and water for a set time, matched to the seriousness of each sin. Separate sections cover monks, clergy and laypeople. The work helped spread the Irish system of private, tariffed penance through Frankish Gaul.

The Instructiones, a collection of thirteen short Latin sermons, are traditionally attributed to the Irish missionary abbot Columbanus (d. 615). Scholars have disputed the attribution, but many now accept it. If they are his, they date from the years of his work on the Continent, roughly 590 to 615. The first sermon sets out faith in the one and triune God. The others address monks on the brevity and illusion of earthly life, self-denial, compunction, love of God and longing for the heavenly homeland. They are an important witness to early Hiberno-Latin spirituality and preaching.

This is a collection of Latin letters by the Irish monk and missionary Columbanus (d. 615), written between about 600 and 613 while he was working in Gaul and Lombard Italy. It opens with a letter to Pope Gregory the Great defending the Irish method of dating Easter, which drew on Anatolius of Laodicea. Other letters in the set are addressed to popes, to Frankish bishops and to his own monks. Written in an ornate Hiberno-Latin style, they are key evidence for the Easter controversy and for Irish monasticism on the Continent.

The Carmina are a small group of Latin poems traditionally ascribed to the Irish monk Columbanus (d. 615), founder of Luxeuil and Bobbio. They include verse epistles to Hunaldus, Sethus and Fidolius, and a series of moral monostichs. In a plain, admonitory style the poems urge their readers to despise riches and passing pleasures, remember how short life is and how close death is, and live by God's law and the example of the Fathers. Whether they are authentic is disputed. Some scholars assign some or all of them to a later Carolingian Columbanus, sometimes identified as Columbanus of Saint-Trond.

The Instructiones is a Latin didactic poem by Commodian, a Christian poet who said he had converted from paganism. It is usually dated to the mid-third century, though some scholars place it later. It has 80 short poems, nearly all of them acrostics, written in rhythmic hexameters that depend on stress rather than classical quantity. The first part mocks the pagan gods and addresses Jews and heathens. The second deals with Antichrist, the end of the world and the resurrection, and gives advice to Christians, penitents and clergy.

This is a record of a synod of North African bishops at Carthage under Cyprian, usually dated to about 251–253, although some editions place it later. Its best-known ruling, preserved in Cyprian's synodal letter to the bishop Fidus, rejected the view that baptism should wait until the eighth day after birth by analogy with circumcision. It held instead that newborn infants should not be denied grace. The record also covers disciplinary matters, including an insolent deacon and a layman who named a presbyter as guardian in his will. It is an early witness to infant baptism.

This is the record of an African council held at Carthage under Cyprian, usually dated around 254, though some older editors place it later. It survives as a synodal letter, counted as Cyprian's Epistle 67. Spanish Christians had asked for its judgement on Basilides of León and Martial of Astorga. Both bishops had lapsed during the Decian persecution as libellatici and were deposed. Basilides then won support from Pope Stephen. The council upheld the deposition and their replacement by Sabinus and Felix, holding that lapsed bishops could not keep their office.

This is the synodal record of the first of the councils held at Carthage under Cyprian on the baptism of heretics, usually dated around 255, though some sources give 256 or 258. Numidian bishops had asked whether people baptized by heretics, including Novatianists, should be baptized again when they joined the Church. The assembled African bishops replied that baptism outside the one Church is invalid, so such converts must receive true baptism. Their reply survives as Cyprian's Letter 70. The ruling began the controversy with Pope Stephen I.

This is the record of a council of 71 bishops from Africa and Numidia that Cyprian of Carthage called in 256 during the controversy over heretical baptism. It was the second of his councils on the question. It confirmed two decisions. Clergy who had lapsed from the faith were to be readmitted only to lay communion. Baptism given by heretics was held to be null, so converts needed true baptism, not rebaptism. Cyprian reported these decisions to Pope Stephen I, who rejected them and upheld Roman practice.

The Sententiae episcoporum is the Latin record of the council of North African bishops that met at Carthage under Cyprian on 1 September, usually dated to 256, though some headings give 258. After letters exchanged with Bishop Jubaianus were read, Cyprian and each of the eighty-seven bishops from Africa, Numidia and Mauritania gave a short opinion in turn. All held that heretics joining the Church must be baptized. The record opposed the position of Stephen of Rome and was later debated in Augustine's writings against the Donatists.

The Seventh Council of Carthage met in 256 under Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, and dealt with the baptism of heretics. Its record, usually called the Sententiae episcoporum, preserves the individual votes of the roughly eighty-seven African bishops present. They agreed unanimously that people baptized outside the Catholic Church must be baptized again, a position opposed to that of Pope Stephen I of Rome. The Western Church later rejected this view. The Greek canonical collections still kept the council's decision, together with related letters of Cyprian.

This short Latin entry in collections of African church councils concerns a supposed assembly at Carthage, conventionally dated after 256–257. Jerome, in his Dialogue against the Luciferians, claimed that the bishops who had approved the rebaptism of heretics with Cyprian later met again, went back to the older custom and reversed their decree. The editor includes the council only for completeness and argues that it probably never took place. Rebaptism, he notes, persisted in Africa, Donatists still appealed to Cyprian's council, and Augustine found no evidence that Cyprian ever changed his view.

This is an editorial collection of the records of the councils of African bishops held at Carthage under Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, around 251–252, while Cornelius was bishop of Rome. They dealt mainly with the lapsed, Christians who had sacrificed or bought certificates during the Decian persecution, and set terms of penance for readmitting them. The councils also rejected the envoys of the Roman schismatic Novatian and excommunicated Felicissimus and his supporters. Little survives in the form of formal acts. The councils are known chiefly from Cyprian's letters, and their synodal letter to Cornelius is lost.

The First Council of Orange (Arausio, in southern Gaul) was a Latin synod held in 441 under Hilary of Arles. It issued about thirty disciplinary canons on matters such as penance, the right of sanctuary, chrismation and the conduct of clergy. The name is closely tied to the Second Council of Orange of 529, presided over by Caesarius of Arles. Drawing on Augustine, its canons on grace and free will condemned Pelagian and so-called Semipelagian teaching. Those canons became a landmark of Western teaching on original sin and grace.

These are the doctrinal canons of the Second Council of Orange (Arausio), a synod of bishops held in southern Gaul on 3 July 529 when a basilica was dedicated. Caesarius of Arles presided. The council answered the teaching on grace associated with Faustus of Riez, later called Semi-Pelagianism. Its canons and closing definition of faith teach that Adam's sin damaged both body and soul and passed to his descendants. They also teach that even the beginning of faith is a gift of God's grace. The decrees broadly followed Augustine and were confirmed by Pope Boniface II in 531.

This is the synodal letter of the bishops who met at Constantinople in 382, written in Greek to Pope Damasus, Ambrose of Milan and the other Western bishops gathered at Rome. It describes the sufferings of the Eastern churches under Arian rule and declines an invitation to attend the Roman synod. It sets out the Nicene faith in one Godhead in three hypostases. It also defends the appointments of Nectarius at Constantinople, Flavian at Antioch and Cyril at Jerusalem. The letter survives in Theodoret's Ecclesiastical History and is a key witness to the theology of 381.

This is the short synodal letter that the bishops of the First Council of Constantinople, summoned by Emperor Theodosius I in 381, sent to him at the close of their meeting. Written in Greek and later known in Latin, it thanks God for the emperor's support of church peace. It reports that the council restored concord, confirmed the Nicene faith, condemned the heresies that arose after Nicaea and issued canons on church order. It asks Theodosius to ratify the council's decrees by imperial letter.

This Latin synodal letter was sent by the bishops gathered at the Council of Paris in 573 to Sigebert I, the Frankish king of Austrasia. Its more than thirty signatories include Germanus of Paris and Pappolus of Chartres. The bishops protest the irregular ordination of Promotus as bishop at Châteaudun, which lay within the diocese of Chartres, and call it contrary to the canons. They politely but firmly ask the king not to defend Promotus. The letter shows how Merovingian royal politics and church discipline came into conflict over episcopal appointments.

This short dossier gathers records of the third-century dispute over whether converts from heresy needed to be rebaptized. It opens with a brief notice of a Roman synod said to have been held by Pope Stephen I around 255–256, preserved in the much later Libellus Synodicus. According to that notice, the synod excommunicated African bishops who required rebaptism, though how reliable the report is remains uncertain. It then lists the Carthaginian councils held under Cyprian between 253 and 256, including the three councils on baptism. These councils are known chiefly through Cyprian's letters and the Sententiae episcoporum.

This Latin document is traditionally presented as the decree of a Roman synod of seventy bishops held under Pope Gelasius I in 494, and is better known as the Decretum Gelasianum. It lists the books of the Old and New Testaments accepted by the Roman Church. It also asserts the primacy of the Roman see, names the councils and Church Fathers to be received, and catalogues apocryphal and rejected writings. Modern scholars widely regard it as a later compilation, probably of the sixth century, and the attribution to Gelasius is disputed.

This Latin decree is known as the Decretum Gelasianum, or "On books to be received and not received". Tradition presents it as issued by a Roman council under Pope Gelasius I around 494–496, but some manuscripts name Damasus or Hormisdas instead. Modern scholars generally regard it as a later compilation, probably from sixth-century Italy or Gaul. It lists the canonical books of Scripture, ranks the major sees and councils, names approved Church Fathers, and condemns many apocryphal and heretical writings. It is an important witness to how the Western canon and early ideas of orthodox authority were defined.

This is the Latin record of a synod held in Rome on 13 May 495 under Pope Gelasius I, with several dozen bishops and presbyters present. It records the reconciliation of Misenus, bishop of Cumae. As a legate of Pope Felix III to Constantinople, Misenus had entered into communion with Patriarch Acacius and was condemned in 484. At the synod his written petition of repentance is read again and he is absolved. The record is an important document of the Acacian schism and of papal procedure for restoring clergy who had lapsed.

This is the conciliar record of a Roman synod held under Pope Dionysius, usually dated about 260–262 (the heading gives 263 but calls the year doubtful). Christians of the Libyan Pentapolis had accused Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria of teaching that the Father and the Son differed in nature. He had made these statements while writing against Sabellianism. Summoned to explain his faith, he answered by letter and in four books of apology. Athanasius later reports that he was cleared. The episode is important early evidence for the Trinitarian debates that came before Nicaea.

The bishops who met at the Council of Serdica (modern Sofia), usually dated to 343, sent this Latin synodal letter to Pope Julius I of Rome. Julius had not attended, and the letter explains that his envoys, the presbyters Archidamus and Philoxenus and the deacon Leo, will report the council's acts and decisions in detail. It survives among the historical fragments of Hilary of Poitiers and in early canon collections.
