This is the prefatory letter that Gregory, bishop of Tours (d. 594), placed before his four books on the miracles of Saint Martin (De virtutibus sancti Martini). Addressed to the clergy and faithful of the church of Tours, it says that the miracles at Martin's tomb confirm those recorded in the earlier Life of the saint. Gregory explains that recurring dreams moved him to record them. He calls himself unlearned and wishes that Sulpicius Severus, Paulinus or Venantius Fortunatus could have done the task instead.

The Miracles of Saint Martin is a Latin hagiographical work in four books by Gregory of Tours, written over many years between his consecration as bishop of Tours in 573 and his death in 594. It belongs to his collection of miracle books. Gregory begins by naming earlier writers on Martin, notably Sulpicius Severus. He then records healings and other wonders worked at Martin's tomb and through his relics, including cures Gregory said he received himself. The work is an important source for the cult of saints in Merovingian Gaul.

The Prosa de Sancto Martino is a short Latin liturgical piece praising Martin of Tours, followed by a prayer. It survives in a manuscript from the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, alongside Gregory of Tours' books on Martin's miracles, which is why it is sometimes attributed to him. The early editor who printed it thought it was more likely taken from old missals. It celebrates Martin's Pannonian birth, his upbringing in Italy, his miracles and his destruction of idols, and asks for his intercession.

The Decretum de Ecclesia Toletana is a royal decree issued by Gundemar, Visigothic king of Hispania from 610 to 612, and addressed to the bishops of the province of Carthaginensis. It complains that some bishops of the province had disregarded canon law and ignored the authority of the metropolitan church. In response it rules that the bishop of Toledo, the royal city, holds primacy over all the churches of the province. It also forbids dividing the province between two metropolitans. The decree is an important witness to the rise of Toledo as the leading see of Visigothic Spain.

This is the collection of surviving Latin writings of Hadoindus (Hadoind), bishop of Le Mans in the seventh century under the Merovingian kings. Its main document is his testament. In it the bishop says that he dictated the will while sound in mind and body, to a deacon who wrote it down. It is dated to the fifth regnal year of King Clovis II, which scholars usually put at 642, and Hadoindus is thought to have died around 653. The testament is accepted as genuine. It is a valuable record of property, church institutions and legal practice in Merovingian Gaul.

This is the collected correspondence of Jerome of Stridon. It spans roughly fifty years, from his earliest surviving letter to Innocent (c. 370) until shortly before his death at Bethlehem in 420. The collection also includes letters written to Jerome by correspondents such as Pope Damasus and Augustine of Hippo. The letters deal with ascetic and virginal life, biblical interpretation and the principles of translation, as well as the Origenist controversy and personal disputes. They are polished examples of Latin prose and an important source for the church and society of the late fourth century.

The Life of Paul the First Hermit (Vita Sancti Pauli Eremitae) is a short Latin saint's life by Jerome. He wrote it around 375–376, probably while living as a hermit in the Syrian desert. Jerome argues that Paul of Thebes, not Antony, was the first Christian hermit. In his story, Paul flees the Decian persecution and lives for decades in an Egyptian desert cave, fed by a raven. Antony visits him and later buries him, and lions dig the grave. Jerome's first saint's life, it strongly shaped medieval monastic devotion, though scholars have questioned whether Paul really existed.

This is Jerome's Latin translation of the treatise On the Holy Spirit by Didymus the Blind of Alexandria, with whom Jerome had studied. Pope Damasus urged him to begin it in Rome, and he finished it in Palestine around 387–390. He dedicated it to his brother Paulinianus. Didymus argues that the Spirit differs in nature from the angels and creatures and shares the divinity of Father and Son, and that the Spirit must be invoked in baptism. The Greek original is lost, so the treatise survives only through Jerome's version.

The Dialogue Against the Luciferians is a Latin polemical dialogue by Jerome. It is one of his early works, usually dated around 379, though some scholars place it a few years later. In it, a follower of Lucifer of Cagliari debates an orthodox Christian. The Luciferians refused communion with bishops who had compromised with Arianism. Against them, Jerome argues that such bishops, especially those who signed the formula of Ariminum in 359, should be received back, and that baptism given by heretics is valid. The work includes his famous remark that the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.

Jerome wrote this Latin polemical treatise in Rome around 383, while Damasus was bishop there. It answers Helvidius, a layman who claimed that the Gospels' references to the "brothers" and "sisters" of the Lord show that Mary had other children with Joseph, and who ranked marriage as equal to virginity. Jerome argues that Mary remained a virgin, that these "brothers" were the Lord's cousins, and that virginity is superior to marriage. Helvidius's own work is lost and is known only through this reply.

Against Jovinianus is a Latin polemical treatise in two books by Jerome, written in 393. It answers Jovinian, a Roman monk condemned at synods in Rome and Milan. Jovinian had taught that virgins are no better than wives, that abstinence is no better than eating with thanksgiving, that the baptized cannot sin, and that all sins and rewards are equal. Book I praises virginity over marriage, and Book II rejects the other claims. Many readers found its attack on marriage excessive, and Jerome defended it in letters to Pammachius. The treatise was later widely quoted in medieval writing against marriage.

Against Vigilantius (Contra Vigilantium) is a short polemical treatise by Jerome, written at Bethlehem in 406. Jerome says he dictated it in a single night. It answers a lost work by Vigilantius, a presbyter from Aquitaine who had once been Jerome's guest. Vigilantius had attacked the veneration of martyrs' relics, vigils at their tombs, clerical celibacy, monasticism and the sending of alms to Jerusalem. Jerome defends these practices in fierce, sarcastic terms, mocking his opponent as "Dormitantius" ("the sleepy one"). The treatise is an important witness to the cult of the saints in the early fifth century.

To Pammachius Against John of Jerusalem is a Latin polemical treatise by Jerome, written in the late 390s during the Origenist controversy. It is addressed to his Roman friend Pammachius. Jerome attacks John II, bishop of Jerusalem, for allegedly sheltering Origenist errors on the resurrection of the body, the soul and related doctrines. He also defends himself and Epiphanius of Salamis in the quarrel over Epiphanius' ordination of Jerome's brother Paulinian. The work is an important source for the controversy in Palestine and for church politics there at the time.

Jerome wrote this polemical Latin treatise at Bethlehem in about 401–402, during the Origenist controversy. Its first two books are addressed to Pammachius and Marcella. They answer Rufinus of Aquileia's Apology, which Jerome knew only from summaries sent to him and from passages his brother Paulinianus had memorized. A third book followed after Rufinus sent a letter in reply. Jerome defends his own orthodoxy and his translations, attacks Rufinus's Latin version of Origen's On First Principles and its preface, and denies any sympathy for Origen's errors. The work marks the bitter end of a long friendship.

The Dialogue Against the Pelagians is a Latin polemical work in three books by Jerome. He wrote it in Bethlehem late in life, around 415 to 417, and it was his last major controversial writing. It takes the form of a debate between Atticus, a Catholic, and Critobulus, who speaks for Pelagius. The work attacks the claim that a person can live without sin by free will alone and defends the necessity of divine grace, drawing heavily on Scripture. It was written while Pelagius was in Palestine, and it set Jerome beside Augustine in the Pelagian controversy.

The Life of Saint Hilarion is a Latin hagiography written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 390. It tells the story of Hilarion, a fourth-century hermit from near Gaza who was a disciple of Antony of Egypt and is regarded as the founder of monastic life in Palestine. It follows his ascetic struggles, miracles and later wanderings, which took him to Egypt, Sicily, Dalmatia and finally Cyprus, where he died. Jerome wrote it to promote the ascetic ideal. Alongside his Lives of Paul and Malchus, it shaped Latin monastic hagiography.

De viris illustribus (On Illustrious Men) is a Latin collection of short biographies and bibliographies of Christian writers. Jerome compiled it at Bethlehem in 392–393 and dedicated it to Nummius Aemilianus Dexter. It has a preface and 135 chapters, running from the apostles to Jerome himself. He modelled it on Suetonius's lives of pagan men of letters, presented it as a defence of Christian learning and took much of the early material from Eusebius. It was continued by Gennadius of Massilia and later by Isidore of Seville, and it is a key source for early Christian literary history.

The Liber de nominibus Hebraicis, also called Liber interpretationis Hebraicorum nominum, is a Latin glossary of the Hebrew proper names in Scripture. Jerome compiled it at Bethlehem around 390. Its preface says Jerome first meant to translate a Greek onomasticon credited to Philo and Origen. He found the copies so confused that he reworked the material instead, going through the biblical books in order and listing the names alphabetically with their meanings. Medieval writers used it widely for allegorical interpretation, and the title Stella Maris for Mary may come from a mistaken reading of one of its entries.

The Onomasticon, more fully On the Place Names in Holy Scripture, is a gazetteer of biblical place names in Palestine and Transjordan. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, compiled it and dedicated it to Paulinus. It is traditionally dated to before 324. The entries are arranged alphabetically and grouped by biblical book. Each gives a site's location and its name in Eusebius's own day. Jerome translated and revised it in Latin as the Liber de situ et nominibus locorum Hebraicorum. It is a key source for the historical geography of Roman Palestine and influenced the Madaba map and early pilgrim accounts.

The Excerpta de aliquot Palaestinae locis is a Latin gazetteer of passages taken from the writings of Jerome (c. 347–420) and arranged alphabetically by place name. It is a later compilation, not a treatise Jerome wrote himself. Its entries come mainly from his biblical commentaries and his Hebrew Questions on Genesis. They identify biblical sites such as Anathoth, Ar, Azotus and Beersheba, giving distances, their current names and Roman administrative details. They draw on Jerome's long residence at Bethlehem and are a useful witness to the geography of late antique Palestine.

The Hebrew Questions on Genesis is a Latin philological commentary by Jerome, written in Bethlehem in the early 390s. It works through selected passages of Genesis and compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint and the other Greek versions. It explains Hebrew names, place-names and readings, often drawing on Jewish tradition. In the preface Jerome answers his critics, comparing himself with Terence, Virgil and Cicero. He planned it as the start of a larger series that he never finished. The work prepared the way for his translation of the Old Testament from the Hebrew.

The Commentarius in Ecclesiasten is Jerome's Latin commentary on the biblical book of Ecclesiastes, written at Bethlehem around 388 and dedicated to Paula and her daughter Eustochium. In the preface, Jerome says the work grew out of his reading of Ecclesiastes in Rome with Blesilla, Paula's daughter, to encourage her to reject worldly things. Her sudden death had interrupted the project. He gives his own Latin version made from the Hebrew, compares it with the Septuagint and other Greek versions, and draws on Jewish interpretation. The commentary combines literal and spiritual readings and shaped later Latin exegesis of the book.

The Life of Malchus, the Captive Monk is a short Latin hagiography written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 391. Jerome says he heard the story from Malchus himself, an aged monk living at Maronia in Syria. Malchus had left his monastery and was captured by Bedouin raiders. He was enslaved and forced to marry a fellow captive, but the two lived together chastely and finally escaped. The work celebrates chastity and monastic obedience, and it is the only record of Malchus.

Jerome's Latin translation of two homilies by Origen on the Song of Songs, made around 383 in Rome and dedicated to Pope Damasus. In the preface, Jerome says that Origen surpassed himself in his ten-volume commentary on the Song. He set that work aside as too great a task and translated these simpler sermons instead, offering "a taste, not a meal" of Origen's thought. The homilies read the Song as a wedding drama between Christ and the Church or the soul. The Greek original is lost, so this translation is the main witness to the text.

This is Jerome's Latin translation of the monastic rules of Pachomius, founder of communal monasticism in Upper Egypt, together with writings of his successors Theodore and Horsiesius. Jerome made it in 404, soon after the death of his companion Paula. The texts had been sent from Alexandria through the presbyter Silvanus. He worked from a Greek version of the Coptic originals, for Latin-speaking monks in Thebaid monasteries and at Metanoia near Canopus. His version is the main witness to the Pachomian Rule and shaped later Western monastic legislation.

The Instituta form part of the monastic rules of Pachomius (d. 348), founder of communal (cenobitic) monasticism in Upper Egypt. Jerome translated them into Latin at Bethlehem around 404, working from a Greek version of the Coptic originals. These short numbered regulations govern the daily life of the brethren: gathering for prayer and instruction, the duties of the monastery's officers, the care of books, tools and clothing, and correction for negligence. In Jerome's Latin, the Pachomian rules became a significant influence on Western monastic legislation.

The "Precepts and Judgements" is one section of the Rule of Pachomius, the founder of cenobitic monasticism in Upper Egypt. It survives in the Latin translation Jerome made at Bethlehem around 404 from a Greek version of the Coptic original. This section is a penal code for the monastic community. It lists offences such as slander, habitual anger, false accusation and leading simpler brothers astray, and sets graded penalties: repeated warnings, demotion in rank, separation with bread and water, and expulsion. Jerome's version was the main channel through which Pachomian legislation reached Western monasticism.

The Praecepta ac leges is the monastic rule of Pachomius (died 346), founder of communal (cenobitic) monasticism in Upper Egypt. It survives mainly in the Latin translation Jerome made at Bethlehem around 404 from a Greek version, because the Coptic original is largely lost. Its numbered precepts govern prayer gatherings, manual labour such as weaving palm leaves, and discipline and penance. They also set out the authority of each house's superior and his second. The rule shaped later Western monastic legislation.

The Monita S. Pachomii is a short Latin collection of spiritual admonitions for monks, attributed to Pachomius, the founder of communal monasticism in Egypt. It survives with the Latin versions of Pachomian writings that Jerome made in 404 from a Greek translation of Coptic originals. It urges its readers to honour God and stay of one mind in their calling. It also stresses obedience to God's law over one's own will and steadfast faith in times of trouble, citing Scripture throughout. Its exact origin and its place within the Pachomian material are uncertain.

This is a collection of short letters and sayings by Pachomius (d. 346), founder of communal monasticism in Upper Egypt, and his disciple and successor Theodore. They were written in Coptic and survive in a Latin version made by Jerome. He translated them from a Greek intermediary around 404, together with the Pachomian Rule. The letters are addressed to heads of other monasteries, such as Cornelius of Mochansis. They are famous for their obscure "spiritual alphabet", in which Greek letters serve as cryptic signs whose meaning was already unclear to the translator.

This Latin commentary on the Book of Isaiah, in eighteen books, was written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 408–410. He dedicated it to the ascetic Eustochium, fulfilling a promise made to her late mother Paula and her brother-in-law Pammachius. It follows his commentaries on the Twelve Prophets and Daniel. Jerome compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint and other Greek versions and joins historical with spiritual interpretation. He presents Isaiah as evangelist as well as prophet. The prologue contains his famous saying that ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.

This is a Latin translation of nine homilies by Origen on the Book of Isaiah, traditionally credited to Jerome. When it was made is uncertain, and some scholars have questioned whether Jerome was the translator. Origen's Greek originals are almost entirely lost, so this version is a key witness to his preaching on the prophet. The first homily treats Isaiah's vision in the year King Uzziah died. Origen reads it morally: the sinful "king" ruling in each soul must die before a person can see the glory of God.

Jerome wrote this Latin commentary on the Book of Ezekiel in fourteen books at Bethlehem, roughly between 410 and 414. He dedicated it to the virgin Eustochium. Its preface describes how he had to break off the work at the news of the sack of Rome and the deaths of Pammachius and Marcella. The commentary sets out both the literal and the spiritual sense of the prophet, often comparing the Hebrew text with the Greek versions. Gregory the Great later drew heavily on it for his own homilies on Ezekiel.

This is a Latin commentary in two books on the prophet Micah, written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 392–393. It was one of the first in his series of commentaries on the Minor Prophets and, like others in that series, is dedicated to Paula and her daughter Eustochium. Jerome compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint, explains Hebrew names (he reads Micah as "humility") and places, and sets a literal-historical reading alongside a spiritual one. In this he draws on Jewish learning and on earlier Greek exegetes, especially Origen.

This is Jerome's Latin commentary in one book on the Old Testament prophet Nahum. He wrote it at Bethlehem around 392–393 as one of the first in his series of commentaries on the twelve Minor Prophets, and he dedicated it to Paula and her daughter Eustochium. Jerome compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint and with Aquila's version. He explains the prophecy against Nineveh historically, as comfort for Israel under Assyrian oppression. He also reads it figuratively, taking Nineveh, whose name he renders "beautiful", as a figure of the world.

This is a Latin commentary in two books on the prophet Habakkuk by Jerome. He wrote it in Bethlehem around 392–393, as part of his series of commentaries on the Minor Prophets, and dedicated it to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia. Jerome begins by discussing the prophet's name, which he explains from the Hebrew as "embrace" or "wrestling", and the meaning of the Hebrew term massa ("burden"). He then works through the text verse by verse. He compares the Hebrew with the Septuagint, Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, and gives both historical and spiritual interpretations.

This Latin commentary on the Book of Zephaniah, ninth of the twelve Minor Prophets, is in one book. Jerome wrote it in Bethlehem around 392–393 as part of his series of commentaries on the Minor Prophets. He dedicated it to the Roman ascetics Paula and her daughter Eustochium. The preface defends writing for women, citing biblical heroines such as Huldah, Deborah, Judith and Esther, as well as learned women of antiquity. The commentary explains the prophecy both historically and spiritually. It draws on the Hebrew text and compares it with the Septuagint and other Greek versions.

This is a Latin commentary in one book on the prophet Haggai by Jerome. He wrote it at Bethlehem around 392–393 as part of his series of commentaries on the Minor Prophets, and dedicated it to Paula and Eustochium. Jerome begins by dating Haggai's prophecy to the second year of Darius, linking it with Zechariah, Ezra and Roman history. He then explains the text verse by verse, giving both a literal reading of the rebuilding of the Jerusalem temple under Zerubbabel and Joshua and a spiritual one. He often compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint.

This is a Latin biblical commentary in two books on the prophet Zechariah, written by Jerome at Bethlehem around 406. It belongs to his series of commentaries on the twelve Minor Prophets and is dedicated to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, whose letter the monk Sisinnius had brought to him. Jerome comments on the Hebrew text, which he compares with the Septuagint, and gives both a literal-historical and a spiritual reading. He draws on Jewish teachers and on earlier Greek exegetes, notably Origen and Didymus the Blind.

This is a one-book Latin commentary on the prophet Malachi by Jerome, part of his series of commentaries on the twelve Minor Prophets, usually dated to about 406 during his years in Bethlehem. Jerome compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint and explains the literal and spiritual sense of the prophecy. He takes the name Malachi to mean "my messenger" and rejects the Origenist idea that the prophet was an angel who took a human body. He also reports the Jewish tradition that Malachi was Ezra the priest, and places him after Haggai and Zechariah.

Jerome wrote this Latin commentary on the Book of Daniel in one book at Bethlehem, around 407. It goes through the prophecy verse by verse, and its prologue answers the pagan philosopher Porphyry. Porphyry had argued that Daniel was written in the time of Antiochus IV Epiphanes and recorded past events rather than predicting future ones. Jerome holds that no prophet spoke more clearly of Christ. He reads the fourth kingdom as Rome and gives an account of the seventy weeks. The work matters most because it preserves much of Porphyry's lost argument.

This is Jerome's Latin translation of fourteen homilies on the Book of Jeremiah by the third-century Alexandrian theologian Origen. It is generally dated to around 380, early in Jerome's career, and was made together with his version of Origen's homilies on Ezekiel. In the preface, addressed to his friend Vincentius, Jerome sorts Origen's biblical works into scholia, homilies and tomes. He also says he chose a plain style suited to the Church. The translation helped bring Origen's preaching on the prophets to Latin readers.

This is Jerome's Latin translation of fourteen homilies on the Book of Ezekiel preached by Origen of Alexandria in the third century. Jerome made it early in his career, usually dated to around 380 during his stay in Constantinople, alongside his versions of Origen's homilies on Jeremiah and Isaiah. The homilies give a spiritual and moral reading of the prophet, beginning with Ezekiel among the exiles in Babylon. Origen's Greek originals are largely lost, so this Latin version is the main witness to the series.

The Commentary on Hosea, in three books, is a Latin biblical commentary by Jerome (c. 342/347–420). He wrote it at Bethlehem around 406 as part of his series of commentaries on the twelve Minor Prophets. Jerome works through the prophecy verse by verse. He compares the Hebrew text with the Septuagint and gives both a literal-historical and a spiritual reading. His preface deals with the scandal of God commanding Hosea to marry a prostitute and stresses how obscure the book is. The work shows how Jerome combined Hebrew scholarship with allegorical exegesis.

This is a Latin biblical commentary in one book on the prophet Joel by Jerome. It is one of his commentaries on the Twelve Minor Prophets and is generally dated to about 406, when he was living in Bethlehem. Like its companion volumes on Hosea and Amos, it is dedicated to Pammachius. The preface compares the order of the Twelve in the Septuagint with the Hebrew order and explains the meaning of each prophet's name. The commentary then works through Joel, comparing the Hebrew text with the Septuagint and giving both literal-historical and spiritual interpretations.

This Latin commentary in three books on the prophet Amos is by Jerome. He wrote it at Bethlehem around 406, as part of his series of commentaries on the twelve Minor Prophets. It opens by separating Amos, the third of the twelve, from Amoz, the father of Isaiah, by pointing out how their names are spelled differently in Hebrew. Jerome works through the text verse by verse. He compares the Hebrew with the Septuagint, gives a historical and literal explanation, and then offers a spiritual reading. The work shows his Hebrew scholarship and his skill as an interpreter of Scripture.

This is a Latin commentary in one book on Obadiah, the shortest book of the Old Testament prophets. Jerome wrote it at Bethlehem around 396, as part of his series of commentaries on the twelve Minor Prophets, and dedicated it to his friend Pammachius. In the preface he recalls an allegorical exposition of Obadiah he wrote in his youth, before he knew the prophet's historical setting, and apologizes for it. The new commentary works from the Hebrew text and sets historical explanation beside spiritual interpretation, showing how Jerome's method as an exegete had matured.

This is Jerome's Latin commentary on the Book of Jonah, written in one book at Bethlehem around 396. In the preface Jerome says that about three years had passed since his commentaries on Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah and Haggai, and that other works, including On Illustrious Men and Against Jovinian, had kept him busy. He explains the text both literally and spiritually. He reads Jonah as a type of Christ, whose three days in the whale prefigure the Resurrection, and he draws on both the Hebrew text and the Septuagint.

Jerome's Commentary on Matthew in four books is a Latin exegetical work written at Bethlehem in 398 for his friend Eusebius of Cremona. By Jerome's own account he wrote it in haste, in about two weeks. The preface separates the four canonical Gospels from apocryphal and heretical ones and links each evangelist to one of the four living creatures of Ezekiel and Revelation. The commentary itself is concise and mostly historical and literal, drawing on earlier writers such as Origen. It became one of the most widely used Latin commentaries on Matthew in the medieval West.

The thirty-nine homilies on Luke's Gospel were preached by Origen of Alexandria, probably at Caesarea in the third century. They survive complete only in a Latin translation by Jerome, made around 390 at the request of Paula and Eustochium, while the Greek original is preserved only in fragments. Most of the homilies treat the first four chapters of Luke, especially the infancy narratives, and a few cover later passages. They are an important witness to Origen's preaching and exegesis and to Jerome's activity as a translator.

This Latin commentary in three books on Paul's Epistle to the Galatians was written by Jerome in Bethlehem around 386–387. It is dedicated to Paula and Eustochium, and was written to console Marcella in Rome after the death of her mother Albina. It follows his commentary on Philemon and belongs to a group that also covers Ephesians and Titus. Jerome drew heavily on Origen and other Greek exegetes. His reading of the clash between Peter and Paul at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14) as a staged dispute led to a well-known exchange of letters with Augustine.

This Latin commentary in three books on Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians is by Jerome. He wrote it in Bethlehem around 386–387 and dedicated it to Paula and her daughter Eustochium. It belongs to a group of commentaries on Pauline letters written at that time, alongside those on Philemon, Galatians and Titus. Jerome drew heavily on Greek exegetes, especially Origen, and acknowledged doing so. This later made the work contentious: during the Origenist controversy, Rufinus pointed to passages in it to accuse Jerome of sharing Origen's views.

Jerome wrote this one-book Latin commentary on Paul's Epistle to Titus in Bethlehem around 386–388. In the same period he also wrote commentaries on Philemon, Galatians and Ephesians. The preface defends the authenticity of the letter against Marcion, Basilides and other heretics who rejected it and the Pastoral Epistles. It also notes that Tatian, although he rejected other Pauline letters, accepted Titus as genuine. The commentary then works through the text verse by verse, drawing on Greek exegetes, especially Origen. It discusses church order, the qualifications of bishops and presbyters, and Christian conduct.

Jerome wrote this Latin commentary in one book on Paul's Letter to Philemon in Bethlehem around 386–387. It was the first of a group of commentaries on Pauline letters that also covered Galatians, Ephesians and Titus. The work opens by defending the letter's place among Paul's epistles against critics who thought a short personal note about a runaway slave unworthy of divine inspiration. Jerome then explains the text verse by verse, drawing on earlier Greek exegesis, especially Origen. It is an early witness to debates over the authority and value of this brief epistle.

The Chronicle is a universal chronicle that Jerome wrote in Latin at Constantinople around 380–381. It translates and expands the chronological tables in the second book of Eusebius of Caesarea's Greek Chronicon, adding material on Roman history, and carries the record on from 325 to 378. In its preface, addressed to Vincentius and Gallienus, Jerome discusses how hard it is to translate faithfully. Although it contains errors, the work preserves Eusebius's tables, whose Greek original is lost. Later chroniclers such as Prosper of Aquitaine and Victor of Tunnuna wrote continuations of it.

This is a Latin prefatory letter by Jerome to Desiderius, an otherwise little-known friend who had asked him to translate the Pentateuch into Latin directly from the Hebrew. It was probably written around the turn of the fifth century. Jerome defends his work against critics who accused him of undermining the Septuagint. He rejects the legend that its seventy translators worked in separate cells, arguing that a translator is not a prophet. He later quoted the preface in full in his Apology against Rufinus. It became one of the standard prologues of the Vulgate.

Jerome wrote this Latin preface for his translation of Isaiah from the Hebrew, part of the version of the Old Testament that later became the Vulgate, probably in the 390s. He explains that he set the text out in clauses and phrases (cola et commata), as was done with Demosthenes and Cicero, and not in verse. He praises Isaiah's refined eloquence and calls him an evangelist more than a prophet. He also defends his new version against critics as a companion to the Septuagint.

The Prologus in Jeremiam is a short Latin preface written by Jerome for his translation of the Book of Jeremiah from the Hebrew, made around the 390s and later part of the Vulgate. Jerome says that Jeremiah's style is plainer than that of Isaiah or Hosea but equal in meaning. He describes the prophet as a priest from Anathoth, notes the alphabetic structure of Lamentations, and says he restored the order of the visions, which was confused in Greek and Latin copies. He also leaves out the Book of Baruch because it is not in the Hebrew canon.

This is the short Latin preface Jerome wrote for his translation of the Book of Ezekiel from the Hebrew, part of the work later known as the Vulgate, probably in the early 390s. It explains that Ezekiel was taken captive to Babylon with King Jehoiachin and prophesied there while Jeremiah was in Judaea. It describes his style as neither very eloquent nor very rough, and notes how obscure the book's beginning and end are. Jerome also defends his translation, which is set out in sense-lines (per cola et commata), against critics.

This short Latin preface by Jerome introduces his translation of the twelve Minor Prophets from the Hebrew, made in the early 390s and later included in the Vulgate. It is addressed to Paula and Eustochium. Jerome explains that the Hebrew order of the prophets differs from the Septuagint's, and he follows the Hebrew. He briefly describes the style of Hosea and Joel and insists that the Twelve form a single book. He also gives guidance on dating prophets whose titles name no king.

Jerome wrote this preface to his Latin translation of the Book of Job, made directly from the Hebrew around 392–393, while he was living in Bethlehem. He defends his work against critics who saw it as an attack on the Septuagint. He points out that Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion had already produced other Greek versions, and that Origen had marked the Old Testament with obeli and asterisks to show where the older Greek was defective. Jerome stresses that this was especially true of Job, where the Septuagint lacked many passages. The preface shows how he justified translating from the Hebrew.

This is Jerome's Latin preface to his translation of the Psalms made directly from the Hebrew, the version later called the Psalterium iuxta Hebraeos. He wrote it in Bethlehem around 392 and addressed it to his friend Sophronius. Following Hebrew and apostolic usage, Jerome argues that the Psalter is a single book rather than five, which is why he discusses the Hebrew "amen" that the Septuagint renders as "fiat, fiat." He also holds that each psalm belongs to the author named in its title. The preface shows his commitment to "Hebrew truth" in translating the Old Testament.

This short Latin preface was written by Jerome for his translation of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs from the Hebrew. It is addressed to the bishops Chromatius of Aquileia and Heliodorus of Altinum and is usually dated to the 390s. Jerome thanks them for paying for his secretaries and copyists, and says that, though weakened by illness, he finished the work in three days. The preface is best known for its view of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus: the Church may read them to build up the people, but not to establish doctrine.

Jerome wrote this preface to his Latin translation of the Book of Daniel from the Hebrew and Aramaic around 392 and addressed it to Paula and Eustochium. He explains that the churches read Theodotion's Greek version rather than the Septuagint, which he judged far from the original. He notes that parts of Daniel are written in Aramaic ("Chaldee") and recalls how hard he worked to learn that language. He also observes that the Jews counted Daniel among the Hagiographa rather than the Prophets, and that the Greek additions, such as Susanna, are absent from the Hebrew.

This is Jerome's Latin preface to his translation of Chronicles (Paralipomenon) made directly from the Hebrew. He wrote it in the 390s as part of his new version of the Old Testament, and addressed it to Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia. Jerome argues that the Septuagint no longer survives in its pure form. Instead, rival recensions circulated in different regions, linked to Hesychius in Egypt, Lucian at Constantinople and Antioch, and Origen in Palestine. He defends going back to the Hebrew text, and the preface is an important witness to his views on translation and the history of the biblical text.

The Praefatio in Ezram is Jerome's Latin preface to his translation of the Book of Ezra directly from the Hebrew, made as part of the work later known as the Vulgate. Written in Bethlehem, usually dated to the mid-390s, it is addressed to his friends Domnion and Rogatianus, who had urged him for three years to undertake the translation. Jerome complains of critics who attack his work, asks that Hebrew names be copied carefully, and explains that Ezra and Nehemiah form a single book. He rejects the third and fourth books of Esdras as apocryphal.

This short Latin preface by Jerome introduces his translation of the Book of Esther, made directly from the Hebrew. It belongs to the series of prefaces he wrote for his new Old Testament version, the project he pursued between about 391 and 405 that became part of the Vulgate. Jerome says that earlier translators had corrupted the book. He contrasts his close, word-for-word rendering with the common Latin version, which he criticises for stretching the text with wordy additions that resembled rhetorical exercises on a set theme.

The Preface to the Book of Joshua is a short Latin prologue by Jerome (c. 342/347–420). He wrote it for his translation of Joshua made directly from the Hebrew, which later became part of the Vulgate. It dates from the first decade of the fifth century, after he had finished the Pentateuch. The preface introduces Joshua, Judges, Ruth and Esther and gives their Hebrew names. It asks copyists to keep the Hebrew proper names and the division of the text into sense-lines exactly as written. Like his other prefaces, it also defends his translation from the Hebrew.

The Prologus galeatus, or "Helmeted Preface," is Jerome's Latin preface to his translation from Hebrew of the books of Samuel and Kings, written about 391–392 and addressed to Paula and Eustochium. It was the first of his prefaces to his Hebrew-based translations. In it he sets out his method and lists the books of the Hebrew canon, which he counts as twenty-two to match the Hebrew alphabet. He classes Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit and the Shepherd of Hermas as outside the canon. This made it a key text in later debates over the Old Testament canon.

This Latin dedicatory letter, known from its opening words as Novum opus, is the preface Jerome addressed to Pope Damasus I with his revised Latin text of the four Gospels. It is usually dated to about 383. Jerome explains that, at the pope's request, he corrected the widely differing Old Latin copies against Greek manuscripts. He expects to be attacked as a forger and defends the work. He also explains how to use the Eusebian Canons. The letter introduced the Vulgate Gospels and was copied at the start of many medieval Gospel books.

This is Jerome's short Latin preface to his translation of the Book of Tobit, made around the turn of the fifth century. It takes the form of a letter to the bishops Chromatius of Aquileia and Heliodorus of Altinum, who had asked for the translation. Jerome notes that the Hebrews set Tobit apart from the canon of divine Scriptures and counted it among the apocrypha. He says he worked from a text in "Chaldean" (Aramaic), with help from someone who knew both that language and Hebrew. The preface is an important witness to Jerome's views on the biblical canon.

This short Latin preface was written by Jerome for his translation of the Book of Judith, which became part of the Vulgate. He notes that the Jews count Judith among the apocrypha and that it was written in Chaldean (Aramaic). However, the Council of Nicaea was reported to have counted it among the Scriptures, so he agreed to his correspondents' request. He says he translated it in a single night's work, rendering sense for sense and cutting out corrupt variant readings. He ends by praising the widow Judith as a model of chastity for both women and men.

This is Jerome's Latin preface to his revision of the Book of Job, made from the Greek Septuagint as found in Origen's Hexapla. He probably wrote it in Bethlehem in the late 380s, and it is addressed to Paula and her daughter Eustochium. Jerome defends himself against critics who called him a forger. He explains his critical signs: obeli mark passages missing from the Hebrew, and asterisks mark material added from the Hebrew. The preface sheds light on his early method of biblical revision, before he translated directly from the Hebrew.

This is a short Latin preface by Jerome to his translation of the Books of Chronicles (Paralipomenon) based on the Greek Septuagint. He addressed it to his friends Domnio and Rogatianus, probably after he settled in Palestine in the later 380s. Jerome argues that anyone who has seen Judaea understands Scripture more clearly. He says he checked the book with a Jewish teacher of the Law from Tiberias. He also complains that copyists, not the Seventy translators, had badly corrupted the Hebrew names in Greek and Latin manuscripts. The preface shows his growing reliance on Hebrew scholarship.

This short Latin preface by Jerome introduces his revision of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, based on the Greek Septuagint. He addressed it to Paula and Eustochium, probably in Bethlehem in the late 380s. Jerome explains that he marked superfluous passages with obeli and inserted missing material under asterisks. He also corrected faulty earlier Latin renderings and restored misplaced sentences. He says he left Wisdom and Sirach untouched because he wished to emend only canonical Scripture. Some editors suspect the surviving text is a fragment with later additions.

The Sermo de vita S. Honorati is a Latin funeral panegyric by Hilary of Arles in honour of his kinsman and predecessor Honoratus, founder of the monastery of Lérins and bishop of Arles, who died around 429. Hilary delivered it at Arles on the anniversary of Honoratus's death, probably soon after he became bishop. In elaborate rhetorical prose it praises Honoratus's conversion, his ascetic life, the founding of Lérins and his time as bishop. It is a key source for early monasticism in southern Gaul and for the circle of Lérins.

This is a brief Latin letter from Hilary, bishop of Arles (c. 403–449), to Eucherius, bishop of Lyon. It was written during Hilary's episcopate, probably between about 429 and 449. Hilary says he has returned the books Eucherius sent him because the messenger insisted. He had read them through only once and admired them all. He asks to receive the Instructiones again soon, calling himself one of the young men for whose instruction they were written. The letter is early evidence for Eucherius's Instructiones and for the ties between the bishops of southern Gaul.

This Latin letter to Augustine of Hippo, preserved as Letter 226 in his correspondence, was written around 429 by Hilary, a layman in Gaul who admired Augustine. It is not certain whether he is the same person as Hilary of Arles. Written alongside Prosper of Aquitaine's Letter 225, it reports objections raised in Marseilles and elsewhere in Gaul to Augustine's teaching on predestination, grace and the beginning of faith. Augustine answered with On the Predestination of the Saints and On the Gift of Perseverance, which makes the letter a key early document of the so-called Semi-Pelagian controversy.

De Trinitate is a Latin theological treatise in twelve books by Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. He wrote most of it during his exile in Phrygia in the later 350s, and it was completed by about 360. Its first book opens with an autobiographical account of Hilary's search for truth, which led him to faith. The treatise argues against Arianism, defending the full divinity of the Son and his unity of nature with the Father from Scripture. It is the first major Latin work on the Trinity, and it brought Eastern theological debates to Western readers.

The Liber contra Constantium is a Latin polemical treatise by Hilary of Poitiers, usually dated to about 360–361, near the end of his exile in the East. It is a fierce invective against the emperor Constantius II. Hilary calls him a forerunner of Antichrist and a persecutor more dangerous than open pagan tyrants, because he undermined the faith through flattery and imperial pressure. The work attacks the emperor's support for Arian and Homoian creeds after the councils of Rimini and Seleucia. It urges bishops to speak out openly in defence of Nicene orthodoxy.

The Liber contra Arianos vel Auxentium is a Latin polemical letter by Hilary of Poitiers, written around 364–365 to the bishops and faithful who held to the Nicene faith. It describes Hilary's failed attempt in Milan, under Emperor Valentinian I, to expose Auxentius, the Homoian bishop of that city, as an Arian, after Auxentius won imperial favour with an ambiguous profession of faith. Hilary calls the Arian bishops forerunners of Antichrist and protests that the Church must not depend on worldly power. Auxentius's own profession of faith is preserved with the letter.

The Collectanea Antiariana Parisina, also called the historical fragments (Fragmenta historica), is a collection of documents on the fourth-century Arian controversy associated with Hilary of Poitiers. It survives in two series, A and B, and is usually thought to come from Hilary's lost polemical history directed against the bishops Valens and Ursacius. It includes synodal letters, creeds and correspondence connected with the councils of Serdica, Rimini and Paris. Together with Hilary's own commentary, these documents are an important primary source for the conflicts over Nicene doctrine under Constantius II.

This is a collection of fragments from lost works of Hilary of Poitiers (c. 315–367), the Latin bishop and opponent of Arianism. The fragments survive only as quotations in later writers. The collection opens with passages from Hilary's lost treatises or homilies on the Book of Job, which Augustine quoted in his Contra Julianum. Those passages present the devil's constant attacks through the weakness of the flesh as the occasion for the Christian's victory and purification. The fragments preserve evidence of Hilary's exegetical writing that is otherwise lost.

This Latin sermon for the feast of a church's dedication has come down under the name of Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–c. 367). It is generally regarded as spurious or of doubtful authenticity, and its true author and date are unknown. The preacher describes the night vigil, with its lamps, readings and psalms. He urges his hearers to adorn their hearts with good works as the church walls have been adorned. He reads Moses' tabernacle and Solomon's temple, with their firm foundations, incorruptible wood and pure gold, as types of the Church.

De Synodis ("On the Councils", also called "The Faith of the Easterns") is a Latin treatise by Hilary of Poitiers. He wrote it around 358–359, while exiled in Asia Minor during the Arian controversy. Hilary addressed it to the bishops of Gaul and Britain. In it he sets out and comments on the creeds of several Eastern councils, including those of Antioch, Sirmium and Ancyra. He argues that the term homoiousios ("of like substance") can be understood in an orthodox sense. The work sought to bring together Western Nicene bishops and the moderate Eastern Homoiousians against the more radical Arians.

The Apologetica ad reprehensores libri de Synodis responsa is a short Latin work by Hilary of Poitiers, probably written soon after his De Synodis of 358–359. It answers critics of that treatise, among them Lucifer of Cagliari, whom it addresses directly. In brief notes tied to particular passages, Hilary explains why he spoke well of the Eastern homoiousian bishops and of the creeds of Ancyra. He also argues that "similar substance," rightly understood, means unity of substance. The work sheds light on Hilary's efforts to reconcile Nicene and moderate Eastern opponents of Arianism.

This short Latin letter is addressed to Abra, said to be Hilary of Poitiers' only daughter. It is traditionally dated to 358, during Hilary's exile in the East. Using an allegory, Hilary explains his long absence. He says he has travelled far to ask a beautiful young man, meaning Christ, for a priceless garment and pearl for her. He urges her to refuse earthly marriage and adornment and keep her virginity for this heavenly gift. Venantius Fortunatus knew of the letter, but many modern scholars doubt that Hilary wrote it. It is said to have been sent with a hymn.

This Latin morning hymn, beginning "Lucis largitor splendide", is traditionally attributed to Hilary of Poitiers. He is said to have sent it to his daughter Abra together with a letter urging her to devote herself to Christ. It is written in short metrical stanzas. The hymn praises Christ as the true light-bringer, brighter than the morning star, and asks for protection against the devil's deceits and for chastity of body and mind. It closes with a Trinitarian doxology. Scholars widely doubt that the hymn and the accompanying letter are authentic.

The Liber ad Constantium Augustum is a Latin petition by Hilary of Poitiers to the emperor Constantius II. Hilary wrote it in Constantinople around 360, during his exile for opposing Arianism. In it he asks the emperor for a public hearing where he could debate his opponents face to face, and he defends the faith of Nicaea against the shifting creeds of the period. It is one of three writings by Hilary addressed to Constantius, and scholars have long debated their number, order and dating. It is valuable evidence for the church controversies of the 350s and 360s.

The Tractatus super Psalmos is a Latin series of homilies on the Psalms by Hilary of Poitiers. It is generally dated to his last years, after he returned from exile in the East around 360. Only part survives, covering selected psalms, including Psalms 1, 53 and 130. Hilary drew heavily on Origen's exegesis. He reads the Psalms mainly as speaking of Christ, and he holds that interpretation begins by asking in whose person the psalmist speaks and whom he addresses. The work is among the earliest substantial Latin commentaries on the Psalter.

This is a Latin set of commentaries on Psalms 15, 31 and 41 (Vulgate numbering), attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, the fourth-century bishop and opponent of Arianism. They were published apart from his main Tractatus super Psalmos as texts missing from earlier editions, and scholars have doubted that Hilary wrote them. The treatment of Psalm 15 reads it as a prophecy of Christ's passion and resurrection. It links the psalm's title to the inscription on the cross and stresses that Christ's flesh did not see corruption.

The Commentary on Matthew is a Latin exegetical work by Hilary of Poitiers. It is generally dated to the 350s, before his exile to Phrygia in 356, and is the earliest surviving complete Latin commentary on the Gospel of Matthew. It is divided into chapters, or canons, that follow the Gospel story from the Nativity onward. Hilary reads the text mainly through typology and allegory, often treating events as figures of the Church, the Jews and the Gentiles. The work is an important witness to Western biblical interpretation before Hilary's later contact with Greek theology.

This Latin collection gathers the letters of Pope Hilarius (Hilarus), bishop of Rome from 461 to 468. It opens with a letter he wrote while still a deacon and legate of Leo I to the Empress Pulcheria. In it he describes the Second Council of Ephesus (449), Dioscorus's faction and his own escape. The papal letters deal mostly with church discipline and jurisdictional disputes among bishops in Gaul and Spain. They include decrees for the bishops of Tarraconensis on who may be ordained, based on Scripture and the canons of Nicaea.

The Decreta are short Latin decretal fragments attributed to Pope Hilarius, bishop of Rome from 461 to 468. They were not transmitted with his letters. Instead they survive as excerpts quoted in later canonical collections, including Gratian's Decretum and Burchard of Worms. One fragment teaches that each communicant receives the whole body of Christ in a single portion. It compares the Eucharist with the manna of Exodus 16. Another, citing Paul, says that contentious persons should be censured until they mend their ways. As with many excerpts in medieval canon law, their authenticity is uncertain.

A short Latin excerpt that its heading assigns to the third book of a treatise by Hincmar, archbishop of Reims (d. 882), against the objections of the Greeks, addressed to Bishop Odo of Beauvais. The heading also links it to the third book of Ratramnus of Corbie's Contra Graecorum opposita. It probably belongs to the Frankish response to Byzantine criticism of Latin practice during the Photian controversy of the late 860s. The passage cites Fulgentius of Ruspe as an authority for the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son (the Filioque).

This is a Latin letter of consolation by Antoninus Honoratus, bishop of Constantina (ancient Cirta) in Numidia. He wrote it to Arcadius, a Catholic layman whom the Vandal king Genseric (Gaiseric) had sent into exile for refusing Arian Christianity. It probably dates to about 437–439. Drawing on Job, Adam and the Gospels, Honoratus urges Arcadius to stand firm as a "confessor of unity." He tells him not to let love of wife or family turn him from his faith, and promises him a martyr's crown. The letter is an early witness to the Vandal persecution in Roman North Africa.

The Epistolae are the surviving Latin letters of Pope Honorius I, bishop of Rome from 625 to 638. They deal with church and political affairs in Italy and beyond. One asks the exarch Isaac of Ravenna to restore the Catholic Lombard king Adaloald against the Arian Arioald. Another deals with the deposition of Fortunatus of Grado. Others address the Anglo-Saxon church. The most important are his letters to Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople, which spoke of one will in Christ. Because of them, the Third Council of Constantinople (681) condemned Honorius for supporting Monothelitism.

The Epistolae et decreta are the collected Latin letters and decrees of Pope Hormisdas, bishop of Rome from 514 to 523. Most of the correspondence deals with the Acacian schism between Rome and Constantinople. It includes exchanges with the emperors Anastasius I and Justin I, with eastern bishops and with papal legates, and it led to the reunion of the churches in 519 on the basis of the Formula of Hormisdas. The collection also contains disciplinary rulings and letters to Western bishops. Some of these are spurious, such as the letter naming Remigius of Reims papal vicar in Gaul.

This is a short Latin letter on church discipline, addressed "to all the provinces" and attributed to Pope Hormisdas (514–523). It is generally considered spurious, partly because it praises a "Pope John" as an earlier authority, and every pope of that name came after Hormisdas. The letter survives in the ninth-century penitential of Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai. Citing the 318 fathers of Nicaea and Gallic canons, it holds that clerics convicted of adultery or confessing to it may not return to their rank. It also attacks those whose misplaced leniency would ease the old canons.

The Chronicle is a Latin historical chronicle by Hydatius (c. 400–c. 469). He was a native of Lemica in Gallaecia and bishop of Aquae Flaviae, probably modern Chaves in Portugal. Hydatius presents the work as a continuation of the chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea, which Jerome had translated and extended. It records events year by year from 379 to about 468, and was completed near the end of his life. It concentrates on Hispania, especially the Suebi, the Visigoths, the Priscillianist controversy and the collapse of Roman rule. It is the main source for fifth-century Iberian history.

The Descriptio consulum is a Latin list of the Roman consuls, dated by years from the founding of Rome. It begins with Brutus and Collatinus, the first consuls of the Republic, and runs into the fifth century AD, with short notes on notable events added to some years. It has traditionally been attributed to Hydatius, the fifth-century bishop of Aquae Flaviae in Gallaecia and author of a chronicle. Modern scholars doubt that he wrote it. They usually call it the Fasti Hydatiani or Consularia Constantinopolitana and regard it as an important source for late Roman chronology.

This is the collected Latin correspondence and decretals of Innocent I, bishop of Rome from 401 to 417. The letters deal with church discipline, liturgy and doctrine. They include a letter confirming the authority of Anysius of Thessalonica over the churches of Illyricum and a decretal for Victricius of Rouen. Others are addressed to Exsuperius of Toulouse, with a list of the canonical books of Scripture, and to Decentius of Gubbio on liturgical practice. Further letters back John Chrysostom and confirm the African councils' condemnation of Pelagianism. Together they are an important early witness to the growth of papal authority.

This short Latin text is a summary of the canons of the Council of Nicaea (325) in numbered points. It survives in an old canonical collection from Lucca and is headed as taken from a letter of Pope Innocent I (401–417). It is unclear whether Innocent wrote a single letter on the Nicene canons or whether a later compiler gathered them from several of his letters. It covers clerical discipline, how bishops are ordained, holding synods, and the precedence of Alexandria, Rome and Jerusalem. It is among the earliest Latin versions of the Nicene canons.

This is a short Latin letter by John, bishop of Arles in the mid-sixth century. He wrote it to the nuns of the monastery of Saint Mary inside the walls of Arles, which his predecessor, Bishop Aurelian, had founded and given a rule. John calls that rule complete but adds further precepts to protect the community. Above all, he forbids the sisters to drink with visitors, whether lay or religious, relatives or strangers. They may offer guests small cups out of charity, but they must abstain themselves.

This short Latin chronicle by John of Biclaro, a Visigothic monk and later bishop of Girona, continues the chronicle of Victor of Tunnuna, which in turn followed the work of Eusebius, Jerome and Prosper. It covers roughly 567 to 590 in yearly entries dated by the reigns of Byzantine emperors and Visigothic kings, and draws partly on what the author saw himself. It is a key source for the reign of Liuvigild, Hermenegild's revolt, Reccared's conversion to Catholicism and the Third Council of Toledo in 589.

A short Latin commentary on John Cassian's Conferences (Collationes). Despite being catalogued under Cassian, it is not his own work. It was written much later by a commentator whose name is not given, and it collects passages that seemed doctrinally doubtful and need a "pious interpretation". These include the claim, taken from the Shepherd of Hermas, that a good and an evil angel accompany each person, and statements about the assurance of salvation. Citing Scripture, Jerome, Tertullian and the Gelasian decree, the commentator explains how these passages can be read in an orthodox way.

This Latin letter was written around 500 by John, a deacon of the Roman church, to Senarius, a high-ranking layman and old friend who had asked him about church practice. John answers Senarius's questions in order. He explains the rites leading to baptism, including the catechumenate, exorcism, the breathing on candidates (exsufflation), the giving of salt, the scrutinies, the anointings and the white garments, along with other matters of discipline. It is an important early witness to the Roman baptismal liturgy. Some scholars identify its author with the later Pope John I, but this is uncertain.

This Latin biography of Pope Gregory I (Gregory the Great) in four books was written by John the Deacon of Rome around 873–876. He dedicated it to Pope John VIII, who had asked why Gregory had no Life in his own Roman Church when the English and the Lombards already had accounts of him. It opens with dedicatory verses. John drew heavily on Gregory's letters and writings, and on Roman tradition. The result is the fullest early account of Gregory's life, pontificate and mission to the English, and it shaped his later medieval image.

The Epistolae are a small collection of Latin letters attributed to Pope John I, bishop of Rome from 523 to 526. The first, addressed to an Archbishop Zacharias, deals with accusations against bishops. It insists that sheep may not accuse their shepherd unless he has strayed from the true faith. It also rules that bishops who have been despoiled or expelled cannot be tried until their sees and property are restored. The letter's themes and borrowings from earlier popes and from Prosper are typical of the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals. Its authenticity is therefore generally rejected.

The Latin letters of John IV, bishop of Rome from 640 to 642, are a small surviving collection. One letter was written in 640 by John, then pope-elect, together with the Roman clergy, to bishops, priests and abbots of the "Scoti", meaning the Irish. It warns them against keeping Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon with the Jews and against a revival of Pelagianism. Bede preserves part of it. Another, written around 641 to Emperor Constantine III, defends Pope Honorius against Monothelite readings of his letter to Sergius of Constantinople.

The Etymologies (Etymologiae, or Origines) is a Latin encyclopedia compiled by Isidore, bishop of Seville, in Visigothic Spain during the early seventh century. It was still unfinished at his death in 636, and his friend Braulio of Zaragoza arranged it into twenty books. It covers the liberal arts, medicine, law, chronology, Scripture and the Church, languages and peoples, animals, geography, building, warfare and everyday objects. It explains things mainly through the supposed origins of their names. Drawing on many classical and Christian authors, it became one of the most widely copied reference works of the Middle Ages.

The Differentiae, or "On the Proper Meaning of Words", is a Latin work in two books by Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), usually counted among his earlier writings. The first book, on differences between words, takes near-synonyms in alphabetical order and briefly defines how each pair differs. Its preface names Cato as the first Latin writer on the subject. The second book, on differences between things, distinguishes theological and moral ideas. The work shows the interest in exact meaning and word origins that later shaped his Etymologiae.

De fide catholica contra Iudaeos is a Latin treatise in two books by Isidore of Seville, written in the early seventh century and dedicated to his sister Florentina, a head of a community of nuns, at her request. It gathers Old Testament prophecies about Christ's divine birth, incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, kingdom and judgement. Isidore presents them as proofs of the Catholic faith against Jewish objections. The work was widely read in the Middle Ages. An Old High German translation made in the late eighth century is one of the earliest major prose texts in German.

The Sententiarum libri tres (Three Books of Sentences) is a Latin handbook of Christian doctrine and moral teaching by Isidore of Seville, written in the early seventh century. It is also known as De summo bono from its opening words. It draws heavily on Augustine and Gregory the Great. The first book covers God, creation and doctrine, and the second and third treat virtues, vices, prayer and the duties of clergy and rulers. It was widely copied and was an early model for medieval collections of sentences.

De ecclesiasticis officiis (On Church Offices) is a Latin treatise in two books by Isidore of Seville, written in the early seventh century. It is addressed to his brother Fulgentius, bishop of Écija. The first book explains the origins of the Church's worship: prayers, psalmody, readings, the Mass, feasts and fasts. The second describes the clergy, monks, penitents, virgins, widows, married people and catechumens, along with baptism and chrism. Compiled largely from earlier authors, it became an influential source for medieval liturgical commentary.

The Synonyma, also called the Lamentation of the Sinful Soul or Soliloquies, is a Latin devotional dialogue by Isidore of Seville, written in the early seventh century. A sinner weighed down by the troubles of this world laments himself almost to the point of despair. Reason then comforts him, restores his hope of forgiveness and teaches him to reject the world and take up a spiritual life. The work is famous for its style, which piles up near-synonymous phrases, and it was widely read and imitated in the Middle Ages.

The Regula Monachorum ("Rule for Monks") is a Latin monastic rule by Isidore of Seville, archbishop of Seville, written in the early seventh century. Some versions address it to the brothers of a monastery called Honorianense. Isidore says he drew on the precepts of earlier Fathers and chose a plain, "rustic" style so that monks could easily understand it. It covers the abbot, prayer, work, reading, meals, clothing, property and discipline. Its authenticity was once questioned but is now generally accepted. It is an important witness to Visigothic monasticism in Spain.

The Epistolae are a small collection of Latin letters attributed to Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), archbishop of Seville and the leading scholar of Visigothic Spain. They were written in the early seventh century to fellow churchmen and other correspondents. The best known are his exchanges with Braulio of Zaragoza, which bear on the making of the Etymologiae. The first letter, addressed to Bishop Leudefred, sets out the duties of each clerical grade, from doorkeeper upward. Its authenticity has long been questioned, as has that of some other letters in the collection.

Liber de ordine creaturarum is a Latin treatise on the order of creation that has come down under the name of Isidore of Seville (d. 636). From the ninth century, Aeneas of Paris quoted it as Isidore's. Modern scholarship generally rejects that attribution and assigns the work to an anonymous Irish author of the seventh century. Starting from the distinction between the uncreated Creator and created things, it treats the Trinity, angels, the heavens and their lights, the waters, the earth, humanity, sin, and the final destiny of souls. It is valued as evidence of early Hiberno-Latin cosmology and theology.

De natura rerum is a short Latin treatise on cosmology and natural phenomena. Isidore of Seville wrote it for the Visigothic king Sisebut, who had asked him about such matters, and it is usually dated to about 612–613. Drawing on classical and Christian authorities, it covers days, months, years and seasons, the elements, the sun, moon and stars, weather and winds, the position of the earth and the tides. Its circular diagrams earned it the name Liber rotarum, and it was widely copied in early medieval schools.

The Allegoriae quaedam Sacrae Scripturae is a short Latin handbook of biblical allegory by Isidore of Seville, written in the early seventh century and dedicated to a bishop named Orosius. It gives brief figurative interpretations of the best-known names in the Old and New Testaments, taking them in order. Adam, for example, is read as a figure of Christ and Eve as the Church. Isidore offered it to Orosius for correction. The work handed down patristic typology in a compact form and served as a reference aid for medieval readers of Scripture.

The Chronicon, often called the Chronica maiora, is a Latin universal chronicle by Isidore, bishop of Seville (c. 560–636). It summarises history from the Creation to the reigns of the emperor Heraclius and the Visigothic king Sisebut, and a later revised version carries the account a few years further. Isidore follows the tradition of Julius Africanus, Eusebius, Jerome and Victor of Tunnuna, and arranges events in six ages of the world. Its compact scheme of world history was widely copied and used by early medieval chroniclers.

The History of the Kings of the Goths, Vandals and Suebi is a Latin chronicle by Isidore, bishop of Seville. It survives in a shorter and a longer version, the longer usually dated to around 624, during the reign of the Visigothic king Suinthila. It opens with the famous "Praise of Spain" (Laus Spaniae). It then gives brief, reign-by-reign accounts of the Visigoths, followed by shorter sections on the Vandals and Suebi. It is a key source for the history of Visigothic Spain and for how the Goths saw themselves as Spain's rightful rulers.

De viris illustribus is a Latin catalogue of short biographical notices of Christian writers, composed by Isidore, bishop of Seville, in the early seventh century, before his death in 636. It continues the works of the same name by Jerome and Gennadius of Marseille. Its subjects come mostly from the fifth and sixth centuries and are chiefly Spanish and African bishops and authors, though popes, poets and the emperor Justinian also appear. Some notices in the transmitted text are probably later interpolations. Braulio of Zaragoza added a notice on Isidore himself, and Ildefonsus of Toledo later continued the series.

De ortu et obitu patrum ("On the Birth and Death of the Fathers") is a short Latin handbook attributed to Isidore of Seville, archbishop of Seville (d. 636), and written in the early seventh century. Its preface says it sets out, briefly, the origins, deeds, genealogies, rank, deaths and burials of notable figures praised in Scripture. It starts with Adam and covers figures from the Old Testament and then the New. Meant as an aid to memory for readers of the Bible, it was widely copied in the Middle Ages, and some passages in it were added by later writers.

The Prooemia is a short Latin handbook to the Bible by Isidore of Seville, archbishop of Seville, who died in 636. It opens with a prologue listing the books of the Old and New Testaments accepted in the Church's canon "according to the ancient tradition of the forefathers". Brief prefaces follow, one for each book, giving its author, subject and main contents. A teaching aid for clergy and readers, it reflects Isidore's wider work of passing on inherited learning in compact form. It also shows how the biblical canon was understood in Visigothic Spain.

The Liber numerorum qui in sanctis Scripturis occurrunt is a short Latin treatise on the symbolism of numbers in the Bible, attributed to Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636). Braulio of Zaragoza includes it in his list of Isidore's works. It opens with basic arithmetical definitions of number, unity, and even and odd numbers. It then treats particular numbers in turn, explaining the mystical meaning each carries in Scripture. The treatise draws together classical arithmetic and the patristic tradition of allegorical number exegesis, and helped pass that tradition on to medieval readers.

De Veteri et Novo Testamento Quaestiones is a short Latin catechetical work in question-and-answer form, attributed to Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), though the attribution is doubtful and the work is usually counted among his spurious or dubious writings. Each question begins "Dic mihi" ("Tell me") and is followed by an answer. It contrasts the Old and New Testaments, counts the books of Scripture and explains basic biblical and ecclesiastical terms. It belongs to the early medieval tradition of simple didactic dialogues used in teaching.

The Mysticorum expositiones sacramentorum, also called Quaestiones in Vetus Testamentum, is a Latin commentary by Isidore, archbishop of Seville, written in the early seventh century. It reads Genesis and the following historical books of the Old Testament allegorically. Its preface says that the plain historical sense comes first and that the figurative sense, pointing to Christ and the Church, follows from it. Isidore drew on earlier church writers, calling his work a gathering of flowers from many meadows, and kept it short for readers who dislike long works. It helped pass patristic typological reading on to the medieval West.

This short Latin allegorical commentary on the Books of Kings is transmitted as an appendix to the Mysticorum expositiones sacramentorum (Questions on the Old Testament) of Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636). Its attribution to Isidore is uncertain, and it may be a later addition to his work. It reads the opening of 1 Samuel spiritually, using the meanings of Hebrew names. Elkanah's two wives, Hannah and Peninnah, are compared with Sarah and Hagar, and the text develops themes of the unity of faith and of charity as the fulfilment of the law.

De vita contemplativa is a Latin treatise in three books by Julianus Pomerius, an African-born priest and teacher of rhetoric at Arles. He wrote it around 500 at the request of a bishop named Julian. It compares the contemplative and active lives. It also covers the duties of bishops and clergy, including preaching, managing church property and personal conduct, and the virtues and vices. In the Middle Ages it was often attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine. It was widely read as a guide for pastors, especially during the Carolingian reforms. It is the only one of Pomerius's works to survive.

A collection of writings under the name of Julius I, bishop of Rome from 337 to 352. Its main authentic document is his letter of about 341 to the Eusebian bishops gathered at Antioch. In it he defends Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra and asserts Rome's right to review their depositions. The letter survives in Greek because Athanasius preserved it. The set also includes another letter, to the church of Alexandria. A treatise on the union of body and divinity in Christ circulated under Julius's name, but it is generally regarded as an Apollinarian work falsely attributed to him.

This letter was written by Pope Julius I of Rome around 341, after a Roman synod, to the Eastern bishops who had met at Antioch. They included Flacillus, Narcissus, Eusebius, Maris, Macedonius and Theodore. Julius rebukes their contentious reply to his invitation and defends Athanasius of Alexandria and Marcellus of Ancyra against their deposition. He argues that such cases should have been referred to Rome according to custom. The letter survives in Greek in Athanasius's Apology against the Arians. It is a key early witness to Roman claims of appellate authority.

This is a letter from Julius I, bishop of Rome (337–352), to the presbyters, deacons and people of Alexandria. He wrote it when Athanasius was returning from exile to his see, an event usually dated to 346. Julius congratulates the Alexandrians on their bishop's return. He praises their steady faith and loyalty to Athanasius through his long absence and offers them his prayers and blessing. Athanasius preserved the letter in his Apology against the Arians. It shows the support Rome gave Athanasius during the Arian controversy.

This is a collection of Christological fragments transmitted under the name of Julius I, bishop of Rome from 337 to 352. They come from a sermon on the homoousion and from letters, and stress the union of divinity and humanity in Christ, speaking of "one nature" and "one person" by analogy with the union of soul and body. Modern scholarship generally regards much of this material as Apollinarian writing falsely attributed to Julius. Under his authority it was later cited by Cyril of Alexandria and by Miaphysite theologians in the Christological controversies.

This is a small Latin collection of ten short canonical decrees attributed to Pope Julius I, bishop of Rome from 337 to 352. They survive as excerpts in the medieval canon-law compilations of Ivo of Chartres and Gratian. The rulings condemn profiteering from hoarded grain and wine, require priests to grant penance to the dying, and declare that the marriages of slaves cannot be dissolved. They also forbid marriage within seven degrees of kinship, or to the betrothed of a dead relative. Such attributions to early popes are generally regarded as later and spurious.

This Latin letter is attributed to Pope Julius I (bishop of Rome 337–352). It rebukes the Eastern bishops for condemning and expelling Athanasius of Alexandria and Marcellus of Ancyra. Its chapter headings claim that only the Roman pontiff may summon councils, judge bishops or approve their condemnation, and that bishops deposed without the apostolic see's consent must be restored. Scholars since Baronius have regarded it as spurious. It belongs to the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals and is distinct from Julius's genuine letter of about 341 to the Eastern bishops, which survives in Greek in Athanasius's Apology against the Arians.

This Latin decretal letter is attributed to Pope Julius I (bishop of Rome 337–352). It presents itself as his reply to the Eastern bishops in defence of Athanasius and other deposed bishops. It is in fact a forgery from the ninth-century Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals. It reworks the historical conflict, which is known from Julius's genuine letter preserved in Greek by Athanasius, into a set of canonical rules. These cover appeals by accused bishops to the apostolic see, the rights of metropolitans and primates, who may bring accusations and testify, and limits on judging bishops outside their province.

This Latin handbook in two short books introduces the study of Scripture. Junillus Africanus, quaestor of the sacred palace under Justinian at Constantinople, wrote it around the 540s and dedicated it to the African bishop Primasius. Junillus based it on rules taught by Paul the Persian, a teacher trained at the School of Nisibis. Set out as questions from a disciple and answers from a master, it explains the kinds, authority and themes of the biblical books. The work carried Antiochene exegesis, shaped by Theodore of Mopsuestia, to the Latin West.

This short Latin document is a profession of faith that tradition attributes to the emperor Justinian I and links to Pope Boniface II (530–532). It closely follows the Formula of Hormisdas, the libellus of 519 that ended the Acacian schism, and an annotation notes that the original was addressed to Hormisdas. The signatory promises to follow the apostolic see in every respect, to condemn all who oppose the Roman Church, and to keep the names of those outside its communion out of the liturgy. Whether the text is authentic and when it was written are uncertain.

This treatise is also known as the Letter to Menas. Emperor Justinian I addressed it to Menas, patriarch of Constantinople, in 543. It was written in Greek and survives in Latin translation. It attacks Origen and his followers, charging that his teachings on the Trinity, the pre-existence of souls and the final restoration of all things share the errors of pagans, Arians and Manichaeans. It ends with anathemas against Origen. According to Liberatus, the deacon Pelagius urged its issue. The edict led to a synodal condemnation of Origenism in Constantinople and later shaped the Origenist controversy of the sixth century.
