For each figure, including Andrew, James son of Zebedee, Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, Simon the Canaanite and Matthias, it briefly records the regions where he preached and where he died or was buried. Its date and author are unknown.

The Epistola ad Desiderium de duodecim doctoribus is a short Latin letter that briefly describes twelve Church writers, presented as "luminaries" shining across the world. It was long transmitted under the name of Jerome, and also under Bede's as De luminaribus ecclesiae, but its author and date are unknown. Erasmus and later critics rejected it as spurious, pointing to its clumsy style, its chronological errors and its odd judgments of the writers it discusses. It also mentions heretics such as Pelagius and Jovinian, whose writings it censures.

This short Latin letter is addressed to a "brother Desiderius" and falsely attributed to Jerome. Its author and date are unknown. The writer says he will describe, briefly and kindly, the church writers who shed light on the obscurities of Scripture. He compares them to lights shining in the firmament. He then offers short, image-filled sketches of individual authors, beginning with Augustine as an eagle soaring over mountain peaks, Hilary as a lamp of the churches and Origen as a lofty but wandering thinker. It belongs to the many spurious works that circulated under Jerome's name.

The Liber nominum locorum ex Actis is a short Latin gazetteer of the places named in the Acts of the Apostles. It was transmitted among the works of Jerome but is not by him, and its author and date are uncertain. The entries are arranged alphabetically, from Acheldema, Asia, Egypt, Arabia and Ethiopia onward. Each gives the biblical reference with a brief geographical or historical description. The material draws on earlier Latin geographical writing and on Jerome's own work on biblical place-names. Like other early medieval aids to reading Scripture, it was meant to help readers understand the biblical text.

The Hebraici alphabeti interpretatio is a short anonymous Latin glossary that gives the meanings of the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. For example, aleph is glossed as "thousand" or "teaching" and beth as "house". It has come down among the spurious works of Jerome, and most of its glosses are taken from his writings. Its date and author are unknown. A brief list of ten Hebrew names of God, such as Sabaoth, Adonai and El, follows it and is attributed to a certain Symeon the Jew. Works like this show how medieval Latin readers learned about Hebrew.

De Deo et nominibus ejus ("On God and His Names") is a short Latin treatise wrongly attributed to Jerome. Its author and date are unknown. It opens by praising Jerome as the first to translate the interpretation of Hebrew names into Latin. It then explains the ten Hebrew names of God, including El, Elohim, Sabaoth, Elyon and Ehyeh, and gives their Latin meanings and etymologies with a Trinitarian reading. Its wording closely follows the opening of Book VII of Isidore of Seville's Etymologies.

De benedictionibus Jacob patriarchae is a short anonymous Latin commentary on the blessings Jacob gives his twelve sons in Genesis 49. It has been handed down among the spurious works of Augustine and has also been linked with Jerome; its real author and date are unknown. Written as questions and answers, it says the blessings should be read both historically and allegorically. Historically, they refer to the division of the Promised Land among Jacob's descendants. Allegorically, they point to Christ and the Church in the last days.

This is an anonymous Latin commentary on the blessings Jacob gave his twelve sons in Genesis 49. It has come down under the name of Jerome but is not his work, and its date and real author are uncertain. The author says the patriarch's prophecy can't be read purely literally, but its historical meaning shouldn't be lost in allegory either. So he first sets out the literal sense as a foundation. He then turns to the spiritual meaning where the letter falls short, taking each son in turn, beginning with Reuben.

The Decem tentationes populi Israel in deserto ("The Ten Temptations of the People of Israel in the Desert") is a short Latin exegetical tract once wrongly attributed to Jerome. Its real author and date are unknown. It takes the place names of Deuteronomy 1:1 as Moses' brief and veiled rebuke of Israel, and links each one to a separate occasion in Exodus and Numbers when the people tested God in the wilderness. The ten are counted to match Numbers 14:22, where God says Israel has tempted him "ten times."

This is a brief Latin summary, falsely attributed to Jerome, that lists the ten times Israel tempted God in the wilderness, alluding to Numbers 14:22. In order it names the Red Sea, the golden calf, the complaints about food and the fiery serpents, the waters of contradiction before and after Miriam's death, the rotting manna, the quails, Korah's rebellion and the spies. It works as a recapitulation of a longer treatise on the same subject. Its author and date are unknown.

The Commentarius in canticum Debborae is a short Latin commentary on the Song of Deborah in Judges 5. It was once attributed to Jerome and printed among his works, but it is now considered pseudonymous; its real author and date are uncertain. It goes through the song verse by verse, mixing historical and etymological explanation with allegory. For example, it identifies Barak as Deborah's husband Lapidoth by playing on the meanings "lightning" and "flash", and it reads the shaking earth as the theophany at Sinai. Some of its explanations parallel traditions found in Jewish exegesis.

The Quaestiones Hebraicae in libros Regum et Paralipomenon is an anonymous Latin commentary on the books of Samuel–Kings and Chronicles. It was long passed down among the works of Jerome, but it is not his, and its author and date are uncertain. It is generally placed in the early medieval or Carolingian period. Working verse by verse, it explains Hebrew names and draws on Jewish traditions and interpretations, for example on Elkanah's descent. Rabanus Maurus used it in his commentary on Kings, which makes it a witness to Jewish learning reaching Latin biblical scholarship.

The Excerpta ex commentario in Job is a short Latin commentary on the Book of Job. It was once attributed to Jerome but is now classed as pseudonymous, and its author and date are unknown. It opens by explaining that Scripture is read historically, allegorically and morally, and that some verses of Job cannot be taken literally. Its methods and images, including Scripture as a river where the simple can wade and an elephant can swim, closely follow Gregory the Great's Moralia in Job.

This is a short Latin commentary on Isaiah, a "little abridgement" on a few chapters, traditionally attributed to Jerome but not his work. Its author and date are unknown. A prologue presents the prophets as spiritual physicians treating the wounds of the soul. The twelve minor prophets set out in brief the same pattern that the major prophets develop at length: humanity, sick through its own fault, is healed after death by Christ, the true physician. The commentary then glosses selected verses in both their historical and their tropological sense.

In Lamentationes Jeremiae is an anonymous Latin commentary on the Lamentations of Jeremiah. It was handed down among the works of Jerome but is not by him, and its author and date are unknown; it is generally placed in the early Middle Ages. The commentary works through the alphabetic acrostic of the Hebrew poem and reads each letter for its symbolic meaning; aleph, for example, is taken to mean "doctrine". It explains the laments in three senses: historically, of Israel in captivity; spiritually, of the Church as the city of God; and morally, of each individual soul.

Commentarii in librum Job is an anonymous Latin commentary on the Book of Job, handed down among the works of Jerome but not by him. Scholars usually connect it with the Job commentary of Philip the Presbyter, a fifth-century disciple of Jerome, of which it appears to be a reworking. Its date and exact authorship remain uncertain. The commentary reads Job allegorically. Job is a figure of Christ, his three friends stand for heretics who blaspheme Christ under his name, and Elihu represents philosophers outside the faith who lie in wait for the Church.

The Breviarium in Psalmos is a Latin commentary on the whole Psalter, long transmitted among the works of Jerome but now regarded as spurious. Its preface borrows from Jerome's genuine Commentarioli in Psalmos, which presents the notes as brief remarks supplementing Origen's Enchiridion on the Psalms. Its true author and date are uncertain, and it is generally considered a later compilation, probably early medieval. Psalm by psalm, it offers short explanations of titles and verses, reading all the psalms as referring to Christ.

A Latin commentary on the Psalms handed down under the name of Jerome but generally treated as pseudonymous. Its date and author are uncertain. It works through the Psalter psalm by psalm. It opens with a comparison, taken ultimately from Origen, of the Psalter to a great house: the Holy Spirit is the key to its main door, but each psalm is a room with its own key. The comment on Psalm 1 rejects reading the "blessed man" as Christ. The work shows how Jerome's name and Origen's methods of exegesis shaped Latin interpretation of the Psalms.

This is a short Latin preface to the seven Catholic Epistles that circulated in Vulgate Bibles under the name of Jerome. Its style and wording show it is not his, but it was written by the mid-sixth century, since it appears in the Codex Fuldensis. It argues that the Latin codices should follow the Greek order of the letters: James, Peter, John and Jude. It is best known for accusing unfaithful translators of leaving out the witness of Father, Word and Spirit in 1 John. This makes it early evidence in the debate over the Comma Johanneum.

This is a collection of Latin letters and short treatises that were handed down under the name of Jerome (d. 420) but are not his work. Early modern editors of Jerome set them apart as spurious. Their authors, dates and origins vary, and many are unknown. The collection opens with the Letter to Demetrias, which Bede had already rejected as Jerome's. Augustine's testimony shows that Pelagius wrote it around 413. Such misattributions helped circulate writings that might otherwise have been lost, including some by authors whose teaching was condemned.

The Gospel of the Nativity of Mary (Libellus de Nativitate Sanctae Mariae) is an anonymous Latin apocryphal narrative, probably written in France in the tenth century, though possibly the late ninth. It reworks the first chapters of the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew together with material from Matthew and Luke. It tells of Mary's parents Joachim and Anna, her birth, her upbringing in the Temple, and events up to the Annunciation. It long circulated under Jerome's name and was widely used in the medieval West, including in the Golden Legend.

The Liber comitis, or Comes, is a Latin lectionary that sets out the readings from the epistles, the prophets and the Gospels for Mass through the liturgical year, starting with the vigil of Christmas. Medieval tradition attributed it to Jerome, but that attribution is spurious. Its prologue says that this form of the book was expanded by Theotinchus, a priest, at the request of Hechiardus, count of Amiens. It probably dates from the early medieval Frankish period, though the exact date is uncertain. It is important evidence for the history of the Latin liturgy and of systems of biblical readings.

The Expositio quatuor Evangeliorum is a Latin commentary on the four Gospels that was handed down under the name of Jerome, though he did not write it. Modern scholarship generally regards it as an early medieval work, probably Hiberno-Latin, from around the seventh or eighth century. Its author and exact date are unknown. The commentary uses allegory and numerical symbolism heavily. It links the four evangelists to the four elements, the four rivers of Paradise and the four cardinal virtues. It also offers brief glosses on passages of the Gospels.

This Latin commentary on the Gospel of Mark was transmitted among the works of Jerome but is not by him. It is usually dated to the first half of the seventh century and is often thought to be the work of an Irish author; Cummian has been suggested, though this is uncertain. The preface says that earlier interpreters had largely passed over Mark because his Gospel overlaps so much with Matthew's. The commentary combines historical and mystical readings, and it is among the earliest surviving Latin commentaries on Mark.

This short Latin preface to the Gospel of Luke belongs to the so-called Monarchian Prologues. These prefaces to the four Gospels circulated in Vulgate manuscripts and were long falsely attributed to Jerome. It presents Luke as a Syrian of Antioch, a physician and companion of Paul, who never married and died in Bithynia at seventy-four. It says he wrote his Gospel in Achaia after Matthew and Mark, and it explains his genealogy and his authorship of Acts. Its date and origin are disputed; many scholars place it in the fourth century.

De Martyrio Maccabaeorum is a short Latin poem in hexameters retelling the martyrdom of the mother and her seven sons under the Syrian king Antiochus, the story told in 2 Maccabees 7. The king first offers the mother wealth and then threatens torture, but she refuses to abandon the law of God and encourages her sons to remain faithful. Its authorship is uncertain. Manuscripts give it to Hilary, and it has also been attributed to Marius Victorinus. It probably dates from late antiquity.

The Metrum in Genesim ad Leonem papam is a short Latin poem retelling the opening chapters of Genesis. Manuscripts attribute it to a Hilary, but its true author is unknown. It has been linked to Hilary of Arles and to Hilary of Poitiers, and it is usually placed in 5th-century Gaul. The poem opens with elegiac couplets addressed to a Pope Leo, who had asked for the work. Hexameters follow, praising the eternal, self-originating Creator and describing how the world was shaped out of formless chaos. It belongs to the late antique tradition of biblical epic.

The Conflict of Vices and Virtues is a Latin moral treatise by Ambrose Autpert, the Frankish Benedictine abbot of San Vincenzo al Volturno, written between about 760 and his death in 784. In the Middle Ages it circulated under the names of Augustine and Isidore of Seville. Taking up Paul's saying that all who live godly lives will suffer persecution, it argues that in peaceful times Christians are persecuted from within by the vices. It then pairs each vice with the virtue that opposes it. The treatise was widely copied and read as a guide to the spiritual life.

The Exhortatio humilitatis (Exhortation to Humility) is a short Latin moral treatise by Martin of Braga, the sixth-century bishop and missionary among the Suevi of Gallaecia. It was written between about 556 and 580, and some manuscripts wrongly attribute it to Isidore of Seville. It is addressed to someone who holds authority over others. In a deliberately plain style, it warns against flattery and pride and urges rulers to prefer useful truth to pleasing words. The treatise belongs to Martin's group of short moral writings influenced by Seneca.

De ecclesiasticis dogmatibus ("On Church Doctrines") is a short Latin summary of Christian belief, set out in numbered chapters. It is generally attributed to Gennadius, a priest of Marseilles who died around 496, and was written in the later fifth century. It begins with a confession of the Trinity, saying the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. It then condemns heresies and deals with the Incarnation, the soul, free will, grace and church practice. In the Middle Ages it was widely read, and copies passed it down under the names of Augustine and Isidore of Seville.

Ad Ecclesiam ("To the Church"), also called Adversus Avaritiam ("Against Avarice"), is a Latin treatise in four books by Salvian, a fifth-century priest of Marseilles. It was issued under the pseudonym "Timothy", which Salvian later explained in a letter to Bishop Salonius. Written as a letter to the whole catholic Church, it attacks the greed of Christians who hold on to their wealth. It urges clergy, ascetics and lay believers to give their property to the Church and the poor, especially in their wills, so that their riches serve their salvation.

A letter in Greek from the church of Rome to the church of Corinth. It names no author, but it is traditionally attributed to Clement, bishop of Rome, and most scholars accept this. It is usually dated to about AD 96, although some scholars place it before 70. Members of the Corinthian congregation had deposed their presbyters, and the letter urges them to repent and to restore these leaders, who had been appointed in succession from the Apostles. One of the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament, it was read aloud in churches and copied into some biblical codices.

The so-called Second Epistle of Clement is an early Christian sermon in Greek, usually dated to the mid-second century. Its author is unknown. Tradition attributed it to Clement of Rome, but scholars generally reject that attribution. The text begins by urging its hearers to think of Jesus Christ "as of God," the judge of the living and the dead. It then calls for repentance, self-control and steadfast faith in view of the coming judgment. Often counted as the oldest surviving Christian homily, it appears alongside 1 Clement in Codex Alexandrinus and is grouped among the Apostolic Fathers.

The Epistle of Barnabas is an early Christian Greek treatise in letter form, usually dated between about 70 and 135. Clement of Alexandria and other early writers attributed it to Barnabas, the companion of Paul, but most modern scholars think it was written by an unknown teacher. It reads the Hebrew Scriptures allegorically as prophecies of Christ and argues that the Jews misunderstood their law by taking it literally. It closes with the "Two Ways" teaching on moral conduct. Counted among the Apostolic Fathers, it was once a disputed writing and appears after Revelation in Codex Sinaiticus.

This Greek epitome condenses the Pseudo-Clementine Homilies, a romance falsely attributed to Clement of Rome. Its exact date and compiler are unknown, but it belongs to the Byzantine period. Like the Homilies, it opens with Clement's letter to James, "bishop of bishops" in Jerusalem. Clement then describes how, as a young Roman troubled by questions of death and immortality, he searched for the truth. This leads to his meeting with the apostle Peter, whose travels, preaching and debates with Simon Magus he records. The epitome shows how this apocryphal narrative was reshaped and kept in circulation in later Greek Christianity.

The Clementine Homilies are a Greek Christian romance in twenty books, falsely attributed to Clement of Rome and probably composed in the fourth century. Clement narrates his youthful search for truth, his conversion, and his travels with the apostle Peter. The work records Peter's discourses and his debates with Simon Magus, and ends with the reunion of Clement's scattered family. It is prefaced by letters of Peter and Clement to James. With the Recognitions, it is one of two surviving reworkings of a lost earlier source and is valuable evidence for Jewish-Christian thought.

The Epistle to Diognetus is an anonymous Greek apology for Christianity, addressed to an otherwise unknown enquirer named Diognetus. It survived among the works of Justin Martyr, but he is not thought to be its author. Estimates of its date range from about AD 130 to the later second century. The writer rejects Greek idolatry and Jewish worship and explains God's plan of salvation through his Son. The epistle is best known for its description of Christians as living in the world like the soul in the body. Its closing chapters may have been added later.

The Shepherd of Hermas is an early Christian apocalyptic and moral work written in Greek at Rome, generally dated to the first half of the second century. It has three parts: Visions, Commandments (Mandates) and Similitudes (Parables). Its narrator, Hermas, a former slave, receives revelations from a woman representing the Church and from an angel in the form of a shepherd. The book's main concern is repentance after baptism. The Muratorian fragment names its author as Hermas, brother of Pius, bishop of Rome. It was widely read and sometimes treated as scripture, and it appears in Codex Sinaiticus.

The Epistle to Polycarp is one of the seven letters Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote in the early second century while under guard on his way to martyrdom in Rome. It is his only letter to an individual. Ignatius writes to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, urging him to preserve unity, pray without ceasing, endure hardship like an athlete and care for every member of his flock. He also gives counsel on widows, slaves and marriage. The letter survives in a shorter, authentic recension and a longer, later interpolated recension.

This is a group of Greek letters falsely attributed to Ignatius of Antioch, the early second-century bishop. They are addressed to the Tarsians, the Antiochians, the deacon Hero and the Philippians, and they include an exchange with Mary of Cassobola, called Mary at Neapolis. They were composed in the later fourth century, probably in Syria, alongside the interpolated long recension of the genuine letters. The compiler is often identified with the author of the Apostolic Constitutions. The letters attack docetism and promote church order, and their Christology has been called subordinationist.

The Martyrdom of Polycarp is a Greek letter from the church of Smyrna to the church at Philomelium and to all churches. It describes the arrest, trial and execution of Polycarp, the aged bishop of Smyrna, usually dated to around 155–160, though some scholars place it later. It is the earliest surviving Christian account of a martyrdom outside the New Testament. It presents Polycarp's death as an imitation of Christ's passion and gives early evidence of honouring martyrs' relics and anniversaries. It is traditionally grouped with the Apostolic Fathers.

The Epistle to the Philippians is a Greek letter by Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, and his presbyters, written to the church at Philippi in the first half of the second century. Many scholars think it combines two letters written at different times. It urges faith, righteousness and good conduct, warns against greed and docetic error, and draws heavily on New Testament writings. It also mentions the letters of Ignatius of Antioch. Irenaeus praised it, and it is Polycarp's only surviving writing and one of the Apostolic Fathers.

This synodal letter was written in Greek by Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, to Victor, bishop of Rome, during the Quartodeciman controversy, probably about 190–195. It survives only in fragments quoted by Eusebius in his Church History. Writing for the bishops of Asia, Polycrates defends their custom of keeping the Pascha on the fourteenth day of the lunar month. He appeals to the apostles Philip and John, to Polycarp, Melito and other revered figures, and to his own family's line of bishops. It is an important early witness to disputes over the date of Easter and to the authority of Rome.

The First Apology is a Greek defence of Christianity written by Justin Martyr, a philosopher from Flavia Neapolis in Palestine. It was addressed to the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius and his adopted sons, and is usually dated to about 150–155. Justin argues that Christians should not be punished for the name alone. He defends their morals, presents Christ as the incarnate Logos and appeals to the fulfilment of prophecy. The work contains some of the earliest descriptions of Christian baptism and the Eucharist, and it is a founding text of Christian apologetics.

The Second Apology is a short Greek defence of Christianity by Justin Martyr. It was probably written in Rome in the 150s and is traditionally said to be addressed to the Roman Senate. It was prompted by the execution of the Christians Ptolemaeus and Lucius under the city prefect Lollius Urbicus. Justin protests that Christians are condemned for the name alone and blames such persecution on demons. He also develops his teaching on the "seminal Logos" present in philosophers such as Socrates. Scholars still debate whether it was a separate work or a supplement to the First Apology.

The Dialogue with Trypho is a Greek apologetic work by Justin Martyr, generally dated to about 155–160. It presents a debate over two days between Justin and Trypho, a Jew who fled the recent war in Judaea. Eusebius places the conversation at Ephesus. The work opens with Justin's account of how he moved from philosophy to Christianity. It then argues from the Hebrew Scriptures that Christ has replaced the Mosaic Law, that prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus, and that Christians are the new Israel. It is the earliest surviving full-length Christian work addressed against Judaism.

To Autolycus is a Greek apology in three books by Theophilus, bishop of Antioch, addressed to a learned pagan friend and written shortly after 180. It is his only surviving work. Theophilus defends the Christian name, attacks idolatry and Greek myths and philosophy, and explains the Genesis account of creation. He also builds a world chronology to show that Moses and the prophets are older than Greek writers. The work is notable as the earliest known Christian use of the word "triad" (trias) for God, his Word and his Wisdom.

Against Heresies, originally titled Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So-called, is a five-book treatise by Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, written in Greek around 180. It sets out and refutes the teachings of various Gnostic groups, especially the Valentinians. Against them it defends the one God who created the world, the unity of Scripture, and apostolic tradition handed down through the succession of bishops. Only fragments of the Greek survive, but there is a complete early Latin translation. It is a key witness to second-century theology and to the fourfold Gospel.

The Protrepticus, or Exhortation to the Greeks, is an apologetic treatise written in Greek by Clement of Alexandria, probably near the end of the second century. It is usually seen as the first part of a trilogy with the Paedagogus and the Stromata. It exposes and ridicules the myths, mysteries and idol worship of Greek religion, and urges pagan readers to turn to the divine Logos, Christ, the "new song." Its many quotations from classical poetry and philosophy make it a key witness to early Christian engagement with Hellenistic culture.

The Eclogae propheticae (Prophetic Extracts) is a collection of short exegetical and theological notes in Greek by Clement of Alexandria, written in the late second or early third century. It survives alongside the Excerpta ex Theodoto, after the eighth book of the Stromata. The notes are loosely connected. They comment on scriptural passages, especially from the prophets, and on topics such as creation, baptism, angels and spiritual powers. They cite texts like Enoch and the Apocalypse of Peter. Their exact purpose is uncertain, and they may be preparatory notes.

The Excerpts of Theodotus are a collection of notes by Clement of Alexandria, probably made around 200. They quote and summarise the teaching of Theodotus, a Valentinian Gnostic of the Eastern school, and of other Valentinians. Clement often adds his own critical comments. The notes cover the Pleroma, the Saviour, the origin of the world, the classes of humanity and baptism. They are among the most important first-hand evidence for Valentinian thought. They survive alongside Clement's Prophetic Eclogues, a related set of notes on Scripture, and some translations have printed the two together under one title.

A Greek treatise or homily by Clement of Alexandria, written around the turn of the third century, though its exact date is uncertain. The work ends with the story of the apostle John and the young robber, which Eusebius later preserved. It is an important early Christian statement on wealth.

The Acta Archelai is a fourth-century anti-Manichaean polemic, traditionally attributed to an otherwise unknown Hegemonius, although the attribution is uncertain. It is the oldest major anti-Manichaean text and shaped later polemic in Late Antiquity and the Middle Ages.

This Greek anti-Montanist treatise survives only in fragments quoted by Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History (5.16–17). Its author is unknown. Some editors named him Asterius Urbanus, but that is a misreading, because Asterius Urbanus is only a writer whom the treatise itself cites. The work is addressed to Avircius Marcellus, often identified with Abercius of Hierapolis, and was written in Asia Minor in the late second century. It attacks the "new prophecy" of Montanus, Maximilla and Priscilla, describing their ecstatic utterances and condemnation by local synods. It is an important early witness to the Montanist controversy.

This early third-century Greek treatise against the Roman Adoptionists, followers of Theodotus the tanner and later Artemon, survives only in fragments quoted by Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 5.28). It denies their claim that the apostolic teaching of Christ as a mere man lasted until Bishop Victor. Against this it cites Scripture, earlier writers such as Justin, Irenaeus and Melito, and Christian hymns honouring Christ as God. It also tells of the confessor Natalius. Theodoret calls the work the "Little Labyrinth." Its author is uncertain: it has been credited to the Roman presbyter Caius and, by some scholars, to Hippolytus.

Against Celsus is an apologetic treatise in eight books by Origen of Alexandria, written around 248 at the request of his patron Ambrose. It refutes The True Word, an attack on Christianity by the second-century pagan philosopher Celsus. Origen answers him point by point, defending faith, the identity of Jesus, allegorical reading of Scripture and Christianity's relation to Greek religion. It survives complete in Greek and is among the most important works of early Christian apologetics. It also preserves most of what is known of Celsus's lost work.

On Prayer (Peri euchēs) is a Greek treatise by Origen of Alexandria, usually dated around 233–234 and addressed to his patron Ambrose and to Tatiana. It is the earliest surviving systematic Christian study of prayer. Origen asks why prayer is worthwhile if God already knows all things, explains the kinds of prayer named in 1 Timothy 2:1, and argues that prayer in the strict sense should be offered to the Father through the Son. He gives a long commentary on the Lord's Prayer and ends with advice on posture, place and times for prayer.

This Greek letter is Origen's reply to the Christian chronographer Julius Africanus, written from Nicomedia, probably around 240. It is one of the most important early Christian writings on the meaning of martyrdom.

Selecta in Deuteronomium ("Selections on Deuteronomy") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Deuteronomy attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The notes survive as fragments rather than as a continuous commentary, mostly drawn from later catenae, and the authorship of some passages is uncertain. They comment briefly on individual verses. Topics include Moses as the prophetic voice of God, Joshua as his successor, the inheritance of Reuben and Gad, and how the divine "voice" at Sinai should be understood without suggesting that God has a bodily nature.

The Selecta in Exodum are Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Exodus attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive only in fragments, mostly preserved in later catenae (chains of excerpts from biblical commentators), and their exact relation to Origen's lost commentaries is uncertain. They comment on selected verses. A notable passage deals with the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, where Origen distinguishes between a heart described as "hardened", "strengthened" or "made heavy". This question of divine action and human free will recurs elsewhere in his writings.

Selecta in Genesim is a collection of Greek fragments of Origen of Alexandria's (c. 185–c. 253) exegetical writings on Genesis. Most survive in later catenae, the chains of excerpts that Byzantine compilers made from earlier commentators. Origen's own Commentary on Genesis, written in Alexandria, is largely lost. The collection opens with a passage from its third tome, preserved by Eusebius, on where the apostles went to preach. The other excerpts discuss particular verses: grammar, punctuation, the blessing to increase and multiply, and the creation of humanity in God's image. They are an important witness to Origen's lost interpretation of Genesis.

The Selecta in Jesum Nave are short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Joshua attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts, mainly through catenae, and so their exact wording and authenticity are not always certain. The notes comment on individual verses and mix literal remarks with allegorical readings. Rahab, for example, is presented as a figure of the Church gathered from the nations, and her lowering of the spies through the window is compared to Paul's escape from Damascus.

The Selecta in Job is a collection of short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Job attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like other Origenian "selecta", the comments survive as fragments rather than a continuous commentary. They are mostly preserved in later catenae, so some attributions are uncertain. The notes explain individual verses, often morally or allegorically. For example, they read Satan's attacks on Job's household as possible only through drunkenness, and they treat harsh words from Job's friends as a heavy burden on the soul.

Selecta in Judices ("Selections on Judges") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Judges attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as fragments, mainly in exegetical catenae, so how much of the material is genuinely Origen's is uncertain. The notes take up individual verses. They discuss whether the Spirit was behind Jephthah's rash vow, the "shibboleth" password test, Samson's Nazirite hair, the ephod and teraphim, and the defeat of Benjamin. They also add to what survives of Origen's Homilies on Judges, which are preserved in Latin.

Selecta in Leviticum ("Selections on Leviticus") is a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Leviticus attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). Like other fragments of his biblical commentary, they survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, so how much of the wording is Origen's own is uncertain. The comments explain the book's title and defend its laws on priesthood and sacrifice against critics who thought them unworthy of the Creator. Drawing on Paul's statement that "the law is spiritual," they read the ritual prescriptions as hidden teaching worthy of God.

The Selecta in Numeros ("Selections on Numbers") is a set of short Greek exegetical notes on the Book of Numbers attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). The notes survive as fragments, mainly through the catenae, the medieval chains of patristic commentary, and their authenticity is not always certain. They comment on individual verses, including the meaning of the word "manna", the prophesying of the seventy elders, Miriam's exclusion from the camp and the sending of the spies. They also read Joshua, son of Nun, as a type of Christ. The notes add to Origen's better-known Homilies on Numbers.

The Selecta in Psalmos are a collection of Greek exegetical fragments on the Psalms attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive mainly as excerpts in later catenae, and their authenticity is doubtful in part because some passages may come from other writers, such as Evagrius Ponticus. The opening gathers philosophical definitions of "end" from Aristotle and Stoic sources to explain psalm titles. Even so, the fragments remain an important witness to Origen's lost commentaries and homilies on the Psalter.

Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253) preached this series of sermons on the Book of Jeremiah at Caesarea in Palestine, probably in the 240s. The homilies are important evidence for early Christian preaching and for Origen's exegetical method.

This is a collection of short Greek exegetical comments on the Book of Jeremiah, attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive as excerpts in the Byzantine catenae on the prophets, the chains of patristic comment arranged verse by verse. Some may come from Origen's lost homilies or notes on Jeremiah, though catena attributions are not always reliable. The fragments show his usual allegorical and moral reading, applying the prophet's images to sin, temptation and the soul's struggle, and they add to the Greek homilies on Jeremiah that survive in full.

These Greek exegetical fragments on the Book of Lamentations are attributed to Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–c. 253). They survive in the Byzantine catenae, or chains of commentary, on the prophets. They probably come from the commentary on Lamentations that Eusebius says Origen wrote at Alexandria and which is otherwise lost. The fragments discuss the alphabetic acrostic structure of Jeremiah's laments. They also read the Babylonian captivity allegorically, as the soul's captivity to hostile spiritual powers, from which Christ sets it free.

This is a large Greek exegetical work by Origen of Alexandria, written for his patron Ambrose. He began it in Alexandria around the early 230s and continued it after moving to Caesarea. It originally ran to at least 32 books, but only a few survive, among them books 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 19, 20, 28 and 32. Origen reads the Fourth Gospel at both a literal and a spiritual level. He often argues against the Gnostic commentary of Heracleon, which makes this one of the earliest surviving Christian commentaries on John.

The Refutation of All Heresies, also called the Elenchus or Philosophumena, is a long Greek polemical treatise from the early third century. It is traditionally attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, but some scholars assign it to an unknown "Pseudo-Hippolytus", and it was once credited to Origen. The work argues that Christian heresies come from Greek philosophy, the mysteries and astrology. It surveys pagan thought and then describes some thirty-three Gnostic and other systems, which makes it a major source for early Christian heterodoxy. Books II and III are lost. Books IV–X were rediscovered at Mount Athos in 1842.

The Banquet of the Ten Virgins is a Greek dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. Its title and form deliberately echo Plato's Symposium. Gregorion tells Euboulios about a banquet held by Arete (Virtue) in a garden, where ten virgins give speeches in turn praising chastity and virginity. They draw heavily on allegorical readings of Scripture. Thekla gives the fullest speech, and the work ends with her hymn to Christ the Bridegroom. It is Methodius's only work to survive complete in Greek and an important early Christian treatise on virginity.

On Things Created (De creatis) is a Greek theological treatise by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. The full work is lost. It survives only in a summary of excerpts made by the ninth-century patriarch Photius in codex 235 of his Bibliotheca. The surviving passages argue against Origen and his followers. They criticize his allegorical reading of texts such as "cast not your pearls before swine" and dispute his view that the created world is coeternal with God. The work is an important witness to early opposition to Origen.

Concerning Free-Will (De libero arbitrio) is a Greek theological dialogue by Methodius of Olympus, a bishop and martyr who died around 311. In it, a speaker called Orthodoxus argues against a follower of Valentinian Gnosticism about where evil comes from. He rejects the idea that matter has always existed alongside God and is the source of evil. Instead, he argues that God created everything good and that evil comes from the misuse of free will by rational creatures. The work is an important early Christian treatment of human freedom and of why evil exists.

This Greek panegyric by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, was delivered in Constantinople in 336 to mark the thirtieth anniversary of Constantine the Great's reign. Eusebius presents the emperor as the earthly image of the divine Logos and his monarchy as a reflection of God's heavenly rule. It also praises Constantine's suppression of polytheism and his support for the Church. Its later chapters are generally thought to come from a separate speech on Christ's sepulchre. The work is an important early statement of Christian imperial ideology, which later shaped Byzantine political thought.

This letter was sent by the Christian communities of Vienne and Lyon (Lugdunum) in Gaul to the churches of Asia and Phrygia. It gives an eyewitness account of the persecution of about 177, under Marcus Aurelius. It describes mob violence, trials and the deaths of martyrs such as the aged bishop Pothinus and the slave woman Blandina. Its author is unknown, though some have suggested Irenaeus. The letter survives only in the excerpts Eusebius of Caesarea quoted in Book 5 of his Ecclesiastical History. It is one of the most important early Christian martyr accounts.

The Oration to the Assembly of the Saints is a Greek speech attributed to the emperor Constantine the Great. Eusebius of Caesarea preserved it as an appendix to his Life of Constantine. The speech was given on Good Friday. Scholars disagree about its date and place, and they once doubted that Constantine wrote it, though many now accept it as his, probably translated from Latin. It attacks pagan polytheism and fatalism and defends divine providence and Christ's work. It is especially known for reading Virgil's Fourth Eclogue and an acrostic of the Erythraean Sibyl as prophecies of Christ.

The Life of Constantine is a Greek work in four books by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, written in honour of the emperor Constantine the Great. Eusebius composed it after Constantine's death in 337 and left it unfinished when he died in 339. It mixes panegyric and biography. It presents Constantine as a model Christian ruler and recounts his conversion, including the vision of the cross, his wars, his church building and his religious policy. It is one of the fullest sources for the religious history of his reign, and it quotes several imperial letters and documents.

The Preparation for the Gospel is a Greek work of Christian apologetics in fifteen books by Eusebius of Caesarea. He began it around 313 and dedicated it to Bishop Theodotus of Laodicea. It argues that Christians were right to give up pagan religion and philosophy for the Hebrew Scriptures. It surveys Phoenician, Egyptian and Greek theology and claims that Greek philosophers owed a debt to the Hebrews. It was written as a companion to the Demonstration of the Gospel, and it is valued for preserving many passages from authors whose works are otherwise lost.

The Proof of the Gospel (Demonstratio evangelica) is an apologetic treatise in Greek by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, probably written in the 310s. It is dedicated to Theodotus, bishop of Laodicea, and follows his fifteen-book Preparation for the Gospel. Eusebius uses the Hebrew prophecies to argue that Christ and the Church fulfil the Scriptures, and explains why Christians follow the faith of the patriarchs rather than the Mosaic Law. Of the original twenty books, only the first ten survive, along with a fragment of the fifteenth. It is a major source for early Christian interpretation of prophecy.

The General Elementary Introduction is a Greek work in ten books by Eusebius of Caesarea. Its date is disputed: it may come from before the Great Persecution of 303 or from somewhat later. Only books six to nine survive, known as the Prophetic Extracts (Eclogae propheticae). They gather Old Testament prophecies about Christ, arranged by scriptural book and given brief commentary. They follow earlier books that argued for the faith without relying on Scripture. The work is an early source for Eusebius's exegesis and apologetic method.

Contra Marcellum (Against Marcellus) is a polemical treatise in two books by Eusebius of Caesarea. It was written around 336–337, after Marcellus of Ancyra was deposed by a synod at Constantinople. Eusebius accuses Marcellus of attacking respected churchmen out of envy, among them Asterius the Sophist and Eusebius of Nicomedia. He charges him with Sabellianism for denying that the Son exists as a distinct person. Eusebius continued the argument in his Ecclesiastical Theology. Both works are important because they preserve many fragments of Marcellus's otherwise lost writings.

De ecclesiastica theologia ("On Ecclesiastical Theology") is a Greek theological treatise in three books written by Eusebius of Caesarea late in his life, probably around 337–338. It is dedicated to Flacillus, bishop of Antioch. It follows Eusebius's earlier two books Against Marcellus, which mostly quoted Marcellus of Ancyra's own words. Here Eusebius refutes Marcellus's teaching directly. Eusebius saw that teaching as Sabellian. Against it, he argues that the Son exists as a distinct being alongside the Father. The work is an important witness to the theological debates that followed the Council of Nicaea.

The Theophania, or "Divine Manifestation", is an apologetic treatise in five books by Eusebius of Caesarea. It was probably written in the later years of his life, though its exact date is disputed. The Greek original survives only in fragments, but a complete early Syriac translation is extant. The work argues against atheism and polytheism and presents the divine Word as creator and governor of the world. It then treats the incarnation, Christ's teaching and miracles, and the fulfilment of prophecy. Much of its material overlaps with Eusebius's Demonstratio Evangelica and his oration in praise of Constantine.

De Decretis is a Greek treatise in the form of a letter by Athanasius of Alexandria, usually dated to the 350s. It is written to an unnamed correspondent who had argued with supporters of Arius, including friends of Eusebius. Athanasius answers the Arian objection that the Council of Nicaea (325) used unscriptural terms, "of the essence" and "one in essence" (homoousios). He argues that these words express the meaning of Scripture about the Son's true divinity. The work is a major early defence of the Nicene formula. It also preserves documents connected with the council.

On the Incarnation of the Word is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius of Alexandria. It is the second part of a double work that opens with Against the Pagans, and both are addressed to a certain Macarius. Its date is disputed: some place it before the Arian controversy, around 318, while others place it in the 330s. It explains why the divine Word, through whom the world was made, took a human body to restore humanity from corruption and death. It also answers Jewish and pagan objections and remains a classic of Christian thought on the incarnation.

The second of the Orations against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. Its date is debated, though it is often placed in the late 330s or 340s. It continues his defence of the Nicene faith by examining scriptural texts that his opponents used to argue that the Son of God is a creature. These include Hebrews 3:2, "faithful to him that made him", and Proverbs 8:22, "The Lord created me a beginning of his ways". Athanasius reads such passages as referring to the Son's incarnation rather than to his eternal being.

The third of the Greek Orations (Discourses) against the Arians by Athanasius of Alexandria, generally dated to around 340, though the exact date is debated. Its authenticity was questioned in modern scholarship but is widely accepted. Continuing the earlier discourses, it explains texts used by Arian opponents such as Asterius the Sophist, starting with John 14:10, "I in the Father and the Father in me." It argues for the mutual indwelling of Father and Son, who share one essence. It then attributes the Gospel accounts of Christ's ignorance, growth and suffering to the humanity the Word took on.

The Fourth Discourse Against the Arians is a Greek theological treatise that has come down with the three Orations Against the Arians of Athanasius of Alexandria (4th century). Most scholars doubt that Athanasius wrote it, and its true author and date are uncertain. It is a series of short arguments rather than a continuous discourse. Using Scripture, it argues that the Word is substantial and is the Father's own Son, and so preserves the single "Monarchy" of the Godhead. It attacks Arian teaching, and also views that separate the Word from the Son or merge Father and Son into one.

The First Discourse Against the Arians is the opening book of Athanasius of Alexandria's Greek polemical treatise against Arianism. Its date is disputed: scholars place it either around 339–346, during his exile in Rome, or in the later 350s. Athanasius argues that the Arians are sectaries named after their founder rather than Christians. He attacks the teaching of Arius's Thalia and defends the eternity of the Son and his unity of essence with the Father. He also begins interpreting disputed biblical texts such as Philippians 2:9–10 and Hebrews 1:4. It is a central text of Nicene theology.

Oration 27 is the first of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople in 380, while he led the small Nicene community there. It serves as an introduction to the series and is aimed at the Eunomians, radical Arians known for their skill in dialectic. Gregory does not yet discuss the Trinity itself. Instead he asks who may speak about God, when, before whom and how far, arguing that theology requires purity of life, quiet and restraint rather than clever debate.

Oration 28 is the second of the five Theological Orations by Gregory of Nazianzus. He preached them in Constantinople around 380, when he led the small Nicene community there against the Eunomians, who claimed that God's essence could be fully known. The first oration set out who may practise theology and under what conditions. This one argues that God's nature cannot be grasped by the human mind. Using the image of Moses on Sinai seeing only God's "back parts", Gregory shows that creation reveals that God exists, not what God is. The work is a classic statement of divine incomprehensibility.

The third of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arian groups. After setting out the monarchy of the Father, Gregory defends the full divinity of the Son. He argues that the Son is eternally begotten without time or passion, and answers his opponents' arguments from the terms "begotten" and "unbegotten." The oration closes with a set of antitheses contrasting Christ's human lowliness with his divine glory. Oration 30 continues the argument with a fuller treatment of the disputed passages of Scripture.

Oration 30 is the fourth of the five Theological Orations (Orations 27–31) that Gregory of Nazianzus delivered in Constantinople around 380 against the Eunomians and other Arians. It is his second discourse on the Son. Gregory answers, one by one, the scriptural texts his opponents used to make the Son subordinate, such as "The Lord created me" (Proverbs 8:22) and "the Father is greater than I." He assigns the exalted expressions to Christ's divinity and the lowly ones to his assumed humanity. The oration ends with a discussion of the titles of the Son.

Oration 31 is the last of the five Theological Orations that Gregory of Nazianzus preached in Constantinople, probably in 380, against the Eunomians and the Pneumatomachi, who denied that the Holy Spirit is fully divine. Gregory openly calls the Spirit God and consubstantial with the Father and the Son. He separates the Spirit's procession from the Son's generation and answers the objection that Scripture is silent on the matter with a theory of progressive revelation. The oration was an important statement of Cappadocian Trinitarian theology shortly before the Council of Constantinople of 381.

The Panarion ("medicine chest"), later known in Latin as Adversus haereses, is a Greek treatise against heresies by Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis (Constantia) in Cyprus. He began it around 374–375 at the request of the Syrian archimandrites Acacius and Paul and finished it about three years later. It describes and refutes eighty sects and schools of thought, from the time of Adam to the late fourth century. The work preserves many otherwise lost documents and reports, including fragments of Jewish-Christian gospels such as the Gospel of the Ebionites.

The Ancoratus ("The Well-Anchored") is a Greek doctrinal treatise by Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia (Salamis) in Cyprus. He wrote it around 374 at the request of presbyters in Syedra in Pamphylia, whose letters stand at its beginning. It explains Christian teaching from Scripture and tradition: the consubstantiality of the Trinity, the full incarnation of Christ, and the resurrection and judgment. It argues against pagans, Jews and heretics, and lists the eighty heresies that Epiphanius later treated in the Panarion. It ends with two creeds, one of which closely resembles the creed associated with the Council of Constantinople of 381.

The Ecclesiastical History of Philostorgius (368–c. 439), a Cappadocian historian who followed the Anomoean teaching of Eunomius, was written in Greek in twelve books and appeared between about 425 and 433. It covered church history from the Arian controversy into the early fifth century from a non-Nicene point of view. The original is lost. It survives mainly through the epitome made by Photius of Constantinople in the ninth century. Photius summarised the work critically, but his epitome keeps a rare account of the period from the side of the losing party.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in seven books by Socrates of Constantinople, also called Socrates Scholasticus. It was written in the 440s and continues Eusebius's history, covering events from 305 to 439: Constantine's conversion, the Arian controversy, the councils, and the affairs of the churches of the eastern empire. Socrates aimed for a plain style and drew on documents and on eyewitnesses. Sozomen used the work as a source. In the sixth century it was put into Latin as part of the Historia Tripartita, which carried it into the medieval West.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in nine books by Sozomen, a lawyer at Constantinople. He wrote it around the 440s and dedicated it to Emperor Theodosius II. It was meant to continue the work of Eusebius and covers events from the 320s to the 420s. The ninth book seems unfinished and stops short of the end date the author announced. Sozomen drew heavily on Socrates Scholasticus but added much material of his own, especially on monasticism, missions and the Church outside the empire. It is a key source for fourth- and early fifth-century Christianity.

Cyril of Alexandria, patriarch from 412 to 444, wrote this Greek commentary on the twelve Minor Prophets, from Hosea to Malachi. It is usually dated to the earlier part of his episcopate, before the Nestorian controversy. The preface admits that many have already explained the prophets but argues that further interpretation still helps readers. Cyril reads each prophet first in its historical setting and then spiritually, as pointing to Christ and the Church. It is the fullest surviving patristic commentary on these books.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in five books by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria. It was written around 449–450 and continues the history of Eusebius of Caesarea. It begins with the rise of Arianism under Constantine and ends in 429, with the death of Theodore of Mopsuestia. Theodoret writes from a firmly Nicene and Antiochene viewpoint and focuses on the struggle against Arianism. He quotes many letters, creeds and synodal documents in full. Along with the histories of Socrates Scholasticus and Sozomen, it is one of the main sources for fourth-century church history.

The Historia Religiosa, also called the Philotheos Historia ("History of the Lovers of God"), is a Greek hagiographical collection written by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, around 440. It gives thirty accounts of ascetics of Syria and Mesopotamia, beginning with Jacob of Nisibis. Among them is Symeon the Stylite, who was still living when Theodoret wrote. Theodoret knew many of these monks personally, and he tells of their hardships, miracles and teaching. A short treatise on divine love closes the work. It is a key source for early Syrian monasticism.

The Ecclesiastical History is a Greek church history in six books by Evagrius Scholasticus, a lawyer at Antioch and aide to Patriarch Gregory of Antioch. He completed it around 593–594. It continues the histories of Socrates, Sozomen and Theodoret, covering the period from the First Council of Ephesus in 431 to the reign of Emperor Maurice. Written from a Chalcedonian standpoint, it is a major source for the Christological controversies after Chalcedon, for imperial and Persian affairs, and for the plague of the 540s, which Evagrius survived.

The Chronicon Paschale, or Paschal Chronicle, is an anonymous Greek world chronicle written in the seventh century, probably at Constantinople during the reign of Heraclius. Its author called it an epitome of the ages from Adam to the seventeenth year of Heraclius. Its name comes from its dating system, which follows the Christian Easter cycle. It opens with a discussion of the date of Easter that cites Philo and Peter of Alexandria. Although much of it draws on earlier works, it is an important independent source for events of the late sixth and early seventh centuries.

This Greek commentary on the Book of Revelation is by Andrew, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and dates from the late sixth or early seventh century. It explains the Apocalypse verse by verse, mainly through spiritual and moral readings, and often draws on and corrects the earlier commentary of Oecumenius. Andrew divided it into twenty-four discourses and seventy-two chapters. It became the standard Greek interpretation of Revelation and helped the book gain acceptance in the Eastern Church. It also shaped how the Greek text of Revelation was handed down.

This is a Greek commentary on the Book of Revelation attributed to Arethas, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the early tenth century and a leading Byzantine scholar. It relies heavily on the earlier commentary of Andrew of Caesarea, which it abridges, supplements and sometimes corrects. It works through the Apocalypse in numbered sections, beginning with the prologue, the letters to the seven churches and the opening of the seals. Its interpretation is mainly spiritual and ecclesial. The work is a witness to how Revelation was received in the Byzantine Church.
